items.label: March 1970
items.sum: Editorial celebrating Will Wesch's R.W.A. National 10 miles and Inter-Counties walking titles and the walkers' National team win, praising the Youth and Senior cross-country teams and questioning the track and field prospects.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial celebrating Will Wesch's R.W.A. National 10 miles and Inter-Counties walking titles and the walkers' National team win, praising the Youth and Senior cross-country teams and questioning the track and field prospects. This issue will be reaching you about two weeks later than usual but it's delay in going to the printers has enabled us to feature the highlight of the edition as you now find it---WE HAVE FOUND OUR FIRST NATIONAL CHAMPION OF THE 70'S! WILL WESCH, whose popularity soon overflowed from the Walking Section into the rest of the Club when he joined us only 18 months ago, is the new National R.W.A. '10' and Inter-Counties Champion. Belgravians everywhere offer him their hearty congratulations. Pat Duncan's account of the Liverpool race on another page covers the details of his great effort and tells of the hard work Will had to put in to reap his success. It was truly "a tremendous performance by a man who has worked hard for every second and every yard, earning our respect in the process, and making us very proud to have him as a clubmate". Our joy at finding our first National Champion since 1965 (Ray Middleton) received a further boost when Carl Lawton, Ray Middleton and Len Duquemin produced top form to clinch the team title too---thus winning the only National R.W.A. title to elude them last year. Our congratulations go out to the team and the officials who have served us so well. Our walkers have certainly gone into the 70's on the crest of a wave; but they are only a whisker ahead of our Youth runners who have just completed a cross-country season deserving of the highest praise. Second in the 'Southern' and fourth in the "National" were performances of high merit, but our lads are not yet ready to leave the Youth class until they have made a real mark and, astonishingly, all six of our National team qualify for this category again next year. The weight of favourites is an unkind burden for Youths to bear, but there is no doubt that it is in this section that Belgrave's main hopes lie for emulating the walkers. A word too for our Senior cross-country runners who nowadays have to face a thousand opponents in National Championships with standards rising at a remarkable rate. They had struggled rather through the season and it is to their credit that they produced their best effort on Mational day. In finishing sixth they beat the holders, Tipton Harriers, and had a points score low enough to have given them bronze medals last year. So the picture at the beginning of a new decade bodes well for Belgrave at running and walking---but one part of the picture is not too clear. Will our track and field men win that Southern League and get us back into the National Divisions where we belong?. Will Wesch WILL WESCH new National R.W.A. 10 miles and Inter-Counties champion; joined the club 18 months earlier WILL WESCH Will Pat Duncan Pat Duncan wrote the account of the Liverpool race Ray Middleton Ray Middleton previous Belgrave National champion (1965); member of winning National R.W.A. 10 team Carl Lawton Carl Lawton member of winning National R.W.A. 10 team Len Duquemin Len Duquemin member of winning National R.W.A. 10 team R.W.A. items.sum: Hon. Secretary's notes: Bill True resigns as walking handicapper, congratulations to Peter Hilliar and Charlie Speechley, the 1970 GLC track meeting and open event dates, Battersea Park track changes, the Five Star Award Scheme, the Youths' second place in the Southern and the history of the Walter C. Jewell Trophy, Ken O'Kell's honours boards, Arthur Kendall's retirement, and Belgrave's ECCU Championship record since 1935.
items.s: HON. SECRETARY'S NOTES Hon. Secretary's notes: Bill True resigns as walking handicapper, congratulations to Peter Hilliar and Charlie Speechley, the 1970 GLC track meeting and open event dates, Battersea Park track changes, the Five Star Award Scheme, the Youths' second place in the Southern and the history of the Walter C. Jewell Trophy, Ken O'Kell's honours boards, Arthur Kendall's retirement, and Belgrave's ECCU Championship record since 1935. Owing to a change of job involving difficult hours, Bill True has been obliged to resign from the office of Hon. Handicapper (walking), a position he has held for many many years and in which he has given universal satisiaction. Our Vice President would have liked to carry on for a few more years yet but circumstances will not permit and we extend our warm thanks to Bill for all his hard work and our congratulations on the high standard of handicapping he has always given us. Our hearty congratulations go to Track Captain, Peter Hilliar, on his recent marriage and we wish Mr. and Mrs. Hilliar years of happiness and good health ahead. Congratulations to CHARLIE SPEECHLEY who had his 82nd birthday recently and is still very active indeed - and in a competitive way at that! He confides that he covered 1,100 miles in training and racing last year! Charlie is one of our oldest members, having competed in the first Belgrave Open Walk in 1919. The following dates have been allocated to us by the GLC for our track meetings and these will, of course, be supplemented by many other fixtures. All members, athletes and officials alike are asked to note the dates given below and give full support so ensuring a successful Summer season. April 25 (Sat) Battersea Park May 6 (Wed) Battersea Park May 20 (Wed) Battersea Park June 6 (Sat) Club Track and Field Championships at Hurlingham Park (2.30 p.m.) June 10 (Wed) Battersea Park June 24 (Wed) Battersea Park July 1 (Wed) Invitation Inter Club Walks - Battersea Park July 15 (Wed) Battersea Park July 27 (Mon) Battersea Park Aug 5 (Wed) Battersea Park Other dates to note are:- April 4 (Sat) Southern and Belgrave 12 Stage Road Relay (Wimbledon) July 11 (Sat) Belgrave 20 Miles Open Run (Wimbledon) Oct 17 (Sat) Belgrave Open Youths Road Relay (Wimbledon) Nov 28 (Sat) Belgrave 51st Annual Open 7m Walk (Wimbledon) The GLC are altering the track at Battersea Park to a 400 metres lap which may assist our mathematics - or will it? New hurdles are promised and also improved facilities in the jump pits. The Five Star Award Scheme for young athletes at school and within the clubs has proved a tremendous success and last year 85,000 certificates and 24,000 badges were awarded in the South. It is anticipated that even greater numbers will qualify this coming season and no doubt we as a Club will gain considerable benefit from the scheme. Several of our younger members have already qualified in the highest grade and we hope that each season will add to their number. We also hope that many young athletes will continue with the sport and join our ranks when they will receive a very cordial welcome. The Commonwealth Games are to be held at Edinburgh on July 16 to 25 and we hope that we shall be well represented in the competing teams. Congratulations to our Youth's team on their second placing in the Southern Cross Country Championships at Parliament Hill Fields. They ran really well and showed that our teams of the future will rise above all opposition. We have yet to win this championship inaugurated in 1948 but we may be sure it won't be long now. We were second in 1950 at Eastbourne and again in 1954 (Parliament Hill Fields). Third place was ours at Ewell in 1961 and the following year at Reading and now we are among the medals again! The trophy for this event 'The Walter C. Jewell Trophy' should naturally gravitate towards us for in pre-War days this rather handsome cup was known as the 'Jockey Cup' and was won three years in succession by Belgrave in a two mile team race on the track and was on permanent display at our mid-week quarters of those days 'The Rising Sun', Ebury Bridge Road. During the War we held it in safe keeping and later when the clouds cleared it was re-claimed and adopted for use as a Cross Country trophy. We had a sentimental regard for this cup for it was the first open team trophy to be won by the Club. Let's hope our young runners will take a year's lease on it when the 1971 championships come round. We pay tribute to Ken O'Kell's continuing generosity in keeping up-to-date our Honours Boards showing our 'Presidents' and 'Internationals' which he kindly presented to the Club some years ago. Ken, a Club champion of the '20's, manages to keep very fit thanks to his walks in Epping Forest and an interest in bowls. ARTHUR KENDALL, of Shaftesbury Harriers, and Hon. Secretary of the Southern Counties AAA for many years past (and previously of the Middlesex County AAA) is resigning this year. It is impossible to even begin to assess his value and competence over so many years to the Association and its affiliated Clubs and we can only express grateful thanks for all his efforts, and good health in his retirement. No less than 35 years have passed since Belgrave won the ECCU Championship at Beaconsfield, our team consisting of BERT FOOTER (11), DAN PATIENCE (14), JIM GINTY (15), ALF TAYLOR (18), TOM CARTER (19) and HARRY SHIELDS (20). Other wins came in 1939, 1946 and 1948 and we had a sequence of being 'in the medals' from 1933-1948, War years omitted. We have striven hard in subsequent years and accomplished some excellent performances but team medals have eluded us. This is written ahead of this year's championship and let's hope this statement proves false when it comes to be read! It is interesting to note that since our initial win in 1935 no Club has a record superior to our four wins. Birchfield H. have recorded three, Bolton U.H. one, Coventry Godiva two, Derby & County A.C. three, Mitcham A.C. one, North Staffs and Stone one, Portsmouth A.C. three, Sheffield U.H. two, South London H. three, Sutton Harriers and A.C. four, Tipton H. one and Victoria Park A.A.C. (Scotland) one. Time we went ahead again! There's always Birchfields' 28 wins between the years 1880 - 1953 to overtake and surpass! Bill True Bill True Vice President; resigned as Hon. items.sum: Tongue-in-cheek 'situations vacant' advertisement by retiring Hon. Secretary A.A. Harley seeking his successor, ending with a serious appeal for a new Hon. Secretary.
items.s: SITUATIONS VACANT Tongue-in-cheek 'situations vacant' advertisement by retiring Hon. Secretary A.A. Harley seeking his successor, ending with a serious appeal for a new Hon. Secretary. HARLEY - OUT! OUT! OUT! - - - - - WHAT'SNAME - IN! IN! IN! SITUATIONS VACANT WANTED - a brand new Honorary Secretary to take place of present incumbent who has been suffered since 1938 and is about to be put out to grass. Candidate must possess all the virtues and some of the vices, be house-trained, of patient disposition and regular habits, capable of turning the other cheek and spending his own money generously. Ability to address envelopes, stick stamps, record minutes, shift chairs, split infinitives etc. an advantage. Small knowledge of Amateur Athletics might possibly be helpful but not essential. Prospects non-existent, no help given with removal expenses, all fringe benefits carefully cut away. Office conditions lamentable, pension by arrangement with Minister of Social Security. Applicants should queue at the door of the Presidential sanctum in ranks of three, equipped with 48 hours emergency rations and bed-rolls, pending interview, and be prepared to swear an oath of continence, abstinence, celibacy and eternal loyalty to the Belgrave Harriers (founded 1887 - semper paratus). Or telephone 01 946 6859 (ANSA-BACK system installed) quoting Ref. NBG/BEL/HONSEC and giving the ancient passwords 'Nine in six, Up the Bels'. Seriously, we need a competent, enthusiastic Hon. Secretary soon. Are you the man for the job? A.A.H. A.A. Harley HARLEY Hon. Secretary since 1938, standing down HARLEY A.A.H.

items.label: March 1970
items.sum: Light-hearted account, told as a ship's voyage, of the club children's party at Wimbledon on 11 January 1970 with games, a film show and Father Christmas.
items.s: CHILDRENS PARTY Light-hearted account, told as a ship's voyage, of the club children's party at Wimbledon on 11 January 1970 with games, a film show and Father Christmas. On Sunday 11th January the good ship Belgrave paid a return visit to Wimbledon and Captain Hoppy and his motley crew welcomed aboard a handsome bunch of girls and boys; the galley provided a fine tea, cakes, sandwiches, jelly, orangeade etc., etc. This was soon polished off and the decks were cleared for action when pirates came aboard. These were soon subdued and clapped in irons, a promise of good behaviour was gained from them and games were organised. Crew and passengers all had great fun. It was then reported by the look-outs that the ship was crossing the Equator. The ship was hove to and who should climb over the side but King Neptune himself. The crew were then subjected to the crossing-the-line ceremony, much to the delight of our young passengers; Captain Hoppy, Pete the pirate, Blackdog Paddy and young Jim Gillings and the rest hastily abandoned ship. All the Company now retired to the main lounge where the Purser, Bill Laws, had arranged a film show. Soon the whole ship was filled with laughter, children's and adult's, at the antics of Tom and Gerry and company. Ice cream was distributed and soon consumed. All eyes were now turned upwards when an old friend made his appearance, without his trousers, but in his normal long flowing red robe. Yes, Father Christmas had returned and it was apparent from his stooping shoulders and slow pace that his sack was heavy. Nobody had been forgotten, he had a toy for all. Eight bells now being sounded it was time for the good ship to make its way over the horizon and all good children to be on their way home, but not without saying thanks to all the crew, ladies and gentlemen who served in the galley and those who swabbed the decks later. Captain Hoppy Captain Hoppy nickname used for the party's host Pete the pirate Pete the pirate nickname at the children's party Blackdog Paddy Blackdog Paddy nickname at the children's party Jim Gillings Jim Gillings helper at the children's party Bill Laws Bill Laws arranged the film show Belgrave Children's Party Wimbledon

items.s: OBITUARY Obituary notices for E.R. (Bob) Jessop, a former first-class footballer and long-time club supporter, in his 91st year, and for W.F.C. Davies of Chiswick. We have to advise the death of a very old member, E.R. (Bob) Jessop in his 91st year. Bob who had been a first class footballer in his day, was for many years a great supporter of the Club, and was to be found at all the major Championships sporting his colours and encouraging the Club teams. We mourn his passing. It is with regret that we also have to advise the death of W.F.C. Davies of Chiswick who died recently in his 63rd year. Our sympathies are extended to his widow. E.R. items.s: STANDARDS 1970 Table of club and A.A.A. grade I-III standards for 1970 for Seniors, Juniors and Youths, with a commentary on the changes (the commentary ends on page 6, 'Continued from opposite page'); the table is printed in two side-by-side halves, here each age group is one table. STANDARDS 1970 The A.A.A. Senior Standards for 1970 show many changes, all of course for the tougher. The Juniors are let off lightly with only the long jump being revised, the three grades being increased by 12",6" and 3" respectively. The Youths get off scot free with all marks remaining as last year. It is the Seniors that take a hammering---no less than ten events being upgraded. Grade I in the 200 and 400 are cut by a tenth of a second only, but in the 800 all three grades are cut by 0.9, 1.2 and 0.3 respectively. The 1500 cut is 1.0, 1.0, 2.0 but the 3,000 Steeplechase is slashed by a mammoth 10, 10, 20 seconds! The marathon men do not escape by any means, the cuts in their three standards being 5 mins, 5 mins, and 10 mins. In the Field, the shot mark is increased by an imposing 10%, the biggest change of all; the increases in each grade are 5'-0", 4'-0" and 3"-0. The hammer goes up by 10'-0", 15'-0", (Continued from opposite page) 15'-0" and the discus 10'-0" in each grade. Dave Ansell's jumpers will be pleased to see their long jump marks preserved but the triple men will not feel too happy at having to find another 1'-6", 1-2" or 1'-6" according to which grade they are aiming. As for our own Club marks, which are unchanged, except for a 1" increase in the Senior and Junior high jumps, it looks as though they are due for a big overhaul. items.sum: Article praising the spirit and results of Belgrave's Youths and Boys and the influence of section officials Reg Hopkins and Tom Carter and their moderate training policy.
items.s: YOUTHS & BOYS Article praising the spirit and results of Belgrave's Youths and Boys and the influence of section officials Reg Hopkins and Tom Carter and their moderate training policy. One of the most pleasing aspects of Belgrave Club life today is the quality of our Youths. Not just their fine performances on track, road and country, but also their spirit, enthusiasm and general behaviour. A lot is said daily in the National Press about the youth of today but generally it portrays only one side of the coin. In Belgrave we seem to have the other. It is not just running ability that has brought the results enjoyed this last cross country season. Nor is it just due to the number of miles put in during those many dark, cold winter evenings. It is also due to the character and general approach of the Youths themselves. This is not something they were necessarily born with of course and it is probably fair to say that they have benefitted a great deal from the influence of our Club structure generally and from their section officials in particular. Reg Hopkins and Tom Carter have played a large part over the years in building up this important part of our Club. The Youths and Boys mean a great deal to Reg and it is doubtful whether anyone could quite share the joys and sorrows as he does. Sometimes it looks as though he gets his emotions the wrong way round. He looked like crying and was lost for words after the Southern and National performances which pleased him so much, yet when a disappointing result comes along now and again he is the chirpiest, cheerful man around. This latter quality must be a great help to young runners who can get dismayed so easily. In this era of Bedford-type training and 200 miles a week it is easy for youngsters to be badly influenced by the publicity and made to believe that other people's schedules will make them champion runners too. It is not easy to understand that one man's meat is another man's poison and that there is a mental approach to training as well as a physical one. The moderating influence of Reg and Tom in training policy has made itself felt. The Youths' successes have been chieved on a maximum of 50 miles a week. They have many years ahead of them on which to build up their training in both quality and quantity----and they realise it. Belgrave are proud of their Youths and Boys, but the Youths and Boys will tell you that no pride could be greater than that which they have in Belgrave Harriers. items.s: Youths Win County Title Report and results of the Surrey Youths cross-country championship at Milford Heath on 3 January 1970, won by Belgrave's team with 19 points, Peter Carton third, with a Ron Linstead photograph of the start (page 9). Milford Heath---January 3rd Everything went very much to form in this first Championship of the 70's and it was nice to know that that meant Belgrave were to run out easy team winners with the remarkably low score of 19 points. The Aldershot pair Ford and Adams were reckoned to be certainities for medals but our own Bill Curtin, the reigning County Boys Champion, pushed them hard in the early stages, but he had to give way in the second mile as Ford proved invincible. Peter Carton moved up on Bill and got away in the final stages for an excellent third place (how this lad improves!) while Bill was outkicked by his almost inseparable rival from Mitcham AC, M. Fromant. John Stowe was only 120 yards further back with Tony Binda a similar distance behind John, but closing fast. Our Press Honorary Secretary, Don Maclean, was an interested spectator as he was a winner of this race in the early 1950's. We went into the 50's winning this Championship in 1950,51, and 52. items.s: A SOUTHERN SILVER ! Report and results of the Southern youths cross-country championship at Parliament Hill on 7 February, where Belgrave youths won team silver behind T.V.H. Parliament Hill - February 7 Parliament Hill may have been at it's treacherous, muddiest worst but it was shining silver all the way for Belgrave's youths on this murky February day. Carton and Curtin got a good start but Peter was unable to keep in touch with his team-mate for long and didn't look quite so happy in the mud. Nevertheless, he pressed on in his most determined style to finish an excellent 13th - 38 seconds behind Bill who looked 'out on his feet' over the last 600 yards. One who was far from 'out' was Tony Binda whose slight frame skimmed over the muddy surface of the closing stages faster, probably, than any of the field. It is unusual to see a cautious start in one so young. He was fast catching John Stow who had put in some very hard work in the middle stages and was hanging on to his forward position with great determination. It was a fine display by our youths and Reg Hopkins was the proudest man at Parliament Hill that day. They all deserved the accolade of congratulations that showered upon them. ( 166 finished) 1. J. items.label: March 1970
items.sum: A parody of Henry V's 'Once more unto the breach' urging Belgrave's young runners on, with apologies to Shakespeare.
items.s: A BELGRAVIAN'S Call To Battle! A parody of Henry V's 'Once more unto the breach' urging Belgrave's young runners on, with apologies to Shakespeare. Once more onto the track, dear friends, once more; And run your heart out down that final straight! In school there's nothing so becomes a boy As modest stillness and humility: But when that last lap bell sounds in your ears, Stiffen the sinews, summon up the blood, Disguise fair nature with hard-favoured rage; Then set the teeth, stretch the nostril wide. Gasp in the breath and bend up every spirit to its full height! On, on, you noble Belgraves whose past is filled with veterans of sure proof-- Veterans that, like so many Zatopeks, Have in these parts both morn and evening run and packed their spikes for lack of argument:- Dishonour not your seniors; now attest That those whom you call seniors won't despise you! Be copy now to boys of grosser clubs, And teach them how to run. I see you stand like greyhounds in the slips, Straining upon the start.------the games' afoot: Follow your spirit; and upon this charge Cry-God for Lucas! Carter! and Belgrave! (With apologies to "Will") Lucas Lucas named in the poem's closing line Carter Carter named in the poem's closing line Zatopek Zatopeks used figuratively

items.s: SURREY C.C. LEAGUE YOUTH/BOY DIV. 1 Report of Belgrave's runaway win in the 1969/70 Surrey Cross-Country League Youth/Boy Division 1, with the final table and results of races 2-4, Curtin and Carton finishing together in race 4 at Coulsdon (Race 3 lists 37th M. Clancy in 15:35, faster than places above, as printed). FINAL TABLE With the second lowest total ever, Belgrave chalked up a runaway win in the 1969/7o league season. True, that Bill Curtin and Peter Carton gave us a proud start each time out, but true also that with five to score three other runners had a vital part to play, And indeed no less than six different athletes played their part in filling those supporting places. Three places down after the first race to Mitcham and a further seven down after the second made the victory prospects look tough at the halfway mark. But with a fantastic effort on Mitcham's own course our lads rubbed our host's noses into the mud by filling the first five places. To show that the outcome was no more than a formality, Curtin and Carton, in the final fixture, coasted away together to cross the line equal first. A fine performance and a fine show by a fine bunch of lads. Bill Curtin took the individual award with impressive placings of 2nd, 1st, 2nd and equal 1st. He also had the unusual experience of sharing the winning time in every race. The first race was reported in the December issue of 'The Belgravian'. The next three races went as follows:- RACE NO. 2 - Petersham, Richmond Park - December 13 Having been inched out of victory in the first race by Fromant of Mitcham, Bill Curtin was out for revenge. This time he reversed the decision by a similar number of inches. Walton's Francis pipped Peter Carton again for third place and Tony Binda ran through strongly to secure 11th place, just two places ahead of Vic Butcher who closed in our scoring four. (47 finished) RACE NO. 3 - Morden Park, December 27 It would take more than the upheaval of Christmas festivities to upset our lads when it comes to running. So, instead of fielding depleted teams like some of our rivals, we turned out no less than 14 of the 44 runners! And what a riot it was too! With the terrible twins getting well clear early on, John Stow and Richard Langley gradually consolidated third and fourth places. Tony Binda had his usual steady start and made his way through the field in great style to finish furiously over the final 400 yards or so and clinch the clean sweep that all Belgravians were longing for. (44 finished) RACE NO. 4 - Farthing Downs, Coulsdon, February 21 There was little to fear from the opposition over the snow-covered North Downs. More important to keep injury free on the treacherous surface and think of the following week's National. Once again the 'twins' performed their famous duet to look in a class of their own. Tony Binda regained his third scorer position from John Stow and Richard Langley to finish seventh - a fine effort. (54 finished) 1. BELGRAVE HARRIERS 142 pts 2. Mitcham A.C. 221 pts 3. items.sum: Report by R.H. of the Mitcham Young Athletes 4x2 miles relay at Morden Park on 14 February, where Belgrave's youths led through three legs before finishing fifth (A team) and ninth (B team).
items.s: Mitcham Young Athletes Relay Report by R.H. of the Mitcham Young Athletes 4x2 miles relay at Morden Park on 14 February, where Belgrave's youths led through three legs before finishing fifth (A team) and ninth (B team). Morden Park, February 14th (4X2 Miles Relay) This race included juniors under 20 years of age. Not having any juniors available on this occasion our team was composed of our youths team minus Bill Curtin who was competing in Ireland. We did not, in these circumstances, expect our lads to fare very well thinking that they would be outclassed. Peter Carton opened the first leg for us and disappeared from view in around 4th or 5th spot. This being a 2 mile course round Morden Park it wasn't long before the runners came into sight and much to our delight and surprise who should be in the lead but Pete, going like the clappers and holding on right to the changeover with 8 secs on the second team, Aldershot. Full of congratulations for Peter we just caught the back of John Stowe going away for the second leg. We thought that we had had our moment of glory and that John, although he would always try his best, must lose several places during his stint. But once again we were all mistaken: John was not to be outshone by Peter and he covered the distance in exactly the same time as his team mate and only Adams of Aldershot (6th in the Southern) passed him. Surely we couldn't keep this up "Who said so," cracked Tony Binda, flying over the third leg. He knew we were in with a chance now and he certainly made the most of it. We already knew how tenacious he could be and this was a situation he gloried in, holding on to our second position in fine style. Then we had to face the moment of truth. Vic Butcher was to run the final leg that would normally have been Bill Curtin's. Vic is keen and dedicated to our club and sport and he trains hard and often, but he has yet to find the form we know he could produce. Vic was very nervous and he had to face several good runners on his leg, including one of the Tuck twins. We did our best to inspire him with confidence but it was to no avail. He ran much below form dropping us to fifth position. Vic did his best of course and it didn't exactly cheer him up to know that any one of our 'B' team runners would have gained third place. Never mind, that's the way it goes; we did much better than we had expected anyway. R.H. Fastest Individual:- G. Tuck (Camb. & Col.) 9:57 1. Walton AC 42:09 2. Ald. F. & District 42:50 5. Morden Park---February 14th Strong, gusting winds and a snow-bound course with stretches of treacherous ice did not detract from some fine racing and Belgrave were only just pushed out of bronze medals. items.sum: Report and results of the National youths cross-country championship at Stanley Park, Blackpool, on 28 February, where Belgrave's first-year youths narrowly missed medals in fourth place.
items.s: Youths 4th in National Report and results of the National youths cross-country championship at Stanley Park, Blackpool, on 28 February, where Belgrave's first-year youths narrowly missed medals in fourth place. Stanley Park, Blackpool---February 28th What a performance! The future holds no bounds for these lads. Every outing supercedes the previous one and in asking "Where will it all end?" one hopes the answer will be "In England's Senior team of 1975!" All six of our lads are first year youths and watching them on the sidelines, with itchy feet, was Richard Langley who will be fighting to displace one of our scoring four next year when gold is the target. This year, the only possible target was silver(Small Heath were known to be invincible) but no one really expected us to pick up medals. After all, it would be a big enough task to put Shaftesbury and our Southern conquerors T.V.H. behind us without considering the Midlands and North. How wrong we nearly were! With Carton and Curtin grimly hanging on to their places around the twenty mark, John Stowe going well in the early sixties and Tony Binda only another twenty places back, a count at two miles placed us second, yes second. Could we hold it? Gateshead and Pembroke were both pressing furiously and slowly cutting their scores. Peter held on well, Bill dropped a place or two, John was slipping rather more having put everything into the first half and Tony Binda was making ground (as usual) as the finish approached. It was a very close thing. Only 13 points covered the three teams and we were the unlucky ones to miss medals. The lads deserved some memento of their great effort but perhaps next year will be known as "the year after Blackpool". One cannot really single out any of the scoring four. They all ran at their best and are such good prospects that the order of finishing could change yet again next season. In a club such as ours they should be able to realise their full potential. They have the right connections, the rest is up to them. (365 finished) (52 teams finished) 1. C. Falconer (Springburn H.) 20:50 2. R. Smedley (J.Willmott GS) 20:59 3. J. items.label: March 1970
items.sum: Profile by AAH of Harry Parker, a Belgrave stalwart from 1912 until his death in 1950 and the man behind the 'Pyramid' Cup and the Harry Parker Memorial Bowl, with photographs from 1921 and 1941.
items.s: THE MEN BEHIND THE TROPHIES Profile by AAH of Harry Parker, a Belgrave stalwart from 1912 until his death in 1950 and the man behind the 'Pyramid' Cup and the Harry Parker Memorial Bowl, with photographs from 1921 and 1941. HARRY PARKER Harry Parker was born in Westminster and lived and worked for the greater part of his life in this area which will always be associated with the Club's beginnings. In 1910 Harry joined the Westminster Harriers and here he met many sportsmen he was to know for the rest of his life. A dispute in the Westminster club, which was an organisation of many sections, led to the formation of the Chelsea Harriers but in 1912 this club was absorbed into the Belgrave Harriers. Harry and several others quickly settled down and devoted themselves to a lifetime with the 'Bels', and this continued for 38 years until Harry passed on in 1950. Harry was a keen and enthusiastic team man in his active days and thereafter proved himself to be one of the finest Belgravians ever by reason of his unremitting work for the Club. He rarely missed a fixture. He served in many capacities at various times. He was in turn our Running Hon. Secretary, Assistant Hon. Secretary, Hon. Treasurer, President and a Life Member and working all the time for the Club he held so dear. We joked about his little black memo book, in and out of his pocket with staccato notes entered therein, the innumerable postcards he sent to rally the faithful, his bias towards everything Belgravian, his contemptuous feeling for those who had sneered at Belgrave in earlier days and made use of the club for their own purposes only. His greatest work, however, was undoubtedly done during War years when almost single handed he kept in touch with hundreds of members distributed throughout the world and managed to act as a clearing house for all the news he gathered. To Harry, as much as anyone, goes the credit that Belgrave was a real club, very much in being, and financially sound when we re-assembled to resume, more or less, where we had left off. Harry had served as President of the South of the Thames C.C. Association, as an official at the 1948 Olympic Games, as an AAA Handicapper and in 1950 became President of the English Cross Country Union (and Southern Counties C.C. Association) - the highest honour to be accorded in cross country running councils, and the first Belgrave Harrier to attain this position - only to die in his year of office, much to our sorrow. So passed a great Belgravian. Harry had earlier presented us with the 'Pyramid' Cup for our Weight Put Championship and on his death his many friends subscribed to present to the Club 'The Harry Parker Memorial Bowl' which is awarded to the first Club man to finish in the ECCU Senior Championship. These two trophies will assuredly remind us as long as the Club shall exist of one of its finest workers and of one who never gave anything other than the best that was in him to the Belgrave Harriers. items.h: FROM 'The Belgravian' 25 years ago ●●●●● and 40 years ago
items.sum: Extracts from The Belgravian of 25 years earlier (Victory in Europe, wartime club life, Derrick Burfitt's National youths win) and 40 years earlier (cross-country and walking successes, the Bishop of Birmingham's Cup).
items.s: FROM 'The Belgravian' 25 years ago ●●●●● and 40 years ago Extracts from The Belgravian of 25 years earlier (Victory in Europe, wartime club life, Derrick Burfitt's National youths win) and 40 years earlier (cross-country and walking successes, the Bishop of Birmingham's Cup). 25 years ago As we go to press so comes the good news that we have all waited for, Victory in Europe. Amidst the rejoicing and thanksgiving, members' thoughts may have been turned towards the Club, and how it has fared during these last five odd years. The Club has many good reasons to be proud of its services to athletics and to its members. Belgrave Hall was open not only to our own members but to members of clubs less fortunate and to visiting athletes and servicemen. Much could be written of the fortunes of our many members. A large number, probably the majority, of our active members was called up for service in the Forces. We had, however, many members in reserved occupations, the Police and Civil Defence. These, in spite of long working hours and extra duties and less leisure time, have been able to keep the Club going. We were also pleased to welcome services members when on leave, and they proved valuable helps to the Club's teams. We have also been fortunate in having a live and efficient Committee of hard working officers. They gave up much valuable time in the interests of the Club. It is perhaps little realised how much work is done behind the scenes. We do not know how long it will be before athletics are restored to their pre-war scale and scope but we can confidently say that when they are Belgrave will be to the fore. The past winter has shown us that we can still lead the way and we congratulate our runners and walkers on a good season's work. Once again Derrick Burfitt has merited special mention. He won the National Youth's Cross-Country Race by a convincing margin. He also took other junior titles in his stride. Soon, many of our Services men will be coming back to us and we look forward to seeing them line up with our teams. Others will be drafted to the Far Eastern zone where we already have a number of members. To those who will still be serving we send our best wishes for a speedy and safe return. Until that much-awaited day, they will often be in our thoughts. and 40 years ago The past month, the climax of the winter season, has been wonderfully successful for our runners and walkers. The cross-country men have been placed in the 'Southern' for the first time in the Club's history and followed this up by what is, perhaps, an even better performance - sixth in the National - another 'best yet'. The walkers have won the Junior Championship again and now Belgrave hold both Senior and Junior Championships. Incidentally, we are the first Club to have won the Junior title three times. A team went to Birmingham on March 22 and brought back the 'Bishop of Birmingham's Cup' - our first visit to the Midland town for this race since 1921, when we won the trophy for the first time. Derrick Burfitt Derrick Burfitt won the National Youths' Cross-Country race (1945) National Cross Country Championships Southern Cross Country Championships Bishop of Birmingham's Cup Belgrave Hall Birmingham Far Eastern zone

items.s: ROAD RUNNING Gordon Biscoe's introduction to the 1970 road season, noting the AAA Marathon combining with the Poly Marathon, a proposal to hold the Surrey 20 with the Belgrave 20 on 11 July, and a request for members' times. GORDON BISCOE WRITES: At the time of writing the Road season will once again be getting under way with its familar pattern of races, and after last year's successes our obvious aim must be to try and improve on these. There has been no news of any of our long distance men contemplating retirement so it's expected that the usual faces will be there. The unknown quantities are, as to whether Chas. Dabbs can make another of his come-backs and recapture some of his previous form; and as to what new distance men may emerge from our ranks as has happened in previous years with Tony Brien and Clive Shippen etc. The tendency to try and simplify events continues slowly, this year the AAA Marathon once again combines with the Poly Marathon and there is a strong proposal that the Surrey 20 should be held in conjunction with our own Belgrave 20 on July 11th. We always try to give as complete a record of club performances as possible in the Belgravian as well as the ranking lists introduced in the last issue. So if during the season anyone sets any times they think we may not know about, would they please let Lionel Mann or myself know about them as we're interested in all results. Hog's Back----December 20th The usual large field set off in excellent running conditions. Geoff North cut out the early pace with a group which gradually reduced to about a half dozen. Just after the seven miles mark however the Holt twins sped away leaving their adversaries to fight for the minor placings. Geoff secured sixth place in an excellent time of 44:55 just over 200 yards down on Bob Holt. Dick Piotrowski and Lionel Mann provided excellent backing in 15th and 19th places respectively, enabling us to take second place in the team race to the consistently strong Hercules Wimbledon outfit. The rest of the boys had typical pre-Christmas runs spreading the Belgrave spirit of goodwill throughout the lower echelons of the field. Despite this we provided four men in the first ten in the Veterans Section----Arthur Bruce (4th), Denis Jones (5th), Ken Stimpson (9th) and Geoff Pearson (10th). RESULT Teams:- 1. R. We were 4th in the Jim Peters Trophy with three to score and second in the Fry Trophy with six to score. The race was won by Alan Domleo from Badgery and Lem. Pat O'Connor led in the Belgrave squad followed by Lionel Mann, Clive Shippen and Brian Joines. John Hall motored up from Wales to compete and informed us that he is giving up his first claim on Belgrave and expecting an addition to his family. items.sum: Reprinted newspaper cutting on Mr Norman Capener's call for special sports injury clinics, open at weekends, to reduce the 1,500,000 sports injuries a year.
items.s: Sport clinics sought to reduce loss from injuries Reprinted newspaper cutting on Mr Norman Capener's call for special sports injury clinics, open at weekends, to reduce the 1,500,000 sports injuries a year. WAYS of reducing the suffering, disability and economic loss caused by sports injuries are outlined by physicians and surgeons. It is estimated that there are 1,500,000 such injuries every year, which result in the sufferer being unable to continue his sport. Ten per cent. of the injuries cause absence from work. Special sports injury clinics are advocated by Mr Norman Capener, consultant adviser on orthopaedics to the Department of Health, in the Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine. Such clinics, he says, should be open at weekends to permit immediate treatment. Sports injuries should no longer be regarded as insignificant. They were no less important than industrial injuries and equally might lead to economic loss. Hundreds of thousands of amateurs were engaged in sport. Games and athletics were on balance greatly to man's good. That there were hazards was the price of achievement, and it was here that medicine came in. The important contributions which medical science could make to sports had been neglected. Three shifts Life was lived in three shifts of eight hours each—work, sleep and pleasure. The last one was lengthening greatly. The danger was that passive viewing, whether in the arena or in front of the domestic viewing box, might sap the very vitality of mind and body which games should encourage. Norman Capener Mr Norman Capener consultant adviser on orthopaedics to the Department of Health

items.label: March 1970
items.sum: Article urging athletes to think in metric measurements before British athletics goes fully metric, criticising the A.A.A. for introducing the centimetre, with a feet-and-inches to metres conversion table.
items.s: THINK METRIC NOW ! Article urging athletes to think in metric measurements before British athletics goes fully metric, criticising the A.A.A. for introducing the centimetre, with a feet-and-inches to metres conversion table. It will not be long before British athletics goes metric completely and no more will our field events men and statisticians have to get involved with fractions of an inch when recording performances. Once we have become familiar with the new set of "barriers" this change will bring, the metric result will mean more to us tan it does at present. To the non-specialist each field event has a mark he regards as a barrier. The mark is usually determined by the roundness of the figure rather than the difficulty in obtaining it, with the result that some events have no convenient barrier for the spectator. The long jump fills the latter category perhaps. Twenty feet is commonplace, but thirty feet is unattainable In the javelin and hammer 250 feet doesn't sound quite so magical as 200 feet did and 300 feet will. In domestic triple jumping 50 feet means something, just as 60 feet does in the shot. Soon it will all change. Those events which had convenient "barriers" are likely to lose them and those that were stuck in no man's land will have a new lease of life. In the long jump for instance our club men will aim for 7 metres (23'-0") and the internationals the already magical 8 metres (26'-3"). For Britons at any rate the popular high jump target will be 2 metres (6'-6½"). The shot will become tougher; the old 60 feet barrier will now stretch out to 20 metres (65'-7½"). And the javelin throwers will have to take their choice in 10 metre steps until someone achieves the 100 metres throw, then they'll really have something to throw for! The 4 metre and 5 metre marks are conveniently situated for Britain's pole-vaulters, the imperial equivalents being 13'-1½" and 16'-5" respectively. So one could go on; but the moral should be clear. THINK METRIC FROM THE BEGINNING. Fix in your mind new salient points for each event and work around them---just as mile times are evaluated on the number of seconds either side of 4 minutes. For your guidance we are reproducing a metric conversion table, but we hope you will soon overcome the desire to convert metric into imperial. The table converts imperial into metric (you can read it in reverse of course) and you will notice that the metric figures are given in millimetres. The third decimal place will not apply in athletic results as marks are recorded to the nearest 10 millimetres. At this point it is worth mentioning that the metric system being adopted is the new Systeme Internationale (S.I. units) which will result in the Engineering and Science world adopting a completely new terminology which will be just as new to other European countries as ourselves. As far as linear measurement is concerned our European colleagues have a head start, as the metre and millimetre have been retained. However, THE CENTIMETRE BECOMES AS EXTINCT AS THE INCH. It would therefore be quite wrong for us to fall into the habit of using a non-standard term and, in this respect, it is unfortunate that the A.A.A. should have chosen to amend their measurement rules this year by introducing the centimetre. They could quite easily have ruled that measurements be taken in ten millimetre increments instead of introducing a revision to the wording later on. Someone didn't do his homework! The centimetre markings on the present metric tapes will eventually be changed from 1,2,3,4 etc. to 10,20,30,40 etc.---all helping to confuse those who have just digested the centimetre! The metric system is upon us. THINK METRIC NOW. items.s: IAAF DELAY SHOE BAN Reprinted newspaper cutting reporting that the International Amateur Athletic Federation had postponed its ban on shoes bearing trade marks until October and set up a sub-committee on advertising and sponsorship. Athletics IAAF DELAY SHOE BAN By A Special Correspondent The International Amateur Athletic Federation has postponed its proposed ban on shoes bearing trade marks until October and a sub-committee has been set up to "consider and report on the wider aspects of advertising and sponsorship in relation to amateur athletics." The Federation had previously decided that, as from May 1, athletes taking part in international competition should wear only white shoes with no distinguishing marks. This followed rumours that 'some athletes had received large sums for wearing shoes of leading manufacturers at the Mexico Olympics. The Federation may now follow a similar line as the international body of ski-ing, who are making arrangements for manufacturers to pay national federations for the privilege of using their equipment. If athletics adopted this policy several countries would welcome increased revenue. A Special Correspondent A Special Correspondent Mexico Olympics Mexico International Amateur Athletic Federation

items.label: March 1970
items.sum: Pat Duncan's preview of the 1970 walking season, praising the unbeaten Belgrave 'A' team and naming rival clubs, with an editorial note that the National '10' result appears on page 29.
items.s: WALKING Pat Duncan's preview of the 1970 walking season, praising the unbeaten Belgrave 'A' team and naming rival clubs, with an editorial note that the National '10' result appears on page 29. Pat Duncan writes: A clean sweep in the Open '7's is an encouraging start to 1970, nor should we forget that the Belgrave 'A' team has not been beaten since last Easter. Since then Carl Lawton, Wilf Wesch and Bob Coates have really developed, benefitting no doubt from hard sessions together both on the road at Wimbledon and during the summer on the track. Barry Ingarfield is the latest addition to the Wimbledon school and his times have also improved steadily through the winter. Our older established walkers also seem determined to make their mark so we enter the National season as confident as we can be that some good results should be coming our way. Looking around for rivals Bristol are coming on and while in the Midlands Leicester seemed to have slipped a little Bromsgrove have come on a lot. Further North our old rivals Wakefield will be around over the distance but the real threat must come from Lancashire who could probably be our most dangerous rivals. In the South there are a number of clubs who, with just one or two more class men could really give us trouble. Basildon, Ilford and Metropolitan all have the potential but no depth. If things go well Belgrave should take all the National titles this year. Unbeaten before next Christmas would be even better and this requires not just the odd good performance but sustained training and continuing good results from all in the club. Wilf Wesch and Ray Middleton fit this description and it will be these two who form the core of our future teams. The National '10' result and peport on Page 29 came in after Pat Duncan's above preview. It's now, one down with three to go! items.sum: Humorous poem about Belgrave's walkers written from a wife's point of view, signed 'A. Nony. Mouse'.
items.s: ODE TO THE BEL-BOYS Humorous poem about Belgrave's walkers written from a wife's point of view, signed 'A. Nony. Mouse'. The Belgrave boys are special breed, All living by a mighty creed - Strict training schedules very tight Adhered to fiercely every night. Out in gale force winds, 'tis true They all return a dangerous hue! Diets planned - no fatty feasts Must confront these athlete beasts - They live an die this tough old sport, On Saturdays their nerves are wrought 'What's going to happen?' is the cry As they warm up and gently fry. The starter starts, the men are off, Some passers by just stand and scoff. 'Come on the Bels' the cry rings out The women folk all stand and shout; Claret and gold well up in front, The men now start to groan and grunt. Judges pulling suspect styles Even though they've walked for miles! The pace speeds up, the race is ending The Belgrave name is worth defending. Time keepers waiting at the end, Now they round the final bend Has all this training been in vain? Oh no, the Bels have won again. In the showers all talk is loud, The winners are so very proud. One by one they dress and go To where the tea does freely flow - Lumps of cake and various feed Disappear with frightening speed! The men could sit and talk all night In fact it looks as though they might. Us women banished to the loo Must now encroach on this taboo But my men, of you we're proud We sometimes tell you out aloud. Although we often rant and rave We really think you're very brave. I suppose we'd rather sit and knit Whilst you're out doing your bit It's better that you train like hell And thus end up a better 'Bel'. A. NONY. MOUSE Clue - one of the wives, who devotes her entire time to cleaning, washing and feeding one of these special breed - but he's lovely really. A. NONY. MOUSE A. NONY. MOUSE pseudonym; one of the walkers' wives Bels

items.s: POLICE '7' Report and result of the Metropolitan Police Open 7 walk at Imber Court on 10 January, won by Paul Nihill, with Belgrave taking the team race to complete a clean sweep of the London Open 7s. IMBER COURT - Metropolitan Police Open '7' - January 10th. Great walks from Wilf Wesch, Carl Lawton and Len Duquemin with good support from Ray Middleton gave Belgrave a clear victory in this police race which, for many walkers, is the unofficial championship of the year. This victory gave Belgrave a clean sweep in the London Open '7's, yet another great achievement by the boys. Bob Coates hung grimly to Paul Nihill from the gun but it was too good to last and at four mile Bob was pulled out. items.sum: John Keown's preview of the 20 miles road walk at the 1970 Commonwealth Games in Edinburgh, recounting the campaign to include a walk and profiling Belgrave hopefuls Gerry Cameron, Bob Coates (Scotland), Len Duquemin, John Moullin (Guernsey) and Ray Middleton (England); the piece starts on page 27 and ends on page 26.
items.s: Five Bels at Edinburgh ? John Keown's preview of the 20 miles road walk at the 1970 Commonwealth Games in Edinburgh, recounting the campaign to include a walk and profiling Belgrave hopefuls Gerry Cameron, Bob Coates (Scotland), Len Duquemin, John Moullin (Guernsey) and Ray Middleton (England); the piece starts on page 27 and ends on page 26. THE COMMONWEALTH WALK by John Keown The 9th British Commonwealth Games will be held in Edinburgh from the 16th to 25th July. Included in the programme will be a Men's 20 Miles Road Walk. This event will start at 10.30 a.m. on Saturday July 18th. The inclusion of such an event in the Games owes much to the hard work and tenacity of the British Athletic Authorities, especially the officials of the Race Walking Association. The fight to get a walk included in the Games began in 1934 when Ernest Neville proposed and the late Jack Crump seconded a motion at a meeting of the Southern Area R.W.A., calling upon that body to urge the Road Walking Association (title changed in 1954), to appoint a special sub-committee to take such steps, on behalf of the Association, as it might deem expedient to obtain the inclusion in the next Empire Games of a 50 Kms. Road Walking Race. Such a sub-committee was set up. Despite the enthusiasm of the R.W.A. for the idea it was to be over 30 years before a walk was included in the Games. During the late 1950's and the early 1960's the Association, through their Hon Secretary, L.W. 'Timber' Woodcock, and the British representative on the Walking Commission of the I.A.A.F., Harold Whitlock, continually pressed athletic authorities in Commonwealth countries to support the appeal for the inclusion of a walk in the Games. On 6th August, 1966 the first Commonwealth 20 Miles Road Walk was held at Kingston, Jamaica. Walkers from England filled the first two places. Ronnie Wallwork from Lancashire Walking Club took the gold medal in 2 hours 44 minutes 42.8 seconds whilst the silver medal was taken by our own Ray Middleton in 2 hours 45 minutes 19.0 seconds. Norman Read, and exile Englishman from Steyning, walking in the colours of New Zealand, took the bronze medal in 2 hours 46 minutes 48.2 seconds. This year Belgrave could have a greater interest in the walk. We could have four, possibly five, club walkers representing between them three different countries. Both Gerry Cameron and Bob Coates have as their ambition representing the host country Scotland. Gerry, who did much work behind the scenes to get race walking re-established in Scotland a couple of years ago, will find it very difficult to make the team. Business commitments and a growing family curtail the amount of time he can devote to training and racing. Bob, on the other hand, has an excellent chance of m king the Scottish team. He is one of Belgrave's brightest hopes for the future. It is only two years since Bob competed in his first walking race, the 1968 Belgrave 20 Miles Championship. Prior to this he was an amateur racing cyclist for four years. During 1969 this young Scotsman made steady progress from being an average club walker to a top class one. Two performances of note during the summer of 1969 were a 3,000 Metres at Brighton when he clocked 13 minutes 16.4 seconds and an 8th place in the 'Birmingham 25' when he clocked 3 hours 49 minutes 18 seconds. In the last few months when Bob has been training five days a week, despite some trouble with the judges, he has recorded some very fast times over 7 and 10 miles. Now we await with interest to see what will happen when he tackles the 20 mile races. Here, we hope his mode of progression will make the judges happy. He should be capable of a time inside 2 hours 50 minutes. His greatest rivals for places in the Scottish team will be Bill Sutherland (Highgate H.) and Alan Buchanan (Brighton & Hove A.C.). In 1967 Len Duquemin won the Southern 'Garnet' 10 Miles Championship and lead Sarnia Walking Club from Guernsey to success in the team championship. Another member of the winning team was John Moullin who finished third in the race. Shortly afterwards these two walkers came to work in the London area and joined Belgrave Harriers. Their arrival came at an opportune moment when the club was struggling to rebuild its walking section. Since then both have played an important part in the many club team successes recorded during the last two years. Now both hope to be included in a small team which Guernsey will be sending to the Commonwealth Games. Len, now 39 years old, has been walking since 1963. Besides his 'Garnet' win he has won the 1968 Highgate Open Seven and last summer he finished first in the Belgrave 10,000 Metres Track Championship. His best 20 mile time is 2 hours 45 minutes 35 seconds. 28 year old, John, began race walking in 1964. During 1969 he performed well over many distances. Pride of place must go to his 4th place in the Open London to Brighton when, in his very first race over the course, he recorded the excellent time of 8 hours 22 minutes 35 seconds. In the 1968 National 20 miles he clocked 2 hours 53 minutes his best performance so far over this distance. Our other candidate for a place in one of the National teams is Ray Middleton who finished second in the inaugural race back in 1966. Ray, a very experienced International, is a truly great Belgravian. His first major success was winning the Southern 'Garnet' 10 miles in 1959. Since then he has seldom been outside the scoring four in club teams at all distances from 5 to 38 miles. His best distance is probably 50 Kms. Between 1961 and 1969 Ray has finished outside the first three in the National 50 Kms only once, in 1968, when he was 4th. As he has to try for a place in the England team the strongest as regards walkers in the Commonwealth his task is extremely difficult. Competition for the three places in this team will be Continued opposite Continued from opposite page fierce. With European 20 Kms. champion Paul Nihil certain, barring accidents, to fill one of the places that only leaves two for the other leading contenders. Besides Ray others in the fight for a place will probably be Ronnie Wallwork (The Commonwealth title holder), Shaun Lightman (Metropolitan W.C.), Roy Lodge (Bromsgrove & Redditch A.C.), Bryan Eley (Bristol W.C.) and Jake Warhurst (Sheffield U.H.). Although walkers for the English team will not be chosen exclusively on their performances in any particular race all the leading contenders will have their eyes set on the first three positions in the National 20 Miles Championship. This race will be held in the Midlands on June 13th. Both Guernsey and Scotland will be holding their own local trials. The winner at Edinburgh should be Paul Nihil with a tough fight for the minor placings between Gardiner (Australia), Sutherland (Scotland) and the other English walkers. items.s: WESCH WINS NATIONAL 10 Report and result of the National 10 Miles walk championship at Liverpool on 21 March 1970, won by Wilf Wesch in 72:07, with Belgrave also taking the team title; includes a profile of Wesch's rise over the previous 18 months. WESCH WINS NATIONAL 10 BELS Take Team Title March 21st 1970 - LIVERPOOL - The National 10 Miles Championship So just 18 months ago 2 walkers started training in Battersea Park. They were approached by a flabby German called Wesch who reckoned he'd done a bit of walking - naturally being Belgrave men they smashed him into the ground leaving him at the furthest point from the changing rooms. Gradually,'Yer Kraut' as he is known to his close friends, began to improve. Victory in the Surrey 10 mile championship last year followed good results in the Club 10 and the Basingstoke. Then came disaster with disqualification in the National and second place for Belgrave, a setback which Wilf took harder than his clubmates but which was soon forgotten with victories in the Club 20 and some fine track performances. By August it was clear that Belgrave had another champion in the stable but it took a trip to Frankfurt to really show the world. Here before his own crowd Wilf destroyed the East German Junior star Schuster and held off Ray Middleton in his peak Athens form. Throughout the winter Wilf has been putting away 90 - 100 miles a week, in all weathers, preparing himself for the season to come. Victories in the Belgrave 10, the Basingstoke and the Surrey Championship set the stage and on Saturday at Liverpool Belgrave once again had a National Champion to lead the team. Remembering the dying words of one of his sparring partners during a particularly fierce blizzard "I'm not going through all this bloody suffering to see you beaten in the last mile by some scrubber" Wilf caught Ron Wallwork at 9 miles and after a desperate neck and neck struggle for nearly ¾ of a mile the Belgrave man's superior strength and fitness paid off and he surged away for a brilliant 72:07 victory. The Belgrave Team all produced their best. Carl Lawton " I'd have done 74:30 if I had'nt cracked" winning his Honours Badge with a tremendous 75:00 11th position. Then, just 46 seconds later Len Duquemin our fourth scoring man. Ray Middleton produced a good one just 10 years after he first made the Belgrave National 10 Team,in fact it was his second fastest ever. With the addition of Bob Coates, slouching along in 77 minutes the Belgrave boys also took second place in the County result. With such performances the team race was a formality and for all the club the the pleasure came from the front where a lean hard Belgravian defeated some of the finest walkers in the world to take the National Title. A tremendous performance by a man who has worked hard for every second and every yard, earning our respect in the process, and making us very proud to have him as a clubmate. RESULT 1. items.label: March 1970
items.sum: Poem by a veteran member of over forty years recalling his first prize, the friendships of club life and those who have gone before.
items.s: An Old-un's Reverie Poem by a veteran member of over forty years recalling his first prize, the friendships of club life and those who have gone before. An Old-un's Reverie HOW LONG A BELGRAVIAN HAVE I BEEN: WEL SIR, I'D SAY FOR FORTY YEARS OR MORE, I JOINED WHEN MY YEARS WERE JUST NINETEEN, NOW I HAVE SAID GOODBYE TO O'ER SIXTY FOUR. RACES ON TRACK AND ROAD I HAVE OFT' RUN, AND ACROSS COUNTRY, SO GREATLY ENJOYED; THIS WAS MY PLEASURE; REGRETS HAVE I NONE; FOR THUS WAS MY SPARE TIME MOSTLY EMPLOYED. WHAT WAS THE FIRST PRIZE I EVER RAN FOR? THE THREE MILE ROAD HANDICAP, I BELIEVE, AND WITH A FAIR START, I MANAGED TO SCORE FOR WHICH A SUGAR BOWL I DID RECEIVE. RIGHT PROUD OF THIS ACHIEVEMENT I WAS SIR; ELATED WITH THE THOUGHT THAT I HAD WON, I PONDERED, AND TO ME IT DID OCCUR, THAT RUNNING AND RACING COULD BE GOOD FUN.. WITH THIS IN MIND, DOWN TO TRAINING I GOT, AND BEFORE LONG I WAS MAKING THE TEAMS, THAT STARTED OUR WINNING WAYS ON THE TROT, WHICH GAVE US REALITY, NOT DREAMS 'TIS THE COMPANY I VALUE THE MOST, AND SO MANY A FRIENDSHIP'S BEEN MADE, TO WHICH I RAISE MY GLASS AND GIVE A TOAST THAT THEY MAY LAST MANY A DECADE. FOR MUTUAL WARMTH OF GREETING YOU'LL SEE, WHEN AND WHEREVER BELGRAVIANS MEET, FOR IT IS IN EACH OTHERS COMPANY THE SPIRIT SHOWS, THAT MAKES THE BOND COMPLETE I REMEMBER THOSE WHO HAVE DEPARTED AND RUNNERS AND WALKERS OF YESTERYEAR, FOR IT WAS THEY WHO HELPED TO GET STARTED ALL THAT HAS BEEN ACHIEVED AND HELD DEAR. CHAMPIONS GREAT AND CHAMPIONS SMALL WITHIN OUR RANKS, THROUGH THE YEARS, HAVE EMERGED AND MAY THEY ALWAYS PASS THROUGH BELGRAVE HALL AS IF A PLACE FOR THEM HAS BEEN RESERVED THERE ARE SO MANY WHO HAVE DONE SO MUCH TO PICK BUT ONE, WOULD CHOOSE ANOTHER'S PEER, FOR ALL HAVE NEVER LOST THE COMMON TOUCH THAT HAS BROUGHT US MEMBERS FROM FAR AND NEAR. TO ALL BELGRAVIANS WHO ARE YET TO BE, LET NOT YOU, THE SPIRIT OF BELGRAVE DIE, FOR WE WILL FADE TO JUST A MEMORY WHEN IT BECOMES OUR TIME TO SAY GOODBYE. SEM E. SERKEL SEM E. SERKEL SEM E. SERKEL apparently a pen name; member for over forty years, joined aged nineteen Belgrave Hall

items.s: Postbag: Postbag column with news from Ranjit Bhatia in Delhi, Chris Steer's travels in North America and meetings with Belgravians abroad, and thanks to past president Harry Hare for sending old club material. Postbag: Reg Hopkins is not the only one to have youngsters under his wing. In his latest letter RANJIT BHATIA tells us that six of Otto Peltzer's best young athletes have joined Ranjit at Delhi's St. Stephen's College. He endeavours to guide them whenever he can and particularly enjoys training in company again. Two of the sixteen years old runners recently clocked 4:10 (1500m) and 8:54 (3000m)---seems to be scope here for a postal competition! Ranjit, himself, was unable to compete in most of India's major meets through work committments. Nevertheless, he still managed to finish 3rd in the State 1500m and 4th in the Northern Championships over 5,000m. Our Indian Vice-President has been spending a lot of time on athletics journalism. He is a regular contributor to an Indian newsweekly and sends news to Athletics Weekly also. He has just completed a chapter for Brian Mitchell's new book and is in the throes of writing for the American, Fred Wilt. He was hoping to cover the Commonwealth Games in a journalistic capacity but is unable to find a sponsor. Has anyone any ideas? Ranjit appeals once again to our globe trotting members to make an effort to visit Delhi if they are travelling East, and compete in races there. * * * * * Talking of globe-trotters, CHRIS STEER is just about as far away from Delhi as one could get---Canada---and he sends greetings to all Belgravians. For 5 months he has been roaming around the U.S.A. and Mexico in an old van. He is now in Vancouver "tanned, unfit and broke!" He hopes to be back here in the Summer when he has earned his return fare. He has managed to do a bit of racing and finished 19th in the Pacific A.A.U. cross country championship in San Francisco. While training in Golden Gate Park, San Francisco, Chris was astounded to hear the cry "UP THE BELS". It was U.S. walker Tom Dooley who joined us last summer during his stay in the U.K. with an American team. It's a small world alright, particularly for Chris it seems, for when he was told that Frenchman Guy Monnet had joined us he remarked "That was the guy I accidentally tripped up in a cross-country race here in Canada a few months back". It sounds as though Guy will be looking forward to Chris's return! * * * * * Your Editor's appeal in the last issue for old photographs and literature did not go unheeded for Past President and former Editor, HARRY HARE, sent in a lot of material which has proved to be of great interest. Harry did a tremendous amount for Belgrave during those vital years in the "twenties" when we were building for the future and striving to make our mark in the major championships. Much of his work was the cornerstone of what we have today and Belgravians have not forgotten it. Harry has not been in very good health of late so we wish him a speedy recovery and perhaps we will have the pleasure of seeing him at one of our fixtures in the near future. * * * * * Reg Hopkins Reg Hopkins coaches youngsters Ranjit Bhatia RANJIT BHATIA Indian Vice-President of the club; at St. Stephen's College, Delhi; 3rd State 1500m, 4th Northern Championships 5,000m; athletics journalist RANJIT BHATIA Ranjit Otto Peltzer Otto Peltzer coach whose young athletes joined Bhatia at St. Stephen's College Brian Mitchell Brian Mitchell author of a new book with a chapter by Bhatia Fred Wilt Fred Wilt American writer for whom Bhatia is writing Chris Steer CHRIS STEER travelling in the U.S.A., Mexico and Canada; 19th in the Pacific A.A.U. cross country championship, San Francisco CHRIS STEER Chris Tom Dooley Tom Dooley U.S. walker who joined Belgrave the previous summer Guy Monnet Guy Monnet Frenchman who joined Belgrave Guy Monnet Guy Harry Hare HARRY HARE Past President and former Editor; sent in old photographs and material; active for the club in the 1920s HARRY HARE Harry Pacific A.A.U. Letter from Mrs. Savage I would like to thank the Walking Section for the lovely bouquet they gave me at the Open Belgrave Walk. It was the first one I had ever had given me. I remember the first open walk quite well, and I have seen a good many others. Belgrave Harriers is very dear to my heart, I have spent some happy times with the runners at races and social evenings. I enjoyed doing the teas and refreshments which I had to give up as my health is not too good these days. I wish the Club every success in the future and hope to see the Claret and Gold on top in all sections Mrs. Savage Mrs. Savage long-time helper with teas and refreshments; presented with a bouquet by the Walking Section at the Open Belgrave Walk Open Belgrave Walk

items.label: March 1970
items.sum: Gordon Biscoe's review of Belgrave's 1969-70 cross-country season, with successes in the N.S. (Surrey) League and G.L.C. Championship but disappointments in the Surrey and Southern, and an improved 5th in the National.
items.s: CROSS COUNTRY Gordon Biscoe's review of Belgrave's 1969-70 cross-country season, with successes in the N.S. (Surrey) League and G.L.C. Championship but disappointments in the Surrey and Southern, and an improved 5th in the National. CROSS COUNTRY GORDON BISCOE writes:- One must inevitably look back over this years cross country season with mixed feelings for although one could not call it a failure there was a lot left to be desired. Our only noteable successes were the N.S.League once again and the G.L.C. Championship. With most of our best runners barred, not a great deal was expected from the two South of Thames races although if all those eligible had pulled their weight and turned out we could have had a more respectable placing. No one will deny that the Surrey County Championship was just given away, to be followed by our biggest defeat of all,the Southern. Its fair to say that for a team already weakened by injuries etc, there was good reason why two of the team ran poorly on the day, unfortunately however these things do not count in the final analysis. Finally to the National, true we did not realise that ambition of winning but but at least we improved upon last years position of 7th by two places with the 9 man cup thrown in for good measure. To mention once again, that but for injuries to two of the team the result could have been much better, seems to highlight our theme in all this year's major events; and that when once again we have everyone running together again 100% fit,and as a team,success will improve accordingly. Personality-wise,congratulations are due to Adrian Major for his best overall individual position in the N.S. League and to John Bicourt for his run in the National. One cannot end without highlighting Gerry North's fine run, yet once again, in the 'National'. He must by now have established a record which many of his younger rivals, for all their words, will find hard to emulate. With the Southern and National Road Relays immediately ahead maybe we can end the season as we started (with the Johnston Relay)---on a winning note! items.s: Surrey Championships Report and result of the Surrey cross-country championship at Milford Heath on 3 January, where four Belgrave runners missed the start and the club finished third in the team race; R. Holt won with Gerry North second. Surrey Championships MILFORD HEATH-----January 3rd If ever a championship was thrown away it was this one. Yet it was not because of the way our runners performed, but simply because few of them didn't even start! The course was about a mile away from the school used for changing and was not easy to find. Even so, everyone managed to allow sufficient time to succeed except Messrs. Satchell, Walker, Kerr and Black who were still on a grand tour of the Surrey roads when the starting pistol was fired. Bad luck of course but one would expect to find experienced runners acquainting themselves with the course a good half hour before the start. As it happened, any one of this quartet only had to make the first 41 places and become our sixth scorer to give Belgrave the Championship. Although Gerry North was not expected to retain his title on this very fast course which favoured Bob Holt (H/W) he fought with great tenacity. At halfway he had to give ground to Holt who opened a sizeable lead but Gerry came again at the finish to run home about 80 yards down. Meanwhile, Major and Bicourt were going great guns on a course which seemed to suit them and enabled us to finish three in six and be well represented in the County team. On the other hand, Tony Fairclough was run off his feet and was heard to be pining for Parliament Hill with mutterings of "Wait 'till the Southern". Charlie Dabbs and John Kelly supported well and deserved their bronze medals---but that big 'IF' still remains. RESULT (84 finished) Teams:- 1. R. Holt (Hercules-Wimb) 34:15 16. A. SOUTH OF THAMES Crawley - January 13 With most of our leading runners still barred from this race we had no hope of the team award, but in John Bicourt we had high hopes of an individual place. Unfortunately John was suffering with another bout of severe catarrh, which plagues him from time to time, and was unable to continue after the halfway mark when he was a well-placed eighth. Another casualty was Clive Shippen who fell after only half a mile and retired with a sprained ankle. Tony Brien put in a surprise appearance and although short of competition and looking a little overweight ran into an excellent 25th place: R.A.F. life is obviously doing him no harm. RESULT Teams 1. items.s: SOUTHERN CHAMPS. Report and result of the Southern cross-country championships at Parliament Hill on 7 February, won by D. Bedford, where Belgrave finished fourth behind Hercules Wimbledon, Reading and Blackheath. SOUTHERN CHAMPS. PARLIAMENT HILL---February 7th A race our runners will wish to forget, with Hercules Wimbledon getting five men home before our second and, to rub it in, Reading and Blackheath pushing us out of the medals altogether. Gerry had been very short of training in the preceding week or so through pressure of work and although he was up in 7th place at 5 miles,uncharacteristically blew-up over the last mile and dropped 21 places---Geoff passing him on the run-in. Of the remainder, little also can be said. They were never in it and morale was pretty low afterwards. An injured and frustrated Fairclough was obliged to be a spectator but even he at his best would not have saved the day. Everyone hoped that our runners had got rid of their bad runs all in one day. items.s: VETS AVENGE SENIORS Report and result of the Belgrave v Blackheath veterans' 5 mile cross-country match at Hayes, won by Charlie Walker from Jack Brown, with two photos of the pair at the 1963 National credited to C.Shipp. VETS AVENGE SENIORS This was the match we've been waiting for, a 5 Mile cross country race at Hayes against the veterans of Blackheath with the added interest of the meeting between Jackie Brown and Charlie Walker brought together for the first time as Vets by the Cross Country Secretary through devious means known only to himself. Unlike the seniors the previous week at Parliament Hill the Vets overcame Blackheath, but what hopes had the Heathens with Jack and Charlie, arch rivals over two decades, out to run each other into the ground. Unfortunately, both went off course twice and although the younger man won on this occasion we shall wait to see if more racing will prove Jack still has the beating of Charlie.
