items.s: Old Contemptible ELECTION SPECIAL Spoof newspaper 'Old Contemptible Election Special' lampooning club affairs ahead of the A.G.M. in general-election style, with mock reports on the editor Clive's resignation, Colin Pearson's 'Broken Promises' speech, an 'Autumn Budget' and A.A. Harley standing down as Hon. Secretary with Peter Hillier's spoof manifesto as successor, plus jokes, slogans and captioned photos. 1s 6d CHOOSE THE RIGHT MANN DONT GET LEFT WITH O'CONNOR Who really knows how to assess election issues? Read THE INFORMERS! As a reader of the "Belgravian" you are already aware of its authoritative presentation of views and news about challenging subjects of national importance. The A.G.M. merits special assessment of the issues involved and you are now offered a unique opportunity to be comprehensively informed by writers who live and know athletics 52 weeks a year. When you read the Belgravian, the gossip ends and the facts begin from all points of view - left,right and centre. ELECTION REPORT-1 Quo Vadis Clive? On hearing of your recent announcement to surrender the editor-ship of the 'Belgravian' one is forced to ask "What is the true signifieance underlying this decision?" Is it possible that the Belgravian is to be the only casualty, or shall you SCAN the horizon for fresh fields to conquer? Are your sights on the higher echelons of our sport? Shall we lose you to sink in the morass of Heavy Titles and Light Deeds? Will your undoubted ability with the pen and courageous expurgation of silly rules and regulations be stilled? Shall your voice, strong in its support of your club weaken; not from choice, but dilution by pompous Committee bilge. C.E.M. ELECTION REPORT-2 Broken Promises This was the theme of an "under the showers" speech by Colin Pearson in Belgrave Hall last night. Quoting from last December's issue of the Belgravian he recalled Gordon Biscoe's promise that ... "this year we would win the Polytechnic Marathon as well as the National Cross Country Championship". "However, it is beyond doubt," he continued, "that the Hon. Member will be returned with an even larger majority than last year, proving again the value you can place on the opinion of the 'man in the street'. "I'm not really to blame,your worship, I was foodless, friendless and homeless," pleaded the burglar. "My man," replied the judge, "you move me deeply. Food, shelter and companionship shall be yours for the next nine months!" ELECTION REPORT - 3 Autumn Budget After a detailed examination and an Emergency Finance Meeting, the Rt. Hon. John Baker, who last year took office as the Chancellor of the Exchequer recently disclosed at a Cabinet meeting that the state of the economy was worse than he had been led to believe prior to taking office. His final figures have not been revealed in the national interest but informed sources speculate that worse is to come following a complete dossier being handed to the Director of Public Prosecutions and that an Autumn Budget seems inevitable. Footnote: Following Interpol's investigations a Home Office spokesman, Mr. Frank Jarvis, categorically stated that the short, smiling gentleman found at his luxurious sheep farm in Jerusalem was not the man thought to be able to assist Scotland Yard in their enquiries. A BLATENT BRIBE Every man has his price - is this the cancellation of Concorde - secret negotiations with the People's Republic of China - No! - He wants Peach Melba instead of Ice Cream at the Club Dinner. Tom found out that his best golfing friend was having an affair with his wife. Rather than get involved in anything unpleasant like a row, they decided to play eighteen holes - the winner to have complete ownership of the lady. "...and just to make it more interesting", said Tom, "let's play for a pound". ELECTION REPORT-4 A CHANGE OF GOVERNMENT At the end of the current administration in September, yet another of our elder statesmen has intimated that he will not be standing for re-election. We, of course, refer to the Party Secretary, the Rt. Hon. A.A.Harley. His name is legion to the many athletes and unions throughout the country and no doubt many more words will be written and said in tribute to him before he finally stands down. However, much interest will be focused on the man who has the timerity and gall to accede to this vital post and who was recently announced by the Official Party Office as Mr. Peter Hillier. What sort of man is this? Let us quote from his manifesto ..... Peter Hillier ..... recently married, in an unguarded moment, your prospective candidate for Hon. Sec. has not involved himself into the cauldron of athletic politics and is consequently eminently suitable for the role of neutral referee at the monthly bun fights at "The Ship". Educated at the 'ampshire Parish School for backward children, he was prematurely discharged with a note to prospective employers that said they could, "teach him no more". With such qualifications he naturally gyrated to the Stock Exchange. The frequency with which he changed Brokers was only matched by the swiftness with which he changed his disguises. items.s: TRACK AND FIELD Track captain Peter Hilliar's event-by-event assessment of Belgrave's 1970 track prospects (sprints, 400m, 800m, 1500m, 5000/10000m, steeplechase), with photos from the Club Championships 800m and discus. TRACK AND FIELD PETER HILLIAR (Track Captain) WRITES: It is my task once again to put pen to paper in order to assess our track prospects this season. To put this into financial terms, I have to offset our assets against our liabilities (yes- we do have them!). Prospects have invariably been set out in tabular form in past years and who am I to depart from such a practice? SPRINTS:- We started 1970 realising that we had lost the valuable services of John Mitchell- a crushing blow. Nevertheless, we are hardly short of class with Steve White , already a county champion at 200 metres, and Jim Vivian available. We have annexed a fine sprinter from Switzerland in Bruno Hafner, who has already given Steve a couple of close races. 400 M.:- Mel Ford has already given a glimpse of his true potential with his 49.5 at the club championships, although his versatility means that he does not get a great deal of opportunity for competition over this distance. Our second ranking man, Charlie Gillett, is also a class hurdler. We have a very promising youth coming through in Martin Bloice, who has already done times that would do most seniors credit. We must not forget Philip Gee, ever-willing to turn out despite being short of real fitness, and Dave Rees, just back from 'birdless' West Wales. 800 M.:- This event has always been one of our weak spots in spite of the willingness of our competitors. However, the emergence of a 1st year junior as our leading runner is a healthy portent for the future- keep up the good work Peter Carton. We also Have John Boardman, Mel Ford and another junior, John Stowe, under the 2 minute barrier and Colin Pearson and John Kelly should also be shortly. 1500 M.:- John Thresher reigns supreme at this distance, although John Stowe's Surrey Junior run, when he broke 4 minutes and led home the Stowe/Carton/Curtin triumvirate, was a fine achievement. Other promising runs have come from Peter Carton, Bill Curtin, Bill Kerr, Adrian Major, Bob Smith and Jim Rimmer. This could be one of our stronger events. 5000/10000 M.:- Potentially our strongest events, but we very rarely get 2 of our top men out at the same time. Outstanding performers so far are Bob Smith, Gerry North, John Bicourt and Bill Kerr. Geoff North's retirement is a sad blow(if it is true!). Steeplechase:- Another potentially strong event. John Bicourt is already well under 9 minutes and it is good to see Alan Black and Dick Piotrowski back in action again after injury. A word of encouragement to such as Nigel Bacon, who has deputised for others absent on innumerable occasions- keep plugging away, Mate, we need you! Photo:J. items.s: BILL COUZENS (Field Captain) WRITES: Field captain Bill Couzens's assessment of Belgrave's jumping and throwing talent in 1970, naming Eric Barker, Glyn Ratcliffe, the Swiss members Bruno and Henry, Nick Head, Steve Inman, Mel Ford, Charlie Gillett and John Martin. BILL COUZENS (Field Captain) WRITES: From some of our recent results it may seem that the jumping and throwing side of the Club is down and out but in fact, to my knowledge, we have never had such all round talent on our books. Just to illustrate, we have a new member from the Grenadier Guards (just demobbed) Eric Barker. You cannot miss this mountain of a man at 19½ stone. He competes in the Hammer, Discus, Shot and even the High Jump if it will get points for the Club. He is a real asset. His performances this year include 155 feet Hammer, 43 feet Shot and 138 feet Discus. With Eric partnering Glyn Ratcliffe in the Shot and Discus we take some beating. Our two new Swiss members Bruno and Henry are very talented, with Bruno able to turn out electrifying sprints, and a very good long jump, whilst Henry's main event is the Pole Vault, his best height to date being 14 feet. Nick Head is back in the country again and is already finding form with the Javelin, with Steve Inman close on his heels. This partnership has already given us maximum points in the Malkin Trophy. Another "Dynamic Duo" is Mel Ford and Charlie Gillett Middlesex and Surrey 400m Hurdle champions respectively. It must be the first time in Belgrave's history that we have had the winners in both counties John Martin seems to have had one personal best after another this year and is now only a few inches short of 40 feet in the Shot Putt, I wonder how many athletes with a body weight of 11½ stone can achieve this distance with the 16lbs Shot, not many I'm sure. This is only some of the talent in Belgrave and you may wonder why we have had such poor turn outs. It may be that we lean heavily on Chelsea Barracks but one thing I am sure of------ when we field a full team we are going to win. items.s: THE NATIONAL LEAGUE P.H. explains Belgrave's relegation from the National League to Division 1 of the Southern League, their 5th of 6 finish in the first fixture, and appeals for athletes to turn out for the remaining meetings at Reading and Wimbledon Park. THE NATIONAL LEAGUE The National League was introduced last year to provide a national inter-club competition.The organisers believed that it would raise standards and enable new talent to be recognised more easily. Last year, we were invited to compete in the 3rd. Division of the National League and, on finishing last, we were relegated to Division 1 of the Southern League. We have already competed in one League fixture this year and were surprised to find the standard somewhat higher than in the lower echelons of the National League. We were unlucky to be without the services of most of our regular field-event men,who were unable to compete due to other unavoidable commitments. However, we were most seriously inconvenienced by two leading runners, both of whom were either too proud or casual to get in touch with the Track Secretary or Captain, who had assumed that both were available. As a result, we finished 5th out of 6 clubs and are in danger of relegation again. This from the 9th strongest track club in the country, judged on our best performances! We are a superb walking club, a fine road and cross-country club and we have the athletes to make us a great track club.Only one quality seems to be lacking and that, quite bluntly, is club spirit - the will to win at all costs. The National League is surely a clear indication of a club's strength and the support its athletes give it. Judged on our recent results, we don't get the support although we have tha athletes. So, let's confound the cynics who say that Belgrave are a lot of has-beens. All track athletes can help by competing in the remaining two meetings (July 4th at Reading and August 22nd at Wimbledon Park), if selected. If unable to compete, please let the Track Secretary or Captain know as soon as possible so alternative selections can be made. Finally, a plea for support. Please come along whoever you are, whether you feel aggrieved at being left out of the team or otherwise. Every bit of support helps and it could mean that we win promotion instead of relegation! items.sum: P.H.'s report and Belgrave results from the opening Southern League Division 1 match at Crickelfields Track, Ilford, on 16th May 1970, where Belgrave finished fifth.
items.s: SOUTHERN LEAGUE DIV. 1 - DISMAL START TO SEASON P.H.'s report and Belgrave results from the opening Southern League Division 1 match at Crickelfields Track, Ilford, on 16th May 1970, where Belgrave finished fifth. SOUTHERN LEAGUE DIV. 1 DISMAL START TO SEASON OPENING MATCH - Crickelfields Track, Ilford on 16th May Belgrave fortunes reached their highest point in the first event to be held on the track, the 400 metres hurdles, where we placed 2nd and 1st respectively. Subsequently,progress was generally downhill despite one or two excellent performances. Basically, we could not afford to field a weak team in a competition where the standard is possibly above that of Division 3 of the National League. Even our strongest team would have been hard-pushed to come out on top. Our outstanding performers were Steve White, winner of the 'B'100 metres, 2nd in the 'A'200 metres and a member of both relay teams; Jim Vivian, 4th in the 'A' 100 metres, 1st in the 'B'200 metres and a member of the winning sprint relay team; John Thresher and Bob Smith, 2nd respectively in the 'A'1500 and 5000 metres. Both of our relay teams ran exceptionally well,despite their relative positions. Finally, I should like to single out a very promising performance by 1st year junior Peter Carton. His 1 min.57.4 secs in the 'B' 800 metres was a portent that we could have another Dave Cocks emerging from our junior ranks- given Dave's appetite for a great deal of hard work, of course! items.sum: Report and results for Belgrave at the 1970 Surrey Championships (Wimbledon Park, 9/10 May, and Motspur Park, 27/28/30 May): Martin Bloice's Youth 400m and 200m wins, Steve White's Senior 200m title, a 3000m walk clean sweep, junior 1500m, and senior, junior and youth results.
items.s: Surrey Championships Report and results for Belgrave at the 1970 Surrey Championships (Wimbledon Park, 9/10 May, and Motspur Park, 27/28/30 May): Martin Bloice's Youth 400m and 200m wins, Steve White's Senior 200m title, a 3000m walk clean sweep, junior 1500m, and senior, junior and youth results. Surrey Championships May 9/10 Wimbledon Park May 27/28/30 - Motspur Park The outstanding Belgravian at this year's Championships was undoubtedly Martin Bloice who successfully defended his Youth 400 metres title and also annexed the 200 metres for good measure. Drawn in Lane 5 for the one lap event he ran a perfectly judged race to hit the final straight three yards clear and moved away still further to break the tape eight yards to the good. His time of 51.3 was 1.3 seconds better than his winning time of last year and a tenth better than the Junior champion recorded. In the 200 metres it was a much tighter thing. Gerry Quarry of Tulse Hill School (runner-up in the 100) was leading ten yards from the tape but Martin's stamina and judgement edged him ahead just when it mattered. He certainly is a fine prospect. The man whom Martin eyed with most interest was another former Youth star, now fulfilling the promise he always showed, Steve White. Steve showed all the majesty of a true champion as he smoothly powered his way to the Senior 200 title; in this his first year too. Richard Langley, runner-up last year in the Youth 800, tackled this year's event in a most forthright way. He shot into the lead and towed the strung-out field thro' a first lap of 58.7. At 600 he had only four rivals near him but as they ran down the final straight it became a blanket rush for the tape. The straight was just about 20 yards too long for Richard who slipped to fourth in those final few strides. Nevertheless, it was a courageous run and he obviously has a great chance of winning a County title in future years. The 'terrible triplets' (Peter Carton, Bill Curtin, John Stow) were on view in the 1500, which became a Belgrave v Aldershot F.D. match with Adams and Ford in the line-up. Unfortunately it was a case of Belgrave doing the work and Aldershot collecting the awards, for Bill led the first lap, Peter the second, and John made the final determined effort to break clear with 600 to go - but he was 'jumped' in the last 200 and got a bronze for his attempt. Once again our lads had displayed courageous attacking running against tough opposition. It will soon pay off. Photo:Ron Linstead Peter Carton leads winner Adams (AFD), Bill Curtin (hidden), Ford (AFD), and John Stow in the final of the junior 1500 metres. In the 3,000 metres walk, Wesch, Coates and Lawton made a clean sweep of the medals, following the example of Paddy Breslin and Eddie McNally who, three week's earlier, took the first two places in the Junior steeplechase. Other winners were Lee Sullivan (Junior long jump), our Senior sprint relay team and Colin Gillett (400 hurdles) who also featured prominently in the flat 400. John Thresher made a gallant attempt to win the 1500 title, making his break with 600 to go. Only Mike Davis (TVH) stuck with him and although he had covered the distance faster than his previous best he just had enough left to move past John in the last few strides. Just over an hour later Bob Smith also gained a County silver, his first Surrey medal, in the 5000. With John Bicourt(3rd), Trevor Hart (5th) and Bill Kerr(10th) in this race,we were very well represented. Altogether the Championships were a fine affair. The final day at Motspur Park is always a treat to see. It not only illustrates that Surrey are perhaps the best organised County in the land but that they also have the talent to lay on one of the most attractive meetings in the athletics calendar. All non-Surrey men are invited to see for themselves next year - one presumes that our Surrey members are there in any case! 100: 1. C. Cheetham (Ports) 11.0, 3. J. Vivian 11.1, 4. S. items.sum: Report on the 1970 Belgrave Club Championships at Hurlingham Park on June 6th, with trebles for Lee Sullivan and John Cambridge, doubles for Steve White, Mel Ford and Glyn Ratcliffe, the junior 800m/1500m duel, and full results for every event.
items.s: CLUB CHAMPIONSHIPS Report on the 1970 Belgrave Club Championships at Hurlingham Park on June 6th, with trebles for Lee Sullivan and John Cambridge, doubles for Steve White, Mel Ford and Glyn Ratcliffe, the junior 800m/1500m duel, and full results for every event. CLUB CHAMPIONSHIPS HURLINGHAM PARK - JUNE 6th For the first time in many years our Championships were blessed with a hot, dry and sunny day. A pleasant enough setting for the spectators perhaps, but a "horse-ride" of a track and an unusually strong wind up the finishing straight made it the usual bad-conditions verdict for the runners. The afternoon saw two "trebles" and three "doubles". Heaviest loaded with trophies and medals were Lee Sullivan (Jun), who notched the senior long jump title in addition to the Junior's sprint double, and John Cambridge (Boy) who scooped an unusual trio in the Boys 100, 800 and high jump. The "doubles" went to Steve White (100/200), Mel Ford (400/800) and Glyn Ratcliffe (Shot/Discus) - all in good form. Martin Bloice, our new Surrey County Youth Champion, had no need to repeat his 51.3 of the previous week in winning the Junior 400 - but he was chased hard by Elliott and Langley. Another Surrey Champion on view was Will Wesch, but he was unable to match Martin Bloice's example. He set the pace in the 10,000 metres walk for 85% of the race and then had to see Bob Coates "jump" him to go on to an impressive win. Fancy letting a honeymoon affect your racing! Photos: Ron Linstead LEFT: Lee Sullivan adds the Senior long-jump title to his Junior sprint double. RIGHT:The moment of truth. Peter Carton wins the junior 800m in the last stride from an exhausted John Stow. There were many interesting contests during the afternoon but excitement built up for the clash between Bill Curtin, Peter Carton and John Stowe in the Junior 800 and 1500 events. Bill was the holder of both titles but Peter had clocked the fastest 800 this year (1:57.4) and John the fastest 1500 (3:57.0). Bill sized up the odds and withdrew from the 800 leaving his rivals to sort out who should be his successor. John set a fearsome pace and gradually stretched a lead to the 600 mark where he began to tire. Peter bore down on him but still seemed to have little chance, till John seemed to mistake the finish and momentarily stumble allowing Peter that valuable split second to squeeze past for the title. Fine efforts by both, in the second lane too, 1:59.5 to 1:59.8 - times even the Seniors couldn't better! And so to the 1500 where they renewed their battle alongside a fresh Bill Curtin. Bill shot to the front as usual but soon the trio were together again and clear of the field, with 600 to go the slight frame of John Stowe stole ahead and one wondered whether his stronger looking rivals would repeat the story of the 800. But this time there was no mistake and it was the followers who struggled the last 200. John's fine win of 4:08.6 would have placed him third in the Senior race. He is a fine prospect indeed. John Thresher had no difficulty in retaining his Senior 1500 title but it was good to see Guy Monnet tag him closely for 1200 metres before fading badly in the final straight. Photos: Ron Linstead LEFT: Bill Kerr leads Guy Monnet (116) and John Thresher, the winner, on the second lap of the Senior 1500 metres. RIGHT:Bob Coates on his way to an impressive win over Wil Wesch in the 10,000 metres walk. The 400 promised much, with Steve White meeting 800 winner Mel Ford and our Surrey 400 hurdles champion, Charles Gillet. However, it proved to be an anti-climax with Mel showing himself a winner all the way and Charles and Steve crossing the line together 15 yards back - the latter unusually comfortable for a race of this severity. The best field event performer was Glyn Ratcliffe whose discus throw was well ahead of his rivals. Once again the meeting ran smoothly and to time and much credit for this goes to Bob Taylor, who is the only one pleased to see this meeting end. Charlie Manning enjoyed himself organising the children's races in a scene of utter confusion, but there seemed to be no upsets and as the champions of the future left clutching their hard-won prizes it became apparent that some semblance of order must have prevailed. items.sum: Pat Duncan's walking notes praising Wilf Wesch's run of wins, regretting Bob Coates' omission from the Scotland team, and looking ahead to the National 20 Miles and 50 Kilos.
items.s: WALKING Pat Duncan's walking notes praising Wilf Wesch's run of wins, regretting Bob Coates' omission from the Scotland team, and looking ahead to the National 20 Miles and 50 Kilos. Pat Duncan writes: Wilf Wesch goes from strength to strength following his National 10 Mile win by dominating the 20 Kilometres, the 20 Miles, his new wife and the inter-counties 10,000 Metres not to mention numerous other victories including a world class time in the Met WC 20 Kilos. Ray Middleton and Carl Lawton have also turned in some magnificent performances and Bob Coates must count himself badly done by in not being selected for Scotland to accompany Len Duquemin and John Moullin who have both been picked for Guernsey. It is incredible that Scotland, the host country, can overlook Bob's claim to selection; he is one of the most competitive walkers in the country and would certainly have performed with credit before his home crowd in Edinburgh. Barry Ingarfield and Brian Ward have also come to the fore and Pat Duncan is now busy trying to convince Dave King that he is needed for the longer ones. Victory by over 50 points in the National 20 Miles should set us on our way to a similar victory over 50 Kilos in August. items.s: National 20 kilos ~ Title Lost ~ But Wesch Wins Report, photo and results of the RWA National 20 Kilometres walk at Crystal Palace on May 9th, won by Wilf Wesch, where Belgrave lost the team title to Lancashire Walking Club by one point. May 9th Crystal Palace - RWA National 20 Kilos Over this tough 9 lap motor racing circuit Belgrave reckoned to have a good chance but we failed to reckon with Lancashire Walking Club's great junior prospect Chris Eyre who flashed past the post in 7 th place for the surprise result of the year. Wilf Wesch walked his customary race from the front for his secnnd National victory over Wallwork and with the lads all backing well we looked all set. Disaster struck when Len Duquemin dropped out and John Moullin was pulled leaving Bob Coates in 16th position to close the team in. Although only one point separated us from victory this was not to be,although if Ray Middleton or Carl Lawton had been aware of the position these two great walkers could surely have pulled something out. A disappointing day for Belgrave although that vocal Irish newcomer John Johnson staged an entertaining finale to his first national. Team ChampionshipResult 1st. Lancashire W.C.(38) 2nd. Belgrave H. items.label: June 1970
items.sum: John Keown's profile of the veteran Belgrave walkers Joe and Percy Wilson: Joe's 50 km, London to Brighton and centurion record since joining in 1939, and Percy's racing, Boys Brigade walks and years as a helper and feeding-station organiser.
items.s: SPOTLIGHT ON ............ The Wilson Brothers John Keown's profile of the veteran Belgrave walkers Joe and Percy Wilson: Joe's 50 km, London to Brighton and centurion record since joining in 1939, and Percy's racing, Boys Brigade walks and years as a helper and feeding-station organiser. An athletic club is composed of many different age groups with the active members tending to come from the younger and middle groups and the officials and supporters from the older groups. Yet each club has a number of athletes who remain competitors for most of their lives, few of whom ever achieve greatness. They are the unsung heroes who in their younger days help fill the non-scoring positions in club teams and in their later years act as counsellors, guides and unofficial coaches to successive generations of athletes. They are the backbone of the club, without whose support, year after year, many clubs would find it extremely difficult to survive the lean years through which each club passes from time to time. Belgrave Harriers has always been blessed with such men. Each section has its own stalwarts; quiet, unassuming men who are as much a part of the club as Belgrave Hall. Men, who year after year, lead the slow packs during training sessions and thereby help turn the raw novice into a budding athlete. Two such men are the Wilson Brothers Joe and Percy, both members of the Walking Section. Sixty-one year old Joe, joined Belgrave in September 1939. He was introduced to the club by Charlie Churcher, one of Belgrave's top walkers just immediately before and after the Second World War. Joe has been walking ever since, although now barred by age from competing in National Championships, he still manages to turn out in various club and inter-club events. Before taking up walking he was a keen amateur footballer, winning several league and cup medals. A serious knee injury meant giving up that sport. He was also a good performer at Ballroom Dancing, winning several open competitions and being placed in the first three many times. Later he acted as a Judge and Demonstrator at Dancing Competitions. During the war Joe competed in various races and joined London Vidarians as a second claim member. By 1947 he had turned into an above average performer at all distances from 10 miles to 53 miles and became a regular member of Belgrave's first team over distances of 20 miles and above. His times in the National 50Kms. Championship in 1947, 48 and 49 were 5h.17m.28s., 5h.12m.30s (his fastest ever) and 5h.16m.48s respectively. During his long competitive career he competed in 14 London to Brighton races, finishing all inside 10 hours (Second class standard time). In 1947 he was the second Belgravian to finish, thus securing 2nd place in the club long distance Championship. His time was 9h.27m.40s. In each of the next three years he reduced this time, until in 1950 he clocked 9h.16m.22s., his fastest for the Brighton course. One of his proudest memories was helping Belgrave to finish 2nd team in a big Open 50Kms. at Eastleigh in 1949. Other scoring members of the team were Jack Rutland and Tommy Green. Joe himself also took third handicap prize and a time standard medal. In the 1951 Brighton and Back race he became Centurion No.164 with a time of 21h.59m.30s. in what Joe himself describes as his most satisfactory race. At about 43 miles in the 1957 'Brighton' he was hit by a car and spent the next three weeks in the Royal Sussex Hospital, Brighton recovering from a broken jaw bone and facial injuries. Percy, the younger brother, at 57, joined Belgrave in 1943/4. Prior to this he had played football, table tennis and tried his hand at Boxing. Although not as successful in competition as his older brother he has in his own way contributed much to the success of Belgrave walkers and race walking in the London area. During the last 26 years he has competed in numerous National Championships and 10 London to Brighton races. His fastest 'Brighton' was accomplished in 1953 when he clocked 9h.25m.07s. That year he was the 5th club walker to finish only a few minutes behind the 4th scoring man A.J. Stirling Wakeley. In 1955 with the help of brother Joe he became Centurion No.246, passing the 100 mile point in 21h.53m.55s. Perhaps his greatest contribution on the Brighton road has been as a helper to other walkers and for a number of years now chief organiser of a feeding station just after Gatwick Airport. There is no more welcomed sight than to see Percy standing at the side of the road with his special tray of drinks after one has fought one's way around the two miles of difficult roadway which skirts the airfield. One usually finds him in action again near Preston Park, where with a cheerful greeting, a drink and a sponge, he and his friends see each competitor safely away on the last leg of their journey to Brighton front. Percy has on a few occasions provided a similar service for the long distance runners in their annual race over the same historic course. For a number of years Percy organised a Boys Brigade Walk in his native Earlsfield. The first year he had 27 boys, 8 years later this figure had risen to 127. An Open 3 Miles Walk was held at the same time. This walk was always well supported by walkers from the London Area. The money to pay for the prizes for the walks was collected by Percy from the local shops. Unfortunately in 1968 Percy had to go into hospital for two operations and despite the efforts of brother Joe to keep the walks going, lack of sufficient local support made this impossible, so London lost a popular summer fixture. Down the years both brothers have helped many Belgravians and others to achieve success in race walking. Amongst their most notable achievements in the role of helpers have been assisting that great Belgravian, A.J. Stirling Wakeley to win a 24 Hour Track Walk at Motspur Park in 1948 and helping fellow Belgravians, Gordon Doubleday and Syd. Spencer compete successfully in races at 100 miles and over. Dickie Green (Surrey W.C.), many times winner of the Stock Exchange Brighton, has had Joe as his attendant on 10 occasions. The Wilson brothers both have a great love and respect for Belgrave and the sport of race walking. Percy sums up this respect with the words, "Belgrave is a great club, one of the best. Race walkers are a wonderful lot of chaps, in their ranks I have met some of the greatest sportsmen to be found in any sport." items.sum: Comic poem by 'Aphrodite' about a day out with the Belgrave walkers at the National 20 Miles at Redditch, where Belgrave won the team title and the Nijmegen Shield.
items.s: A DAY AT THE RACES Comic poem by 'Aphrodite' about a day out with the Belgrave walkers at the National 20 Miles at Redditch, where Belgrave won the team title and the Nijmegen Shield. The Duncanmobile sways to and fro As off to Redditch we all go With "Doub", 3 Johns, and Brian too Wilf, Carl, Pat, Barry; who'd be blue? After a coffee we all pile Back into the Duncanmobile - Morris wades through fruit and rice Giving him energy that should suffice. All talk is centred on the race, Each wondering who will set the pace 20 miles of tough terrain Should expose those men that train. We arrive and meet the rest, They all seem fit and full of zest, Jean's bargain car is packed with gear So that the men will have no fear Of passing out without a drink, We have the sponges too - I think! Up to the start we all make tracks Late comers' numbers pinned on backs Nerves are wrought and tension high Awaiting for the starters cry. Now they are off - the climb uphill Watched speculatively by Paul Nihill. Us women make for Jean's auto A quick ice cream then off we go. The day is hot, conditions tough, Racing round this course is rough. We sponge away and hand out drinks, Into a ditch poor Jenny sinks! Our stalwart "kraut" hotly pursues The vanishing hind of Bob Hughes. Wilf out in front now, pace gets hot The Bels are giving all they've got. One by one the men come in No one's surprised at who did win It's the lad that's full of fun Our handsome, friendly, little "Hun". Belgrave win and sweep the board Of medals, quite a just reward We even got the Nijmegan shield With thanks to Barry Ingarfield. All over now for a little while It's back into the Duncanmobile Off we speed to nearest pub To cheer the victory of our club. Its been a gorgeous day I think As Duncan whips my shandy drink! You lovely bunch of handsome men If I'm asked I'll come again. A day with you lot is a treat And one that I'd find hard to beat It's great to see you all do well And thus preserve the name of "Bel". Now I am back among the chores Of cooking washing cleaning floors Look out my window see it's raining Where's my man? - Oh, he's out training! items.label: September 1970
items.sum: The departing Editor's last editorial, warning the Gazette may cease without volunteers, urging attendance at the AGM and thanking the contributors and typists of the 1960s.
items.s: EDITORIAL The departing Editor's last editorial, warning the Gazette may cease without volunteers, urging attendance at the AGM and thanking the contributors and typists of the 1960s. This is the last Editorial to flow from the pen of the present Editor, and it is with a feeling of some sadness that he parts company with his charge. Sadness, not only at the separation but at the distinct possibility of the Gazette discontinuing in it's present form: for there appears to be a reluctance on the part of members to step forward and fill the breach. If this reluctance is because the interests of members are confined to a particular section of the Club, rather than the whole gamut of our activities then we appeal to them to volunteer their services in respect of that section alone. A sub-Editor for each facet of our journal could well preserve continuity of production, and we ask members to consider this seriously. This edition should be in members' hands on Annual General Meeting day---September 17th. This is, perhaps, the most important day in the Club year, for on that day the Club's officers are elected or re-elected. It is vital that we get the best men for the fifty or so elections that are made, for on them depends our success in the long term. The right selections can only be made by a well attended A.G.M. A well attended A.G.M. is only forthcoming from an enthusiastic membership; and an enthusiastic membership will be found in a well organised and successful club. This is the circle of effects which can spiral downwards so easily if too many members are unwilling to play an active part in the running of club affairs. Finally, a thank you to all those helpers who have done so much to assist in the production of this Gazette during the "Sixties". Our contributors have been too numerous to name in full, but particular mention should be made of Gordon Biscoe, Pat Duncan, Alf Harley, Bill Lucas and Charlie Manning for the written word; and Ron Linstead and Ed. Lacey for the visual word. Also to former co-Editors Mal Robinson, Dave Mitchell and Alan Mead---wish you were here. The ladies have also played their part, and our appreciation is extended to Sally Lucas, Margaret North, Gwenda Couzens ana Barbara Mitchell for their typing assistance. Last, but by no means least, your departing Editor extends his thanks to Elizabeth Shippen who not only typed the majority of the last 1200 odd pages in difficult circumstances but who showed the forbearance which enabled your Editor to continue for so long. items.label: September 1970
items.sum: Hon. Secretary's notes by A.A.H.: the Gazette may end with Clive Shippen's retirement as Editor, an appeal for the Supporters Football Scheme, Joe Flower at the Track Championships, the winding-up of the Association of London Athletic Clubs, and an appeal to sell AAA Draw tickets via Frank Webb.
items.s: HON. SECRETARY'S NOTES Hon. Secretary's notes by A.A.H.: the Gazette may end with Clive Shippen's retirement as Editor, an appeal for the Supporters Football Scheme, Joe Flower at the Track Championships, the winding-up of the Association of London Athletic Clubs, and an appeal to sell AAA Draw tickets via Frank Webb. In our last issue our Hononary Editor reminded us all of his intention to lay down the Editorial blue-pencil at the end of the Club year, and asked for anyone with the requisite abilities to consider this important office, and volunteer his name to the Committee. At the moment of writing there has been no such volunteer, and unless between now and the publication of this current issue someone has come forward, we may well have to look upon this issue as the end of the road, and the last of the "Belgravians". There were Lectographed copies of a Club circular in the very early 1900's, but a printed "Belgravian" did not appear until 1925. It would be a very great pity if, 45 years later, we had to tell ourselves that we no longer have members with the enthusiasm, the ability and the determination to carry on an old tradition! The foregoing paragraph has the imprint of sadness upon it but we must not allow these thoughts to rob CLIVE SHIPPEN of the sincere Vote of Thanks that is due to him, as well as the individual thanks of us all. Eleven years have been bridged by Clive and his various associates in putting before us a Club gazette which would compare favourably with any in the country; and we have all eagerly awaited the quarterly appearance of the "Belgravian", with the possible exception of the Hon Treasurer! We do normally rather tend to take these things for granted, but now that Clive has decided he can no longer undertake these duties, we become aware more intensely than at any other time, of his great work on behalf of us all and of the pleasure he has given us (and will continue to give us in retrospect), over a decade. His standards have been high and earned commendation from many directions, and our gratitude must be equally high and may perhaps be best expressed by the emergence of someone who even at this late hour is prepared to carry on the torch! Incidentally some additional expert typing volunteers might possibly help to solve our problems on the production side; and allow a member to come forward as Hon Editor who could concentrate on the written material side. It should perhaps be explained that to save the high costs of professional type-setting; we, in effect, do our own setting by typing the material on to foolscap sheets, which are reduced photographically to our page size by our printing suppliers, and the required quantity run-off. So further expert typing volunteers might yet help us out of our difficulties; and we would thank all those who have helped in the past. Our Supporters Football Scheme continues, thanks to the efforts of Leslie and Mary COHEN, and without its aid many of our activities would of necessity disappear, or be considerably reduced. Our income from this source has tended to fade somewhat in the last ten years, but it still brings in more than our subscription income and without it we should look sick indeed. Our competition is still one of the best of its kind with generous prizes relative to its membership; and well worthy of the support of every member from one ticket at 1/- a time payable weekly, upwards. Leslie Cohen, Jack Goswell, Adrian Major, John Baker, Norman Dewberry, Dave Shepherd and many others will all give you the details, or they can be had by post. Some years ago we had a solid nucleus of sellers who disposed of hundreds of tickets each competition (averaging three weeks); but many have retired from business, and they have not been replaced. We should welcome a number of new agents who could handle regularly twenty tickets or more, and be happy to ensure they are not out of pocket, by paying them a commission. The need for more money in substantial terms to maintain and improve, or even replace, our Wimbledon Headquarters weighs heavily with us; and on the competitive side our ever-widening range of activities makes more and more demands on us. Yes----on us! We are the people to ask ourselves if we are doing all we ought to be doing for the finances of the Club. Our Competition is a very agreeable little affair, easily understood, rewarding weekly a number of members, benefiting our Club and its activities. If you are not a regular supporter right now, we hope you will change your status right away and join the Belgrave Supporters club; introducing your friends and relatives at the same time. How pleasant to see JOE FLOWER, now retired, at our Track Championships----but a little chastening to be reminded that it was 40 years earlier that he had won the Mile Championship! In 1951 the Association of London Athletic Clubs came into being. Its principal objects were to promote Inter-City Athletic matches; to give financial assistance to member clubs and the sport generally and so help amateur Athletics in the most effective way. With the sponsorship and the help of the "Evening News" and the labours of a succession of hard-working amateur officials who never spared themselves, great success was achieved. The annual Meetings held at the White City Stadium under floodlit conditions attracted some of the largest crowds ever seen at the White City: and some of the most memorable athletic performances of all times were recorded at these meetings. In 1954, the first visit of a team of Russian Athletes to this country saw every seat and place taken; with a financial surplus available of over £7,300 for distribution to member-clubs and to be ploughed back into the Sport. Prague made an impressive visit to London the following year succeeded by BUDAPEST (1956) NEW YORK (1957) WARSAW (1958), and so on! On all occasions the Inter-City match events were supplemented by other top-class athletic presentations and provided marvellous sport and entertainment. Over the seven years 1954-60 interest was at a tremendously high level and the general public enjoyed their athletics, particularly under floodlit conditions. Clubs who were members from the inaugural meeting (as we were) received over £1000 each over the years; and nearly £40,000 was ploughed back into Athletics as a result of these Meetings. In 1961 sponsorship was withdrawn and the Association decided to "go it alone" with a June meeting which gave some excellent running, particularly by the New Zealand athletes, but the public did not attend in sufficient numbers and the first financial setback was sustained. Since then the Committee has not embarked on any major promotions. The obvious, almost pathetic, falling away in public attendance at sports meetings generally, lack of suitable sponsorships, the constantly rising costs of travel, hotel and all other expenses, the lack of really suitable opposition, the introduction of a new style television contract, and now the possible loss of the White City (with its tremendous capacity) to athletics, all combine to make the thought of a major promotion not only unwise, but downright foolhardy. The Association has had the pleasure in recent years of fulfilling some engagements abroad in connection with British Fair Weeks etc. which B.A.A.B. have been unable to undertake, and these have served a very useful purpose. In all the circumstances, and by unanimous vote of the constituent Clubs, the Association has now decided to go out of existance---and it's last act is to distribute the reserve funds among the member-clubs, and we shall benefit to the extent of £68-0-0. Our General Hon. Secretary was elected to the Committee of the Association at its first meeting in 1951 and had served ever since; for many years past with the double job of Chairman and Hon. Treasurer. He, and many others, will feel a little sad at the passing of the Association with its tremendous store of memories of top-class competition presented under almost ideal conditions; but will derive some satisfaction from the thought that financial benefit went back into the Sport via the Clubs; and that some of the events (e.g. first visit of U.S.S.R. team, Chataway V KUTS, five men in 4 minutes or under in the Mile, Ibbotson's record Mile for example) will stay in the memory for many years to come! Most members will receive with this copy of the "Belgravian" some Draw Books issued by the Amateur Athletic Association. Half of all the sales made to Club members and friends will directly benefit our Club funds, the balance will be used by the A.A.A. to assist our Sport. The prize list is very attractive----see for yourself, and give your maximum support! There are those who say they can never sell draw tickets---would they please try on this occasion and perhaps surprise themselves? Others say "I would rather pay "double subscriptions"---well, it will not be refused! A few suggest "there are far too many of these Draws about"---to which we can only reply that our Club and our Sport should take priority. So we ask all members to help---please don't leave it to "the others"; don't push your share of our financial responsibilities on to other shoulders. Our Past-President and Trustee, FRANK WEBB once again generously gives of his time and energies to organise the Draw on our behalf. Please send counterfoils and cash as soon as sold, and definitely not later than Nov. 10th to: FRANK WEBB, BELGRAVE HALL, DENMARK ROAD, WIMBLEDON, S.W.19. Cheques and P.O.s should be made payable to F.R.WEBB, and crossed. Unsold tickets (counterfoils only) should also be sent to him; and, of course he can supply extra books of tickets to those who are really making a good job of helping the Club in this respect. items.s: Resignations Notice of the resignations of sprinter and timekeeper Frank Kemp and steeplechaser Dick Piotrowski. It is with regret that the Club have accepted the resignation of FRANK KEMP. Frank will be remembered for his excellent sprinting as a Junior in the early "fifties". He was Belgrave Junior Champion at both sprints and Surrey County Champion at 220 yards. He also had some success at 440 yards. He has been a Grade I timekeeper for some time now and has been in great demand in the Southern Counties. All this has to end because Frank's business committments now require that he is available at a moment's notice. We shall be sorry to lose his membership but wish him the best of success in his career. Another to resign recently is DICK PIOTROWSKI. Dick joined us three years ago when in the Army and stationed at Chelsea Barracks. He had belonged to Bracknell A.C. but switched his allegiance to Belgrave because of the proximity of Battersea track and the competition we could provide. He made his mark very quickly and regularly supported our teams on track, road and country. In 1968 he won the 10 miles cross-country championship and his name will be on the "Macher Shield" for all time. His main event is the steeplechase and he has been half a stride outside the 9 minutes barrier for some time. In 1969 he was 4th in the Southern Track Championships. Continued overleaf Cont'd from previous page We shall miss his valued membership, his prescence in our main teams and his friendly company. However, our runners will meet him from time to time in competition for Dick, now married, has bought a house in Reading and will shortly be wearing a blue and white hooped vest. We wish him luck. items.sum: Retiring President Gordon Doubleday's farewell, recalling his illness at the time of his election, the season's highs and lows, and thanking officials and helpers.
items.s: A PRESIDENT'S Adieu Retiring President Gordon Doubleday's farewell, recalling his illness at the time of his election, the season's highs and lows, and thanking officials and helpers. I would like to thank all Belgravians who have made my term of office such a pleasant one. To be President of the Belgrave Harriers is indeed a great honour and the warmth of feeling extended to me added to the pleasure in serving the Club has made 1969/70 a year to remember. At the time of my election I was a hospital patient (I was on a six weeks ' course of antibiotic injections for baterial endocarditis) and the obvious faith the Club had in my recovery was a great spur to make progress and I was able to return home on the day that the treatment ended. I am grateful to the Past Presidents who acted for me in my absence. If I have one regret it is that I was unable to meet members at meetings---I was invariably at the finishing line timekeeping. Nevertheless I have followed the Bels' ups and downs and I was proud to support our teams when I could. If I have to admit to supreme moments it was surely when I saw Wilf Wesch win two Individual titles backed up by others to give us R.W.A. Team Championships; and when we won the Southern Road Relay Championship. At the other end of the scale I wasn't feeling very happy (nor were the others) when the coach broke down on the way to the National Road Relay Championship. I thought how bad it would be to miss a place (or even a win) by default. Fortunately the team arrived in instalments and put up a great fight to finish fifth after an experience which, to say the least, was very unsettling. None of our activities, whether our efforts in the big events, or in the promotion of a Club or Open Event would be possible without the help given by the Club officials and that enthusiastic band of helpers who mark courses, act as pointsmen, lap scorers, or measure jumps or throws. These have all been active athletes and having hung up their shoes, devote themselves to the sport so that others can enjoy participation. Their valued service is greatly appreciated. Our younger members, by their efforts and prominent positions in their categories, give us great hopes for the future of the Club. They show great pride in representing Belgrave and many already show signs that they will bring future honours to the Club. We must give them all the support and encouragement that we can. We look to the future with confidence and anticipation, and I hope to serve under future Presidents to foster the good name of the Belgrave Harriers. Gordon S. Doubleday. Gordon S. items.sum: Postbag of news from letters by former members Peter Whewell in South Africa, Life Member Harold King and Tony Whincup.
items.s: Postbag: Postbag of news from letters by former members Peter Whewell in South Africa, Life Member Harold King and Tony Whincup. PETER WHEWELL, who played a large part in many of our team successes a few years ago, writes from South Africa to say that he hopes to be back in England this December for a short period and looks forward to renewing old acquaintances. For those with insatiable appetites for letter writing, his address is: 5, Cardigan Road, PARKWOOD, Johannesburg. It was nice to receive a letter from Life Member HAROLD KING, whose picture appears on another page. Harold, who lives in Erith, Kent, did some rummaging last month and came across the Club Handbook for 1922/3 which records the leading performances of members during the 1921/2 season, the year following that of the "Men Behind The Trophies" article in this issue. H.F. King's successor to the A.J. Sawyer Cup was A.F.P. Spendlove, but Harold was still our most notable performer. He won the R.W.A. Junior title and the Kent County title and took the "Murphy Shield" for what was then the Club '9'. It was interesting to see that our Boys and Youths coach, Micky Pyer, who is on the 1969/70 Committee was Belgrave mile champion and a Committee member almost 50 years ago! Harold King's address is: 19, Ramsden Road, ERITH, Kent. TONY WHINCUP found that the flashback photo in the June BELGRAVIAN brought back many memories of fine athletes and administrators. He also recalled that the picture was taken when he was trying to get a boat home from India. Unfortunately he brought home a weird spinal disease which has got progressively worse these last ten years or so, and in June this year he had to retire from work at the early age of 48. "We are not despondent here, however," writes Tony from his Shirley, Croydon home, " and hope that a light local position will come along----and, of course, the chance for a few visits to Belgrave Hall". Tony sends best wishes to all members and in particular to Gordon Doubleday, Tom Morrell, Frank Simmons, Arthur Penny, Joe MacDonald, Alf Harley, Ted Stimpson, and that highly skilled tactician who will never be forgotten, Bert Footer". items.s: J. R. 'Jock' McKay Obituary of Past President J. R. 'Jock' McKay, sprinter, Hon. Treasurer and President 1933-35, illustrated with a 1934 Club Championships presentation photograph. As we go to press comes the news of the death of our Past President "JOCK" McKAY, and we extend sincere condolences to his widow and son, and to brother FRED, on their sad loss. Jock joined Belgrave in May 1921 and was active as a sprinter for several years and a great supporter of our relay teams. For four years he was the Club Hon. Treasurer, and later as one of our Auditors and as a Committee man he served us extremely well; and when Jimmy Belchamber proposed JOCK McKAY as his successor in the Presidential Chair in 1933 the suggestion was agreed with acclamation. CLUB CHAMPIONSHIPS 1934-----Presentation of Awards Jock R. McKay (left), President of Belgrave Harriers, assists the Mayor of Battersea during the Presentation. To the right is the bespectacled W.L. Bayliss, Hon. Secretary, and to the far right (applauding)W.Redgrave, a Vice-President for many years and now in his 90's. He was re-elected the following year and throughout his two years as President he gave the Club inspiration and guidance at a time when Belgrave was really going ahead. Our first Southern Cross-country Championship was won during his term of office; followed later by our first E.C.C.U. triumph; our first London-Brighton Road Relay win was achieved; and on the track,athletes such as TOMMY SCRIMSHAW, JIM TOSH and JOHN CLEMENS were carrying our colours with distinction. They were great days and our successes owed not a little to the man who held highest office in the Club at that time. We are truly grateful for his personality and services, and glad to have had him in membership for almost fifty years. A.A.H. CLUB CHAMPIONSHIPS 1934-----Presentation of Awards Jock R. items.label: September 1970
items.sum: Profile of Alfred A. Harley on his retirement after 32 years as General Honorary Secretary: joining in 1926, switching to walking, editing The Belgravian, wartime R.A.F. service, organising the 1948 Olympic 50 km walk and his presidency of 1950-52, ending with a list of milestones in his career.
items.s: SPOTLIGHT ON ... ... ... ... ALFRED A. HARLEY Profile of Alfred A. Harley on his retirement after 32 years as General Honorary Secretary: joining in 1926, switching to walking, editing The Belgravian, wartime R.A.F. service, organising the 1948 Olympic 50 km walk and his presidency of 1950-52, ending with a list of milestones in his career. The 14th day of September 1970 marks the end of an era in Belgrave History. On that date ALFRED A. HARLEY relinquishes the Chair of General Honorary Secretary after a period of 32 years---a span of service broken only by the hiatus of World War II. Alf Harley's service during this period to his Club, County, Area and National Associations is well known throughout the athletics, walking and cross-country worlds. His ambassadorial efforts on behalf of Belgrave have done much for the stature of our Club, and it is no small part due to him that we occupy our present position amongst the leading clubs in the land. But what sort of man is Alf Harley? Past President Frank Jarvis has referred to him on many occasions as "Mr. Belgrave". Surrey County Past President Ron Goodman has gone one better with "Lord Harley" of Belgrave". There is no doubt that for statesmanship and diplomacy he is ideal ambassadorial material. However, none of these titles or qualities portray the extent of his devotion to the Club all these years and the immense amount of hard work he put in. It all started at the A.G.M. of 1926. Life Member George Powell proposed Alf for membership at the instigation of A. Harley Senior, for whom George worked. George's prowess with the javelin had led the Harleys to an affinity with Belgrave which resulted in Alf's membership while still in his 'teens. He wasted no time and his enthusiasm for any Club activity was soon noticed. He became a regular member of pack runs led by Albert Macher and Harry Hare, and he soon found his way into the Belgravian (Dec.1926) when he finished 28th in the Club 5 miles cross-country handicap held in conjunction with a match between T.V.H. and Ashcombe A.C. Three months later he ran in the Club 10 miles "Macher Shield" Championship, finished 11th and led the "Belgravian" to remark "-----and A. Harley did better than the handicapper anticipated and deservedly gained second place in the sealed handicap". He continued to have moderate success on track and cross-country during his first three years of membership, but his 6'-3" well-built frame was not ideally suited to the rough terrain of the country or the speed of the track, and in 1930 he was persuaded by Oscar Horwood and Jimmy Belchamber to give walking a trial. The switch was successful and to his liking. He finished third in a 5 mile Novices Walk and was soon amongst the handicap prizes in subsequent races. As always, Alf put everything he had into his efforts, and our President, Gordon Doubleday, recalls that his face had a tendency to redden with his exertions; so much so it was said that one knew how many laps had gone by the colour of Alf's face! It may have seemed to some that Alf, having now found his true sporting vocation, would be totally immersed in a training and competition programme. They could not have been more wrong. Alf Harley had taken an interest in the legislative side of Club affairs from his earliest days. He was a regular member of the Sunday morning strolls which the Club held during those times, and used those occasions to ask questions and put forward ideas to improve Club activities. It was in 1927 that he made his proposal for the formation of a subsidiary club which would enable our Middlesex-qualified members to compete as a team-----a proposal which eventually led to the formation of Cadogan AC which has only just been disbanded due to a rule change(see Belgravian article "Goodbye Cads", June 1970). Incidentally, this illustrates how any member, not only members of Committee, can and should put forward their ideas. His election to the Committee was inevitable and at the A.G.M. of 1928 he was duly elected. This was the platform from which he was able to rise to many heights. He was so immersed in Club affairs and had such a prodigious appetite for work that it was simply a question of time before he took on some major responsibilities. In fact, it was 7 months. In April 1929 he succeeded Ben Knifton as Honorary Editor of "The Belgravian", the third man to hold the position. It was typical of his approach to the job that in his first year he produced a record 10 editions! We have no knowledge of how this was received by the Hon. Treasurers of that period, Albert Macher and Harry Parker, but like most Club officers they would no doubt have been very reluctant to curb their young colleague's enthusiasm. On the other hand it has been rumoured that the financial stability of the Gazette was assured by the number of Club ties sold by the Editor! Alf Harley was Honorary Editor for 9 years during which time he produced no less than 59 editions of "The Belgravian". Charlie Redgrave, "The Banjulele Boy", passes Alf Harley only feet from the tape to win the 1929 Boxing Day Walk Handicap. It was only a year after his election as Club "Scribe" that Alf took on the additional responsibility of Walking Hon. Secretary, a position he held for 10 years. By 1935 he had contributed so much to Club affairs that he was elected a Life-Member, yet he was still only in his twenties. His dedication to Club work did not, however, mean that he stood aside from the activities themselves. Whatever the activity,he always played his part. In the"Thirties" there were numerous Socials (some were multi-club affairs), theatre and concert visits, all-day strolls and Youth Hostelling at long week-ends. None of these would be complete without Alf, and after a full day's activity he would always be ready for a hand of cards, a game of chess or even talk someone into a table-tennis match. His enthusiasm was boundless and he eagerly awaited the next Club function. Even if it was a stroll in the hay-fever season (he was a sufferer) Alf would manfully and tearfully sneeze his way across fields of long grass rather than miss the companionship of his club mates. Club morale was high during this period. As Editor, he had the privilege of recording Belgrave victories in practically every team championship and race of any importance in both running and walking. As Walking Hon. Secretary he had guided our teams to many fine wins. It was time to move on. At the A.G.M. of 1938 Alf Harley was elected the General Honorary Secretary of Belgrave Harriers, in succession to W.L. Bayliss. To prove he was an ordinary mortal after all, he relinquished the Editorship to Gordon Doubleday. Our new Secretary had not been at the helm of Club affairs for long when the disaster of World War II was upon us. The happy band of Belgravians gradually broke up, as one by one they volunteered or were drafted into the various armed forces to serve throughout the World. Some were never to return. Alf found himself commissioned into the R.A.F. who were soon to find out the advantages of having A.A.H. on their strength. Alf's efforts and flair for organisation soon had athletic meetings established wherever his duties took him; at R.A.F. Yatesbury (where he included a mile walk and won it himself!), Great Yarmouth and Blackpool; and eventually in North Africa and Italy. At the end of the war the Mediterranean Area R.A.F. Games were held in Rome and, as one would expect, Alf Harley was there as Chief Track Judge. As athletics' representative on the Mediterranean Area Committee he frequently crossed the Appenine Mountains by private 'plane to attend committee meetings! He probably wishes he had the same facility now when required in so many places at once. Alf Harley (12) competing in the Chiswick Annual Sports----August 1933. Despite all this part-time activity over and above his war-time duties, he never lost contact with Belgrave Harriers. On the contrary. The high volume of correspondence he produced, enabled him to have a better idea of what was going on in the Athletics world than many at home. He was always eager to meet athletes, wherever his duties took him. Imagine Alf Miller's surprise, for instance, when he was recovering from wounds on the Italian front to find Alf Harley at his bedside. By the time the War had ended Alf had reached the rank of Squadron-Leader. If the hostilities had continued for much longer we would probably have had an Air Vice-Marshall on our books! Alf returned to the fold in 1946 and resumed his General Hon. Secretary duties which had been ably handled by Harry Parker during his absence. He was soon serving, with characteristic energy on the Committee of Middlesex County, Southern Counties A.A.A., Road Walking Association and the General Committee of the A.A.A. itself. It was no surprise, therefore, when he was given the task of organising the 50 Kilometres Walk at the London Olympic Games of 1948. With the help of many Club members the event was carried through with great success. In 1950 Alf was accorded the highest honour our Club can bestow, that of President. The editorial of "The Belgravian" for December 1950 read, "As for our new President, Alf Harley, it is difficult to find any page in the Club history over the past 20 years that has not some reference to him". Has this not been just as true of the last 20 years? The following year he was re-elected as President, and it was fitting that his two-year term of office should see almost every major championship come our way --- the one important exception being the National Cross Country Championship where we were placed "only" 7th and 5th. Despite this, the roll of honour was impressive, for we were champions of, R.W.A. 20 Miles R.W.A. 50 Kilos Surrey County Walk National Road Relay London-Brighton Relay Southern Counties Cross-Country South of Thames (Senior) Cross-Country South of Thames (Junior) Cross-Country Surrey County (Senior) Cross-Country Surrey County Youth) Cross-Country In time, life-memberships, vice-presidencies and even presidencies of the various bodies to which we are affilliated fell to Alf Harley. In retrospect, it seems as though the honours fairly rained upon him. Many men would have found themselves drifting away from Club affairs in such a situation, but at no time has Alf's devotion to Belgrave waned,and wherever he goes you can be sure he will enhance the good name of Belgrave. His work on the various bodies has brought him a wide knowledge of athletics, and whilst some may have a more specialised knowledge of certain branches of our sport, for all-round knowledge of athletics and it's personalities Alf can have few equals. His advice is often sought and his opinions highly respected. 21st JUNE 1952. Five months after her accession to the throne HER MAJESTY QUEEN ELIZABETH II visits the A.A.A. Championships at the White City. On the left is A.A. Harley and to the right The Marquess of Exeter. On our own Committee, which has been blessed with his prescence for a 42 years span, even long standing members remark on the tact and patience shown by our Secretary, whether the subject of debate is highly controversial or borders on the trivial. Perhaps his desire to see all viewpoints fully aired stems from those early days when he successfully used the Club procedures himself to get ideas implemented. He has always been a great advocate of strong reasonably-efficient clubs on the principle that strong clubs means a strong A.A.A.; and a great believer in the enthusiasm generated in the clubs to get things done---as in fact Belgrave have done for many years past. And now his term of office comes to an end. At last he relinquishes the reins of General Honorary Secretary. He does so because he feels, with great conviction, that our Club needs an infusion of young blood. Furthermore, that he can best serve our interests as a "Roving Ambassador". The standards he has set will be hard to emulate, but one can be sure that he will be available to advise and assist wherever he is needed. There are many who have had the privilege of working alongside Alf Harley, there are many who treasure his friendship and many who value his wise counsel. But there are even more who are just plain glad to say "I know Alf Harley". C.S. items.h: A Review of ~ PAST GENERAL HON. SECS.
items.sum: Review of the twelve men who have held the post of General Honorary Secretary of Belgrave Harriers in its 83 years, from A.H.N. Edwards to A.A. Harley.
items.s: A Review of ~ PAST GENERAL HON. SECS. Review of the twelve men who have held the post of General Honorary Secretary of Belgrave Harriers in its 83 years, from A.H.N. Edwards to A.A. Harley. With our present Hon. Secretary vacating the position at this year's A.G.M., one's thoughts dwell on the comparatively small number to have occupied the post in our 83 years of history. In the beginning A.H.N. EDWARDS had this responsibility, and his period of office extended to twelve years. Alf Edwards was considered a more than useful miler in his day with the ability to break 4½ minutes; and his close co-operation with H. MORTON CARR (PRESIDENT) gave the Club an excellent foundation on which later generations could build. He was succeeded by FRANK BOOL who held office for five years, and it will be remembered that he died only a year or two ago at his home in Chelsea, aged 93 years. In 1903/4 H.A. SMITH took over for a year during which period he was placed sixth in a London-Brighton Walk. W. MATHEWSON, who later emigrated to Queensland, held the position until 1911, when A.E. GRANT took over, to hand on to H. HAWKES after a year. In 1913 OSCAR HORWOOD became the seventh holder of the office, and, with CLEM ARNOLD, alternated and jointly held the position until 1921. These were, of course, very critical years for the Club, covering as they did the first World War period when activities all but ceased. Oscar's work in re-shaping Belgrave's destiny after difficult years has been recorded in these columns on other occasions; and these were the days when money was short, and the Club only survived by reason of the hard work of the few and the personal sacrifices made. Nineteen-twenty-one arrived and W.H. HARE became Hon. Secretary within a few months of joining the Club; and combined this with a multiplicity of other jobs, including that of Hon. Editor of our first printed gazette. With all this immensity of Club work which he carried, Harry yet had time to win a Club Championship and to score in our winning Walking Championship teams. In 1924 FRANK THOMSON became Hon. Secretary. He had been a member (and a Life member) in the earlier days of the Club but had then followed other interests and came back to the fold in his later years. Frank was to be found at Battersea Park Track every evening and his work for Athletics was tremendous. He was our first President of the R.W.A., and a member of the Southern Committee of AAA for many years on our nomination. He was Hon. Treasurer to the Surrey County AAA, and for many years acted as Hon. Handicapper to the RWA and was Chief Scoring Judge at most of the events in the South. His efforts helped largely to encourage progress in Field Events by his conduct of the Southern Amateur Athletic League Competitions for which he assumed responsibility. In 1927, a former Club Captain and one of the most popular figures ever within the Club became Hon. Secretary and continued in office for eleven years, at the end of which he was also President. This was W.L. BAYLISS ("WALLY") and it is a great pity that his health failed during the War years, and has prevented him from playing a part in our affairs in more recent years. After 11 years in office Wally Bayliss handed over to the subject of our SPOTLIGHT article above-----A.A. HARLEY, of whom no more need be said. Twelve Hon. Secs. spanning 83 years, and a whole realm of achievements by the Club. Its a long while and it has given us much to enthuse over and much to be grateful for. Alf Edwards A.H.N. items.sum: Extracts from The Belgravian of 1945 (club's position at the end of the war and its wartime record) and September 1930 (Tommy Green's record-breaking London-Brighton Walk).
items.s: FROM 'The Belgravian' 25 years ago ●●●●● ●●●●● and 40 years ago Extracts from The Belgravian of 1945 (club's position at the end of the war and its wartime record) and September 1930 (Tommy Green's record-breaking London-Brighton Walk). 25 years ago 'Since the last issue events have moved quickly. The sudden ending of hostilities in the Far East has brought Peace to the World again. A number of our members have already been demobilised and many others hope to return to civilian life soon. We extend a hearty welcome to those who have been away from us and wish them the best of luck in the battles ahead for places in our teams. The Committee has decided that the Club shall return to its full pre-war programme, and a glance at the Fixture List will show that there is a busy season ahead. At the outbreak of war we occupied a position which had never before been attained by any club. We were National Road Walking Champions (20 miles) and English Cross-Country Champions (10 miles). We also won the R.W.A. National "Junior" (qualification basis) Ten Miles' Championship. Our walkers were runners-up in the 50 Kilos Championship, whilst our runners had been placed in the Southern and the London-Brighton Relay. Of our best Individual Performances, Harry Churcher was our brightest star. A.A.A. Champion at Two and Seven Miles, Inter-Counties Road Walking and Track Champion, unbeaten in Open Road Walks for two seasons. Ted Stimpson and Arthur Penny represented England in the International Cross-Country Race. Tom Carter was Southern Counties' Six Miles Track Champion, he also held the Surrey Title, and was fourth in the A.A.A. Ten Miles' Championship. Eddie Pack was Southern and Inter-Counties 440 yards Champion, and runner-up in the A.A.A. title. Charlie Melchior was second in the Southern and third in the A.A.A. Javelin Throw. Joe Colman was third in the A.A.A. Seven Miles and third in the Southern Two Miles' Walk. Stan Botwright was third in the Southern Furlong. Many other members gained A.A.A. and Southern Standards, and won honours in County Races. During the war our runners, walkers and field events men have striven hard to uphold the high position held by the Club, and we can say that no other club maintained such a high all-round level of performance. We can feel justly proud of our war-time record. Now we have to set about the task of defending our titles from teams from all parts of England. We have some very good material for team-building, and the only way to reach championship class is by hard work, regular and systematic training, and a carefully graded racing programme.' and 40 years ago SEPTEMBER 1930----- '------ Every Belgravian (and every athlete, for that matter) will join us in congratulating Tommy Green upon his wonderful record-breaking effort in the London-Brighton Walk (8hrs:2mins:55secs). This momentous feat, accomplished in wretched weather conditions, will live for ever in the history of the Club and of road walking. If Tommy never donned another shoe(and we hope to have his help for many, many years to come) we could, on past performances alone and disregarding the future, which is even brighter, justly claim him as the greatest walker ever seen. We are certain that a better sportsman could not be found anywhere and we are proud to number such a loyal Clubman among our members----one of many, let it be added. Congratulations also to Jim Tosh and Tom Scrimshaw upon finishing first and second, with inches between them, in the Inter-Counties 880 yards.' Harry Churcher Harry Churcher pre-war: A.A.A. With the season far from over we have a string of notable successes behind us, both individual and team. Lionel Mann never ceases to amaze, not only by the range of his repertoire (his aim next season is to race in every event from 100 yds to the "Brighton") but also by his relentless progress from year to year. He is now amongst the top flight of road runners and could be on the brink of great things. Our team wins in the Belgrave '20', Finchley '20' and Feltham '5' were particularly noteworthy in view of the competition. Not far behind were our second places in the Kent '20', Shaftesbury '10' and Reading '10'. One thing can improve. This is the degree of assistance given to Gordon Biscoe regarding entries. items.s: The South Downs Frolic! Description of the course of Worthing A.C.'s '10' road race on 15 August 1970, from Sompting over the South Downs, with the leading and Belgrave results (the fraction in the course-length footnote is hard to read). Saturday, the 15th August, was a fine bright day. It was also the day that Worthing A.C. had chosen to stage their, "sporting '10' ". The prefix has certain romantic 18th century connotations and it described delightfully the treat in store. The course runs East from Sompting towards Shoreham along a rather depressing major road until a left turn takes one out of this age and into a nursery rhyme. Narrow lanes wind up hills through leafy woods----down past cottages and farms----fields of corn slip gently by----sheep graze lazily----cows stare out on Summer. Imperceptibly at first, one starts to climb. Then the way becomes steeper, and steeper; suddenly you are on top of the world. We now follow a ridge of downs with toy villages down below; there's a lot of sky and in the distance the sea is twinkling. If this sounds like a travel agent's catalogue it's no more than the truth---but if you do it next year, it'll look rather different if its peeing with rain! C.E.M.
