items.sum: Report and results of the 19th Belgrave 20 miles open road race at Wimbledon on 11 July 1970, won by R. Richardson, with Belgrave winning the team race and the Lauriston Shield, plus the Surrey County Championship and Belgrave 'Lady Fell' Shield results.
items.s: 19 th. ANNUAL 20 MILES OPEN ROAD RACE INCORPORATING THE SURREY COUNTY TEAM & INDIVIDUAL CHAMPIONSHIPS Report and results of the 19th Belgrave 20 miles open road race at Wimbledon on 11 July 1970, won by R. Richardson, with Belgrave winning the team race and the Lauriston Shield, plus the Surrey County Championship and Belgrave 'Lady Fell' Shield results. Wimbledon-----July 11th This was one of the closest-ever, as well as one of the fastest-ever, Belgrave '20' races. Blackheath's Richardson won by a mere couple of strides from Watson (Cambridge H.), both having run fast enough to have been over a quarter of a mile clear of the field in any of the previous 18 races, apart from that of 1966 when Graham Taylor set the remarkable course record of 1:39:37. Under a strong sun, but with the benefit of a cooling breeze, 110 runners were sent on their way by our President. At the 5 miles point (25:24) the leading group of ten were well clear with Lionel Mann and Trevor Hart nicely tucked in. Five miles later the number had reduced to six, and both of our lads were still in contention. This was the half way mark (51:34) and supporting our key men were Clive Shippen (56:18), Brian Joines (60:49), Paul Pringle (60:49) and Jack Baker (62:03). The leading group split up second time up Copse Hill but Lionel was hanging on tenaciously to third spot as the Richardson-Watson duel hotted up sixteen seconds ahead of him. At 15 miles (1:17:35) Trevor was in splendid isolation in 6th place (1:19:16) with Clive 20th and Belgrave narrowly ahead of Cambridge in the team stakes. The leaders really hummed going up Copse for the third and last time and it was only in the final sprint that Bob Richardson squeezed ahead. Lionel ran magnificently to take third place and knocked something like 2 minutes off his previous best '20' time. His time was good enough to have won in any other year, except 1966. Trevor held his sixth place well and had no one near him for the whole of the final circuit. Meanwhile, back on the by-pass, Haith (Camb.H.) had caught Clive to make the team points level, though this was unknown to either of them. A tremendous tussle developed going into Copse but the hill was kind to the Belgravian and could offer nothing but sickness to the Cambridge man. So it was medals, medals all the way with Belgrave retaining the "Lauriston Shield". In addition to having the third individual and the winning team in the Open race, we also had first and third individuals and second team in the Surrey Championships held in conjunction (thanks to Jack Baker closing in our "County" team). Our Race Secretary, Gordon Biscoe, had everything under control as usual, and once again there were no hitches in the organisation----though he had his worried moments no doubt. items.label: September 1970
items.sum: Don Bonser's report on the International Maxol Marathon in Manchester on 23 August 1970, incorporating the R.R.C. Championship, where Lionel Mann set a club record of 2:24:07 in 9th place.
items.s: INTERNATIONAL maxol marathon Don Bonser's report on the International Maxol Marathon in Manchester on 23 August 1970, incorporating the R.R.C. Championship, where Lionel Mann set a club record of 2:24:07 in 9th place. Manchester INCORPORATING THE R.R.C. CHAMPIONSHIP Sunday 23rd August---Don Bonser reports:- This year's Maxol Marathon incorporated the Road Runners Club Championship. Additional interest was created by a small but high quality overseas entry. The absence of the leading British performers gave the less well-known good-standard runners an opportunity to demonstrate their ability in good class company. Lionel Mann's effort in recording 2:24:07 was an outstanding performance. During the early part of the race he challenged the leaders. Later he adjusted to his own steady tempo and finished strongly in a very creditable 9th place, 12½ minutes faster than his previous best. A new club record also resulted; a just reward for such courageous running. The race was sponsored by W.H. Dean & Son Ltd of Burnley, and it proved to be one of the most well organised I have yet taken part in. Overnight accommodation was at the Owen Park complex of Manchester University. Competitors and officials were provided with single rooms in the 14 storey tower block. The rooms were sound proofed which was just as well when Lionel's left big toe came into involuntary contact with the sharp end of a drawing pin. Otherwise our nocturnal slumbers were undisturbed, apart from the owls hooting in the grounds. Meals were very sustaining. Even "Chef de Royale" was disposed to favourable comment, especially after his plate of toadstools! With regard to the race itself, the course was the same as last year, apart from a couple of humps in the 2 lap section produced by road works. Conditions were rather warm with bright sunshine; humidity seemed high. To introduce us to the mysteries of metrication intermediate times were given at 5km intervals. This seemed to make the miles go quicker and gave us plenty to think about. Sir Matt. Busby started us from the Albert Square at 10am. Road traffic was light and far less hindrance than last year. There were less spectators (one included Ron Hill) but their encouragement was very welcome especially to the plodders in the back half of the field. At about 26km (work the miles out for yourself---we had to!) a group of scruffy lads asked "ah tha' fum Manchester"? My head jolted forward almost involuntarily and this was greeted with tremendous cheers and shouts. The last part of the course took us past the finish at the Manchester United F.C. ground for a final 5kms out and back. This seemed endless. The "turn" was at the carborundum works---most appropriate, as I was just about worn down to the knees. At last the stadium and a final circuit of the perimeter track to the finsh. After the race, and regaining a certain composure, it was very pleasant to have a few words with Bill Dance. He appeared to be recovering from injury and had been training for three months. He wishes to be remembered to his many friends. An excellent end to a most satisfying week-end. RESULT 1. A. Usami Japan 2:13:45 2. Y. Unetani " 2:16:00 3. J. SEPTEMBER Progress - The London Borough of Merton earnestly continue with their contribution towards Conservation Year. Having completed the chopping down of trees on Wimbledon Common, plans are now well under way to exterminate all live stock within a three mile radius against a possible outbreak of Rabies in the unforseeable future. The latest "shoot" includes 3 foxes, 4 badgers, 4,563 birds and Arthur Whitehead. Due to the enormous amount of golf balls being lost, it is envisaged that 2,400 acres of grassland will be concreted - Quotes for plastic grass verges are being sought to satisfy local dog owners. Mr. Tom Carter will investigate this matter in the Club's interest, and report at the next meeting. OCTOBER London hit by a spate of robberies Jewellers, furriers and antique dealers demand more action from Scotland Yard following increased Crime Wave. - Belgrave Jumble Sale reaches a record £4,700 profit. - Club seeks new Field Events Secretary following rapid departure abroad of Bill Couzens. ............... Tragic consequences to Hallo'ween prank. A man was seriously battered on the head with a bloater, having been mistaken for an illuminated pumpkin. ............... Mr. Tom Carter has checked and can't give a definite answer. NOVEMBER London enters its Winter Social scene. One of the first off the mark is Belgrave Harriers with their traditional Dinner and Dance. Following the customary speeches, the remaining five minutes will be taken up by dancing with the President and his Lady leading the assembled company into Auld Lang Syne. November (continued) Charlie McLennan will be discharged from hospital early this month. But for a slight residual fishy smell he will be completely recovered. Mr. Tom Carter will sound him out. DECEMBER The rainfall in Delhi is confidently expected to exceed 7.6 ins. whilst in Battersea Park less than 2.2 ins are predicted. Supplies of red flannel and Ellerman's Rub are parachuted to Ranji Bhatia. Spectral Visitations to St. John's Hall That there are mysterious happenings at the headquarters of an athletic club in S. W. London was evasively denied by spookesman Mr. A. Penstone. Mr. Tom Carter will look into this. JANUARY High Tide: Littlehampton 14 ft. (LITTLEHAMPTON!!) Weather: Temperature will be lower than annual average. Belgrave Hall disappears! Mr. Tom Carter doesn't think so. Anxious moments for Bernard Merry! FEBRUARY Top clubs decimated by phantom illness Coventry Godiva go down with blackwater fever - Birchfield stars have tennis elbow - Hercules Wimbledon have rampant athletes foot (and no athletes) so the extravagent claims and feeble excuses are rife because of the resounding successes of Belgrave Harriers in the National. First man home in this blanket finish of Claret and Gold was C. Manning, who had rather misled outsiders by saying he was concentrating on 800 metres. Next was John Baker in second place - the work this boy had put in 'round the park' was known only to the astute team manager, G. Biscoe. In third place will be T. Wright, who will run rather above himself. In fourth position we predict A. Penny, who has shown a welcome return to form. February (continued) D. Bedford could rob us of fifth place by pushing past Fred Pagett and Ron Linstead (who is supposed to be taking photographs anyway) in the funnel. To take eighth place, and give a score of 1, 2, 4, 6, 7 and eighth will be Howard Satchell, fresh from a season 'on the boards'. With the "National" won - Fairclough 273; Major 302; and Bicourt 392 will complete the first team for the "Nine Cup". Ted Stimpson comments, "If they only trained from the Hall, they would have had six in six". Mr. Tom Carter sends apologies for absence. MARCH Travel agency collapses. Beware of package tours. Dudley Gordon Holidays offer three weeks in Carribean for £2.18s.0d. Mr. Tom Carter will report at next meeting. APRIL On the 1st - at a Foyle's Literary Lunch, T. K. Hart claims that his new book "I was a Record Holder for 70 Days" is destined to become a new best seller. "My Poly Marathon time", he continued, "although superceded by Lionel (Raspberry) Mann was largely technical, like a short course, slow watch and force nine following wind." The book is "ghosted" by J. Macdonald to a modern coloquial turn of phrase to retain the author's amateur status. Mr. Tom Carter absent. MAY Mr. Charles Forte's abortive bid for Bernie Inns accelerates his interest in revitalising the declining canteen facilities at Belgrave Hall. He regards this as an attractive proposition with the promise of a subsidy to be met out of the profits made on the sale of club clothing, i.e. vests, ties, etc. .............. Mr. Tom Carter has nothing positive yet but hopes to for the next meeting. ............... Barry Sawyer requests Training Schedule from Trevor Hart. JUNE Triple Coach Disaster M. F. Jones, C.N.Collis and J.C.Smart ruin Dick Taylor's preparation for Munich Games. "But they don't coach Dick Taylor" "Aren't they Three A's coaches...?" "Yes, but ..." "Well they don't coach Belgravians so who ...." Mr. Tom Carter will make enquiries. JULY INFLATION - THE COST OF LIVING CONTINUES TO RISE Athletics Weekly announce price of their magazine to be 5/- per week (not including postage). This increase will be offset by more pages, allowing Editor, Melvyn Watman to extend his coverage of Athletic data. For the first time, Junior Mixed wheelbarrow, egg and spoon, three-legged and Shrove Tuesday Pancake Races will be recorded in depth. - Thus satisfying the ever increasing demand of athletes thirsting for this type of fatuous waffle. ............... Mr. Tom Carter has nothing to report. AUGUST In planning your holiday the weather will most likely be of importance. Consider then that heavy falls of snow are expected from Balleny Island to Magnet Bay. This naturally includes the Shackleton Ice Shelf and Mertz Glacier. Mr. Carter wants notice of the question. A.A.A. announce intention of introducing National 3 x 1½ miles Road Relay (to be held in Newcastle on Tyne) in response to popular demand!!! .................................... We thank all our readers for their avid interest. As a measure of the enthusiasm, we received how many replies to our Competition in the last issue of the Belgravian? - That's right, None! - Still, there will obviously be nobody complaining at the price of the Dinner Tickets this year. THAT'S YER LOT! items.h: TRACK AND FIELD — MANN WINS GRIFFEN CUP
items.sum: Report and results of the club 5000 metres championship at Battersea Park on 15th July, won by Lionel Mann for the Griffen Cup, with other events (110m hurdles championship, schools relay, 300m handicap).
items.s: TRACK AND FIELD — MANN WINS GRIFFEN CUP Report and results of the club 5000 metres championship at Battersea Park on 15th July, won by Lionel Mann for the Griffen Cup, with other events (110m hurdles championship, schools relay, 300m handicap). Club 5000 metres Championship---Battersea Park---15th July With Peter Morris (the holder) back home in Blackpool, and last year's silver medallist Fairclough still on the way to fitness, this year's event was certain to produce a different result if nothing else. In fact, 3rd and 4th last year simply moved up into the vacant positions, giving Lionel Mann the trophy and Laurie O'Hara the runners-up medal. But it was not quite as simple as that. Twenty five starters toed the line, the same number as last year, and there was much speculation as to how newcomers like Peter Carton and Tony Binda would fare, and as to how much fitness was tucked away in that old campaigner Pat Newell. After 1600 metres the leading group consisted of Mann, O'Hara, Major, Carton, Kerr and North; but Gerry was finding the pace too sharp for his moderate state of fitness and began to tail off. Bill Kerr, for some unknown reason, stopped at half way and resumed some way down the field. Peter lost contact during the second half of the race but held his position very well. At about 3 laps from home Lionel realised he would have to draw Laurie's "sting" and he piled on the pressure splitting the leading trio. Although Laurie closed a little at the end, Lionel is no mean finisher himself and the three second margin was plenty enough to have in hand. Carton and North finished strongly and Peter is certain to be among the medals very soon. The bronze went to Adrian Major, who is getting back to form after injury. It was good to see John Woodcock back again after a period of studying, and Jack Hampshire having a go once again. But the boquet of the day goes to the man who won gold, Lionel Mann, for it was only 4 days earlier that he had placed third in the Belgrave 20 miles road race with a Club record time of 1:44:45! items.s: 'Brockman' Report and Belgrave results from the Brockman Trophy at Wimbledon Park on 1 August, where a weakened Belgrave team finished 6th; Belgrave's points total is overtyped and uncertain. Brockman Trophy at Wimbledon Park on 1st August The "Brockman" saw us field one of our weaker teams - we have sometimes been stronger at mid-week Battersea fixtures. As a result, we did not live up to our record of the last three years, in which we finished first or second; and ended up in 6th place. One athlete who excelled himself was Peter Carton, who beat his personal best 800 metres time by a considerable margin. Peter has emerged this season as our most promising half-miler since Dave Cocks won the Surrey title in 1964, and his future looks very bright. The meeting also saw the pole vault debut in club colours of Henry Pfenninger. He cleared 12 feet at the first attempt, despite admitting to being off-colour, although he failed 12 feet 6 inches. His remark was: "My coach in Zurich would kill me for this performance". Shades of Frank Simmon's at his most fearsome! Apart from these two performances, Arnold Bentt, who finished second in the high jump and our relay team should be specially mentioned. P.H. 100m (Final) 5. B. Hafner 11.4 200m (Final) 3. J. items.s: 2nd Match at Reading on 4th July Report, Belgrave results and league position after the second Southern League Division 1 match at Reading on 4 July, where Belgrave finished second to Reading. 2nd Match at Reading on 4th July A dull morning at Clapham saw most of our team board the coach outside the Granada Cinema for the second Southern League match at Reading. We had a considerably stronger team than at Ilford but we were still weak on the throwing events, the Pole Vault and High Hurdles. Nevertheless, we got men out in every event and managed to finish second to Reading whose all-round strength was too great for us. Our winners were Bruno Hafner ('B' 100 metres), Lionel Mann ('B' 5000 metres), Alan Black ('B' steeplechase), Charlie Gillett ('B' 400 metres hurdles), Arnold Bentt ('A' High Jump), Bob Couillault ('B' Triple Jump) and the 4 x 100 metres relay team of Lee Sullivan, Bruno Hafner, Charlie Gillett and Steve White. Other useful performances came from Steve White, Peter Carton, John Boardman, Adrian Major, Bill Kerr, Lee Sullivan and Glyn Ratcliffe. One can say that it was a good team effort, but just wait and see what we can do at Wimbledon Park! P.H. RESULT 1. Reading 170 pts. 2. BELGRAVE H. 143 pts. 3. Windsor/Eton 125 pts. 4. items.sum: Report, Belgrave results and match result of the third Southern League Division 1 match at Wimbledon Park on 22 August, where Belgrave (134 pts) edged Herne Hill (133) by one point for second place behind Reading.
items.s: Southern League - 3rd match at Wimbledon Park on 22nd August Report, Belgrave results and match result of the third Southern League Division 1 match at Wimbledon Park on 22 August, where Belgrave (134 pts) edged Herne Hill (133) by one point for second place behind Reading. Southern League - 3rd match at Wimbledon Park on 22nd August After one of the most exciting matches seen for some time we edged out Herne Hill by one point to take second place in this match and the league. In addition, we had to suffer two miscounts on the way, which stretched our already taut nerves. Where can one begin to look for highlights when our team, weakened by holidays and injuries, acquitted itself nobly throughout? First of all, let us praise Snowy Brooks who competed in the first event and was involved in the last. On the way, he did 3 personal bests (400 metre hurdles, pole vault and hammer) and covered 7 events, including the long relay. Then, Bill Kerr who is running better than ever this season did a personal best 1500 to pip John Thresher. Mick Marshall, still a youth, recorded 3 very useful second places in the sprints and triple jump and also did a storming anchor leg in the relay. Mel Ford ran two fine races in the 400 metre hurdles and 400 metres and also did a 50.5s. relay split. Last, but by no means least, Gerry North won the 5000 with some ease and then placed 2nd in the B steeplechase, although his hurdling technique didn't please the purists! However, it is invidious to pick out individual performances when the essence of the day was that we performed as a team. This can be taken as a tribute to our hard-working track secretary, Bob Taylor, who seemed to be everywhere, encouraging, exhorting and entreating. Now, we go into the melting pot to see whether we will be asked to go to Leicester for the eliminating contest for the National League. If so, the other clubs had better beware of the new Belgrave! items.s: MANN WINS TOM CARTER CUP Report and result of the club 10,000 metres championship at Battersea Park on 27 July, won by Lionel Mann for the Tom Carter Cup, lapping all but Laurie O'Hara. Club 10,000metres Championship---Battersea Park---July 27th Just twelve days and three races after winning the 5,000 metres title, Lionel Mann rubbed home his superiority even more convincingly in adding the "Tom Carter" Cup to his collection. Once again Laurie O'Hara led the challengers, but it was a lonely chase for he was the only one in the field that Lionel failed to lap. The defending champion, Bob Smith, was down with injury but brought the Cup along and stayed to see who would next be polishing it. Nineteen runners fought for the privilege, but after 1200metres only six were in contention. Kerr and Mann were pushing the early pace with O'Hara, Piotrowski, Fairclough and Major tagging along. The last two named lost contact at about 3,000 metres but the situation ahead of them took a dramatic turn at 5,000 metres when Piotrowski retired with a blistered foot. And again at 6,000 metres when Kerr, who had been pushing the pace with Mann, also called it a day. This left Mann high and dry, and big gaps were the order of the day. Of the chasing procession Laurie was his usual reliable self, and Colin Pearson a praiseworthy 5th----nearly 1½ minutes faster than last year. RESULT (19 started) 1. L. Mann 31:7.4 2. L. items.s: A.A.A.'s: Club Records for Ford, Bicourt Report on Belgrave athletes at the AAA Championships at White City on 8 August, with club records for Mel Ford (400m hurdles) and John Bicourt (steeplechase) and a profile of Ford's progress. AAA Championships at White City on 8th August Our two regular finalists, Derek Boosey and John Bicourt appeared once again on finals day this year. Both performed well and John did a personal best in his heat. But, I would like to draw the attention of readers to a new name, M.Ford (Army A.A.). This was none other than our own Mel Ford, who finished a close-up 5th in the 400 metres hurdles in a personal best time of 53.1s., having come desperately close to getting a place medal. Mel's progress has been rapid since he joined us early last year, when the 2nd Battalion Grenadier Guards came back from Germany to Chelsea Barracks. He then had personal bests for the quarter mile and quarter mile hurdles of about 51.0s. and 57.5s. respectively. He improved rapidly and really broke through in last year's "Brockman", when he recorded 49.3s. for 400 metres. He sliced a large portion off the hurdles time and also ran the odd 800 metres, achieving an unofficial split of 1-56 on a relay leg. Last year's progress has been consolidated this year and he annexed the club 400 and 800 metre titles. In addition, he has won army titles at 400 metre hurdles and 800 metres and is the Middlesex 400 metre hurdles champion. His versatility has led to him being much in demand; on one week this season he ran for 4 organisations - club, unit, army and county. He is still uncertain whether to concentrate on the hurdles or 800 metres, in both of which he could achieve high honours. I have a sneaking suspicion that his best event will prove to be the 800 metres. P.H. 400m Hurdles (Final) 5. M. Ford 53.1 (Club Record) 3000m S/C (Final) 7. J. items.label: September 1970
items.h: THE MEN BEHIND THE TROPHIES — J. SAWYER
items.sum: History of the J.G. and A.J. Sawyer Memorial Cups given in 1921 by Vice-President J. Sawyer in memory of his two sons killed in the First World War, with the reproduced 1921 club championships programme and entry lists.
items.s: THE MEN BEHIND THE TROPHIES — J. SAWYER History of the J.G. and A.J. Sawyer Memorial Cups given in 1921 by Vice-President J. Sawyer in memory of his two sons killed in the First World War, with the reproduced 1921 club championships programme and entry lists. J. SAWYER During the 1920's and later, a rather sad faced man could be seen at all our Battersea Park Track meetings, firmly grasping the rails which separated the public footpath from the finishing straight of the track in those days, intent upon every stride of every race. We had a very considerable following at all our track meetings at that time and it may be that the close proximity of the track helped the athletes of the past to identify themselves with those of the then present. These supporters have now passed on and the present generation of spectators is practically non-existent, in the face of the many competing interests for their leisure time----more's the pity! To come back to our sad-faced man----his name was J. SAWYER, and he was a Vice-President of the Club. A nod of recognition was the most one could expect of him---he rarely spoke to anyone. Perhaps his thoughts were for his two sons, killed in the 1914-1918 War, and commemorated by the two Cups given by MR. J. SAWYER in 1921----"THE J.G. SAWYER MEMORIAL CUP" for the 440 yards (now 400 metres) Championship and "THE A.J. SAWYER MEMORIAL CUP" for the 2 miles (now 3000 metres) Walk Championship. These were two events of the original Club Championships Programme on the Track, held at Prices Athletic Club ground, Earlsfield on Thursday, July 28th 1921. The cover of the programme for that inaugural Club Championships meeting is reproduced above. Alongside, are shown the entries for events Nos. 9 and 13-----the two challenge cups put up by Nr. J. Sawyer. As can be seen, there was no shortage of competitors. The first winners were:-440 yards Championship, L.C. SMITH; 2 Miles Walk Championship, HAROLD KING, who we are glad to report is fit and well, and a frequent visitor to Wimbledon during the Winter season. A.A.H. LEFT: Harold King (left), first winner of the "A.J. SAWYER" Cup, in action with E.L. Reeve during a road race. RIGHT:Len Smith (right), first winner of the "J.G. SAWYER" Cup, in action with C.T. items.label: September 1970
items.sum: The Editor's humorous account of a Sunday Times column on Sports Illustrated correspondent Gwil Brown, who claimed Belgrave Harriers as his club, only for the Assistant Hon. Secretary to find no such name on the club's books.
items.s: THE STORY THAT WASN'T... The Editor's humorous account of a Sunday Times column on Sports Illustrated correspondent Gwil Brown, who claimed Belgrave Harriers as his club, only for the Assistant Hon. Secretary to find no such name on the club's books. THE STORY THAT WASN'T... All journalists, even the amateur ones, like to get hold of a good story---and your Editor is no exception. It was while scanning the sports pages of THE SUNDAY TIMES last month that his eye caught the words "Belgrave Harriers". Not just once, but twice. Now our name is not entirely foreign to that esteemed newspaper and shouldn't, therefore, attract overdue attention: except that in this instance the headline of the article in question read "All Those Shy British Sports Writers". As our readers know, the Editor is shy. He is certainly British (his upper lip is a giveaway) and he writes about sport as well. Was this then fame at last? Had it only taken 11 years for THE SUNDAY TIMES to recognise the quality of our gazette? Was there actually an offer in the post? Such fly-away thoughts took but a split second: just long enough to notice that the photograph in the article bore no resemblance to your resident scribe, and the caption beneath it, however much he screwed up his eyes, still read GWIL BROWN. Further perusal showed that this character was quite unknown to your Editor and in view of the let-down seconds earlier he felt disinclined to become acquainted. But then, thinking of his loyal readers, he felt duty-bound to read the offending column. The following is a brief extract:- BRITISH SPORT loses a friend and a critic next week when Gwil Brown, a likeable American, is recalled to the New York offices of Sports Illustrated, the quality sports magazine with a circulation of two million and, reputedly, a readership of 14 million. Brown, an associate editor of the magazine, has been its resident London correspondent for three years. Brown's language is flecked, in the American style, with italics: astonishing, outrageous, preposterous. "As far as cost and availability are concerned, both public and private, Britain is an absolute paradise for the club-level sportsman. When I first came over I was amazed to see people running through the streets in their running kit. You'd never see that in New York. Unthinkable. Even in Central Park, people get hostile, they elbow you and try to trip you up." He grinned. "What I like here is the casual nature of sport. Practically everybody does something, and they don't talk about it, they just do it. At 42, Brown is thought by his American friends to be a bit of a fitness nut. He belongs to the Cumberland Lawn Tennis Club, Hendon Golf Club, ("me and Harold Wilson"), Belgrave Harriers, and has running rights at the Duke of York's Barracks in Chelsea. All his club costs total about £63 10s. a year. Gwil Brown "You're a nation of soccer players and long distance runners." The Press facilities in almost any sport, with the notable exception of golf, Brown feels, are hopeless compared to the States. The sportsmen, too, are shackled by the amateurish administrations, Brown thinks, and certainly by the lack of money. "You're a nation of soccer players, where you only need a ball, and long-distance runners. People like Lynn Davies are really remarkable for having got going without special facilities." Among sportsmen themselves, Brown sees an odd will to lose. "Maybe it's the English reserve," he said, "or the Baron de Coubertin spirit of participating. That and nerves. Ann Jones, not defending her Wimbledon title because of nerves. That's outrageous. And Virginia Wade. Nerves again. There's something wrong somewhere. "You even see it among the sports writers, with their shyness. But some aren't like that, and produce really literate and informative stuff." Brown grinned. "Is that enough?" he asked, as though we might like another 100cc of criticism. It was noon, and he had some running to do at the Duke of York's. He might even have a go at the Bridges Run, over both the Chelsea and Albert Bridges and round Battersea Park. "The course record is held by Gerry North at 12:02, although you'd better check that," Brown advised, then he added, wistfully, "North's a Belgrave Harrier. That was my club." Your Editor read it once, twice and then a third time, his eyes finally resting on that opening paragraph. Going back to New York eh? Why now? Perhaps there is a connection with "The Belgravian" after all. He's frightened of getting roped in as the next editor and is skipping the country before the A.G.M. That's it! Wants to hang on to his cushy number with "Sports Illustrated"! These were a few of the thoughts that raced through his mind as he continued to smart from the initial disappointment. He may have lost the first story but this second one was probably even better. How could a true Belgravian behave in such a way; hiding his light under a bushel these last three years? Yes, the new story would pursue the line of how a member of Belgrave Harriers defected to the West rather than assist his Club. An excellent idea. And so the story was written, It took many hours of the midnight oil and ran to two full pages, and your Editor felt pretty pleased with himself. It would be controversial for sure, and no doubt Gwil Brown's mates at the "Dukes" wouldn't be too happy, but it would be worth it, just to get a good story. The "i's" were dotted and the "t's" crossed and only one more item of information was needed from our Assistant Honorary Secretary. "Hello! Is that you Bill?----Hon. Editor here----could you give me the date Gwil Brown joined us?" There was a pause, a rustle of paper, the click of a pencil on the receiver, "Hallo! Clive-----there is no such name as Gwil Brown on our books". Gwil Brown "You're a nation of soccer players and long distance runners." items.sum: Walking notes by Pat Duncan paying tribute to Guernsey walker Len Duquemin on his retirement after the 1970 Commonwealth Games, with news of Wilf Wesch, Ray Middleton and others and results from Cambridge, the London Postal Region '6', the Lambeth '5' and the Birmingham Outer Circle '25'.
items.s: WALKING Walking notes by Pat Duncan paying tribute to Guernsey walker Len Duquemin on his retirement after the 1970 Commonwealth Games, with news of Wilf Wesch, Ray Middleton and others and results from Cambridge, the London Postal Region '6', the Lambeth '5' and the Birmingham Outer Circle '25'. WALKING Pat Duncan writes: In October 1967, when Belgrave fortunes were at a low ebb, two Channel Island walkers joined the club. Although members of the winning Sarnia team in the Garnet Cup John Moullin and Len Duquemin were as yet unknown to the British Walking world although we'd heard that Moullin was a bit of a scrubber and Duquemin too old to do anything useful. These two soon adapted to our ways and were soon putting Belgrave back on the map. Prepared to try any distance, whether on the road or in the pub afterwards, Len proved to be the faster but over the longer distances it was John who generally triumphed. In the 1970 Commonwealth Games both were selected to represent their native Guernsey and for Len Duquemin this was to be his final race. What a race he had !"Took a packet at 10 had had enough by 15"and came back to record a personal best 2.42.48 to beat Shuan Lightman by two minutes and 14 years. Len's performance must rank as one of the fastest ever for an "oi not so much of the old" 40 year old but what a way to retire. Freeman may have walked a blinder but for me Len's was the finest performance of all. Although Len's contribution to Belgrave is clear in the record book, he has winning team medals for all the national championships, his sportsmanship and humour must also feature highly. Always ready with a cheerful word of encouragement for novice or champion alike Len has been one of the elder statesmen of the game. His style was superb and he will be remembered as a good athlete and a great team man. He reckons to retire and take up running, " I fancy clay-pidgeon shboting as well". We will miss him but hope that after a couple of months he'll get his shoes out again and, as usual, put his clubmates to shame with some more faultless races. John Moullin finished 10th in the Commonwealth Games 20 Miles, Len was sixth, in 2.48.07 but then he always was the scrubber. * * * * * In his first international appearance for West Germany Wilf Wesch flattened the opposition, from France, Sweden as well as his own team to record as fast 91.21 for 20 Kilometres. Although Wilf's form in the German selection races has been disappointing this certainly showed the German selectors who was boss when it mattered. * * * * * After the disappointment of losing the National 20 Kilometres by just one point the boys have really got down to the hard work of winning races. The ever consistent Ray Middleton, although slightly shaded by some great races from Wilf Wesch, has once again provided a fantastic example for the club. Although 35 Ray is still turning in personal bests at nearly every distance and on his present form must trouble every walker in Britain either at 20 or 50 Kilos. His first attempt at the Brighton could really provide some interest and should ensure yet further honours for Belgrave in this clasic. Wilf has also been impressive and although disappointed by his 4.13. clocking in the German 50 Kilos ( he finished 5th although the styles of those ahead * ! ?) his latest win put him back at the top again. John Moullin has also shaken off his earlier lack of lustre ready for a good Brighton. Pat Duncan is at last coming through a bit although both Brian Ward and Dave King look like catching him ( some hope !) and its good to see Dave Debondi back in the thick of it once more. Gerry Cameron is back training although his recent move to Scotland is something of a problem. Another much improved walker is Bernard Capener who should feature in the international postman's walk in September. Those Belgrave landmarks John Keown, John Morris and George Beecham are still very much alive and will, one hopes shortly be joined by John Johnson. Over the short ones Barry Ingarfield should also feature after a hard summer. On May 30th the Cambridge section scored a one/two for Belgrave with Bobby Barnes winning the 3,000 Metres in 16.42 18 seconds clear of Barry Wallman. Meanwhile Ray Middleton took the London Postal Region '6' in a snappy 45.38. August 9th - London Postal Region Invitation '6'. Carl Lawton burnt off the opposition to record 45.52 over this tough Blackheath course with Pat Duncan 5 minutes behind in 5th position. Tommy Cook made the best of a generous mark to win the handicap. In the afternoon John Johnson held off the best of them to win the London Transport handicap at Wembley Park and once again Tommy Cook scored to take his second pot of the day. June 9th - Brookwell Park - Lambeth '5'. Held just before the National,Belgrave could only muster a reserve squad and had to let Ilford in for the first place honours. Nevertheless Wilf Wesch was right up with the leaders and Barry Ingarfield also pulled out a good one. CARL LAWTON (left) was a well placed 7th in the Lambeth '5', while RAY HALL (right) produced one of his "retirement" outings to finish 24th. July 4th - Birmingham Outer Circle '25'. Even though some of our regular distance men were otherwise involved we still could have won the race but for an unfortunate navigational error which landed Bob Coates and John Keown far from the scene of hostilities just when they were most needed. Ray Middleton held on to a slender lead to win from a much improved Harding of Royal Sutton. Further back Bob Farley and Gerry Cameron both chose this race for their return to active competition although they will need some hard training spins if they are to get back amongst our leading men once again. 1. items.s: Bels Retain National 50k Report of the RWA National 50 Kilometres Championship at East Ewell on 15 August, where Ray Middleton was second to Bob Dobson and Belgrave retained the team title. Bels Retain National 50k August 15th - RWA National 50 Kilometres Championship - East Ewell. After his superb recent form Ray Middleton looked a strong contender for the title and selection, once more, for the British Team. As it turned out Ray had to contend with Bob Dobson who walked an inspired race to win by just 60 seconds from Ray who was fast catching him over the last lap. The race, held over a fairly stiff 8 lap course, was generally fast but the weather contributed to the fairly tough conditions so that Ray's 4.21.22 was a very good clocking indeed. John Moullin was also well to the fore over the early stages but suffered for this although still returning a useful time. Bob Coates fell foul of the judges but Brian Ward and Pat Duncan were close at hand to ensure a comfortable victory for the team. Brian's 4.54.23 was an encouraging sign for the future even if the ever crafty Pat sneaked past in the last lap. Dave King was another to impress with a very rapid return to form. Dave Debondi had a disappointing race, mainly due to an unfortunate fall in training, ( Lawton still denies tripping him!) but George Beecham's defeat of John Keown should certainly strengthen our chances in the Brighton where both will be fighting for a team place. Johns Morris and Johnson found conditions a bit trying and were both forced to retire. 1. R.Dobson Basildon 4.20.22 16. B.Ward Belgrave 4.54.23 2. R.Middleton Belgrave 4.21.22 26. items.s: HASTINGS-BRIGHTON WINNERS Report of the Hastings to Brighton 38 miles walk on 1 August, won by Ray Middleton, with Belgrave taking the team race by three points from Surrey Walking Club. HASTINGS-BRIGHTON WINNERS August 1st - Hastings to Brighton 38 Miles. Ray Middleton and Wolly Wortley were our sole representatives on the grid at one minute to go when to their relief John Moullin, Dave DeBondi, Dave King and Pat Duncan all sped into view and after frantic scenes of nudity in the middle of the road the Belgrave team were on their way. John Moullin took the front but after 20 Kilos in 106 minutes he'd had enough of the heat and by 20 miles we were one short. Ray Middleton was soon forcing the pace and despite the very tough conditions he powered through to a very impressive win in just over 5hrs 40 Minutes. Don Thompson's return to walking resulted in a second place with Colin Young fresh from his Strasbourg to Paris 300 Mile epic closing in third. Behind him our man Duncan recovered from a slow start to overhaul all but Weston of Highgate finishing fifth and once again taking the Sussex distance title. The extreme heat troubled DeBondi, who, coming as he does from the temperate Australian climate is not used to such extremes of temperature. He suffered but hung on gamely to give Belgrave victory by a slender three points from arch rivals Surrey. Dave King marked his return to competition with his slowest time ever,nearly 75 minutes behind his previous best, a performance which said a lot for his courage but little for his fitness, Handicap: R.Middleton 1st Sussex P.Duncan 1. items.label: September 1970
items.sum: Clive Shippen previews Belgrave's 1970 autumn road relay season, regretting the loss of the Johnstone relay and criticising the presentation of A.A.A. relay championships, and lists the fixtures from 12 September to 17 October.
items.s: Autumn Relay Prospects Clive Shippen previews Belgrave's 1970 autumn road relay season, regretting the loss of the Johnstone relay and criticising the presentation of A.A.A. relay championships, and lists the fixtures from 12 September to 17 October. Autumn Relay Prospects Clive Shippen reviews the forthcoming road season Once again a popular point to point relay bites the dust. First it was the classic London to Brighton, then the well established Leyton to Southend, then the Southampton to Bournemouth and now the Johnstone event. This latest casualty was in our fixture list last year and vied with the Dudley to Bridgenorth relay for the high spot of the seven week season. As holders of the trophy we are naturally dissappointed at not having the opportunity to defend it but are even more concerned at this steady erosion of quality events from our fixture list. To suggest that the introduction of A.A.A. Championship events over 12 stages and 6 stages are suitable compensations would raise cries of derision from those who have witnessed these events. Whilst one would not quarrel with the organisation of these races between starting gun and tape there is a great deal more that requires attention in a National Championship than the race itself. Someone should be appointed to deal solely with pre-race publicity, public relations generally and the presentation ceremony itself. It is just not good enough to search around on the day for a place to"hand over" the medals or to ask the teams to shake hands with the Mayor's sixth reserve when the medals do not turn up. It has always been difficult to get a big attendance at after-race presentations but, if the present trend continues, even the successful teams won't bother to go. It is rumoured that the National 6-stage Relay will be held on October 10th at Southport. It is ironical that of all the events in the Autumn calendar this is the only one for which we had not received details at time of press. As it happens, Belgrave will not be sending a team in any case; and we are unlikely to be the only absentees. Unless National Championships are put on with all the publicity, presentation and trappings of a truly National occasion then the longer standing events are in danger of going the same way as the 6 stage relay. Back to the local scene, this year's fixture list covers one of the briefest periods ever---5 weeks. The programme is as follows:- September 12th----Surrey Co. Road Relays (S & Y), Woking Lido. " 19th----Blackheath H. Road Relay, Hayes " 26th----Belgrave 5¾ miles handicap (non-championship). October 3rd----Walton A.C. Road Relay. " 10th----Belgrave 3 miles Yacht Handicap. " 17th----Dudley to Bridgenorth and Back Road Relay. The opening event could see us off to the best start we have had since 1951. In that year we won the Surrey Co. Road Relay for the 4th consecutive time, yet after eighteen further attempts we have failed to record another win. This year there is much determination in the camp to put the record right---an approach which has sadly been lacking in recent years. It coincides with the running into form, just at the right time, of Kerr, Thresher, North, Major and Fairclough. With Bicourt and Hart already in fine fettle we could well be having a celebration dip in the Lido on September 12th. With our Surrey men nicely tuned up after Woking they will be joined by our other big guns, Mann, O'Hara and O'Connor for the Blackheath Relay seven days later. This year's race had been switched to a Sunday with an 11a.m start but just before going to press we hear that the event has reverted to the normal Saturday spot. There are many arguments against a Sunday morning road relay but it would have been interesting to see how well the athletes supported it. The following Saturday (Sept.26th) is the day on which many of our dark horses have been training to reach peak. Secret sessions and time trials ("I've only been out once a week Bill") culminate in that blue riband of the road, the "5¾". All the nervous tension and needle of an international meeting is on show, with the battles becoming more gruelling the further down the field one goes. If you can't run in this one you must at least watch it! October opens with the Walton Relay. This is a popular event over a nice course and we usually manage to enter about five teams. For those who are striving to make our team for the main event of the Autumn season and have had no real luck so far, their final chance comes with the Yacht '3' on October 10th. This popular handicap attracts as many as sixty members and Bill Lucas's handicapping has proved so good in the past that a funnel is required at the finish to produce a correct finishing order. Don't miss this one for, whatever your standard, you could be a winner; and there are prizes for the first three. The short season reaches it's climax on October 17th with Tipton's Dudley to Bridgenorth Relay. This event attracts a top class field and we have done very well the last two years in finishing second both times-----to Derby in 1968 and to City of Stoke in 1969. The programme laid on for the preceding 5 weeks should be ample for our runners to tune up nicely for this race. Gold would be nice compensation for the loss of the "Johnstone". All members, whatever their event or standard, are asked to study the above fixtures, decide in which events they would like to run (everyone runs in the Yacht!) and notify Gordon Biscoe at 34, Pam's Way, Ewell, Surrey. items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial announcing that Clive Shippen has given up the editorship after about ten years and that a committee led by Donald Maclean now runs the magazine. Clive Shippen has given up the Belgravian Editorship after some ten years, in which he achieved a club magazine standard quite exceptional for an amateur athletic club. We still have the benefit of Clive's advice and contributions, but a Committee has been set up to take over the reins. Contributions to the mag. should now be sent to Donald Maclean, 45 Amerland Road, London, S.W.18 (874-1889). Other members of the Committee are John Dear, Dave McMillan, Tony Fairclough, and any members who want to lend a hand - writing, typing, ideas or whatever - and these should get in touch with Don, from whom you are sure of a hearty welcome. items.label: December 1970
items.sum: The President's message thanking the club for his re-election, thanking Gordon Doubleday, and setting targets for relay, walking and cross-country championship wins.
items.s: THE PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE The President's message thanking the club for his re-election, thanking Gordon Doubleday, and setting targets for relay, walking and cross-country championship wins. May I express sincere thanks to the club for electing me President for a second term of office. I would like to think this will coincide with a high measure of success in all branches of Athletics by our teams and members -- and there is certainly no valid reason why it should not be so. Our grateful thanks are due to Gordon Doubleday for the exemplary way in which he served as President during the past Club year. At the time of his election Gordon was laid low in hospital, but a happy and enduring recovery enabled him to work as hard on our behalf as any club has a right to expect, plus a bonus for Good Timekeeping! Thank you, Doub for your great work for a great Club. Three years ago Frank Jarvis, when elected President, made his demands of the Annual General Meeting for even more Trophy wins during the summer season -- and in due course his desires were consummated. I am much more exacting and demanding -- much greedier for the honours that Athletics has to bestow upon a champion Club. I would like Belgrave to win the four senior R.W.A. Championships during my Presidency as against the three won this year and one lost by a single point. I am given to understand that this will not happen again! I would ask for no less than Cross country wins in the Surrey, Southern and English Championships. All these titles have been in our possession before. Why not again? I am confident that the ability to ride high is within our ranks; with adequate reserve strength in addition to play a very substantial part, and to prove to everyone the truth of the adage "that strength is in reserves". I repeat, the talent is there. It needs to believe in itself, to have confidence that the deeds of the past can again be accomplished, to develop an enthusiasm and a determination which will sweep the Belgrave colours to multiple successes within months. The secret key to the success is "Hard-work", Intellegently applied, allied to a burning enthusiasm, and a mutual identity of determined intention over a period of three months or so. Our undoubted strength, if unified, and directed with maximum impact, correctly timed and beamed on our objectives, must prevail, and crown our efforts with success in the events which matter most. In similar vein we could also take a couple of AAA Relay Championships, the twelve aside road-relay Championship and the Sprint Relay, which we won in 1954, for example. And here again on Track and Field lets have a few Trophy successes for good measure! While all this good work goes on we may be sure our Juniors, Youths and Boys will have received the message and I am sure their triumphs will be many. The objectives I have outlined above might well be considered a twelve months programme to daunt any Club but Belgrave; and there may be some in our ranks who doubt our ability to do these things. But consider for a moment the small, almost infinitesimal margins that decide Championships and separate success from failure. Think of the sprinter who loses a race by inches in a hundred yards -- or centrimetres in a 100 metres, if you prefer it that way. The margin is so small, probably of the order of one point in 750. A 1% improvement would easily swing defeat into victory. Similarly a 1500 metre runner winning clearly by a metre is abviously only the slightest possible fraction faster than his opponent. A 1% or 2% improvement by the second man would give a very different result! It would enable him to achieve all his ambitions and more. These slender margins also win or lose team championships. Six men all showing a small percentage of impsoved running can well and truly put us among the trophies! I'll not pretend that that last little final degree of improvement is easy to attain. The 1% extra intensity of effort in training and racing; in the determination to succeed, in the support given to one's colleagues over weeks of preparation -- all this can only mean ultimate SUCCESS. Will you please try and make this extra contribution? In the same way we should endeavour to put that extra 1% effort into the administrative side of the Club. Well as we are served, just the little more extra effort over and above the tremendous work already done will register, and put us in the highest places. The general membership, too, has its part to play in giving that extra little bit of help and support in every possible way. We must be on the constant look-out for new members, and ensure that they are cordially welcomed and quickly assimilated into our activities. We must guard against wastage and loss of talent by reason of our shortcomings; and we must give vocal and other support to our chosen team when the Championship seasons comes round. We have all heard of the tag "for want of a horse-shoe nail the battle was lost!! Let us ponder the truth of this, and let us be on our guard that we do not commit the sins of omission or commission. Let us be warned, and let us aim high when many other subsidiary successes will automatically be sept into the net. We'll even mix our metaphors if its going to help! As your President I look to everyone to pull his weight (+ 2%) during this year. Every member, and certainly every Officer and member of Committee should be seeking for ways and means whereby the maximum amount of thought and action is contributed to matters Belgrave. I feel confident that this will be so, and that the result of our united efforts will be seen this year, and for a long while to come. A.A.H. items.sum: Note thanking Gwen and Bill Couzens for the October 31st jumble sale and appealing for fund-raising support, A.A.A. Draw tickets and prompt subscriptions.
items.s: JUMBLE Note thanking Gwen and Bill Couzens for the October 31st jumble sale and appealing for fund-raising support, A.A.A. Draw tickets and prompt subscriptions. Our thanks to Gwen and Bill Couzens for the great amount of work they once again put in for the jumble sale held on October 31st. It looked to me as if there was more to sell than ever before, and it was a sucess despite the fact that it was a rainy morning. Thanks also to the small band of willing helpers who always turn up although many are already doing jobs within the club. This leads to a question. Do members really want fund raising activities or would they prefer to pay higher subscriptions ? The response to the A.A.A. Draw is very poor considering our membership. There are still a great many members who are not buying a weekly football ticket during the winter. The last improvement to Belgrave Hall was somewhere around 1953 we can improve still further if a little more effort is made by all members. By doing this we can attract more members, with rising costs we need the extra income if we are to remain one of the leading clubs in the country. Current subscriptions became due in September, and I appeal to members to pay promptly. May I wish fellow members a Happy Christmas and a prosperous New Year. Gwen Couzens Gwen organised the jumble sale, October 31st 1970 Bill Couzens Bill Couzens organised the jumble sale, October 31st 1970 A.A.A. Draw Belgrave Hall

HARLEY Announcement of Alf Harley's election as club President for a second term, with a 1950s photo of him receiving the Romulus and Remus trophy and amendments to the previous issue's Spotlight article on his offices. Our President A.A.HARLEY In recognition of his outstanding service and devotion to Belgrave Harriers, ALFRED A. HARLEY was unanimously elected as President of the Club at the Annual General Meeting on September 17th. As readers of our SPOTLIGHT article in the last 'Belgravian' will know, this is Alf Harley's second term of supreme office - the first being for years 1950 to 1952 - and we are proud to have him as our President once again. (Photo: Evening News) Another milestone in the life of ALF HARLEY is reached during the 1950's when, as Chairman of the London Association of Athletic Clubs, he receives the ROMULUS AND REMUS trophy from the Italians at London's Dorchester Hotel Apropos that SPOTLIGHT article, a few amendments and additions need to be made. Alf resigned as Honorary Treasurer of the R.W.A. in September 1969, and was elected a Trustee of the Race Walking Association at the same meeting. Incidentally, he is also a Trustee of the Southern Counties A.A.A. At the Annual General Meeting of the A.A.A. held in October, Alf was elected a Vice-President of the A.A.A. (on the Southern Counties nomination) and this is the first time a Belgrave Harrier has held this office. Not only is this a tribute to Alf Harley himself, but to the Club also. We look forward to a successfull year under his leadership. items.label: December 1970
items.sum: President's column of short notes: thanks for a presentation at the Dinner-Dance, the Tommy Green Cup awarded to Wilf Wesch, an appeal for timekeepers, and a call for a club photograph on March 13th.
items.s: PRESIDENTIAL PARS President's column of short notes: thanks for a presentation at the Dinner-Dance, the Tommy Green Cup awarded to Wilf Wesch, an appeal for timekeepers, and a call for a club photograph on March 13th. On behalf of my wife and myself, may I thank the Club most sincerely and humbly for the really magnificent present that was given to us at the Annual Dinner-Dance. I was certainly over-whelmed and lost for words, and the quiet and secret manner in which the whole affair was managed was worthy of M.I.5, 007, F.I.B. and all the other coded agencies rolled into one. Please accept my very grateful thanks and sincere appreciation. It has been a great privilege to serve the club for 42 years in office, and I hope to be able to continue to do so and to make my small contributions from time to time. There has been a deal of satisfaction to be had in filling various offices, not least that of General Hon. Secretary for 32 years since taking over from Wally Bayliss. I count it a great honour to have been permitted to continue so long with higher councils of the Club; and am further privileged in serving as your President for a second term, in the current year. My thanks to you all. --ooOoo-- Tommy GREEN (our legendary hero of years ago and the winner of dozens of walks in the late 1920s and early 1930s) as many will recall, was selected as one of the Olympic team to go to Los Angeles in 1932. Tommy duly won the first 50 kilometres Olympic Walking title in tropical conditions. Great Britain had two winners only, our Tommy Green, and Tom Hampson (800 metres) who was a second-chain Belgrave man, and scored in some of our Surrey County Relay wins. Later Tommy Green presented us with a magnificient Cup to which his name was given; and it was, decided that it should be held each year by the Club athlete who, in the opinion of the Committee, accomplished the finest individual performance during the Club year. This year a very popular choice was WILF WESCH for his win with RWA 20 Miles Championship -- one of the three main titles that he won. With the Cup's association with our first ever Olympic champion it will be interesting to see whether WILF can emulate the donor at Munich in 1972 -- forty years on -- and take an Olympic walking title. It could well be! --ooOoo-- The death of Ernie KEMP, and retirement for business reasons of his son Frank is likely to handicap us greatly in time-keeping at our various events in the future. Cecil Gittins has always made it clear that he has many other prior commitments to discharge as we are well aware; and this throws the burden on our immediate Past President Gordon Doubleday, and the occasional welcome visits of Harry HATHWAY. With four events being decided simultaneously on one afternoon (as on Jan. 23rd) timekeeping will be a difficult business indeed; and looking ahead we shall certainly need more assistance at track meetings. May we ask those who feel they could be helpful in this field to get in touch? Expensive watches are not essential -- the desire to be helpful and to turn up with regularity are the important assets. --OOOOO-- On another page will be seen an invitation to all members able to do so, to turn up at Belgrave Hall on Mar. 13th for a Club photograph to be taken. We hope to have a representative gathering of Club members of all ages present. As we cannot depend upon the weather it is intended to take the photograph inside Belgrave Hall, where special staging arrangements will be made. It will be necessary for the photograph to be taken at 2.00 p.m., so that the competitors in the following afternoon competitions may have ample time for stripping-off, warming up, and getting on the mark in good time. Ordinary clothes (with Club ties) should be worn for the photograph. So make an entry in your new diary now -- Mar. 13th/Club Photo/2.00p.m. sharp/ --ooOoo-- Wally Bayliss Wally Bayliss preceded the writer as General Hon. items.sum: Note on Past-President Ernie Duffett's recovery from a brain operation and his retirement to South Wales, recalling his 25 years as Running Hon. Sec., with a photo of him third in the Surrey County cross-country championship around 1928.
items.s: Note on Past-President Ernie Duffett's recovery from a brain operation and his retirement to South Wales, recalling his 25 years as Running Hon. Sec., with a photo of him third in the Surrey County cross-country championship around 1928. His many friends in the Club will be delighted to know that Past-President ERNIE DUFFETT is fast recovering from an operation at the Atkinson Morley Hospital, Copse Hill, for the removal of a non malignant growth on the brain. Ernie is gathering strength every day, and after a period of rehabilitation will be moving to his new home in South Wales which had been planned before ill-health intervened. We wish Gladys and Ernie good health and long life on their retirement. Ernie was one of the vital forces in Belgrave and athletics generally in the 25 years he served us as Running Hon.Sec. He joined us in 1927: his influence was tremendous, his enthusiasm great and reflected in our successes during the period. In 1948 he acted as Marksman at the Olympic Games; and there was a time when Ernie knew every runner, his club, and his "marks" in open handicaps -which was just as well for he was an A.A.A. Handicapper for a number of years. He was known as the one-man scrutiny meeting in the world of cross-country running, and his remarkable memory often came to the rescue of confused Event Secretaries! In his younger days Ernie was a more than useful runner, holding the Club mile record at one time, taking place medals in Surrey Championships, and giving valuable support to our teams. items.sum: Club notes on Ray Middleton's London-Brighton Walk debut, the sale of Ranmore Post-Office, the 51st Annual Open Walk on November 28th, and Ken O'Kell paying for names added to the Honours Boards.
items.s: Club notes on Ray Middleton's London-Brighton Walk debut, the sale of Ranmore Post-Office, the 51st Annual Open Walk on November 28th, and Ken O'Kell paying for names added to the Honours Boards. Ray Middleton's amazing first-attempt time in the London-Brighton Walk (in which he finished second) confirms Ray as one of the finest walkers of all time. This is further underlined by his representation of Great Britain in five successive Lugano Walk Competitions -- testimony to his ability, his determination, his strength and his fitness. We look to Ray for further honours yet, for as he grows older he returns faster and faster times! * * * * * * * * Our strollers of yesteryear will be saddened by the news that Ranmore Post-Office and buildings are up for sale as business has declined. Many will remember our steady climb up through the woods until we achieved the heights of Ranmore Common, with the "Post-Office" and it's pots of tea to supplement the sandwiches we carried. Time was when we sheltered in a dilapidated barn, later repaired, with - not unexpectedly - an increase in charges. We pleaded we were part of the goodwill of the establishment, but we still had to pay the extra coppers! * * * * * * * * Our 51st Annual Open Walk received excellent support on November 28th. The weather cleared, the organisation - thanks to Pat Duncan, Jack Goswell and others - was of the usual high order, and Belgrave won the scratch team race. A very good day - with Belgrave Hall stretched to it's limits! A very special "Thank you" to all who assisted for the hungry hundreds after the race. A pleasing feature of the event was the number of former Belgrave champions and athletes to be seen looking on. How nice to see Bob McMullen (now on the 80 mark) and Harry Churcher (Seven times A.A.A. Champion and an Olympic walker) who was prevailed upon to present the awards, and Joe Coleman, Ben Knifton, Tom Scrimshaw, Percy Wright, Harold King - and no doubt old Uncle Tom Cobley was there as well! * * * * * * * * We are again indebted to our one-time Captain and Champion, Ken O'Kell, for defraying the cost of adding names to the two Honours Boards hanging in Belgrave Hall, which Ken presented to us some years ago. items.sum: The new Hon. Secretary's first notes: praise for the annual dinner, a decanter presented to Alf Harley, the committee's move to the Parkway Hotel managed by Wilf Wesch, and a review of the book Today's Athlete.
items.s: HON. SECRETARY'S NOTES The new Hon. Secretary's first notes: praise for the annual dinner, a decanter presented to Alf Harley, the committee's move to the Parkway Hotel managed by Wilf Wesch, and a review of the book Today's Athlete. I must sav that the magazine has come with its usual quick deadlines and has caught me almost literally with my trousers around my ankles. You're probably wondering what I am going to say in my first secretarial jottings, but then so am I! First, let me convey an enormous amount of praise for the way in which the annual dinner was organised. For me, the meal was the best we've had in years and particularly enjoyable for not being that aged bird "Surrey Chicken". Bill Lucas was his usual efficient self as toastmaster and several who spoke later with the aid of the microphone (it worked this time!) wondered how his voice managed to carry to the furthest corners of the room. It was a very moving experience for all present when Bill Laws presented Alf Harley with a splendid decanter set as a worthy presentation for the years he has served the club in an official capacity. The club wouldn't be what it is now without the devotion and hard work that Alf has given it and it is good to see that his efforts have been justly rewarded. The committee has been elevated in status by its move from its former Kennington Lane venue to the more sophisticated ambiance of the Parkway Hotel in Bayswater. We have to thank the hotel manager for this beneficial move - he is none other than our home-grown German walking champion, Wilf Wesch. We wish him many more years at the Parkway. Incidentally, it was noticeable that fewer sub-committees developed during the course of the meeting this time. I have recently been sent a book called Today's Athlete, which is published by Pelham Books at 35/-. This is a compendium of articles on athletics and is edited by Brian Mitchell. It covers a wide range of subjects and its contributors include such notables as Bruce Tulloh, Tony Ward, Tom McNab and our own Ranjit Bhatia, who contributes a chapter on distance running in India. The book is aimed principally at the coach, the school teacher, the administrator and the thinking athlete and makes fascinating reading, although the overall standard is uneven, as it must be in a collective book. I can recommend it wholeheartedly to anyone who wants to get a little extra from the sport. - PH PH PH new Hon. Secretary (P.B.
