items.s: FROM 'The Belgravian' 25 years ago ..... and 40 years ago Reprinted extracts from June 1946 (the club's dominant first post-war cross-country season, including the English National team title) and March 1931 (Arthur Allum's Southern, National and International runs and the walkers' eight successive road wins). FROM 'The Belgravian' 25 years ago ..... JUNE 1946 ------ The first post-war Winter season was a memorable one for the Belgrave Harriers. Our cross-country runners won every open championship. In November we had the first two teams home in the South of the Thames "Junior", and the first three individuals. This in itself was a remarkable feat as all of our pre-war "cracks" cannot run in this race owing to the barring clauses. In the New Year we won the Surrey County Title, whilst our Middlesex members, running for Cadogan A.C., took the Middlesex title. This was not regarded as very extraordinary as it had been done on various occasions before the war. The South of the Thames "Senior" Race resulted in another win for us. Here again, a large number of our best men are barred. The Southern Counties Cross-Country Championship, 7½ miles instead of the usual 10, was held from Belgrave Hall. Our Captain, Tom Carter, gained a well earned and popular victory. With David Main third and four others in the first 20 positions, we gained a 99 points margin over the second team. In fact, our team of 12 was home before any other team had finished its six scoring men! Then to the much awaited English Championship of which we were the proud holders. On March 9th our lads travelled to Leamington Spa and had another battle royal with our famous Midland rivals, Birchfield Harriers. Our team finished in the first 24 positions, and after a breath-taking adding up of the scores we were acclaimed winners with a ten-points margin. We are indeed truly the Champion Club. Of individuals, Tom Carter deserves our thanks and praise for the successful training and nursing of his team, also of course for his own brilliant running. It was a cause for general regret that Tom did not get another International vest. Len Herbert, by finishing seventh, was awarded an England vest and we congratulate Len on adding his name to the distinguished company of Belgravians so honoured in the past. It is of interest to recall them: A. Allum, H.E.Footer (3), A.W.Penny (3), C.T.Carter, J.Ginty and E.S.Stimpson. Pat Parker qualified for an England vest but chose to run for Ireland. David Main has also entered the ranks of the Internationals as he also ran for Ireland. ..... and 40 years ago MARCH 1931 ------ Arthur Allum merits the congratulations of all upon his splendid running in the Southern Cross-country Championship. He is the first Belgrave man to finish in the first three of this race, and it should not be long befores he improves, even upon this. Since writing the above Arthur has very nearly exhausted our supply of superlatives by finishing fifth in the National Championship, and so earned a place in the English team. The Club's best wishes go with Arthur to Ireland. In the International Championship decided at Baldoyle Racecourse, Dublin, Arthur Allum finished ninth in the actual race and was the sixth Englishman to score. Thus England scored a very easy win and we are proud to have supplied one of the victorious team. WITH THE WALKERS: Our scratch teams have continued in the victorious vein and have brought the number of successive wins to eight - without doubt a unique feat in the history of road walking. The successes are as follows:- R.W.A.'7', Enfield '7', Highgate '7', Belgrave '7', S.W.C. Godstone & Back, Cambridge '7', L.C.C. Tramways '7', Ashcombe '10'. Len Fletcher and Frank Elson have assisted the Club in seven of these eight wins; Tommy Green six times; Fred Rickards on three occasions; Harold King, Frank Thorn and Ted Saunders each twice; and Joe King and Jack Field once each. items.label: June 1971
items.h: Winning for three-quarters of the distance
items.sum: Short report of a 3-1 soccer defeat by Buckingham Palace staff, refereed by Tom Carter.
items.s: Winning for three-quarters of the distance Short report of a 3-1 soccer defeat by Buckingham Palace staff, refereed by Tom Carter. Winning for three-quarters of the distance The snag with the soccer match against Buckingham Palace staff was that referee Tom Carter neglected to bring the game to an end while we were still winning. A beautiful first-half goal gave us a lead that we held into the last quarter of the game, then the Palace - with our own Lionel Mann playing a starring role - struck, and we ended up on the wrong side of a 3-1 scoreline. A fitting lead-up to the Cup-final all the same. items.sum: Report of Belgrave's second place in the Surrey cross-country championship on Wimbledon Common, with Gerry North sixth and Guy Monnet 14th, plus Belgrave results in the Middlesex, Bedfordshire and Wiltshire championships.
items.s: SECOND PLACE IN SURREY CROSS-COUNTRY - Wimbledon, January 2, 1971 Report of Belgrave's second place in the Surrey cross-country championship on Wimbledon Common, with Gerry North sixth and Guy Monnet 14th, plus Belgrave results in the Middlesex, Bedfordshire and Wiltshire championships. CROSS-COUNTRY SECOND PLACE IN SURREY CROSS-COUNTRY - Wimbledon, January 2, 1971 Even with a great breakthrough by Guy Monnet, who finished a magnificent 14th in 41m. 57s., we were still kept out of first place in the Surrey Cross-Country Championship, over 7-miles of fog-bound Wimbledon Common. Gerry North finished in sixth place in 40m. 12s., just under a minute behind the winner, Bob Holt of Hercules Wimbledon. Trevor Hart was just one place in front of Guy, who was followed by John Thresher, 18th, and a back-to-form Alan Black, 20th, with Tony Fairclough making up the scoring six. John Bicourt was none too fresh after a run in the Nos Galan meeting in Wales the previous night. In the Middlesex championship , at Cockfosters, Laurie O'Hara was 20th in 43m.53s., and Pat O'Connor 21st in 43m. 58s. Lionel Mann was third in the Bedfordshire championship in 32m. 30s., and in the Wiltshire, Tony Brien was second in 39m. 32s., just one second behind the winner, J. Maskell, of Swindon. 1. R. items.sum: Report of the Inter-Counties cross-country at Leicester, where Gerry North helped Surrey to the title, with other Belgrave runners for their counties and Surrey's youths third.
items.s: INTER-COUNTIES Leicester, January 16, 1971 Report of the Inter-Counties cross-country at Leicester, where Gerry North helped Surrey to the title, with other Belgrave runners for their counties and Surrey's youths third. INTER-COUNTIES Leicester, January 16, 1971 Gerry helps Surrey to title Lancashire went to Leicester as hot favourites for the inter-counties' title, but as at Leicester four years ago, it was Surrey that ran away with the race - and helping them was our own Gerry North. Once again, Gerry showed his capacity to rise to the occasion, covering the near 7½-miles course in 35m. 42s., against 35m. 04s. by the winner, Trevor Wright, of Hallamshire and Yorkshire. Lionel Mann produced a sound run, as usual, to finish 84th in 37m. 06s. for Bedfordshire and Huntingdonshire. But ahead of him was our rapidly improving R.A.F. runner, Tony Brien, who carried Wiltshire colours to 67th place in 36m. 48s. Turning his attention to the mud, also, was our road running member Brian Joines, who finished 287th in 42m. 55s. for Oxfordshire. Apart from winning the Senior race, Surrey took third place in the Youths' event. Three Belgrave runners finished in the Country's scoring four - Bill Curtin coming home tenth in 18m. 58s. - some 32s. behind the winner- while Peter Carton was one place further back in 18m. 59s., and Tony Binda was the third Surrey man, with 26th place in 19m. 32s. John Stow also won his County colours, but was going through a rough patch when this race came round, and finished 99th in 21m. 11s., nothing like the performance we know he can produce. items.s: MACHER SHIELD Report and results of the Macher Shield club 10-mile cross-country championship at Wimbledon, won by Lionel Mann from Guy Monnet, with John Kelly winning the handicap. MACHER SHIELD Mann makes it five in Macher Shield - Wimbledon, January 23, 1971 Lionel Mann won his fifth official club championship of 1970-71 when he added the 10-mile title to his bag after a hard struggle with surprise packet Guy Monnet. Just for good measure, Lionel is also the club darts champ. Guy had been showing good form earlier this winter, and had really come to the fore in the Surrey championship three weeks earlier. In his first ten-miler of the winter, he showed that he was good for the distance, pushing Lionel from start to finish, and being squeezed into second place by a mere five seconds. John Kelly ran himself into a place in the Southern team, and was a deserving winner of the handicap. Scratch time Handicap Handicap time Handicap place 1. L. Mann 58m.51s. 1.15 57.36 6 2. G. items.s: Lionel Mann rescues the "B" team - Ruislip, January 30, 1971 Lionel Mann won the Ruislip race ahead of Pat O'Connor, helping a short-handed Belgrave "B" team to second place behind Oxford City. Lionel Mann rescues the "B" team - Ruislip, January 30, 1971 It was a good thing for our "B" team that first-teamers Lionel Mann and Pat O'Connor wanted a run-out at Ruislip, because of our genuine "B" team men only five made the journey. Lionel won the race from Pat O'Connor, with our road running member Brian Joines taking fourth place for Oxford City, his first-claim club over the country. Denis McKeown was 10th, Charlie Henn 14th, John Blair-Fish 20th, John V. Baker 24th, and John Johnson - playing hookey from the walking section - 26th. Times, unfortunately are not available. The team result is available, however, and scoring six-a-side, we were second, with 71 points, to Oxford City's 37, with Hillingdon third, on 84. items.label: June 1971
items.sum: Report and results of the Southern cross-country championship at Parliament Hill, where Belgrave took team second behind Reading and Gerry North finished fourth.
items.s: A SOUTHERN SILVER! Report and results of the Southern cross-country championship at Parliament Hill, where Belgrave took team second behind Reading and Gerry North finished fourth. A SOUTHERN SILVER ! BELS HIT FORM AT PARLIAMENT HILL Having slipped out of a place in the Southern Cross-Country in 1970 for the first time in several years, the Bels bounced back into form in the Parliament Hill mud this February, with a highly encouraging second place. Reading romped away with the title - helped by our old friend Dick Piotrowski in 37th place. Their total of 137 points went quite unchallenged. Our second place was a nail-biting business, however. With 221 points we had a margin of only 4 points to spare over the up-and-coming Hillingdon side, and only 5 to spare over Brighton & Hove. It was pleasing to be the first Surrey side - ahead of the titleholders, Hercules Wimbledon - and also to take the Oddling Smee Cup, as the first Surrey club to close in a full team of 12 men. The most heartwarming sight of the afternoon for Belgrave supporters was that of the flying figure of Gerry North, who made a thrilling attempt to recapture his title - and had he not been hit by his old enemy, the stitch, might well have done so. As it was, his fourth place in 46m. 55s. gave us a magnificent start, and with another three men in the first 34, and John Thresher in 42nd, it was a good day for the Bels. John Bicourt made a good recovery from his disappointing show in the Surrey, to finish 34th in 48m. 55s. Lionel Mann was two places ahead of John, with 32nd in 48m. 53s., but both these stalwarts were outpaced by that rising star Tony Brien - 30th in 48m. 48s. A below par Tony Fairclough made up the scoring six - in 79th place. Pat O'Connor's 82nd place was closer to his real ability than some of his other performances lately, while it was good to see Bill Dance down from Yorkshire to carry the Belgrave colours again. Trevor Hart must have been disappointed with 123rd, but not as disappointed as Guy Monnet - the most sharply improved runner in the club - who could have expected to finish at least 100 places higher than his 151st. A different Guy might have been seen, however, had it not been for a poisoned tooth. John Kelly was rewarded for his recent improvement with a first run in the Southern. items.s: BRIEN RUNS FOR R.A.F. Tony Brien's runs for the R.A.F.: second to Roger Clark against Wales at Barry, and eighth in a 3,000m at Motspur Park one place behind John Bicourt. BRIEN RUNS FOR R.A.F. Tony Brien was a prominent member of R.A.F. cross-country teams last winter. At Barry on January 9, he helped his side to beat Wales, when he finished second to England international Roger Clark in 26m. 57s., the same time as the winner's. Tony also showed some useful track form at Motspur Park on May 12, in a match between London University, the R.A.F., Borough Road College, and Middlesex, finishing eighth in the 3,000m. in 8m. 44s., one place behind our own John Bicourt, who clocked 8m. 43.2s., competing as a guest. LEAGUE FIFTH SUCCESSIVE SUCCESS IN SURREY LEAGUE - Coulsdon, February 20, 1971 The Surrey Cross-Country League title was well set up for the Bels to take after the first three of the season's four fixtures. The last race, however, provided the club with yet another sweeping victory - to put the seal on our fifth successive League title. For many of our men this run was mainly important as a warm-up for the National two weeks later, and it was good to see Tony Fairclough making more like his real self, and Alan Black also showing up well. National Cross-Country Championships Oh dear, what a calamity! at the Royal Norfolk Agricultural Showground, Norwich, March 6, 1971 Hopes raised at the Southern took a sharp plunge at Norwich. Twelfth place was our worst in the National for a good few years. But that's the way it goes. Lose a few seconds in the National and you lose a lot of places. We still have the men to get a high placing next year - six men in a hundred is a fair target to aim at. And it only wants a bit of application - not 200 miles a week. This year we only managed one in a hundred - Gerry North battling magnificently against a bad cold - and ignoring his doctor's advice to give the race a miss - to finish 18th. Otherwise, our lads were solidy below par. And with only eight finishers, we didn't even challenge for the Charles Otway Cup - awarded to the first team (nine to score) outside the first three in the Championship. m. s. m. s. 1. D. items.s: ROAD RELAYS Review of Belgrave's 1971 road relay season (Thames Valley, Southern, Brighton Seafront and Hornsey relays) with team results from Cranford (fifth), the Brighton Front Relay and the Hornsey A.C. Relay (third and sixth). ROAD RELAYS It cannot be said that 1971 was a vintage year for Belgrave in the road relay field. But the bright aspects are the emergence of our junior stars as forces in the senior ranks, and the continuing enthusiasm to be found in our ranks. Setbacks are inevitable from time to time, but they can also be the springboard for greater things. It seemed that the disappointment of the National cross-country performance was still hanging over us when he went to Cranford for the annual Thames Valley relay, and fifth was the best we could manage. Colin Pearson's 13th place for the"B" team on the first leg was enough to win him his place in the team for ths following week's Southern relay, and there were promising runs from Alan Black and Chris Steer, but otherwise little of note. Setting aside the two championships, however, from this point our form seemed to be improving. Fresh,if that is the word, from seventh in the Southern race , we went to Brighton on April 3 for the Seafront race, and this time we managed fourth place. John Stow showed that he was recovering the form that makes him one of our brightest junior stars, with a good clocking on the first stage for the "A" team, and it was nice to see Derek Crooks turning out for us again. Then, at Hornsey the following week, it was up to fourth place, with our junior runners again making their presence felt, and another good run from Chris Steer. Gerry North, unfortunately, was by this time feeling the full effects of his recent illness - which had possibly cost him his place in the international cross country team. items.s: BITTER NEWS FOR THIRSTY BELS Former relay runner Len Adams has left insurance to become landlord of the Malden Manor pub near Motspur Park. BITTER NEWS FOR THIRSTY BELS Our old friend Len Adams has given up the insurance business to become Mine Host at the Malden Manor pub, opposite Malden Manor Station - just a few javelin throws from Motspur Park. You don't have to go back all that many years (only to the early nineteen-fifties) to remember Len as a stylish last leg man in the London to Brighton Relay. Len still looks good for a sub-fifteen minutes 3-miles - or at least for two-miles in drinking-up time. It may seem a long jump from insurance to licensed victualling, but Len points out that he's always been interest in - er, drinking. A warm welcome from Len and Eve awaits all Bels at the Malden Manor. Road relay trial - Hayes, Kent - April 24, 1971 With a week to go our National Road Relay team was far from picking itself, and we were grateful to Blackheath for putting on a special trial at their Hayes headquarters. Blackheath and Hercules-Wimbledon each fielded one team of four, and we put out three. The course was a slightly longer version of the one used for the annual open Blackheath relay in September, and measured just over three miles. Our "A" team led on each lap, with our "B" team second on each, while our "C" finished fifth. Trials sometimes do something to sort out selection problems, but on this occasion the most important performance was put up by Guy Monnet, whose 15m. 06s. - slightly faster than the times returned by Tony Fairclough and Tony Binda - must have caused some headaches. items.sum: Stage-by-stage report and full team results of the National Road Relay at Sutton Coldfield, won by Birchfield, with Belgrave 14th.
items.s: National Relay Stage-by-stage report and full team results of the National Road Relay at Sutton Coldfield, won by Birchfield, with Belgrave 14th. National Relay BIRCHFIELD BACK - National Road Relay, Sutton Coldfield, May 1, 1971 If it was like old times to see old pals of the Brighton Road, Thames Valley, win the Southern Road Relay, it was doubly like old times to see our London-to-Brighton rivals of the nineteen-thirties, Birchfield, taking the National Relay title. But it was bad times for the Bels. With our Birmingham friends first in 4hrs. 10m. 58s., we were 4hrs. 21m. 00s. But just to show how fortunes fluctuate in this type of running, Southern winners Thames Valley were only 56s. ahead of us, in 12th place. On the same lines as the Southern event, the race consisted of a 5.6 miles leg and a 3.1 miles leg, covered alternately, to make a total distance over 52 miles. Hillingdon led at the end of the first lap, of 5.6 miles, and Coventry at the end of the each of the next 7 laps, except the fifth lap, when Tipton briefly took up the pace-making. Birchfield ended each of the last four laps at the front, but only after a great battle with the reigning champions, Godiva. Laurie O'Hara got us off to a promising start. Though only 14th, his 27m. 11s. was a good time for the distance, and kept us well in touch with the leaders. Only Trevor Hart of our men could get within half-a-minute of his clocking. At the end of the second stage, the outlook still looked promising. John Bicourt went round the shorter leg in a useful 15m. 23s., and gave us our best position of the day - eleventh. Bill Kerr was not at his best, however, on the third leg, falling to 16th, with a time of 27m. 58s. Peter Carton, just turned 18, came into the team, and gave a hint of things to come, returning 15m. 43s. to pick up one place. Pat O'Connor was a shadow of his real self on the next stage, dropping to 18th, with 28m. 27s. Gerry North was still fighting off the effects of his earlier illness, and took a short stage, rather than his customary long. He ran well in the circumstances, however, to cover his lap in 15m. 09s., and pull back two places. Next, it was Lionel Mann's turn, but not his day - a time of 27m. 55s. losing one place. Young Tony Binda had an unenviable task in his first race of this calibre - but he did well to hold his position and clock 15m. 52s. on the eighth stage. Bill Dance stayed in 17th place. with 28m. 05s., and about the only bright speck in the sky at this point was that we were at least ahead of that renowned road relay club, Portsmouth A.C. Tony Fairclough was again fit enough only for a shortage stage, but he caught the Cardiff man to put us in 16th place , clocking 15m. 59s. Trevor Hart remained in 16th place on the 11th lap, but he put in some good work (by the standards of the day), to return 27m. 38s., and provide Bill Curtin with something to go for on the last lap. Bill showed his senior teammates a thing or to, passing the Medway and Bristol runners on his way to 14th place, with 15m. 40s. Fastest laps: short (3.1 miles) - D. items.sum: Leg-by-leg report and results of the Southern Counties Road Relay at Wimbledon, won by Thames Valley, with Belgrave seventh and Dave Bedford breaking the lap record.
items.s: Southern Road-Relay Leg-by-leg report and results of the Southern Counties Road Relay at Wimbledon, won by Thames Valley, with Belgrave seventh and Dave Bedford breaking the lap record. Southern Road-Relay BEDFORD STAGGERS THE CROWD - BELGRAVE STAGGER Wimbledon, March 27, 1971 We are used to success in our own Southern Counties 51-miles Road Relay at Wimbledon - with four wins and one second in the five races held up to this year. We had expected to be pressed to win a place this year - with clubs like Reading and Hillingdon beginning to hit the high spots. But seventh was a bit below our hopes. Sometimes in a relay of this kind it is a blow-out on one or two legs that does the damage. But this was not case here. None of our men ran outstandingly badly, but most were half a minute or so slower than they would be on top form. And that adds up to quite a lot of minutes altogether. Our old pals of the Brighton Road, Thames Valley pulled one out of the bag to win the race in 4hrs. Olm. Ols., after pre-race favourites Reading had made most of the running, while particular congratulations, perhaps, should go to Cambridge Harriers, third, and Medway, sixth. As usual, the race consisted of a 5½-mile lap and a 3½-mile, covered alternately. First leg: John Bicourt took the first stage (5½-miles) for us, and set the tone for most of our men, with a modest 13th place in 24m. 55s. - our local rivals, Hercules Wimbledon heading the field in 23m. 51s. Second leg: Colin Pearson made a sound, if unspectacular debut in this class of competition, and was unlucky in having to run on his own for most of his stage - holding 13th place with 16m. 49s., while Reading moved into the lead. Third leg: On a better day, Lionel Mann might have done much to strengthen our position, but as it was he fell back a place in clocking 25m. 07s. Portsmouth took a turn in the lead. Fourth leg: Bill Kerr pulled us back up to 13th, but can't have been very pleased with his time of 16m. 16s. Reading went back to the front. Fifth leg: Gerry North was still suffering from the illness which hit him ahead of the National cross-country, but showed his usual dermination in covering his lap in 24m. 18s., our best of the day for the long stage, and can count himself unlucky to pick up only one place on balance. Gerry actually passed two men, but was himself passed by a a shatteringly on-form Dave Bedford, who took Shaftesbury from 16th to 10th with a time of 22m. 20s - cutting no less than 54s. of the lap record previously held by Bob Holt of Hercules Wimbledon (if the 23.12 by Medway's Dick Newble, who finished Bedford's stage in second place is left out of account). Sixth leg: Bill Curtin made an impressive entry at this level of senior competition, and from this point our fortunes can be said to have been on the mend. Bill clocked our second fastest short-stage time of 15m. 55s, and moved us up to tenth. Seventh leg: Pat O'Connor - teetering on the brink of a return to top form - picked up another place, with 24m. 45s. Eighth leg: Tony Fairclough made our position look even more respectable, taking us up to eighth. A time of 16m. 02s is not the vintage Fairclough, but Tony clearly ran up to the limits of his fitness. Ninth leg: Trevor Hart's 24m. 30s. was our second-fastest long-leg time - but Trevor still fell back to tenth. Such are the fortunes of war. Thames Valley took the lead. Tenth leg: Bill Dance gave us a boost by pulling us up to seventh, with 15m. 57s., while Reading recovered the lead. Eleventh leg: Laurie O'Hara held our seventh position, though he might have hoped for better than 24m. 58s. Thames Valley took a 12s lead over Reading. items.s: ROAD RUNNING Round-up of Belgrave's early-1971 road racing, including the win in the Jim Peters Trophy at the Mitcham "15" and Bill Weller's five-mile win at Hastings, with results from Mitcham and other road races from February to May 1971 (results continue on page 18 after the Wimbledon Cup report). ROAD RUNNING After the usual spring warm-up, the road running season is now getting into full stride (the full stride, of course, comes on July 17, when we hold the annual Belgrave "20"). Our boys have not been setting the world on fire, but with the National Road Relay championship not being held until the first of May, they have not been firing on all cylinders in the straight road races. Back in January, however, we showed our potential, by winning the Jim Peters Trophy in the Mitcham "15". Lionel Mann, as usual, has been prominent, and Trevor Hart has been showing handy form, as has Pat O'Connor. At the same time, Bill Weller has done enough to indicate what a tower of strength he is going to be in our teams when he has qualified to run first-claim for us in the autumn. Bill, in fact, has been our only winner so far - with first place over five miles at Hastings. Results: Mitcham "15", Mitcham, January 9, 1971 (run over 25 kilometres - 15m. 940 yds.) items.sum: Lionel Mann won the Wimbledon Cup 5¾-mile club road championship by one second from Laurie O'Hara, his sixth current club title, with Bert Stroud winning the handicap; full scratch and handicap results and a photo of the field.
items.s: WIMBLEDON CUP for Mann Lionel Mann won the Wimbledon Cup 5¾-mile club road championship by one second from Laurie O'Hara, his sixth current club title, with Bert Stroud winning the handicap; full scratch and handicap results and a photo of the field. WIMBLEDON CUP for Mann Double hat-trick for Lionel - Wimbledon Cup, Wimbledon, March 13, 1971 If Lionel Mann wants to go on adding to his list of Belgrave championships, he may before long have to start learning the pole-vault. (There is no club pole vault championship, of course, but it may be necessary to invent one). Lionel started off the spring road season the way he finished the way he has been going for the best part of a year - with his sixth current club championship in the 5¾mile road run. Just for the record, Lionel's sideboard now boasts the Lady Fell Shield (20-miles road), the Griffen Cup (5,000m. track), the Tom Carter Trophy (10,000m. track), the Blackstaffe Shield (7 miles c.c.), the Macher Shield (10 miles c.c.), and the Wimbledon Cup, not to mention the Denmark Pot (darts championship). As in the 10-mile c.c., Lionel only just got home, however, and this time he had a margin of only 1s. to spare over Laurie O'Hara. Trevor Hart showed some improved form, in third place, while youths Bill Curtin, Peter Carton, Tony Binda and John Stow added to their growing reputations with fourth, sixth, seventh and twelfth, respectively. The race provided a nostalgic moment for youths' coach Ron Linstead, and some others with longer memories. Ron set a record for the 5¾ course in March, 1954, when he clocked up 28m. 24s., at the age of 18. Now after 17 years comes the Linstead coached Bill Curtin to clock 28m. 00s. - also at the age of 18. By and large, the results of the race were encouraging, after the disappointment of the National Cross-Country . Among a number of good performances was Colin Pearson's 8th place - which put him squarely in the running for the Southern Relay team. Colin only managed second place in the handicap, however - first place going to Bert Stroud, who obviously knows his way around a 10m. handicap. Good to see Pat Newell turning out again - and breaking 30m. yet once more. The 5¾-miles championship field, still hunched after one mile. items.s: HART RECOVERS MARATHON RECORD Trevor Hart regained the Belgrave marathon record with 2hrs. 22m. 50s. in the Maxol marathon, after Lionel Mann had taken it from him in the same race the previous year. HART RECOVERS MARATHON RECORD Trevor Hart first captured the Belgrave Harriers' marathon record when he clocked 2hrs. 25m. 58s. in last year's Polytechnic race from Windsor to Chiswick - lowering Barry Sawyer's 1963 time of 2hrs. 28m. 08s. But he held it only a few weeks, because Lionel Mann went up to Manchester for the Maxol marathon, and turned in 2hrs. 24m. 07s. Trevor, it seems, took a tip from Lionel, and had a crack at the Maxol himself this year - and recorded 2hrs. 22m. 50s. items.s: TRACK AND FIELD Track report previewing Belgrave's 1971 track season event by event, noting the reduced fixture list of four Trophy and three Southern League meetings and the likely runners at each distance. TRACK AND FIELD TRACK REPORT We come yet again to another Track Season. This year the Track Committee decided it would benefit the Club and the athletes concerned to withdraw from a couple of last years trophy meetings which were too long winded or we considered ourselves hopelessly out-classed. So compared with 1970's fixtures of seven Trophy meetings and three Southern League meetings, we have in 1971, four Trophy meetings and the three Southern League meetings. These we thought, were well within our capabilities of winning. That is providing we all get stuck in, as I'am sure you all will. It is fortunate that, at Belgrave, we have at our disposal a reasonable quantity of middle-distance and long-distance runners. Sprints it seems we have only a handful of representatives, but what we have are very useful indeed. The steeplechase seems to be our only setback. 100m - 200m. As we have not heard how fit JIM VIVIAN is, I can only say that STEVE WHITE who is the most promising sprinter we have , will be our main runner this year - when he is not competing for Oxford. He will have fine backing from LEE SULLIVAN, MICK MARSHALL, CLIFF BROOKS and CHARLIE GILLETT. 400m One of the weak spots, although I hope I'am proved wrong. MEL FORD will be our main runner but he will have good backimg from CHARLIE GILLETT and from a very promising MARTIN BLOICE who will I'am sure surprise us all. I must not forget our vice-captain PHILIP GEE, his usual help and eagerness is a good backing for any of these runners. On the sidelines will be DAVE [illegible]EES and CLIFF BROOKS while I cannot be certain of PHILIP SMITH'S fitness at the moment, if he knuckles down to hard training he will also be a useful substitute. 800m Again it seems MEL FORD will be our main contender here, with PETER CARTON. They have numerous runners to back them up notably JOHN BOARDMAN BILL CURTIN, DOUGLAS JARDINE, JOHN KELLY, and LIONEL MANN - training for a fast finishing marathon. Also very capable substitutes will be COLIN PEARSON and JIM RIMMER (saying "wait till the track season I'll show you") another useful youngster is RICHARD LANGLEY. 1500m It seems we have no problem here with JOHN THRESHER and evergreen BILL KERR (a Vet next year by the way) our main contenders. Others aiming to get into the team will be PETER CARTON, BILL CURTIN, JOHN STOW, JOHN BICOURT, LAURIE O'HARA and JIM RIMMER, who says he's fitter than ever("I'am doing my own training this year") and also ADRIAN MAJOR. 5000m Probably the strongest event we have. With great runners such as GERRY NORTH, JOHN THRESHER and BILL KERR to pick from. Good substitutes will be TONY FAIRCLOUGH, the galloping gourmets LIONEL MANN and GUY MONNET as well as TREVOR HART, JOHN BICOURT, LAURIE O'HARA, TONY BRIEN and ADRIAN MAJOR. I think we had better watch out for BRIAN GORMAN I believe he wants to be on the same level as Bill Kerr (both are Vets next year) and is doing 100 miles a week. I hope he can prove to us he is doing the right thing. 300m Steeplechase This year I'am afraid it looks as though this will be our weakest event, with JOHN BICOURT our only sub 9-minute man. ALAN BLACK will back him up and our "Ed" might also have to be called upon. JIM RIMMER and GERRY NORTH also had a go at this event last year to help the Club out and might also consider helping us out again. items.s: Field Event Report Field events report on the first track meeting at Battersea Park, the Southern League fixture dates for 1971, and news of members including a newly married Bob and Mel Ford and others stationed at Caterham Barracks. Field Event Report A cold day greeted our first track meeting at Battersea Park on 24th April, but what a fine start by Cliff Brooks and field events captain John Martin in the Shot Putt, both producing personal bests, over 40 feet and there is little doubt that even better performances are in store. Lee Sullivan also had a good start to the season in the Long Jump winning with 21' 7" and showing fine consistancy by clearing this exact distance on three of his attempts. It is always difficult to keep in contact with everyone during the winter with regard to training and it is hoped that after a solid winter's training, technique work is now in progress, if not for goodness sake start NOW, as we must win the Southern League and get back to the National League. We ought to be able to do it as we were ranked tenth in the N.U.T.S. rankings for 1970 season. Just remember these dates for the League fixtures. 22nd MAY at Ilford 3rd JULY at Enfield 21st AUGUST at Wimbledon Park 18th SEPTEMBER at Crystal Palace (QUALIFYING MEETING) These fixtures for Belgrave are the most important of the year so lets have the supreme effort and give the track and field sections the uplift it needs Bob Cou[illegible]lault, now a "married" man, is back in the ranks this year and is at present suffering from the effects of a broken nose, although I'am assured this happened during a football match and not a domestic match! Anyway, congratulations to Bob and to his wife. Mel Ford is in top form already judging by recent results and he has been invited to represent the Southern Counties in two forthcoming meetings in the 400m hurdles and in the 800m. Mel is now stationed at Caterham Barracks and I know he is finding duties clashing heavily with training sessions but I am convinced that Mel will produce some very fine performances in the 400m hurdles, 400m flat and 800m during the coming season. Also stationed at Caterham with Mel are Glyn Ratcliffe, Steve Inman and Keith Schofield. I hope that guard duties will not eliminate them from the League meetings. items.s: Boxing Day Track Meeting - Battersea Park - December 26, 1970 Report and results of the Boxing Day 2-miles and 120 yards handicaps at Battersea Park, won by Dave Harvey and Philip Smith (the text gives Chris Keavey's allowance as 560 yards, the table as 500 yards). Boxing Day Track Meeting - Battersea Park - December 26, 1970 Sixteen hardy souls gave their Christmas pud a miss (maybe) before turning out in traditional Boxing Day 2-miles handicap. Young Dave Harvey made good use of his 680 yards allowance to win fairly comfortably in 9m. 12s., a highly promising performance. Chris Keavey took second place, off 560 yards, while Guy Monnet raced through to third place, off 220. items.s: Taking off the covers - Battersea Park, April 24, 1971 Report and results of Belgrave's opening track meeting of 1971 at Battersea Park, where the Metropolitan Police won and Belgrave were second. Taking off the covers - Battersea Park, April 24, 1971 The wraps came off all that winter training, or some of it anyway, when we held our opening Track meeting at Battersea Part on the last Saturday in April. The meeting failed to give us a win - the Police, aided and abetted by our very own Frank Glass - made a fair cop. But there were some highly encouraging performances. These included some good sprinting from Cliff Brooks and Lee Sullivan, and some good long-jumping from the same pair. But pride of place undoubtedly went to the shot-putt, where Cliff shoved the benefit of technique training with a distance of 41' 4½", and John Martin was also over 40'. What a difference shot-putting like this could make to our chances in the big meetings. Back on the track, there signs of life returning to Track Captain Adrian Major, while in the 1,500m. Jim Rimmer and young Mark Clancy caught the eye. items.h: BANSTEAD COACHES TROPHY MEETING - Norbiton, May 1, 1971
items.sum: Report and Belgrave results from the Banstead Coaches Trophy meeting at Norbiton, where Belgrave finished fifth of six clubs and second in the 5,000m team race.
items.s: BANSTEAD COACHES TROPHY MEETING - Norbiton, May 1, 1971 Report and Belgrave results from the Banstead Coaches Trophy meeting at Norbiton, where Belgrave finished fifth of six clubs and second in the 5,000m team race. BANSTEAD COACHES TROPHY MEETING - Norbiton, May 1, 1971 This meeting covers senior, youths and junior events, and we achieved a fair spread of success, if not enough to challenge for the Trophy. Although we were well behind the first two teams, we were within a short shot-putt of taking third place of the six clubs, which is another way of saying were were fifth. Our assorted successes can be seen below, but it is worth pointing out that success cannot always be measured by position. Lee Sullivan was probably our outstanding senior competitor, but came up against some exceptionally hot competition in the 100m. and long-jump. It was good to see Paddy Breslin back in action in the junior events, and to see John Stow back in winning form, while there was a promising junior steeplechase from Mark Clancy. In the youths' events, Dave Harvey and Simon Holmes had good middle-distance wins, and weren't afraid to try their hand at field events either. Reg Hopkins cleared 5' 6" in the youths' high jump, but that is commonplace for him these days. Jimmy Rimmer is running with much more fire lately, and won the senior 1,500m. The senior track race providing the most excitement, however, was the 5,000m. team race. With the National Road Relay on at Sutton Coldfield, it looked for a long time as though we were not going to find a team, but a last minute entry by Charlie Walker saved the day. With a lap to go, we were in the hunt, but couldn't quite make it, in spite of good running by Guy Monnet, Charlie, and new member Bob Ker, who looks highly promising. items.label: June 1971
items.h: Cliff Brooks breaks Club Decathlon Record
items.sum: Cliff Brooks set a new club decathlon record of 6,016 points finishing eighth at Leicester on May 1/2, gaining an A.A.A. Grade-One standard.
items.s: Cliff Brooks breaks Club Decathlon Record Cliff Brooks set a new club decathlon record of 6,016 points finishing eighth at Leicester on May 1/2, gaining an A.A.A. Grade-One standard. Cliff Brooks breaks Club Decathlon Record Cliff Brooks looked good at the opening Track meeting, and at Leicester on May 1/2 he proved he was good, when he finished eighth in a decathlon competition with the new Club record score of 6,016 points. This gained Cliff an A.A.A. Grade-One standard, and a Club Honours Badge. Our one man trophy team showed particularly good form on the first day in the 100m. (11.2s.), long-jump (22' 1"), and high-jump (1.74m./5' 8½"). The shot-putt (12.10m./39' 8¼") and 400m. (52.3s.) also produced good marks. The second day's events in the decathlon are the ones in which Cliff perhaps has the most room for improvement - and with his basic ability, a bit of technique training in the pole-vault, discus and javelin is capable of making a radical difference to his score, as his recent improvement in the shot has indicated. His best on the Sunday was the 110m. hurdles in which he clocked 16.3s. In the discus Cliff accomplished 32.28m./105' 10¾", the pole vault 2.80m./9'2", the javelin 34.40m./112' 10¼", and the 1,500m. 4m. 53.8s. items.h: Surrey Championships - SURREY STEEPLECHASE TITLE FOR ALAN BLACK
items.sum: Report and Belgrave results from the Surrey Championships at Wimbledon Park on May 8/9, 1971, with titles for Alan Black (steeplechase), Cliff Brooks (decathlon, 5,913 points), Steve White (long jump), Bill Curtin, Mick Marshall, Peter Carton, Reg Hopkins, Stephen Crosbie, Dave Raffell and Dave Harvey.
items.s: Surrey Championships - SURREY STEEPLECHASE TITLE FOR ALAN BLACK Report and Belgrave results from the Surrey Championships at Wimbledon Park on May 8/9, 1971, with titles for Alan Black (steeplechase), Cliff Brooks (decathlon, 5,913 points), Steve White (long jump), Bill Curtin, Mick Marshall, Peter Carton, Reg Hopkins, Stephen Crosbie, Dave Raffell and Dave Harvey. Surrey Championships SURREY STEEPLECHASE TITLE FOR ALAN BLACK This year's Surrey championships produced some good Belgrave performances, both from established stars like Steve White and up-and-coming men like Philip Gee. One of the most pleasing performances, however, came from Alan Black, who has won a whole collection of second and third place medals in past 3,000m. steeplechase championships, and now ran off with the title. Well done, Alan. Cliff Brooks looked by breaking the Club Decathlon record for the second time this season, but faded a little on the second day of the competition. He still romped away with the championship though. A third senior title came through Steve White's win in the long-jump. University studies prevented Steve defending his 200m. championship, but in the long-jump he edged out the holder, Roy Gilfrin, of Camberley, by just ¾". Wil Wesch surrandered his 3,000m. walk title to in-form Paul Nihill, but in doing so helped his rival to a new world best performance. Bob Coates showed good form after a spell away from competition to take third place, and with Carl Lawton fourth and Dave DeBondi sixth, it was a pity there was no team race. Trevor Hart was second in the 10,000m. in a fair time, while Philip Gee was third in the 400m., and lost second place to former champion Nick Lovatt (Mitcham) only by inches. John Bicourt had a close battle for second place in the 5,000m. with Mike Fuller (Hercules Wimbledon), and although squeezed into third position, can be said to have run well, since he had been sixth in the 1,500m. less than an hour-and-a-half before. Mick Marshall, Philip Gee, Chris Martin and Lee Sullivan were third in the sprint relay, and it was particularly good to see Chris sporting a Belgrave vest again. In the junior 1,500m., there was a nerve-tingling late challenge from John Stow - showing some of his old fire - before Bill Curtin added this title to the 3,000m. he had won earlier. Mick Marshall took the junior 100m., and was third in the 200m., while Peter Carton won a strongly contested 800m. in good time. Reg Hopkins was a double winner in the youths' events, taking the pentathlon and the high-jump, while in this section, we also won the long-jump, through Stephen Crosbie, the shot-putt, through Dave Raffell, and the 800m., through fast-improving Dave Harvey. Stephen also finished third in the triple-jump, and Jim McAffee was third in the 1,500m. The Club had only a few representatives in the boys' events, but they look a promising bunch. R. Jenkins was fourth in the 80m. hurdles, and P. Crosbie fourth in the javelin, while Ian Gillings can look forward next year to showing a sharp improvement on this year's sixth place in his 1,500m. heat, a performance which does not reflect his full talent. The most disappointed man at the championships must have been Colin Pearson, who qualified for the 800m. final as the second of the two fastest losers - and didn't realise it. Colin turned up for the final, as a spectator. Laurie O'Hara was again among the medals in the Middlesex championships, taking third place in the 5,000m. items.s: ANOTHER FAIR COP Report and results of the inter-club meeting at Hurlingham Park on May 8, 1971, where Belgrave were second to the Metropolitan Police. ANOTHER FAIR COP The Met Police can always be relied on to put out a solid team, and at Hurlingham Park on May 8 they gave us a second hammering in a fortnight. But at least we were well clear of the other five teams. Jim Rimmer had a good win in the 800m. in 1m. 58.9s., and Guy Monnet took the 3,000m. in 8m. 50.4s., while Philip Gee gave our quarter-miling strength a boost when he won the 400m. in a personal best time of 51.0s. But the star of the meeting was junior member Mick Marshall, who took second place in the 100m. in 11.3s., second in the 200m. in 23.7s., second in the long-jump with a clearance of 20' 10", and second in the triple-jump with 39' 5". Philip also showed some useful 800m. form, while the "B" 3,000m. went to promising new member Tom McCormack - a man to watch. items.s: ONE-SIDED TRIANGLE Report and results of a three-club match at Battersea Park on May 19, 1971, won comfortably by Belgrave in both the senior and junior contests. ONE-SIDED TRIANGLE Battersea Park, May 19, 1971 If its possible to have a one-sided triangle, this was a fair example, as, with three clubs in the field, we took the first two places in each event except the 100m. Derek Glendinning gave us a sprint double, and our promising quarter-miler Martin Elliott won the 400m., while Philip Gee took 2m. 4.8s. off to show his half-miling potential. Colin got the better of Lionel in the 1,500m., and Adrian Major again made more like Adrian Major in the 3,000m. Tom McCormack's second place in the 3,000m. in 9m. 9.4s. deserves praise, as does a 2m. 5.4s. second place in the 800m. by another new member M. Hodge. John Martin was just under 40' in the shot-putt, while the question on everyone's lips after the long-jump was: Has Belgrave at last produced its answer to Bob Beamon? The junior match produced a more level (two-sided) contest, but a treble from Mick Marshall saw us comfortably home. items.s: Southern League - GOOD PERFORMANCES IN SOUTHERN LEAGUE - Ilford, May 22, 1971 Report and Belgrave results from the opening Southern League Division One fixture at Ilford, where Belgrave finished second to Enfield. Southern League GOOD PERFORMANCES IN SOUTHERN LEAGUE - Ilford, May 22, 1971 Our opening fixture in this season's Southern League (Division-One) competition, was a lot brighter than the National League qualifying competition last September. Our second place, behind the newly promoted Enfield team, put us well in the running for a place in this season's National League qualifying contest. But that apart, our lads put up a number of very good performances. Top of the list were Steve White and Glyn Ratcliffe. Steve fairly set the cinders flying in the 200m., in which he equalled his personal best of 21.7s. to score a clear win; and he also took the long-jump. Glyn was only just under 150' in winning the discus, and gave a dramatic performance in the shot, snatching a narrow victory with his last putt. For promising performances, however, the plum went to Peter Carton, who lowered his personal best to 1m. 53.5s. in finishing third in the 800m. Mick Marshall, with some good sprinting, and Reg Hopkins, top of the "B" high-jumpers at 5' 8". Busiest man of the afternoon, as is often the case, was Navy man Cliff Brooks, who figured in four events, as well as the sprint relay. Together with Army man Mel Ford, Cliff gave us a double in the 400m. hurdles. Arnold Bentt was only 1" away from first place in the high-jump, and clocked 17.1s. in the "B" high hurdles. Philip Gee showed what a force he is becoming over 400m., with a 51.5s. second place in the "B" 400m. In the "B" 800m., Jim Rimmer confirmed that he, too, is now a power to be reckoned with, clocking the same time as the winner. Paddy Breslin made a good job of deputising for our star steeplechasers. Paddy did not have a good winter, but with a run free of injury, he could soon be under 10m. in this event. Paddy is still in the junior ranks. Lee Sullivan is just out of them, and another up and coming athlete. In the "B" long-jump, he was edged into second place by just 1½". Derek Glendinning led the triple-jumpers, with 46' 3½" - over 18" ahead of the second man - and we hope to see him getting even closer to 50' before long. 100m. A 3. S. White 11.3s. B 3. M. items.sum: Steve White long-jumped 24' 0¾" to win for the combined Oxford and Cambridge team against Harvard and Yale at Crystal Palace, within 5" of John Mitchell's club record.
items.s: STEVE WHITE CLEARS 24' Steve White long-jumped 24' 0¾" to win for the combined Oxford and Cambridge team against Harvard and Yale at Crystal Palace, within 5" of John Mitchell's club record. STEVE WHITE CLEARS 24' Steve White has been going great guns in the long-jump this season, and it was no surprise when he cleared 24' 0¾" to win the event for a combined Oxford and Cambridge Universities team against Harvard and Yale at the Crystal Palace. This brought Steve to within 5" of John Mitchell's Club record of 24' 5¾", and can be measured, additionally, against the fact that only ten U.K. long-jumpers managed to clear 24' last season. In the 200m., in the same match, he was fourth in 22.5s. items.label: June 1971
items.h: BELS HELP LAMBETH TO VICTORY IN FRANCE
items.sum: Belgrave athletes helped Lambeth beat Vincennes and Castrop Rauxel in a match in France on May 1, with Steve White the star.
items.s: BELS HELP LAMBETH TO VICTORY IN FRANCE Belgrave athletes helped Lambeth beat Vincennes and Castrop Rauxel in a match in France on May 1, with Steve White the star. BELS HELP LAMBETH TO VICTORY IN FRANCE Belgravians made a strong contribution to a comfortable victory for Lambeth in France on May 1, when, with 174 points, they finished comfortably ahead of French opposition in the form of Vincennes (106), and German in the form of Castrop Rauxel. Steve White was Lambeth's star of the day, winning the 100m. in 10.8s. (wind assisted), and then took the long-jump, with a personal best (since improved) of 23' 4¾". To round off the day, Steve contributed a 50.3s. 400m. leg to help his side to victory in the 4x400m. relay in 3m. 25.5s. Adrian Major was third in the 3,000m. in 9m. 13.2s. Also selected for the senior events was John Martin - a fitting reward for his recent improvement. In the under-18 events, the Bels came out with two winners, Mick Marshall being timed at a wind-assisted 10.9s. in the 100m., and Martin Bloice at 29.7s. in the 250m. items.h: INTER-COUNTIES - Victory for Surrey in Inter-Counties Championship - Leicester, May 28/30
items.sum: Surrey won the Inter-Counties Championship at Leicester, with Belgrave contributions from Wil Wesch, John Bicourt and Lionel Mann (for Beds and Hunts).
items.s: INTER-COUNTIES - Victory for Surrey in Inter-Counties Championship - Leicester, May 28/30 Surrey won the Inter-Counties Championship at Leicester, with Belgrave contributions from Wil Wesch, John Bicourt and Lionel Mann (for Beds and Hunts). INTER - COUNTIES Victory for Surrey in Inter-Counties Championship - Leicester, May 28/30 Surrey scored a surprise win in the Inter-Counties' Championship at Leicester over the Spring Bank Holiday weekend - by a clear 20 points, with 70 points to Yorkshire's and Middlesex's 50. Contributing to Surrey's victory was Wil Wesch, who took fourth place in the 10,000m. walk on the Saturday in 45m. 02.2s., and third in the 3,000m. walk on the Monday in 12m. 33.4s. John Bicourt was selected to run for Surrey in the steeplechase, but missed his train and the race. John was, however, brought into the 5,000m. as deputy for Bob Holt, of Hercules Wimbledon - only to finish an off-key 21st in 15m. 03s. Lionel Mann carried Beds and Hunts colours into 16th place in the 20-miles road race in 1hr. 47m. 17s. items.s: ALAN BLACK NEARS BEST Alan Black was third in the steeplechase for Surrey against Loughborough Colleges and London University at Motspur Park on May 26, with Steve White and John Bicourt also competing. ALAN BLACK NEARS BEST Alan Black wasted little time in improving on his Surrey championship winning performance. At Motspur Park on May 26, Alan took third place in the 3,000m. steeplechase in 9m. 21.8s. in helping Surrey to defeat Loughborough Colleges and London University. On this sort of form, Alan is threatening to lower his personal best of 9m. 13.2s., set up in 1967. An attack of 'flu, unfortunately, kept him out of the Southern championships. But there is still a good part of the season left for an attack on the 9-minute barrier - something which has long been within Alan's capability. Also representing Surrey in the Motspur Park fixture was Steve White, who clocked 22.5s. for second in the 200m., and cleared 21' 6¾" for second in the long-jump. John Bicourt ran as a guest in the 1,500m., and returned 3m. 55.7s. as an unofficial third. Alan Black Alan Black third in 3,000m steeplechase, 9m. 21.8s.; personal best 9m. 13.2s. items.s: WALKING - BELGRAVE OPEN '7' November 28th - Wimbledon Report and results of the 1970 Belgrave Open 7 miles walk at Wimbledon, won in record time by Phil Embleton of Metropolitan Walking Club from Wilf Wesch, with Belgrave winning the team race. WALKING BELGRAVE OPEN '7' November 28th - Wimbledon Our correspondent has seen some impressive performances on this severe 7 Mile course which is generally reckoned to be at least one minute long. 1970's race, the 51st in the history, was to provde a brilliant win for the young Metropolitan Walking Club Phil Embleton. The way he streaked away from our own Wilf Wesch was a wonderful sight for those who appreciate fast walking at its best. For the first lap Wilf was in close attendance and with the hills to come Belgrave supporters could be foregiven for thinking that Wilf's extra strength would prove conclusive over the second lap. But Phil had other ideas and moving down Copse Hill he unleashed a magnificent burst of speed walking which carried him nearly 200 yards clear of Wilf who was himself nearly 2 minutes ahead of Lightman. Embleton came home to win in a new record time with Wilf some 43 seconds adrift but also very impressive. Recent team performances had been disappointing for our boys but on their own course there was no mistake, Carl Lawton had a steady race but John Moullin and a much improved Barry Ingarfield were well to the fore to give Belgrave victory by 9 points from the Basildon squad. Once again Jack and Joan Goswell worked miracles with the results, thanks to Bill Ashford whose kitchen is much preferred to the public bar of the Swan as the Open '7' Administrative HQ. Report and results of the Metropolitan Police Open 7 walk on January 9, 1971, a bad day for Belgrave with Wilf Wesch disqualified and Barry Ingarfield pulled, though Carl Lawton set a personal best in fifth. POLICE '7' January 9th 1971 - Metropolitan Police Open '7'. The first race after Christmas is always full of upsets but for Belgrave this was a bad day. Wilf Wesch was deservedly removed from the reckoning after some 2 miles had been covered. Wilf was seeking to establish a lead at the time and in the manner of a distance runner seeking greater speed his stride tends to shorten. His strike is one of the fastest in the world so that any shortening of the stride throws him off. Less excusable was Barry Ingarfield who put paid to any chances the team may have had when he too was pulled. Carl Lawton once again excelled with a personal best which put him among the really fast boys and ahead of Commonwealth Bronze Medallist Bill Sutherland. items.s: CLUB '10' January 23rd - Belgrave 10 Mile Championship and Junior '5'. Report and results of the Belgrave 10 miles walking championship and junior 5 miles on January 23, 1971, where Wilf Wesch retained the Murphy Shield and police cadet Whitehead won the junior race. A photograph of walkers in the race, taken by Ron Linstead, is printed on page 30. CLUB '10' January 23rd - Belgrave 10 Mile Championship and Junior '5'. As expected Wilf Wesch had little trouble retaining the Murphy Shield. His 74:26 done without exertion shows just how far he has come since last year when he won the title, with all stops out, only 30 seconds faster. Carl Lawton finished a strong second with Alan Callow pushing him has most of the way. John Moullin ducked under 80 and hed[illegible] of Barry Ingarfield by six seconds to take the third place medal. In the Junior the holder, Paul Duckett, was suprised to find the you police cadet Whitehead well ahead. This police boy, introduced by John Bromley could well turn in some useful performances in the future. Result: Match versus Police: Junior '5' Dave King (13), Ray Hall (34), Pat Duncan (54) & John Bromley (45) look as though they've spotted the cameraman. February 13th - Battersea Park - GLC '10' This race is becoming one of the major races of the south with all those either living or working in the Greater London Area eligible to take part. Belgrave suffered when Wilf Wesch was pulled while disputing the lead with Shuan Lightman but this gave Carl Lawton the chance to excell as he pulled back Lightman from over a minute to just 30 seconds at the finish. Dave King was another to come out but Ray Hall, scenting medals, was off like a rocket to make up the loss anchoring Belgrave to a second team position 6 points behind old rivals Surrey. February 27th - County '10' Mile Championships Tragedy struck in the Surrey when Wilf Wesch, last year's winner missed his train leaving Ray Hall to close the Belgrave four in behind Surrey Walking Club. Carl Lawton confirmed his recent strong form with a fine win of just 3 seconds over the tenacious Ken Carter of Surrey. Result: Team: In the Middlesex Championship Barry Ingarfield recorded a sharp 77:43 in 4th Pos while in the Sussex race Pat Duncan was 9th in 85:59 "It's fatal to walk when the Brighton running squad are out" said our man after the race! A notable absentee from the Surrey race was Paul Nihill who was returning a World best 69:00 for 10 miles in the Isle of Man. Second place was taken by Belgrave's Alan Callow in 74:50. In the Metropolitan Police '10' Mile championship Brian Ward finished 4th in 86:54 and Doug Fotheringham 8th in 89:29. items.sum: Report and results of the RWA National 10 miles walk at Redditch, where Belgrave narrowly retained the team title and Phil Embleton beat Paul Nihill, with Wilf Wesch fifth.
items.s: National 10m - March 20th - Redditch - RWA National 10 Miles Championship Report and results of the RWA National 10 miles walk at Redditch, where Belgrave narrowly retained the team title and Phil Embleton beat Paul Nihill, with Wilf Wesch fifth. National 10m March 20th - Redditch - RWA National 10 Miles Championship In one of the closest races yet Belgrave only clinshed the team race in the closing stages when Ian Brooks of Surrey Walking Club retired with just over a mile to go. Before that there was never more than a few points in it as our boys battled for the vital points. From the start it was Nihill and Embleton with the young Essex boy really pulling out all the stops to bring the European Champion to his first defeat in an incredible run of nearly four years. Wilf Wesch, the reigning champion, was concentrating on staying safely in the race and avoiding any possible trouble he finished a comfortable fifth. Behind him Carl Lawton and Alan Callow were not quite their best but the reliable Ray Middleton kept going steadily to ensure that Belgrave retained the title. Barry Ingarfield and Dave McMullen both walked good races, prepared to shoulder the burden if necessary. Belgrave men were also prominent in the county race with Wilf and Carl featuring in Surrey's 2nd position and Alan Callow scoring for Lancashire who finished 3rd. President Alf Harley was well pleased with his first national win! Result 1. P.Embleton MWC 69:29 54. J.Moullin 81:58 2. P.Nihill SWC 71:42 56. D.MCMullen 81:59 3. R.Wallwork Lancs 72:49 94. items.h: National 20 m - BACK TO THE DRAWING BOARD
items.sum: Report and results of the National 20 miles walk at Sheffield, won by Paul Nihill in a world best, with Wil Wesch sixth and Belgrave third team behind Surrey W.C. and Royal Sutton Coldfield.
items.s: National 20 m - BACK TO THE DRAWING BOARD Report and results of the National 20 miles walk at Sheffield, won by Paul Nihill in a world best, with Wil Wesch sixth and Belgrave third team behind Surrey W.C. and Royal Sutton Coldfield. National 20 m BACK TO THE DRAWING BOARD National 20-miles, Sheffield, June 12. 1971 As was to be expected, we made a much better showing in the national 20-mile[illegible] than we did in the 20-kilometres, but it still looked as though team manager Pat Duncan and captain Carl Lawton could do with a bit more brake horse power. It is true that we were without Ray Middleton and Len Duquemin, who were on the Continent for the European Postmen's Championship, while Carl Lawton was not fully recovered from the stomach upset acquired on his Bucharest trip, and Alan Callow had the sort of day that everyone has from time-to-time but nobody wants in National championship. But even so, Surrey, with a score of 23, looked very strong, with four in the first 11 (individual scoring). The race was a triumph for Paul Nihill, as well as his club? Surrey W.C. Paul clocked a world best time of 2hrs. 30m. 35s., which gives our up-and-coming youngsters something to aim at, and left him almost five minutes ahead of the second man, former Commonwealth champion Ron Wallwork (Lancs. W.C.). Last year's winner, our very own Wil Wesch, was sixth. This may seem pretty small beer for Wil, but it represents a good performance. Our man has just taken over the management of an hotel in Bloomsbury, and he'd spent the previous night dealing with a series of crises which had left him short on sleep, which is not a good preparation for 20-miles. items.sum: Notes on Carl Lawton's unlucky first Great Britain 20 km in Bucharest, Ray Hall retiring in the Stock Exchange London to Brighton, and Belgrave walkers in the Barking-Southend.
items.s: International honour for Lawton Notes on Carl Lawton's unlucky first Great Britain 20 km in Bucharest, Ray Hall retiring in the Stock Exchange London to Brighton, and Belgrave walkers in the Barking-Southend. International honour for Lawton Carl Lawton walked brilliantly in the National 20-kilometres, and clearly deserved his first selection to represent Britain in a race abroad - competing over 20-kilos in Bucharest on May 16. But for poor Carl, it was an unhappy start on his international career. Like many a likely lad before him, he was plagued on a trip to this part of Europe by stomach trouble, and obviously it was only his guts that enabled him to finish at all. He is reported to have covered his last 5-kilometres in a nifty 44m. Although his first ten kilos took only about 51m., his time for the full distance, in 36th place, was 124m. Never mind, Carl, you may rue the trip, but don't get a mania about it. Another Bel to have an unhappy time on a long journey was Ray Hall, who - as the reigning Stock Exchange 25 miles champion - turned out in the Stock Exchange London to Brighton, and was then forced to retire. But we still reckon Ray is good for a good 'un in the 50 kilos. Come the Barking-Southend, our first man home was John Morris, tenth in 5hrs. 42m. 35s., with Doug Fotheringham not far behind in 12th place (5hrs. 48m. 35s.). April 17th - Wimbledon - Belgrave 20 Miles Walking Championship In trying conditions Wilf Wesch dominated this race from start to finish and never looked even tired by the effort of recording an excellent 2:39:07. Carl and Ray Middleton were never far apart with Ray just failing to catch a weary Lawton up Lauriston Road. Barry Ingarfield started fast but faded over the second half while Dave DeBondi celebrated his return to fitness by walking the last 10 miles nearly five minutes faster than his first 10. Great to see Len Duquemin out again if only for 10 Miles. The 1971 Stock Exchange 25 mile champ Ray Hall called it a day at the end of the second lap while our latest father Bob Coates was content to stroll round - obviously missing the comforting handle of the pram. items.sum: The editor reproduces the walking secretary's pre-championship comment on Belgrave's strength, then reports the National 20 km at Luton where Belgrave were an unaccustomed fifth and Surrey Walking Club took the title.
items.s: The Editor writes on walking: The editor reproduces the walking secretary's pre-championship comment on Belgrave's strength, then reports the National 20 km at Luton where Belgrave were an unaccustomed fifth and Surrey Walking Club took the title. The Editor writes on walking: The Editor's inability to co-ordinate his contributers' contributions, so that they arrive for the same deadline, means that he is able to relieve our hard working Walking Hon. Sec. of the embarrassment of breaking the news of our performances in the National 20-kilometres and 20-miles championships. To show our hon. sec.'s perspicacity, however, we reproduce below the following Comment, written before those two championships were held:- COMMENT If British walking has been through a bad patch its certainly equal to the best in the world at the present time. Each week brings a fresh crop of times which, only a year ago would have been considered impossible. Phil Embleton has broken 70 for 10 miles, 88 for 20 Kilometres and best of all the Track 10,000 Metres UK Record with a staggering sub 42 clocking. Over 20 Miles Belgrave look strong enough and our distance men can usually be relied upon but the 20 Kilometres at Luton looks to be the risk if we are to achieve an unbeaten national record this year. Fortunately some of the boys have been playing it a bit carefully and we can only hope that they have timed it right. Wilf Wesch is obviously as fit as ever, so is Carl Lawton. Alan Callow is struggling to right a back injury but Ray Middleton is on the rising fitness trail once more. Barry Ingarfield we hope can show consistently the form he has produced on occasions and with Len Duquemin back in training and eligible for the Post Office John Moullin may also reappear. Dave DeBondi and Pat Duncan are both training hard - so is Dave King. Nonetheless although we have the greatest depth and strength of any club in the world - witness those packs at Wimbledon-in the present competitive climate it is impossible to relax. If the team can just pull together on the day then all will be well but there can be no margin of error as Surrey, Met, Lancashire and Southend hover menacingly for the first chink in the claret and gold. * - * - * - * - * - * Now for it. In the 20-kilometres at Luton on May 8, we finished an unaccustomedly low fifth. And our "B" team didn't win, either. They were 16th. The bright spot in this race was Carl Lawton's sixth place in 97m. 21s. Ray Middleton had raced over 50 kilometres in Berlin the week before, and this may help to explain his lowly 56th position, while we obviously missed Wil Wesch, the reigning champion, who was out through injury. We have to congratulate our old friends and rivals Surrey Walking Club on taking the title. items.sum: Reg Hopkins reports on the lively new Colt team and the re-organised junior section, naming the helpers who look after the youngsters.
items.s: YOUTHS & BOYS - Reg. Hopkins reports Reg Hopkins reports on the lively new Colt team and the re-organised junior section, naming the helpers who look after the youngsters. YOUTHS & BOYS Reg. Hopkins reports We have now in the junior section a very lively Colt team, training and racing with a spirit that would put many seniors to shame, running without inhibitions, and showing a strong loyalty to the Club and the team. I have every hope that given the lead and encouragement from older members, teachers, and parents they have a great future and the Club will be as strong in the coming years as ever in the past, and proud of them. Although we have had our teething troubles in the re-organisation of our section, we now seem to have settled down. Ron Linstead is looking after the older, more experienced members with Ray Beaumont and myself watching over the young and novice with the sage advice of Tom Carter to call upon, and Gordon Biscoe and Bill Couzens always ready to help, so we seem to have arrived at the set-up we desired. We also have another string to our bow with Mick Pyer who is doing a good job at Battersea with his team of youngsters. I will not name any particular member for special mention in this issue. I'am pleased with them all, although obviously some have more wins and better times than others I can honestly say that in the things that really matter, ie. dedication, effort and perseverance, all are equal. This gives me great personal pleasure, and I feel it an honour to be in their company and be accepted as their coach. I know they are gaining a reputation amongst other Clubs for their impeccable behaviour and appreciation of their chosen sport. Long may this continue. It is a grand sight to see them crowding round a fellow member to congratulate or console him after a race. Here we see among these very young athletes the true purpose of our sport, each sharing the triumph or disaster. Reg. Hopkins Reg. items.s: Mitcham Young Athletes Relay Report of Belgrave's all-youth quartet winning the Mitcham A.C. Young Athletes' 4 x 2 miles cross-country relay at Morden Park, with Bill Curtin holding off Grenville Tuck and taking the fastest youth award. Mitcham Young Athletes Relay Mitcham A.C. Young Athletes' Cross - country Relay 4 x 2 miles Mordon Park 6.2.71. Although this event was open to runners up to the age of 20, we scored a fine win with an all youth quartet. John Stow took the first stage and handed over to Tony Binda in 4th place recording 9m 2s. Tony clocked 8m 44s to move into 2nd position. A fine effort by Peter Carton (8m 25s) took us into the lead on stage three. On the final leg Bill Curtin took over only yards ahead of Cambridge & Coleridge A.C. Junior international Grenville Tuck. As this runner had finished in the low twenties in the Inter-Counties Senior C.C. only two weeks before, Bill's task appeared to be a formidable one. Tuck caught Bill with half a mile to go and approaching the finish ou[illegible] lad appeared to be absolutely exhausted. Urged on by our supporters, Bill found hidden reserves and pulled out a desperate sprint over the last 200 yards to bring us home first. His effort was a courageous one and will be long remembered by those present. Running for an incomplete 'B' team Mark Clancey and Pat. Breslin did 9.16 and 9.19. respectively. Mark's effort was a fine one for it put him half way up the days overall time list, whereas just a few months previously one could confidently have expected to find him languishing in the bottom few places. items.sum: Report of the Southern cross-country championships at Parliament Hill Fields, where Peter Carton was seventh in the youths (the back-cover caption says fourth) and the depleted junior team dropped out.
items.s: SOUTHERN C.C. - Parliament Hill Fields - February 13th Report of the Southern cross-country championships at Parliament Hill Fields, where Peter Carton was seventh in the youths (the back-cover caption says fourth) and the depleted junior team dropped out. Due to injury, illness and other reasond we failed to start a complete team. Peter Carton ran a hard race to finish seventh, a good performance but not really indicative of his true potential. Mark Clancy was 60th out of 160 odd finishers and he was probably the only Belgrave runner of the day senior junior or youth to really rise to the big occasion and pull out a best ever effort. The less said about the Juniors the better. We started an incomplete team, the members of which decided to run an incomplete race, pulling out at the half distance. Altogether a poor day for us with just the faint consolation that it would be difficult to do as badly again. items.label: June 1971
items.sum: Report of the club boys' cross-country championship for the Jack Hampshire trophy, won by Jimmy McAffee, and the unofficial colts championship won by Ian Gillings on the same time as Andrew Martell.
items.s: Boys Cross-country championships 27-2-71 - 2½ miles Report of the club boys' cross-country championship for the Jack Hampshire trophy, won by Jimmy McAffee, and the unofficial colts championship won by Ian Gillings on the same time as Andrew Martell. Although there was only a small field, this was one of the best boy's races for some time with very little difference in the abilities of the first four it was anyones guess who would triumph in this Club championship, and with the prospect of holding for a year that much coveted Jack Hampshire trophy to spur them on, each was out to be the first man home. Trying to introduce tactics to his aid in his efforts to thwart the others, Reg Hopkins set off at an incredibly fast pace, his object being to open up a big gap and then try to hold them off until the finish. Simon, Dave and Jimmy were content to watch him go, feeling confident that he would soon tire and come back into sight and thinking that the main threat lay among themselves. On reaching the Windmill they were shocked to find that Reg was not in sight; and the realization that they may have given him too much suddenly brought them to life. The Pace was now desperate, and as it happened saved the day for them. It was at the Queensmere that they caught a glimpse of his back. He was now feeling the early effort, but determined to hold his lead. The moment of truth for them all had arrived. Jimmy was leading the chase with Simon and David hanging on, on reaching the avenue the gap was closed and the race for the finish was on. Jimmy took the lead and in spite of pressure opened a gap from Simon which he managed to hold till the end. David caught and passed Reg and thought he had him beaten for third place, but he had reckoned without the latter's finish, and lost it on the line. Final positions and times were: The Colts race over 1¾ miles was no less exciting. With only Stephen Jay absent from the line up, all our regular colts were in attendance for the unofficial Club colts championship and trying to predict the result before the start was impossible. Any one of them was capable of winning, and we were sure all of them would give their best. It was only the experience of Ian Gillings (it seems incredible with one so young, but Ian has been running for four years now) that brought him success from Andrew Martell. With nothing between them in ability the race was neck and neck right to the finishing tunnel. Andrew should have put in a sprint over the last few yards or so, but he failed to do so and Ian who never loses his competitive urge to win stole this race with both sharing the same time. Seven seconds behind in third place came brother Martin, holding off the challenge from new member Adrian Cook. All runners did exceptionally well, all claimed to have thoroughly enjoyed it the only complaint they seemed to have was to claim that the race was too short!, and should have been twice as long. 1st Jimmy McAffee 15.43 2nd Simon Holmes 15.50 3rd Reg Hopkins 16.20 4th Dave Harvey 16.21 5th Tony Holmes 1st I.
