items.s: CLUB '10' MACHER SHIELD Report and handicap result of the club 10 miles cross-country championship for the Macher Shield at Wimbledon on 22 January 1972, won by Gerry North, with Jim Rimmer winning the handicap. CLUB '10' MACHER SHIELD Wimbledon, January 22, 1972 Gerry North's recent running had shown him as a man to reckoned with at any level, and - as the local papers' reports suggested - his win in the Club "10" showed him as a Cross-Country Captain aiming to lead his men from the front in the major championships approaching. New member John Phelan, from the same Irish club as our own Tony Brien, set tongues wagging, however, with his fine second place - ahead of Blackstaffe Shield winner Laurie O'Hara - always a difficult man to beat. John is a first-year student at St. Mary's College, Twickenham - famous as the former Alma Mater of Alan Black and John Bicourt, as well as the current A.M. of Dave Bedford - and looks a good 'un. Jim Rimmer has been improving as fast this winter over the country as he did in the summer on the track. His performance in beating men like Trevor Hart, Alan Black and Pat O'Connor, as well as Bob Smith and Tony Fairclough, gave him a well deserved win in the handicap. Alan, Pat and Bob could all have surprises up their sleeves for the big races, while Tony Fairclough - celebrating a recent addition to his family - looks as though he's finding his running legs again. Gerry North did extremely well to take second handicap place, off scratch, but Bob Glover got the biggest cheer of the afternoon, when his third handicap place was announced. Bob is apparently out to show some of our better vets the way home, and probably will before long. - Handicap m. s. Mark time pos. 1. Gerry North 57 06 Scr. 57 06 2 2. J. Phelan 58 12 - - - 3. L. items.h: SOUTHERN CHAMPS. — BELGRAVE JUNIORS TAKE HONOURS IN SOUTHERN C.C.
items.sum: Report and senior, junior and youth results of the Southern cross-country championships at Parliament Hill Fields on 12 February 1972, where Belgrave seniors were 13th, juniors 3rd and John Bicourt 4th.
items.s: SOUTHERN CHAMPS. — BELGRAVE JUNIORS TAKE HONOURS IN SOUTHERN C.C. Report and senior, junior and youth results of the Southern cross-country championships at Parliament Hill Fields on 12 February 1972, where Belgrave seniors were 13th, juniors 3rd and John Bicourt 4th. SOUTHERN CHAMPS. BELGRAVE JUNIORS TAKE HONOURS IN SOUTHERN C.C. Parliament Hill Fields, 12th February, 1972 Thirteenth place in the Southern Senior C.C. Championship was our worst placing for a good few years. With only three men in the first hundred, however, we could hardly hope for anything better. The race was not without its highlights for the Bels, however, since the race marked a breakthrough in the cross-country field for international steeplechaser John Bicourt, whose fourth position put him clearly in the reckoning for his first international cross-country vest if he could reproduce the form at Sutton Coldfield in the National three weeks later. In addition, it can be argued that the club came within an ace of having the second man home, in Gerry North - who was challenging Windsor's Tony Moore for this place after some miles when he injured a muscle, and was forced to retire - not the first time Gerry has met with an accident in this race, to which he makes a habit of going in unsuspectedly good form. Jimmy Rimmer, in 93rd place, was the third Bel home - Pat O'Connor having finished 65th - and his performance promises even better in coming years. A solid performance by our junior team, of Peter Carton (4th), Tony Binda (12th), Bill Curtin (17th) and John Stow (32nd) gave them a praiseworthy third - not all that far behind the winners, Thames Valley. We are becoming accustomed to these sorts of performances by this quartet. A word, however, of commendation for Mark Clancy, who gave admirable backing with his 47th position. Mark is improving steadily. In the youths' event, Richard Langley turned in a good run for 20th place - and the Bels' team in this race emulated their senior clubmates, with 13th position. items.h: National Cross-Country Championships — CHILL WINDS AT SUTTON COLDFIELD
items.sum: Report and results of the National cross-country championships at Sutton Coldfield on 4 March 1972, where a blizzard hit the senior race and Belgrave were 32nd seniors, 11th juniors and 40th youths.
items.s: National Cross-Country Championships — CHILL WINDS AT SUTTON COLDFIELD Report and results of the National cross-country championships at Sutton Coldfield on 4 March 1972, where a blizzard hit the senior race and Belgrave were 32nd seniors, 11th juniors and 40th youths. National Cross-Country Championships CHILL WINDS AT SUTTON COLDFIELD National Cross-Country Championships, 4th March, 1972 If Belgrave's 13th place in the Southern Senior Cross-Country Championshi[illegible] was the Club's worst for a good few years, the 32nd place secured in the National was the worst in a good few long memories. It is true that a blizzard blew up during the Senior race, and caused a widespread upset of the form book, forcing a large number of retirements, including that of our own "hope" John Bicourt, and that Gerry North had not recovered from his Southern injury. As it was, Tony Brien won the Harry Parker Memorial Bowl, as our first man home, in 170th place, and Pat O'Connor and Jim Rimmer were our only other runners in the first 300. It was good to see Bob Smith (309th) out in the National, however, while Tony Fairclough plugged away as grittily as ever, and we congratulate Colin Pearson on his first appearance in the National scoring six. We also congratulate our old member, Dick Piotrowski (57th) on helping Reading to thrid team place. In the junior race, our famous four were 11th, with Peter Carton, who just missed a junior international,vest getting good support for his 10th place from Tony Binda (58th), Bill Curtin (109th) and John Stow (111th), and Mark Clancy again poised to fill any breach that should appear. Richard Langley put in another fine run in the youths' race, for 41st, and the Bels took 40th place in the team race. One thing that can be said about the Southern and National Championships is that we did finish a team in all three races at each meeting - and that is always worth saying. 1. M. ENGLISH CLUBS v IRISH CLUBS "INTERNATIONAL" ----- Parliament Hill Fields, 19th March 1972. John Bicourt overcame an impressive pack of Irish internationals to take himself and Belgrave Harriers to individual and team victories in this London Irish AC promotion. John was in the lead after a quarter of a mile, closely followed by Eddy Spillane. At the end of the first lap the position was unchanged, with the Irish champion John Buckley fourth. As the Irishmen changed positions, John eased away to a 11 seconds victory. RESULT (69 finished) Teams: 1.BELGRAVE H 34pts, 2.Donore H 49pts, 3.Shaftesbury H 71pts. (8 teams ran) 1. Australian Athletics ~ BY A BELGRAVIAN "DOWN UNDER" Apart from the well known athletes that are household names throughout the world, the general standard of athletics in Australia is surprisingly lower than one would imagine. Schoolboy times and distances are quite often phenomenal, but once school is behind him, the combined attractions of the beach scene, birds and cars take their toll, and athletics is very often pushed aside for the casual life. The State of Victoria is the most athletics conscious, and they usually manage to keep New South Wales at bay in the annual Interstates Championships. The set-up in New South Wales is built largely around a league system and every club provides up to six competitors in different grades, ranging, for example, in the 400m., from 48s. men in the "A" grade down to 58s. in the "F" grade. Each grade is, in fact, run as a separate league, and towards the end of the track season excitement mounts as each club strives to become top dog in at least one grade. Every track and field event is covered in all grades, Pole Vault, Hurdles and all, so each meeting is split into two sections; 100m., 400m., 1500m., etc. on Saturday, and 200m., 800m., etc. on Sunday, or in the following week. These meetings are family affairs, and often last from midday through to early evening, as there are events for boys in age groups from 10 years upwards, and many of these are also graded. Many spectators take a picnic tea and an ice-box full of Aussie beer, and there is general enjoyment all-round. "Old Joe", flogging himself nearly to death in winning the "F" mile, gets just as much applause as the thoroughbreds in the following "A" 100m., where the first three might well dip under 10.6s. Interstates Championships Australia Victoria New South Wales

items.s: TRACK and FIELD 1972 Round-up of Belgrave's 1972 track and field season so far, including Bicourt and Brooks going to the Munich Olympics, club records, Southern League, Inter-Counties and Surrey Championships performances, and the club championship results at Hurlingham. TRACK and FIELD 1972 We start with the good news of two Belgravians going to Munich - John Bicourt in the Steeplechase and Cliff (Snowy) Brooks in the Decathlon, where he represented his native Barbados. Cliff has broken the club record a number of times this season raising it to a mammoth 6389 points. John also set a club record this year of 8m 35.4s. Another record broken is the Junior High Jump by Reg Hopkins who raised the bar in the London Schools Championship to 6ft 3¼ins. Starting with the first meeting in April we had a reasonable turn out, but not many supporters - it must have been too cold. Getting warmer now and into May with the first Southern League meeting at Southall. A creditable third behind Q.P.H. and Met. Police. We must not forget to mention a very good early season performance by the Bel's 4 x 100m team at the Surrey County Relay Championships at Epsom on 6th May. With P. Gee, R. Hopkins, L. Sullivan, and C. Gillett, we finished second in 44.9s. The Epsom Trophy meeting and a poor turn out - but we still managed fourth place, with seven teams competing. We saw Colin Pearson having a go at the Steeplechase and what's this, long jumping too! Still in May and the 10,000m championship saw another win for that will o' the whisp Laurie O'Hara, beating Adrian Major into second place by almost three minutes, with one of the old vets, a runner called Gorman (?) getting third. On the same evening the 300m handicap saw a fine run by the scratch man Lee Sullivan to get a first place. Getting to the end of May now and at the Inter-Counties Championships at Leicester on Monday, 29th May John Bicourt finished second in the 3,000m steeplechase with 8m 46s. Steve White jumped 7.08m or 23ft 2¾ins but only managed seventh and Rodney Heward-Mills qualified for the final of the Triple Jump. An Inter-Club meeting at Chiswick on the last day of May saw the Bel's turn out in force in the 800m to show what depth we have in this event. A battle royal went on between John Martin and Dave McMillan for third and fourth place; & shotputter John just won. But the way he felt he wished he hadn't! Our second Southern League meeting came up on 3rd June at Wimbledon Park and we again finished third, but maintained our challenge to get into the National League. Good wins here by Steve White in the 100 and 200 metres and Pete Carton in the 800m. Steve also won the long jump and contributed to our 4 x 100m winning squad. Our other winners of the meeting were Charlie Gillett in the 400m hurdles and Arnold Bentt in the triple jump. * * * * * * * The Surrey Championships at Motspur Park on June 6th, 8th and 10th provided us with only one winner in the senior events - Cliff Brooks with 50.6s in the 400m. Cliff's time in the heats was even better with 49.9s. But we did manage a winner in the boys' section. P. Crosbie won the javelin with a championship best of 42.22m. OTHER RESULTS:- Senior: 100m 6th L. Sullivan 12s; 200m 4th C. Gillett 23s, 5th L.Sullivan 23.2s; 800m 2nd P. Carton 1m 52.9s (personal best); 1,500m 3rd J. Stow 3m 54.8s (personal best) 5,000m 10th R. Smith 15m 7s, 11th T. Hart 15m11s; 110m hurdles 2nd C. Brooks 16s; Shot 5th J. Martin 11.93m (39' 1¾"); 400m hurdles 3rd C. Gillett 56.8s; Junior: 100m 2nd M. Marshall 11.6s; 200m 3rd K. Bloice 23.5s; High Jump 3rd R. Hopkins 1.75m; Boys: 100m 6th R. Jenkins 13.2s. * * * * * * * On the 17th June Reg Hopkins continued to improve in the High Jump with a win in the Southern Junior Championships at 6' 1½". And four days later at Crystal Palace John Bicourt set his club record in the 3000m steeplechase with an Olympic qualifying time of 8m 35.4s. A good turn out for an inter-club match at Battersea Park on 14th June. The Bel's swamped the opposition and got a runaway victory. And it just goes to show that we have got some good youngsters coming along, when the other clubs can't turn any out to compete against us. A rain swept match at Walton later on in June saw our half milers out in force again - it's amazing how they keep going. The club 5,000m championship gave Laurie O'Hara his double - 14m 32.2s saw him almost 8s clear of the second man Peter Carton with John Stow coming in third. On the same night the 110m hurdles championship produced what can only be described as remarkable hurdling. Bob Hamilton raced to the first hurdle - but could not get over and Dave McMillan's technique was a cross between the scissors and a Fosbury flop. Cliff Brooks however showed us how it was done in a winning time of 17.7s. A double for Cliff with a win in the 200m handicap. Scratch man Cliff won by a hair's breadth from John Martin, who had a 23 yard start. The third Southern League meeting at Haslemere on 1st July saw a fine win by Belgrave. What more can one say than a good all round performance. On a day like that with so many individual winners it would be a shame to pick any out for special mention. Just congratulate them all. And so to the Club Championships at Hurlingham on 8th July. On arriving at the track one had to think twice whether we were indeed an athletic or a swimming club - the conditions were terrible - but the fearless Bel's pressed on regardless, nothing would deprive them of their run - not even continuous rain on a summer's day. items.label: September 1972
items.sum: John Keown's report on the Surrey W.C. open 100 miles walk at Ewhurst on 25/26 June 1972, in which John Moullin won in 16hrs 55m 44s and Keown and John Morris also became Centurions, with results; the text calls Belgrave's 22 points second team place 'between' Amsterdam (15) and Rotterdam (22).
items.s: WALKING — THREE NEW CENTURIONS John Keown's report on the Surrey W.C. open 100 miles walk at Ewhurst on 25/26 June 1972, in which John Moullin won in 16hrs 55m 44s and Keown and John Morris also became Centurions, with results; the text calls Belgrave's 22 points second team place 'between' Amsterdam (15) and Rotterdam (22). WALKING THREE NEW CENTURIONS BY JOHN KEOWN On June 25/26 in an Open 100 Miles Walking Race promoted by Surrey W.C., three Belgravians, John Moullin, John Morris and John Keown became Centurions when they finished the distance inside 24 hours. By definition, a Centurion is one who, as an amateur, has walked in competition, in Great Britain, 100 miles within 24 hours. John Moullin joined the ranks of the Centurions in a most spectacular fashion. With a truly magnificent display of fast, controlled walking, he finished first in the race, with a remarkable time of 16hrs. 55m. 44s., only 1m. 29s. outside Frank O'Reilly's world best performance for 100 miles. Frank had already competed in two previous races o[illegible] 100 miles and above when he set his world best time of 16hrs. 54m. 15s. in the Leicester to Skegness 100 miles on July 1/2, 1960. A search through the Centurions roll of honour shows that no one has entered their ranks with such a high-class performance. To get inside 17hrs. at one's first attempt at the distance is indeed an unique achievement which makes John Moullin one of our top ultra-long-distance walkers. Since the Centurions were founded in 1911, only five other walkers have succeeded in qualifying as members by finishing inside 18 hours; Billy Baker (Queen's Park Harriers) in 1926, Tom Richardson (Woodford Green) in 1936, Johnny Henderson (Steyning A.C.) in 1937, Rex Whitlock (Metropolitan W.C., and brother of Harold) in 1952, and Colin Young (Essex Beagles) in 1960. The British track walking records from 80 miles upwards must now be within John's grasp. In conjunction with the 100 miles race was a 100 kilometres race, which John also won, with a time of 10hrs. 21m. 06s. When asked what special training he did for the 100, John replied: "I did no special training. In fact, I had done no training at all for at least a month, on accoun[illegible] of working till about 9.30 each evening, but I did several races which I used as training for the 100, including the Leicester Mercury '20', Bradford 50 kms., and the National 20 miles." The other two Johns, who have contested many Brightons during the last twelve years, in a spirit of friendly rivalry, surprised themselves and their mates when, on this occasion, they combined forces to to complete the 100 miles together in 20hrs. 49m. 27s. They walked the entire race shoulder to shoulder, each in turn supplying the necessary encouragement to keep going when the other appeared to falter. As is their normal practice, both trained for this race alone. They covered about 40 miles per week, split into four sessions, during the month prior to the 100. Beforehand, they agreed to try to walk at roughly 5 m.p.h. for at least 60 miles. In fact they reached this mark in 11hrs. 58m. The race was held on a 9 lap road course around the village of Ewhurst, near Guildford. There were 73 starters, including walkers from Holland, Belgium, W. Germany, Canada and Ireland. Contesting the team race (three to score) were three teams from Dutch clubs, one from an Irish club, and six from English clubs. On the lap, there were four feeding stations, roughly 2¾-miles apart. One of these stations was run by the Wilson brothers and our second-claim member, Cyril Gittins. The course, which was mostly on country roads, was fairly flat for five miles, then , in typical Surrey fashion, the remainder of the lap was rather undulating. Here and there the road surfaces were bad, especially near the side. Each 5 km. point was clearly marked with a large sign. These signs were lit during the hours of darkness, from about 11 p.m. until 4 a.m. The only successful way of walking through the wooded sections during this period was along the white line in the centre of the road. The weather was fine except for three hours during the night when it rained very heavily. The winner said this of the course: "I really enjoyed it, but I think it would have been a bit more pleasant if one could see where one was walking in the hours of darkness." At 6 p.m. on the Friday evening, the Life President of the Centurions, Ernest Neville, sent the 73 competitors on their way. Alomaine, the Belgian long distance specialist, led for the first lap. John Hedgethorne (Essex Police) and John Moullin passed him at about 14 miles, and completed the second lap together. The Belgravian now took the lead and retained it until the finish. Although feeling a little tired on lap 5, John Moullin reached the 100 Km. mark in 10hrs. 21m. 06s., just one minute and six seconds outside his schedule. He expected to slow down after this point, but was surprised to find that he managed to maintain his pace until the end. The only trouble he experienced during the race was a bit of swelling around one of his big toes. Morris and Keown, ignoring the early rush, started in a steady fashion. After a couple of laps they were passed by Pat Duncan, who had started the race 20 minutes late. Pat retired around the 40 miles mark. The only trouble the two Johns had in the first half of the race was caused by grit, which Keown seemed to attract like a magnet. Morris, with his detailed calculations of possible finishing times and places, kept his companion's spirits up during the period of heavy rain, when the latter was afraid that an old knee injury might give trouble. Around the 75 miles mark, Morris began to experience some trouble with his back and thighs. This was probably caused by his having ridden a bicycle, for the use of a helper, from Dorking Station to the venue. No amount of praise can be too high for the helpers. All three successful Belgravians owe a great debt to the people that manned the feeding stations and to those boys from the Club who looked after their individual needs throughout the race. Prominent among these were Carl Lawton and Pat Duncan. Pat, after only two hours sleep, took on the role of helper. They saw all three walkers safely across the finishing line. Although a friend of John Keown's took over as a helper at 8.30 a.m. on the Saturday morning, the greater experience of our Walking Secretary proved invaluable when a certain amount of quick massage became necessary to Morris's back during the last 20 miles of the race. Australian Dave de Bondi, who had kept an eye on his clubmates during the early stages of the race, snatched a few hours sleep and drove over to Essex for a 50 kms. race on the Saturday afternoon. Belgravian Alan Callow helped fellow countryman J.D. Harrison, from Boundary Harriers, Isle of Man, to complete the course. Our thanks to all these, and to the officials who made the race possible. At the finishing line to clock Keown and Morris home in 16th and 17th places was a Past President of the Club, Gordon Doubleday. To add to Belgrave's long day of success, the three Johns managed to squeeze into second team place, with 22 points, between L.A.T. Amsterdam (15 points) and R.W.V. Rotterdam (22 points). items.s: NATIONAL 50 Kilos. Report of the RWA National 50 km walk at Redditch, where Carl Lawton was third and gained European selection, followed by his retirement in the European 50 km and a comparison of 5 km splits with the Soviet and East German leaders; the sub-heading prints the year as 1971. NATIONAL 50 Kilos. RWA National 50 Kilos - Redditch 1971 Two likely Belgrave prospects for European selection Ray Middleton and Carl Lawton. Carl took the initiative and in his finest race to date pushed Paul Nihill very hard for much of the distance. Carl was overtaken by Bob Dobson in the closing stages but hung on to beat 4 hours 20 minutes and gain selection for the European Games. Ray Middleton headed the second group but his fifth position was not up to the high standards he has set himself in recent years. In the team race Surrey beat Belgrave by three points but some subtle team selection by Carl Lawton left an unfit Pat Duncan to round off a victorious Belgrave eight in the Milan Trophy. Bob Coates walked a fine race only to be pipped away from his honours badge. Milan Trophy - Belgrave Harriers 8th man in 37th team position. In the European Games Carl Lawton got in with the leaders to record a sub 50 for the first 10 Kilos and 100.08 for 20 Kilos. After this he faded badly and retired shortly after 30 Kilos for a disappointing debut in Championship competition. Another casualty was Ron Wallwork and it is possible that both he and Carl put too much into their preparations immediately before the games. Both Carl and Ron returned some outstanding results immediately prior to the games could it be that the longer term approach of the Russians and East Germans who reach for a greater peak than our boys but by a much more gradual build up is the secret of their fantastic performances ? One can only wonder at the following 5 Km splits: The winner's final 20 Kilometres would have placed him second in the National 20 Kilometres, few British walkers have beaten 94.09 for 20 Kilos let alone after 30 Kilos in 2.28 odd. The ability to sustain this kind of pace over the four hours of a 50 Kilo race can only come from a regular programme of racing and training at similar speeds and distances over a period of years. Such an approach is not yet possible in this country without imposing sevem strains on our athletes. 1. P.Nihill SWC 4.15.05 2. R.Dobson Bas 4.17.44 3. C.Lawton Bels 4.19.00 5. items.sum: Obituary of Belgrave walker Jack Stirling-Wakeley, winner of the 1948 Motspur Park 24 hours track walk and the London to Brighton and Back, professional percussionist and first editor of the Road Runners Club Newsletter.
items.s: OBITUARY — A.J. STIRLING-WAKELEY Obituary of Belgrave walker Jack Stirling-Wakeley, winner of the 1948 Motspur Park 24 hours track walk and the London to Brighton and Back, professional percussionist and first editor of the Road Runners Club Newsletter. OBITUARY A.J. STIRLING-WAKELEY We were saddened to learn at a recent Committee meeting that Jack Stirling-Wakeley died suddenly last December from Coronary Thrombosis. Always interested in amateur sport, Jack developed an interest in long-distance walking when serving in the Middle East during the 1939-1945 war. On his return home he joined Belgrave, and soon became a regular member of our walking teams, and helped us to win first team medals in the R.W.A. 50 kilometres championship and the London to Brighton walk. He also represented Hampshire in the Inter-Counties road walking championship. His two outstanding performances were in the 24 hours track walk at Motspur Park in 1948, when, going into the lead after 100 miles, he went on to win with 122 miles 1,411 yards to his credit. Three years later in the London to Brighton and Back race, he led from the start to win in 18hrs. 46m. A few hours afterwards he was at his place at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden, where he was a percussionist, to play in "Die Meistersinger", one of the longest operas! For his Brighton and back performance he was awarded the Tommy Green Cup. He had also held the Club long-distance trophy, and had been awarded a Club Honours Badge for a performance of outstanding merit. It was a tribute to his keenness and determination that he was able to fit in the long and hard training for these performances with his duties as a professional musician. He was also a qualified physiotherapist. Our sympathies have been conveyed to his wife, Stella. It is problematical whether there will be any more London to Brighton and Back races, so his winning time may stand as a Club record for all time. His winning distance at 24 Hours, however, will stand as a challenge to future Belgrave long-distance aspirants. He was the first Hon. Editor of the Road Runners Club Newsletter, and also took over the Belgrave Newsletter, started by Percy Wright during the war. The latter he typed and circulated himself - a labour of love, and typical of his ideals. Jack collapsed at Wimbledon Broadway in the 1950's, and was rushed to hospital to be operated on for a perforated ulcer. He did not compete again. But only the day before his death he performed in matinee and evening productions. - G.S.D. Jack Stirling-Wakeley A.J. items.label: September 1972
items.sum: Feature on Belgrave's 1913 South of the Thames Junior cross-country team (photographed opposite) and how four of its members came to give their names to club trophies, with a note on the 1915 team.
items.s: The Men Behind The Trophies Feature on Belgrave's 1913 South of the Thames Junior cross-country team (photographed opposite) and how four of its members came to give their names to club trophies, with a note on the 1915 team. The Men Behind The Trophies PHOTOGRAPH OPPOSITE---1913 South of Thames "Junior" winners. Left to Right:- Dick Best (17th), Joe Helm (9th), Harry Parker (15th), Ernie Musselbrook (18th) and Oscar Horwood (16th). Belgrave was placed third in the South of the Thames Cross-Country Championship in 1904; and our next appearance in team results was in 1913 when our team won third medals in the South of Thames Junior Race - 59 years ago! This event was held at Weybridge and our scoring team was:- HARRY PARKER 15, OSCAR HORWOOD 16, DICK BEST 17, and ERNIE MUSSELBROOK 18 - five seconds covering the four runners. Marvellous packing, of course; but JOE HELM,who finished ninth, was in the 'B' team and one wonders what happened to the team selection that day! The photograph shows these five runners, four of them in the claret and gold hoops of the period. All five former club-mates of ours are now dead. JOE HELM was killed in the 1914-18 war. DICK BEST, until fairly recent years, was to be seen at our track meetings where he had standing instructions to be entered in every event - and he always paid up! HARRY PARKER was to prove himself one of our finest officials ever, and in due time was Club President and later, in the year that he died, President of the English Cross Country Union and Southern Counties C.C.A. ERNIE MUSSELBROOK must have been the original wearer of a woollen cap - he was never without it! (He presented us with the Cup which bears his name, and is annually awarded for the Junior 1500 M.) OSCAR HORWOOD was another to serve this Club with all his heart and sinew; and became Hon. Secretary in the immediate Post-War (1914/18) period when the Club funds were what you could find in your own pockets! OSCAR became Walking Hon. Secretary and President later and for many years helped the Club in a hundred ways. Our scoring four of yesteryear are all represented in the range of Club trophies. DICK BEST gave us, many years ago, the cup for our Half-Mile Championship. HARRY PARKER presented the "Pyramid"Cup for Shot Put and is also remembered in the "Parker Bowl" which goes to the first Belgrave man to finish in the E.C.C.U. Senior Championship. OSCAR HORWOOD presented the Horwood Cup for Walking, which is contested enthusiastically each December and has done much to raise our standards, and ERNIE MUSSELBROOK also gave us a trophy as mentioned above. So our team of 1913 is remembered 59 years later! In 1915, at Esher, the third position was again ours with 21 seconds covering the four men who were E. MUSSELBROOK 13, C. ARNOLD 15, J.E. OFFEN 16, J.J. SEXTON 17. PHOTOGRAPH OPPOSITE---1913 South of Thames "Junior" winners. items.label: December 1972
items.sum: The new editor's first editorial, asking for contributions to the magazine and urging members to help counter apathy in the club.
items.s: COMMENT The new editor's first editorial, asking for contributions to the magazine and urging members to help counter apathy in the club. You hold before you a new editor's first edition of 'The Belgravian'. I hope you will bear with him as he picks up the threads from those who have gone before and who have done so much to make this magazine one of the best of its kind. Do remember though, that it's success depends upon a team that includes you! Your articles, ideas, letters, photographs and even your criticisms will be well received. At the A.G.M. it was mentioned during a discussion that there seems to be a state of apathy existing in the Club. Whilst we cannot lay claim to being athletic earth-shakers, we are certainly not doing badly. On the other hand, when it comes to organisation, fund raising, stepping forward to help with timekeeping, etc., it is the same old faithfuls every time who make the effort and I think the accusation is fair. You may well say that you joined this Club because you wanted to walk, throw or run but the fact is, if nobody did anything towards keeping our Club going we would be in a fine state. Alright, some people really do not want to become too involved in our activities but if every member took just one weekly football ticket, took one item of jumble up to the hall next time we hold a jumble sale, turned out to support our team at one home fixture, well, the possibilities are enormous. Let's all push towards that improvement in our Headquarters that we badly need; let's sell ourselves to any prospective new member that we can; and let's all strive towards making Belgrave Harriers a vibrant club that knows where it is going. The Editor

items.sum: Clive Shippen, the club's 40th President, thanks members for electing him and appeals for their support for the honorary secretaries and captains.
items.s: THE PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE Clive Shippen, the club's 40th President, thanks members for electing him and appeals for their support for the honorary secretaries and captains. Fellow Belgravians, I am very conscious of the honour, and indeed the responsibility, which you bestowed upon me when you decided that I should occupy the Presidential Chair during the coming year. It is an awesome feeling to be faced with the duty of presiding over the affairs of the finest club in the land; and it is my fervent hope that I will be able to fulfill my duties as effectively as my predecessors did. Over 200 years ago Benjamin Franklin observed, "At twenty years of age, the will reigns; at thirty, the wit; and at forty, the judgement." As your 40th President, and at 40 years of age too, I hope for the Club's sake that JUDGEMENT does reign supreme; also wishing of course that my WIT has not entirely deserted me and that my continued training has prolonged the WILL! During our eight and a half decades of history we have had many years of exceptional success, and I doubt whether our greatest years will ever be matched again, by any club. So it would be unrealistic for me to call for our most successful year yet. I would much prefer to rely on our excellent band of honorary secretaries and captains to produce the best of which we are capable - we can ask for no more. To do this they must have your full co-operation, and I appeal to you all to give them the support they need -- and, who knows, we might yet emulate our best years. Wishing you all the best of success in the coming year, Clive Shippen Clive Shippen Clive Shippen 40th President of the club, aged 40 Benjamin Franklin Benjamin Franklin quoted

items.label: December 1972
items.sum: Report of the club's Annual General Meeting of 21 September 1972, covering the debate and vote to raise subscriptions, new life members and vice presidents, and the election of Clive Shippen as President.
items.s: ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING Report of the club's Annual General Meeting of 21 September 1972, covering the debate and vote to raise subscriptions, new life members and vice presidents, and the election of Clive Shippen as President. SEPTEMBER 21st 1972. The evenings imperceptibly shorten, the air strikes more chill as one leaves the Hall for a canter over the Common; but nothing heralds the approach of the winter season more than the Annual General Meeting, bringing with it the close of another Club year. Speculation was rife amongst those who were there early. Would the Hall manage to hold the massive turnout of Belgravians that were expected to show up and air their views on the running of the Club's affairs, just as they all congregated for that other extravaganza - the Club Track Championships. Well, somehow most of those who were interested managed to get in. Perhaps the 450-odd members who couldn't make it will be luckier next year. Our able Gen. Hon. Sec. opened the proceedings and we reflected upon the reports covering the year's activities. Yes, it had been a slightly disappointing cross country season. Road relay results were better and our track and field team had finished the summer season very strongly. Good to hear that our walking section has been so full of esprit de corps. Somehow though, this was pretty tame stuff. Merely a preamble to the more contentious issue of the Committee's recommendation to raise the subscriptions. Here the meeting suddenly came alive. Two camps were quickly established and verbal battle ensued. Led by some of our financial wizards, the "againsts" took up the initiative. "It's all very well to put the subs up but what is going to be done with the extra. I know we eventually want to improve the Hall but for years we have talked of this and gone no farther. Costs rise and the dead money sitting in our Building Society account becomes worth less and less." Subdued murmers of approval changed to roars of laughter when it was added, "And I'm a life member - I don't have to cough." The voices of the "fors" rose above the clamour. "The subs should keep us going on running expenses, that's why they should go up. Any cash gained through other fund raising must go towards the building fund." "We live in the age of the 10p minimum "tube" fare - I don't consider £3 goes far enough. Make it £5." A vote was eventually taken and the recommendation passed by the sufficient two-thirds majority. Those worthy and energetic members Bill Couzens and Chas. Manning were elected to life membership and the services of John Baker and Joe MacDonald were also recognised - they were made vice presidents. So to the election of Officers and Committee for 1972/73, with Clive Shippen taking over the President's chair from Mickey Pyer. "No change" was the cry as most offices came to be filled but a special note should be made of Bob Taylor's retirement from the Track Sec's job after many years of invaluable service. Suddenly it was over. Chairs scraped in unison as newly elected officers led their followers out into the September night to celebrate their rise to power in the time honoured style. items.sum: Profile of new President Clive Shippen, tracing his running career from joining in 1952 through cross country, road relays and steeplechase to British veterans steeplechase records in 1972, and his service as editor and committee member; with two photos on page 7.
items.s: OUR PRESIDENT Profile of new President Clive Shippen, tracing his running career from joining in 1952 through cross country, road relays and steeplechase to British veterans steeplechase records in 1972, and his service as editor and committee member; with two photos on page 7. Although mildly interested in athletics, largely as a high jumper, during his school days at the Brixton School of Building, our new President did not join a club until he came upon the Belgrave scene at the age of twenty. He was at that time a Rover Scout whose troop visited Belgrave Hall for a few weeks prior to their annual cross country race for special training. Bill Merryman was deputed to lead this pack and was responsible for Clive joining the Club in March 1952. For the first year of his membership he did little or nothing but the Rover Scout championship in 1953 again raised his enthusiasm and he began to enter into club life and first donned the claret and gold vest seriously in the South of the Thames Junior Race in November of that year when he finished 172nd. Due to his engineering training his period of National Service had been deferred but in December 1953 we lost his services to the Army, in which he was commissioned in the Royal Engineers and was responsible for his unit athletic team reaching the Army finals in 1955. The year 1956 was spent settling back into civilian life as a Constructional Engineer and it was not until 1957 that Clive again took athletics seriously. In that year he was 138th in the Southern and 207th in the National. For the next six years he represented the Club in most of the major cross country and road relay races his best performances being in 1961/62 when he won his Surrey County colours for cross country and finished 56th in the Southern and 135th in the National. One of his best efforts was on the Brighton Road in the London to Brighton Relay when he produced the 2nd best time of the day on the Dale Hill slope in a time which stood as a Club record for a number of years. Clive's activities were by no means confined to cross country and rad relays for he began to earn a reputation as a steeplechaser and for a time held the Belgrave record at 9:28 - this will no doubt bring a smile to the face of John Bicourt but in 1962 it was good enough to place our President 3rd in the Sward Trophy race. Unfortunately, late in 1962 Clive picked up a liver virus which kept him out of major events and although appearing in Club races it was not until 1968 that he again trained seriously and took up distance running on the road. In 1970 at the age of thirty-nine he ran a marathon in 2hrs 41minutes 20secs. The highlight of our President's athletic career came recently when on August 24th 1972 at Crystal Palace in the Veteran's International Championships he finished 3rd in the 3,000 metres steeplechase in a British veterans record of 10:04.8. Two weeks later in Cologne he beat the Australian who had finished 2nd at Crystal Palace to finish 2nd in an international race in an improved time of 10:01.6 which still stands as the present British record. Not only has Clive performed well for Belgrave as an athlete but during his twenty years as a member he was Editor of the 'Belgravian' from 1959/1970, was cross country captain for three years and track vice-captain for two years. He has served on our own committee since 1957; was made a Vice-President in 1966 and a Life Member in 1969 and has also found time to serve on the committees of the Surrey County A.A.A. and the South of the Thames Cross Country Association. Everyone who knows Clive respects him as a hard working member of our community always willing to give of his best to help the Club. Any work he undertakes can be guaranteed to be of the highest quality, carried out in a most efficient manner. Clive is endowed with a natural charm which endears him to us all and under his leadership the Club is bound to prosper. We are also grateful to our President's wife Elizabeth who has always graced all our social events and has been prepared to assist with tea making and at jumble sales for many years. Olympian Above. items.s: THE DINNER Light-hearted account of the club's Annual Dinner honouring President Clive Shippen, recalling the guests and moments of the night, with Joe McDonald's remarks printed as mock-expletive symbols. When the Club's Dinner Secretary said to me, "Write a few lines for the 'Belgravian' on the premier night of the year." I said, "OK, leave it to me." Crikey! What a night! What larks! What a whirlwind of glitter and sparkle and what a head the next morning! If this report is inaccurate, exaggerated or even untrue, you must blame the 'POUILLY FUISSE' and the liberal?!? arm of Ken Stimpson. One recalls from this brilliant gathering Gwen Couzens smile and the warmth of Mavis Thresher - the caustic humour of Pat Duncan and Ray Hall. Through the gossamer veils of memory come the gentleness of Evelyn Stimpson and the pleasure of seeing Wynn Shepherd, of the American Belgravian Edmund Donovan and his wife, who flew in, specially for the occasion, from New York. In the kaleidoscope one recalls Bob Glover smiling, Joe McDonald commenting, "∂*! good do en it. No, I mean it's really *[illegible] good, everything's [illegible]** good!" with such honesty that it was a joy to hear him. In this nebulous riot, dimly, I can see June Law's back, can hear the persuasive voice of Jean Middleton selling raffle tickets, admire the towering majesty of Alf's form, watch the palm rubbing of John Baker. What was it all for - our President, Clive Shippen, and Elizabeth and their boys - we could not honour a better chap. A very happy year of office to you and may you remember with pleasure, this wonderful night. C.E.M. items.sum: Club news notes about members and old Belgravians, including tributes to retired President Mick Pyer, visits from past presidents and vice-presidents, Willi Wesch's Olympic walk, Jim Ginty's 1930s international career, appeals for a starter and timekeepers, and Danny Wiseman's return to training.
items.s: GRAPEVINE Club news notes about members and old Belgravians, including tributes to retired President Mick Pyer, visits from past presidents and vice-presidents, Willi Wesch's Olympic walk, Jim Ginty's 1930s international career, appeals for a starter and timekeepers, and Danny Wiseman's return to training. Let us put on record our admiration for our recently retired President, MICK PYER, and express our thanks to him. Mick attended most of our meetings, summer and winter; coached our junior javelin throwers and displayed throughout the utmost enthusiasm for the Club and its activities. And all the while his sight has been fading, and the once champion marksman of the London Irish finds himself groping in the shadows and having difficulty in recognising his friends of many years standing. Needless to say he accepts this situation with courage and humility - and merely asks for continuing opportunities to serve the Club and its members. What a pity there was no photographer present to record an historic occasion at our Club Track and Field Championships, when MICK PYER as President presented the Garnett Cup for the 1500 metres championship to the winner, Peter Carton, fifty years on from the inaugural championship, which Mick himself had won back in 1922. On the occasion of the R.W.A. 20 miles Championship at Worsley, near Manchester we were delighted to see Past President SYD ROBERTS, with his wife who had travelled the long journey from St. Annes-on-Sea to see the Club in action. Our Vice-President EDMUND DONOVAN OBE who has resided in America for fifty years, was able to attend a Southern League fixture at Wimbledon Park Track, and tell us of Belgrave of a bygone age and of the characters who helped to build the Club. BERT MITCHELL, always associated with our Club Marathon Championship Shield, paid us a visit on the occasion of the 20 Miles Open Run and promises that his next visit to Wimbledon will not be so long delayed. At the same event CHRIS STEER showed himself (or the greater part of himself!) and threatened further visits in the future. HAROLD KING, a Club walking champion many times over, celebrated his 51st year of membership at the Club Track Championships. Past President FRANK SIMMONS was able to attend the Annual General Meeting and we were very pleased to see him. Another AGM visitor was SYD SPENCER former 'B' Division Police and Belgrave walker - now on the Judges list. It was a great pleasure when our Vice-President from Delhi, RANJIT BHATIA paid us a visit in late September and competed in our road race. He will be remembered as a great asset to our teams in his Oxford University days, which led to Olympic honours for India in the Rome Olympics. He is striving hard to establish and encourage Athletics in his part of India, with some considerable measure of success. Additional Belgrave representation in the Olympic Games to John Bicourt and Cliff Brooks was provided by WILLI WESCH who represented W.Germany in the 20,000 metres walk. Our thanks and good wishes to JACK OLIVER on his retirement to the Portsmouth area. Jack was of considerable service to us as a walking judge for many years. Having an Olympic steeplechaser in the Club in John Bicourt, reminds us of a former Belgrave Olympic steeplechaser of the 1930's: JIM GINTY. Jim competed at Berlin in 1936; and had the distinction of leading the English team to a win in the 1937 International Cross Country Championship, after finishing 3rd (and scoring 1) in the E.C.C.U. Championship at Stratford-on-Avon. Incidently we scored 94 points and lost to Birchfield by four points! We hope John will succeed in getting double International honours as did Jim many years ago. JACK GOSWELL (with FRANK JARVIS at his right hand as Hon Secretary) has survived a difficult year as President of the Race Walking Assn., and is to be congratulated on the sincerity and efficiency with which he tackled the job. BOB TAYLOR bowed out as Track Hon. Secretary at the AGM, but it is generally understood that this a temporary respite only. Bob is much too good a man to have kicking his heels on the side lines. ARTHUR PENNY, the Empire Games 6 miles Champion of 1934 and an International cross country runner, has officiated as our starter for many years past but he is now anxious to relinquish the position into younger hands. May we have some volunteers please who will approach this office with the seriousness it merits? Timekeepers also are needed if our athletes are to fill up their little black books, and it is emphasised that 100 guinea watches are by no means necessary. Regularity of appearance and the conscientious approach are much more important. DANNY WISEMAN - the very name brings fear to the hearts of those who consider themselves 'two-lappers'. Danny got down to 1:52.2 for 880 yards some years back but then disappeared to qualify as a solicitor and then see a bit of the world. He is now getting back into training and hopes to run on the track next summer. Cheerful letters from ALF TAYLOR and TONY WHINCUP remind us of two stalwarts of years ago. We wish them well. items.sum: Farewell tribute to Dave Ansell, Belgravian athlete and chief jumps coach to the A.A.A., on his move to Leeds, recalling the jumpers he coached.
items.s: Dave Ansell goes North Farewell tribute to Dave Ansell, Belgravian athlete and chief jumps coach to the A.A.A., on his move to Leeds, recalling the jumpers he coached. It's always a bit of a wrench when one of the "old contemptibles" packs his bags and leaves Belgrave territory. Dave Ansell's departure to Leeds, where he is chief design executive for the Burton Group, was no exception to this generalisation. Dave has been a Belgravian for 21 years both as an active athlete and a coach. In both activities he achieved some distinction, particularly the latter where he is the chief jumps coach to the A.A.A. Coaching caught Dave's interest when he was approaching the end of his active career and he quickly built up a young jumps school, where members went from strength to strength. Best known are internationals Alan Lerwill, Britain's successor to Lynn Davies, and Derek Cole - both second claim Belgravians, and Belgravians John Mitchell and Steve White. I think Dave's appeal to the younger athlete is founded on his cheerful philosophy of life coupled with an intense attention to detail. Both John Mitchell and Alan Lerwill testify to his successful ability to harness natural ability to discipline - much of the early spadework taking place in the often depressing surroundings of Battersea Park. Outside his coaching Dave was a good supporter of the Club. I remember several National League meetings where he was to be seen by the trackside, in the pub, or elsewhere. He was not only a cheerful companion on many occasions, but had a becoming modesty about his abilities, from which many could learn. His presence will be missed greatly. P.B.H. items.label: December 1972
items.sum: Tribute by A. A. Harley to Ernest H. Neville, Belgrave Harriers Vice-President and race walking administrator, who died aged 89, recalling his committee work and an anecdote involving Charlie Megnin.
items.s: ERNEST H. NEVILLE Tribute by A. A. Harley to Ernest H. Neville, Belgrave Harriers Vice-President and race walking administrator, who died aged 89, recalling his committee work and an anecdote involving Charlie Megnin. These days we regularly come across the phrase - " a legend in his own life time" - and this could well have originated with Ernest H. Neville who has recently passed on at the age of 89, after a lifetime of inspiration to others and positive action in the service of others. To do justice to such a subject demands a first class biographer with far-reaching research facilities which would go back to the late 1800's and early this century. It is to be hoped that someone, perhaps one of his old Surrey Walking Club or Blackheath Harriers colleagues will be able to fill in the early gaps in such a full life and give us a picture of Ernest in his early days of legal and business training and his earliest contacts with Sport and particularly that of Walking. It could be a really fascinating study. My own personal recollections of Ernest only carry back to the late 1920's when I remember his attendance at the Annual General Meeting of the Belgrave Harriers of which he was a Vice-President - when he enthused over the Club's successes and encouraged to even more success in the future. It was perhaps in the committee and conference room that Ernest was at his absolute best. His erudition combined with his wide knowledge of meeting and administrative procedures, his solid reassuring physical appearance, his sincerity and enthusiasm for his subject, made him formidable indeed, especially when all this was backed by a willingness and an ability to work hard and long in the implementation of committee decisions. He was assisted in this by his wide range of personal contacts, and his ability to persuade Lord Mayors, Members of Parliament, Newspaper Editors right down to the humblest club members to serve and assist with whatever projects he had in mind at a particular time. His enthusiasm communicated itself to all he met, and this was the key to his personality and the mark of a man of true greatness. This quality allied with a determination " to see it through" plus the skill and ability to translate committee decisions and draft plans into positive action and realistic results were in the Neville mould. His physical bulk, command of language and manner of conducting himself gave him a sense of authority wherever he chanced to be. To be with Ernest was to receive the highest possible service and attention normally reserved only for the vippiest of V.I.P.'s. His manner was ever polite and courteous and his personality impress brought forth response from all he met, and his generosity was all-pervading and really something to be seen to be believed. The R.W.A. and our Sport benefit[illegible]d very considerably from Ernest's generous impulses which flared outwards, especially in his 62, London Wall office days of the late 1920's when his business abilities earned him phenominal rewards. Even as an older man Ernest was constantly setting an example to his juniors of undiluted enthusiasm (without which nothing can be achieved), and a willingness to work effectively whether it be as Chairman of an important Committee or as manipulator of the loud-hailer at the conclusion of the Brighton Walk. His enthusiasm was always a delight to see and one can only hope that some of it has "rubbed off" in good measure on to our later generations. Of the respect in which he was held throughout the world of Athletics much could be written, and the influence he exerted in sport is beyond computation. I have confined myself to jotting down some thoughts on Ernest as a man and a friend and a personality who has left his indelible mark on our Sport and bequeathed us something really worthwhile which can be maintained and improved in the way he would have wished in perpetuity. Others will write of Ernest's influence and work on R.W.A. Committees, of his ungrudging services at Club, County, Area and National level, of his yeoman efforts within the Centurians and the Road Runners Club, and over many years internationally, where his work and thinking have earned sincere appreciation. At various times I served on Rules Revision Committees with Ernest and invariably we agreed to commit our ideas to paper and then invite the comments of the other members and so make slow but sure progress. Usually I found myself thinking that there was no great hurry for our work could not be ratified for another six or twelve months - and so my reaction was one of qualified procrastination. Not so with Ernest however! Within 36 hours one received an important legal looking missive timed usually at 4 a.m. (a typical Nevillism) and beautifully handwritten in thin thick copperplate style in black and red ink with marginal title and underlinings in red and black, and embellished with legal red tapes. A real work of art in fact, and although one might disagree with every suggested clause and sentence, nevertheless one was compelled to do something about it and make ones comments, and draft possible alterations. So did Ernest sham his younger colleagues into doing their duty rather quicker than they would otherwise have done, and providing an excellent example for others to follow. To finish with an anecdote which I think deserves to be commited to paper. At an R.W.A. Committee meeting Ernest started the discussion on some subject or other with the words "This morning I consulted my Oxford Dictionary of the English Language....... He was interrupted by Charlie Megnin who had a reputation as a wit who said "I'm shocked. I never dreamed Mr. Neville consulted dictionaries - I thought he wrote them." Ernest enjoyed the joke as much as anyone! Good-bye! Ernest - We cannot fail to miss you! A. A. Harley Ernest H. Neville Ernest H. items.label: December 1972
items.sum: Obituary by G. S. Doubleday of Ernest Neville, Belgrave Vice-President, recording his walking feats, his founding role in the Centurians and the Road Runners Club, and his work for Olympic walking and the London to Brighton races.
items.s: Obituary by G. S. Doubleday of Ernest Neville, Belgrave Vice-President, recording his walking feats, his founding role in the Centurians and the Road Runners Club, and his work for Olympic walking and the London to Brighton races. We are extremely sorry to record the death, in his 90th year, of our esteemed Vice-President, doyen of long distance running and walking, Ernest Neville. His death occurred on Wednesday 1st November, a few days after a stomach operation at St. Georges Hospital, Tooting, where he was a patient in Belgrave Ward. A member of many athletic clubs he joined us before World War I, and was proud of being a Belgravian. He was attracted to athletics in 1897 when he saw the late Teddy Knott walking to Brighton, and, at the age of fourteen he walked from London to Brighton. Four years later he did the double journey, having a meal and a rest at Brighton, within twenty-four hours. In 1902 he promoted the first London to Brighton and Back Walk on behalf of Surrey W.C. From that time on he has been associated with walking and running promotions until a few weeks ago. He was a formidable competitor at running, from the sprints to the marathon, and at walking, from the Mile to 100 miles. He did many feats of long distance walking, and for many years he walked, all duly recorded, 100 miles a week. In 1903 in a Brighton and Back walk, promoted by himself, again for Surrey W.C., he finished third in 21h.13m.50secs. In 1911 he, and other walkers who had walked 100 miles inside 24 hours founded the Centurians, a fraternity restricted to those who had accomplished this feat, he became number seven and at the time of his death was Life President. He was a Past President of the R.W.A. and of the Surrey County A.A.A. and Surrey W.C. His sporting interests were not confined to athletics and he took part in other sports and could speak with considerable authority about them. A great worker behind the scenes he served on many committees of Athletic Associations and Clubs. When the A.A.A. needed information or guidance on matters concerning long distance racing they instinctively turned to him for advice. He was a keen supporter of athletics at County level, and was a tower of strength to his own County, Surrey. Up until 1924 there had only been track walks up to 10,000 metres in the Olympic Games, there had been so much controversy that they were left out of the 1928 Games. It was largely due to Ernest that walking was restored to the 1932 Games at Los Angeles. The race was a 50 kilometres Road Walk, won by our own Tommy Green. He continually pressed for walking at International level and at the 1936 (Berlin) Games he was Chief Judge. After World War II came the Festival of Britain in 1951 and amongst the sporting events was a running race from London to Brighton this was organised by Ernest and was a great success. Subsequently, in order to draw long-distance runners together and to further their interests he founded the Road Runners Club. There were few long distance races in those days and the R.R.C. can claim a large credit for the healthy state and popularity of Road Running today. Not only was he Founder but for many years he was General Hon. Secretary of the R.R.C., and served a term as President. As the years advanced his enthusiasm remained undiminished, most of the present World Best Performances at both Running and Walking were made at events largely organised by him. He was the organiser par excellence, he did the groundwork very thoroughly writing to all potential helpers. His instructions to competitors and officials were models of clarity and precision. After the event letters of thanks would go out to all who had helped. He had a prodigious memory and could recount an event which happened at the turn of the century as if it took place recently. His vast experience of athletic affairs must have been unequalled and his counsels were much sought for and appreciated. Right up to his death he attended meetings and played a full part in the deliberations. His attitudes were always forward looking and he was always receptive to new ideas. This year's London to Brighton run was his last promotion and was a very happy day for him - a great race, a new record, and a surprise presentation to him of a plaque from the Mayor of Brighton for his many years of promoting races from London to Brighton. In the usual letter of thanks to helpers he announced his retirement from promoting, happy in the knowledge that he had found, encouraged and taught others to carry on the good work he had done, as no other man could over 70 years. He also led a very busy life in business, largely connected with Insurance, Finance and the Law. For his services to the City of London as a Fireguard Commander in World War II he was made an Honorary Freeman, an honour reserved for the few. In closing this tribute we say "Good-bye and Thank you, Ernest for all you have done", your name and memory will be honoured by Belgravians for many years to come. G. S. items.sum: Handwritten personal tribute by C.E.M. to Ernest Neville, recalling being recruited as a lap scorer on the Brighton Road, his eightieth birthday party at the House of Commons and his larger-than-life character, with an uncaptioned photo of Neville.
items.s: Handwritten personal tribute by C.E.M. to Ernest Neville, recalling being recruited as a lap scorer on the Brighton Road, his eightieth birthday party at the House of Commons and his larger-than-life character, with an uncaptioned photo of Neville. He was a man - but different from most men - he was so much bigger - big physically - big mentally - more daring - more energetic - he could forsee an organization like the Road Runners Club - he could concieve the master plan - he would then hammer it into shape - with people. Once, seeing me on a remote stretch of the Brighton Road innocently watching one or two well spaced characters in a race, he stopped the car, in which he was a passenger and addressed me, "Hey You!" "Umm ?" "Whats yer name?" "Umm, its Man ..." "You're lap scorer - Saturday week - Walton - 10.30" he said before I had a chance to say anything "But - I'm afraid ..." I began but never got any further because he turned on his heel and with an imperious demand to his chauffeur, "Drive On!" I went to his birthday party - he was eighty - we celebrated it in the House of Commons - Chris. Chattaway proposed his health - he was that sort of man - his business life was lived at full pitch - he danced with Royalty - he trained snails to race, on a ship, in the Red Sea and ran a book on the results - he talked once to my children, not at them, up to them or down to them - he was a Centurian - its probably rather presumptious of me to write this because my connection to him was only tenuous, but because of that I thought I'd just pen these few words as someone not too close to him and because I liked him, as I'm sure you would - if you'd had the honour to know - Ernest Neville. items.label: December 1972
items.sum: Walking notes by Carl Lawton on a disappointing season of 'Nationals' and news of Belgrave walkers including Percy Wilson, Wilf Wesch and Dave De Bondi.
items.s: WALKING Walking notes by Carl Lawton on a disappointing season of 'Nationals' and news of Belgrave walkers including Percy Wilson, Wilf Wesch and Dave De Bondi. General disappointment seems to be the order of the day after the season of'Nationals'. Our failures have certainly not been due to not having the walkers. It has just been a rather bad run of misfortune. With the new blood being produced slowly we should be back on a good footing next season. That stalwart of Belgrave, Percy Wilson, has made a good recovery from the illness that struck him earlier this year and made a welcome return to the sidelines at the Imber Court meeting. Bob Barnes, star of a few years ago was a bystander at the Highgate Hour races and it is rumoured that he is to make his 25th comeback. Gerry Cameron has been putting walking on to the Scottish map although support from South of the border is lacking due to distance. Maybe the Bels can get a team up there next year. Pat Duncan is reportedly returning to training at the beginning of next February, although it is thought that he is looking for another excuse for not doing so. Bob Farley has been at many races taking various scientific measurements including weight loss and it is for this reason that Charlie Maclennan has not turned out for many months. Wilf Wesch cannot be forgotten. He of course represented West Germany at Munich in the Olympic Games, finishing 16th in 1hr.35min. 20.6 secs. With his departure it has left a slight gap in the Belgrave team although with youngsters like Lawton and Middleton we should pull through. Our Australian visitor Dave De Bondi has returned to his country. He is still training in the Australian hills and is hoping to get a little faster. He competed in the Victoria State Championship 50 Km and finished 2nd in 5hrs. and 10 secs. His training has been reduced due to too much time spent thinking about building a'nissen'hut Carl Lawton Percy Wilson Percy Wilson recovered from illness; returned to the sidelines at Imber Court Bob Barnes Bob Barnes spectator at the Highgate Hour races Gerry Cameron Gerry Cameron walking in Scotland Pat Duncan Pat Duncan Bob Farley Bob Farley taking scientific measurements at races Charlie Maclennan Charlie Maclennan Wilf Wesch Wilf Wesch represented West Germany in the Olympic Games walk at Munich, 16th in 1hr.35min. 20.6 secs. Kannenburg in an unofficial world record and Wilf Wesch won the 20 km for West Germany. In an international match - Great Britain v West Germany - Ray Middleton walked one of his best races in the 50 Km but was still 22 minutes behind the winner Kannenburg. items.s: Belgrave lose all in National 50 km Report and result of the National 50 km walk at Badminton on August 15th, won by J. Warhurst, where Carl Lawton's retirement cost Belgrave the team title and they finished third team. AUGUST 15th - BADMINTON. This was an excellent venue regarding the course, almost totally traffic free and apart from one small stretch of rough on each lap, an excellent surface. Amongst the early leaders was Carl Lawton hoping to pull off a performance comparable to last year's and Ray Middleton, starting well but losing ground due to sickness. As the race progressed the hot day began to have its effect and soon numbers of competitors were seen to be retiring. At 20 miles Carl Lawton joined the casualties. This failing of his meant that Bels had little or no chance of winning the team race and as it proved later, a certain victory was once again thrown away. Ray Middleton proved not quite good enough to catch Bob Dobson and Len Duquemin and John Moullin walked their usual races in this event to finish in the first fifteen. With the retirement of Allan Callow and Ray Hall, it was up to John Dunsford to be fourth man home. George Beecham was another to fall by the wayside. Team:- 1. Sheffield 38pts 2. items.sum: Report and results of the Southern R.W.A. Track League final at the East London Stadium on August 19th, which Belgrave won, with John Moullin winning the 5,000m and newcomer Jonathon Dunsford walking in the 2,000m under-18 event.
items.s: Southern R.W.A. Track League Final Report and results of the Southern R.W.A. Track League final at the East London Stadium on August 19th, which Belgrave won, with John Moullin winning the 5,000m and newcomer Jonathon Dunsford walking in the 2,000m under-18 event. AUGUST 19th - EAST LONDON STADIUM. Without much time to get to bed, most of the Bels team travelled over to the East London Stadium for this track meeting. Although it was a rather windy day it still provided a tension filled afternoon. With four races to decide the result, things began to tilt Belgrave's way from the first race and with three walkers in each event and only two to score, there was a battle for team places. The first event of the afternoon was the 3,000m. Due to a rather dusty track Carl Lawton was unable to produce his performance of the previous evening but did finish 2nd to Roger Mills and just held off Ken Easlea's dust storm. John Hall was our second man home. Next on the track with Bels now in a one point lead were the 10,000m boys. A comfortable win by Amos Seddon over Bill Sutherland left Ray Middleton to come in fourth and Len Duquemin 5th. Bels now two points up. It was in the next event that Belgrave pulled out their trump card. In the qualifying round in June we could only produce one junior for the 2,000m under 18 event and Surrey assumed that the same would occur today. It was not to be. Our latest signing, with the ink still wet on the paper, was Jonathon Dunsford thus starting up another father/son walking relationship. Jonathon finished 9th in this event but one cannot go further without giving due mention to our other walker in this event. Martin Bennett, now 16, walked a steady race ('I prefer longer races') to finish third. Not a brilliant performance by any means but when one considers that he had travelled down from Glasgow in the early hours for the race little more need to be said. Appreciation from the other walkers was expressed. Finally on to the last race and although Bels were now 3 points up it was still neck and neck in the 5,000m. John Moullin eventually got the better of Charlie Fogg although battle raged for the minor placings. Initially Surrey men were 2nd and 4th over the first half but they lost ground to the pounding hooves of the Johns, Dunsford and Bromley. The battle between these two lasted up to the finishing line with John Dunsford getting the verdict (and a medal) by four seconds. Overall it was an excellent win for Belgrave and an excellent turn out although one place had to be refilled due to the non-appearance of one walker who had originally been selected. Team:- 1. items.sum: Report and result of the London to Brighton walk on September 2nd, won by Peter Selby, with Len Duquemin and Carl Lawton fifth and sixth and Belgrave second team to Surrey.
items.s: LONDON — BRIGHTON Report and result of the London to Brighton walk on September 2nd, won by Peter Selby, with Len Duquemin and Carl Lawton fifth and sixth and Belgrave second team to Surrey. SEPTEMBER 2nd 6a.m on a Saturday morning is not the best time to be standing shivering on Westminster Bridge. But there we were in an attempt on the Brighton road. Six Bels' lined up to walk and many others carried out their usual timekeeping duties and feeding station attending all so greatly appreciated by us boys. For Carl Lawton and Len Duquemin it was their first attempt on this stroll! For veterans Moullin, King, Keown and Beecham this was far from the case. The dawn slowly broke going up through Streatham as the field spread out. Shaun Lightman was the first leader, a position which he held for much of the race. Carl Lawton made an emergency stop in Croydon to pick up 2p on the road, taking great care that Johnny Morris, this time in the attendants seat on a bicycle, was not there first. Lawton slowly moved through the field and caught Len at 20 miles to take 3rd place. He held this position until Pease Pottage where he lost two places while picking blackberries. At this point Len Duquemin was on the verge of retiring but both men got back on the road again and hobbled on together. John Moullin came through to 5th place at Bolney but he did not hold it for very long due to the increasing power of our struggling pair. Further back Dave King was fighting his usual battle. Brighton was eventually reached, first by Peter Selby who had passed a quietly sitting Lightman at 40 miles. Duquemin got the verdict by 2 seconds from Lawton on the front with John next man 1½ minutes down. Dave King came in as our 4th man although just too far down to give us a team win. items.s: SEPTEMBER 23rd - HIGHGATE HARRIERS ONE HOUR RACES - COPTHALL STADIUM Note on Belgrave's thin turn out at the Highgate Harriers one hour races at Copthall Stadium, where Martin Bennett was second in section 'D' and some older members reappeared. An unfortunately low turn out by Belgrave in this event due to injuries etc. meant that we had no starters in the 'A' section. However, we were represented in all other sections although our only success was Martin Bennett's 2nd position in section 'D'. It was also a meeting place of some of our members who do not get the same opportunity to race as they used to. Namely, Bernard Eglinton down from North Wales and Joe Scammell, not getting any younger but competing in the 'D' section and completing 8324m. Bobby Barnes was spectating and it was rumoured that he was going to make another comeback. Duncan's return (the report gives his time as 48:30, the table 48.38). The opening 5 produced a high turn out of walkers, 17 Belgrave and 23 Met and Essex Police. In addition to this three Belgravians were spectating. Winner on this warm afternoon was Amos Seddon with Ray Middleton strolling in behind. Lou Mockett grabbed 3rd place from John Moullin on the last lap round the Common. A welcome return was made by that stalwart of long distance racing, P.L. Duncan, who fresh from his high altitude training camp in the South of France powered home in 48:30, although it was rumoured, by a certain gentleman of leisure who was taking stock of the situation, that "he didn't half die on the hill". items.s: Bels win Chippenham to Calne '6' Report and result of the Chippenham to Calne 6 walk on October 14th, won by Shaun Lightman, with Carl Lawton third and Belgrave winning the team race. OCTOBER 14th With Carl Lawton a doubtful starter due to injury things did not look too promising. However, throwing cares to the wind he gallantly decided to start with the intention of playing it safe. The course this year was back on the old route and for the competitors it was a welcome return. Bels were not too well placed as the walkers moved easterly towards Calne but as the race progressed Lawton moved up from last place to third which slightly eased the situation. Shaun Lightman managed to break away from Roy (I've forgotten what my heels are for) Court to win and Lawton held off Mal Tolley for third. Ray Middleton powered back onto the scene in 7th place and Len and John brought in our team for another team victory. However, success did not stop there. Dave McMullen was first Veteran, John Bromley picked up fourth handicap and Bob Carter one of the raffle prizes. In fact it was an all round performance with our team of eight all in the first 41 places. Martin Bennett warming up for the National Youth was a little lower down. That performance was without both Allan Callow and Bob Coates, who are rumoured to have retired. Team:- 1. BELGRAVE H. 32pts. 2. Highgate 35pts. 3. Leicester 40 pts. 1. S. Lightman (Met.W.C) 44:03 2. Flynn, with Belgrave taking a fourth consecutive team win and Jack Goswell presented with an attache case for his 21st Open. NOVEMBER 25th - WIMBLEDON Of the 150 starters 19 were Belgravians and some noteworthy performances came from our boys. Carl, John and Ray produced their usuals but Len was the real match winner in 6th place. John Bromley came in together with Munich Olympian Howard Timms. The battle of the Halls continues but on this occasion John got the better of Ray, although the latter gained a team handicap prize as did Martin Bennett. Martin who did not have a very good race has long deserved some reward for his recent performances. Bernard Eglington was obviously tired after his trip from Wales. It was our fourth consecutive win, making some amends for defeat at the hands of Leicester and Basildon in the Enfield '7'. A special presentation of an attache case (donated by J.Johnson) was made to Jack Goswell to commemorate his 21st 'Open' and with usual 'Goswell' efficiency, result sheets were circulated before the hall was closed. items.s: Boxed notice from the Hon. Treasurer giving the new subscription rates agreed at the A.G.M. and the change of the club year to end on June 30th. The members who attended the A.G.M. will already know that subscriptions were increased and are now as follows:- 21 years and over ......... £3.00 17 years and under 21 years £1.50 under 17 years ............ £0.50 I hope members will participate in the fund raising schemes such as the football pontoon and the A.A.A. draw to enable the Committee to continue to provide facilities unequalled by most clubs throughout the country. With the cost of these services continually rising it may well be that a further increase will be necessary unless we can raise money in other ways. Also passed at the A.G.M. was the alteration of the Club 'year', now to end on June 30th. This is to enable the treasurer and auditors to have more time to prepare the balance sheet. In future all subscriptions will be due on July 1st each year. Don't delay, pay your subs now. ~ Hon. Treasurer A.A.A.

"ENGLISH SENIOR CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP" ......... ... "Held at Apsley over a course almost knee-deep in snow, this was definitely not a fair test to the runners, although A.A.Robertson ran in really magnificent style and fully deserved his win. Len Herbert finished 6th and so gained yet another International vest, while Albert Frost ran in great style to finish 17th and so gain his Club Honours badge." "Sutton Harriers, the Northern champions, beat us for the team championship, although we retained the 'Finch-Wayte' Cup awarded to the first Southern club to finish." Thames Valley H. 300." ...... and 40 years ago DECEMBER 1932 ...... ......OUR OPEN WALK ...... "194 entries, comprising 22 teams, entered our Open race which took place over the same course as used in the last year or two. We had four teams entered, Surrey Walking Club sent along three teams and the Polytechnic two. The race resolved itself into a duel between Johnson, of Enfield, and Green, of our's, with Johnson eventually gaining a creditable win. He also had the satisfaction of leading his team to victory, Enfield scoring 28 points to our 36." "H.Latter, one of our young walkers included in the 'B' team, surprised us all by finishing 13th in the scratch race (out of 170 starters), so winning the handicap with an allowance of 5 mins. 50 secs. This success, combined with good walking by A.H.Field, enabled our 'B' team to win the first handicap team prizes, the team being completed by Harley and Brown." 1. J.T.Johnson (Enfield) 54:58; 2.
