items.s: Boxed note that F.M. Stone of Broadstairs congratulates Bill Couzens and Charlie Manning on Life Membership and sends greetings to old contemporaries. F.M.STONE, writing from DENE COTTAGE, RAMSGATE ROAD, BROADSTAIRS, KENT, sends his congratulations to Bill Couzens and Charlie Manning on their election to Life Membership, and would like to be remembered to all Belgravians, particularly Harry Hare or any of his other old contempories. He still keeps in contact with George Powell who is keeping well. items.label: December 1972
items.h: SPOTLIGHT ON LAURIE O'HARA & BILL WELLER
items.sum: Spotlight profile by Gordon Biscoe of Laurie O'Hara, who won veterans 5,000 metres titles at Crystal Palace and Cologne in his first season as a veteran, and Bill Weller, winner of the Belgrave '20' and Surrey 20 miles title, with two photographs.
items.s: SPOTLIGHT ON LAURIE O'HARA & BILL WELLER Spotlight profile by Gordon Biscoe of Laurie O'Hara, who won veterans 5,000 metres titles at Crystal Palace and Cologne in his first season as a veteran, and Bill Weller, winner of the Belgrave '20' and Surrey 20 miles title, with two photographs. It is more than appropriate at this time that our spotlight should fall jointly on Laurie and Bill, for not only are they both completing what has been the most successful year in their respective careers but it is interesting to note that although from different athletic backgrounds and age groups their approach and outlook to the sport is so similar. With the same consistancy with which our various press reports never let us forget who Lionel Mann's employers are, so since June of this year the latest 'in thing' has been to refer to "Veteran Laurie O'Hara". However, with equal consistancy Laurie has produced a string of performances on track and road that have served to prove just how ridiculous it is in these times to stick a 'Veteran' label on 40 year old athletes. Following a very successful cross country and road relay season, Laurie produced a personal best of 30:57.6 to take the Club 10,000 metres championship with an almost solo effort and then proceeded in the following three months to lower his 5,000 metre time on three separate occasions finishing with a time of 14:28s. The highlight of the season, however, was, no doubt, in August and September when at two separate international veterans meetings at the Crystal Palace and Cologne he shattered the opposition to take the 5,000 metres titles. Of the two occasions, the Crystal Palace produced possibly the best veterans 5000 metres field ever assembled with such people as former Australian champion, Dave Power, in contention. As one observer has noted Laurie met the challenge by most uncharacteristically bursting to the front in the first lap and proceeded to open a gap of some 80 yards from the rest of the field. Although this had been cut to 4 seconds at the bell he still won by some 10 seconds having run the heart out of his rivals. Having briefly looked at Laurie's achievements in the last five months since becoming a vet., one must not let these performances overshadow the tremendous years of service he has given to Belgrave since joining, supposedly at a late age. It was in 1961, after a successful career at amateur football, having played for Reading, Bexley Heath and Harrow Town, that Laurie joined the club. Having reached about as far as he could go in football he decided to try athletics, and struck up training acquaintances with Fred Paget and Pat Newell in Fulham and it was these two who were instrumental in getting him to sign the necessary piece of paper! From his first outing on the track in Belgrave's colours his tremendous talents were obvious and that he would be a force to be reckoned with, in and outside Belgrave, was in no doubt. He quickly graduated to our 'A' teams, has effectively stayed there ever since and on his present performances how many are there who can keep him out?!! To try and enumerate Laurie's performances over the years within the limitations of these pages would be an impossible task, the Brighton, Southern and National Relays; Southern and National C.C. Championships; League Races; Local Relays; Club Championships; and just plain inter-club meetings, he has left his mark on them all in his own quiet efficient manner. Possibly his greatest inspiration has been in the Road Relays, a last leg specialist, many are the instances when in a closely fought contest at the closing stages of a race he has driven our supporters wild with delight as he has unleashed that now famous burst of acceleration to drop an opponent and put Belgrave back in the medals. One feels that if Laurie had ever graduated to international ranks on the track, this characteristic alone would have made him a great crowd puller at the White City. Laurie confesses though, that it is Road Running which he enjoys most and recalls that the performance which gave him the most pleasure was winning the first stage in one of the old London - Brighton Road Relays. In spite of first class performances in the country he insists"I only really do it to keep fit - I don't like the country really". Although doing his fair share, he is not one of the present day mileage fanatics, and he's always had to fit his running in with being a family man and his career as an Electrician, which over the years has always involved him in shift work with the result that many's the time he's turned out to race with hardly any sleep behind him. This Summer's bonanza for Laurie was brought to a climax in September when he made his debut over the Marathon distance. Running in the Harlow marathon he finished in a commendable time of 2hr.35mins, but admitted to going too fast early on, very blistered and very tired it was summed up with the comment, "I learnt a lot this time and I'll know better next!" Unlike Laurie O'Hara's 11 years service, Bill Weller has now been with us for exactly two, but characteristically has integrated into the Club so enthusiastically that the time seems much longer and he has long since been considered as part of the furniture. Born in October, 1946, Bill's interest in running stems from the age of 8 years old, when one of his earliest recollections were 2 mile runs along the coast road near Goring, Sussex, having arranged for his father to drive two miles up the road in the car and wait for him. The main awakening came, however, when he changed from primary to secondary school at the age of 11 and found that running was a compulsory sport. To his surprise he found that he could keep going long after his contempories had been forced to stop and drop out, from then on he was 'hooked'! At the age of 13 running seemed a good excuse for not playing football or hockey. Having satisfied the master he would be participating in some such game Bill would quietly slide off for a one and a half hours run over the Downs from his school in Epsom. Unfortunately games periods lasted 1 hour so by the time Bill arrived back search parties were being organised to look for him. However, he maintains that it was these early runs of 9 - 10 miles over the Downs to Headley and back which laid the basis for his stamina in later years, these workouts being augmented by the daily runs from his school into Epsom to catch the early bus home at 4 p.m., those less fleet of foot being forced to wait another half-hour. His early club days were with Redhill and Reigate A.C. from 1961/65 and he recalls at the age of 15 having races and training sessions of 9 miles or more with their Senior team members in Reigate Priory, and anyone who has ever run in the Reigate Relays will know what that involves. Originally Bill confesses to having illusions about being a track star over 880 yards. However, after a considerable amount of track training in 1963 he remembers coming 2nd to Steve Badgery (now Hercules Wimbledon A.C.) over 880 yards in 2:05, so "I soon gave that up". In 1965 he joined Walton A.C. and it was while he was with them, having tried his hand at track, road and country without any great success that he developed primarily into a long distance road man. Spotlight.... Coinciding with the time he joined Belgrave from Walton in 1970 Bill, a Civil Servant, moved with his job from Kingston to Redhill and thus being nearer his home in Reigate was able to devote more time to training. From then on a steady improvement has continued in his performances over the last two years, resulting in rather an impressive tally of placings in this year's road races. These include winning the Belgrave Open 20 miles, Surrey 20 miles Championship, Worthing 11 miles (breaking his own record) and Wimbledon 10 miles, as well as placings in the Bracknell 10 miles (2nd), Walton 10 miles (2nd), Epsom 11 miles (4th) and at the start of the year 4th in the Mitcham 25 Km. Most of these races have been against tough competition and apart from individual achievements Bill has anchored our team to similar successes on these occasions as our results sheets show. After joining us from Walton, he had to serve his waiting period of 9 months but once eligible and once in our teams, like Laurie O'Hara he has stayed there, producing many sterling performances for us earlier in the Spring and this Autumn. Bill also is no lover of cross country running and being subject to injury over it, tends to 'disappear' in the winter months, however, if a league race or the Surrey Championships turn up and we happen to be under pressure, team wise, he'll answer the call and is ready to do battle to, as he puts it, "help keep that other lot at bay". (The 'other lot' being anyone not Belgrave). One could possibly describe Bill Weller as the complete athlete, for when he joined us he brought with him his own supporters club. I refer, of course, to his mother and father who enthusiastically accompany him on most outings and in all weathers, supporting not only Bill but all of the Belgrave team. Having managed, so far, to avoid the marriage stakes, his main interest outside athletics is horse racing; and remembers putting his training to good purpose while still at school to race across Epsom Downs on Derby day to place a bet! Nowadays on Saturday afternoons prior to a race, the way he adjusts his warm up with the checking of the latest results from Kempton or Newmarket etc. on the car radio, is an exercise in precision timing. There is no doubt that in Laurie O'Hara and Bill Weller Belgrave has two great clubmen to be proud of. Both are of that quiet type who do not herald forthcoming performances with selfcentred ballyhoo but who, with a professional-like no-nonsense approach, set out to give of their best with every performance, so characteristic of another Belgravian - Gerry North. From a team managers point of view their general reliability and attitude is a refreshing change to some, and one that others would do well to copy; and to our younger members I would say that these are the characteristics they should seek to mould themselves on. Watching Bill Weller in action during one of the relays this Spring someone remarked to me "I'm glad he's on our side now"! - I would now like to modify this remark and say "I'm glad they're both on our side"!! Gordon Biscoe Opposite. Laurie O'Hara (left) and Bill Weller, all smiles after one of the tightest finishes ever seen on our 5¾ mile road course. Both were given 28 minutes 18 seconds but Laurie got the verdict. KING OF THE ROAD - BILL WELLER makes the Belgrave '20' look easy and wins the race, Belgrave and Surrey titles in 1 hr. 45 min 06 secs. Laurie O'Hara Laurie O'Hara won Club 10,000 metres championship in 30:57.6; won veterans 5,000 metres at Crystal Palace and Cologne 1972; joined Belgrave 1961 after amateur football; won first stage of London - Brighton Road Relays; marathon debut at Harlow, 2hr.35mins; an Electrician Laurie O'Hara Laurie Bill Weller Bill Weller born October 1946; formerly Redhill and Reigate A.C. 1961/65 and Walton A.C. from 1965; joined Belgrave two years ago; won the Belgrave '20' (Belgrave and Surrey titles) in 1 hr. 45 min 06 secs.; a Civil Servant living in Reigate; 1972 wins: Belgrave Open 20 miles, Surrey 20 miles Championship, Worthing 11 miles (record), Wimbledon 10 miles; 2nd Bracknell 10 miles and Walton 10 miles, 4th Epsom 11 miles, 4th Mitcham 25 Km Bill Weller Bill BILL WELLER Lionel Mann Lionel Mann Dave Power Dave Power former Australian champion Fred Paget Fred Paget Pat Newell Pat Newell Alan Black Alan Black Steve Badgery Steve Badgery beat Bill Weller over 880 yards in 1963 Ron Linstead Ron Linstead Gerry North Gerry North cited as another Belgravian of the quiet, no-nonsense type Gordon Biscoe Gordon Biscoe handwritten signature; writes as a team manager Club 10,000 metres championship Veterans international meeting London to Brighton Road Relay Harlow Marathon Reigate Relays Surrey 20 miles championship Worthing 11 miles Wimbledon 10 miles Bracknell 10 miles Walton 10 miles Epsom 11 miles Mitcham 25 Km Surrey Championships Derby Belgrave Open 20 miles Crystal Palace Cologne Fulham White City Harlow Goring Epsom Headley Reigate Priory Kingston Redhill Reigate Epsom Downs Kempton Newmarket Reading Bexley Heath Harrow Town Redhill and Reigate A.C. items.sum: Letter from Ewell by the Race Hon. Sec. 1966-72 (handwritten signature hard to read; it resembles Gordon Biscoe's on page 32) replying to Charlie Manning's thanks for course marking at the Belgrave '20' of July 1971, noting a T.V.H. member had to help with recording.
items.s: POSTBAG Letter from Ewell by the Race Hon. Sec. 1966-72 (handwritten signature hard to read; it resembles Gordon Biscoe's on page 32) replying to Charlie Manning's thanks for course marking at the Belgrave '20' of July 1971, noting a T.V.H. member had to help with recording. 34, Pams Way, Ewell, Surrey. Dear Sir, May I, through the pages of the magazine, clarify a point made by Charlie Manning when writing in the last edition of the 'Belgravian' in September. In that issue he expressed his thanks to seven other members of the Club who assisted with the course marking, etc. for the Belgrave '20' in July 1971 when he was acting as Clerk of the Course. From his remarks it was suggested that I had somewhere in the order of four hundred members helping with the officiating, compared to his seven. Although now just another part of Belgrave's history, I do remember the occasion well and would wholeheartedly endorse his thanks to all members who helped out in any way, however, I would like to point out that on this occasion I had to enlist the aid of a member of T.V.H. to complete the recording teams due to ours just failing to turn up! For further clarification perhaps I should explain that any association between the regular small band of hard working Club members and the remaining crowd of 'Bird Fanciers', 'Name Droppers' and 'Self Appointed Experts' who congregate around the finish on these occasions is purely coincidental. Their sole afternoon's contribution normally being to tell each other of "how it used to be", "how it should be" or even "how well we promote these races". Yours Sincerely [illegible] Race Hon. Sec. 1966 - 72 Charlie Manning Charlie Manning Clerk of the Course, Belgrave '20', July 1971 Belgrave '20' Ewell T.V.H.

items.label: December 1972
items.sum: Gordon Biscoe's road and cross-country column looking ahead to the coming season, saying farewell to Tony Binda (returning to Jamaica) and Tony Brien (studying at Kansas University) and urging other younger runners to step up.
items.s: ROAD AND COUNTRY Gordon Biscoe's road and cross-country column looking ahead to the coming season, saying farewell to Tony Binda (returning to Jamaica) and Tony Brien (studying at Kansas University) and urging other younger runners to step up. To try and comment on our fortunes etc. over the last eighteen months, when the Belgravian was in danger of becoming a collectors item, would be almost an impossible task and in any case much of this has now been collated as history in the recent edition brought out in November. It would thus appear more practical to look forward to what lies ahead, although at the moment it is still a long way off from the major cross country and road relay races, and thus too early to try and predict our chances. However, whatever else may transpire this is no time to relax our efforts for once again we have the unfortunate task of saying good-bye (one that seems to happen all too often for us) to two of our most promising younger stars namely, Tony Binda and Tony Brien. These are two names we can ill afford to lose for I had hoped that we would be able to call upon their talents for many years and thus help rebuild the younger Belgrave team we have been seeking since our disasters in 1971. Tony Binda returns to his native Jamaica and although he has been featured elsewhere in this issue, I would like to add personal thanks for all his efforts, from his races as a youth to his appearances in the senior teams. His cheerful personality will be missed as much as his ability. Tony Brien is now studying in Kansas University, following his departure from the R.A.F. earlier this year. He had already established himself as a 'resident' member in our senior team and his potential was probably more fully realised this summer when he only just missed selection for Ireland in the Olympic Games Marathon. In wishing them both well and every success can we hope that we have not yet seen the last of their appearances in Claret and Gold. For the immediate future, however, who will fill the gaps they leave? - will the Spring of 1973 see Adrian Major and Tony Fairclough back in full cry once more? Can Bill Curtin exploits the talents he's got by making the effort to get fit again and can someone like Doug Jardine, Doug Maughan, Leo Coy or Bob Dixon (a recent but welcome addition to our ranks) do a 'Trevor Hart' of former years and suddenly break through into the 'big time' - all of them have shown considerable improvements this year. The answers for them, and others, will lie in the training they do, but it is worth remembering that our successes as a Club will depend upon our successes as a Team in competitive races, not in private titanic struggles, fought out with Brian Gorman in Richmond Park. items.sum: Boxed note that Don Maclean won the Belgrave Dart Championship and the 'Denmark Pot' on December 2nd, narrowly beating Dave McMillan.
items.s: Boxed note that Don Maclean won the Belgrave Dart Championship and the 'Denmark Pot' on December 2nd, narrowly beating Dave McMillan. A new name was added to those who have held the 'Denmark Pot' when on December 2nd, the Belgrave Dart Championship went to Don Maclean, who gained a narrow victory over Dave McMillan. In the 10 years since this contest was innovated there has not been a more exciting competition for the 'Pot'. All the favourites had fallen by the wayside by the time the semis had been reached, and past champions could only look on in disappointment as 'Adrian Majors' and 'Bernard Merrys', showing all the signs of miss-spent youth, gave scant regard for the more established players. items.sum: Colin Pearson's report and Belgrave team times from the Surrey A.C. cross-country relay in Richmond Park on October 14th 1972, where a depleted Belgrave finished third behind Hillingdon and Borough Rd.
items.s: SURREY A.C. C.C. RELAY Colin Pearson's report and Belgrave team times from the Surrey A.C. cross-country relay in Richmond Park on October 14th 1972, where a depleted Belgrave finished third behind Hillingdon and Borough Rd. OCTOBER 14th 1972 - RICHMOND PARK. Although we fielded a depleted team at this relay we maintained our last year's performance by taking 3rd position, missing stars such as North, Weller, O'Connor and Phelan, who were running at Walton. A fine afternoon and a dry course around the paths of Richmond Park proved to be ideal for fast running, Peter Carton being our fastest man of the day. Another fine run came from Jim Rimmer. Saying that he had just returned from holiday, he was placed in the 'B' team and produced our third fastest time. Adrian Major, now showing that he intends to return to the 'A' team, was second fastest amongst the 'B' men. Lets hope he keeps it up. Colin Pearson. Teams: 1. Hillingdon 95;58 2. items.s: SURREY C.C. LEAGUE (DIV. 1) Report on Belgrave's bid for an eighth consecutive North Surrey (Surrey C.C.) League Division 1 title, with the list of past champions, the standings after two fixtures and results from the Wimbledon match of October 21st 1972 (won by Aldershot, Farnham & District) and the Lloyd Park match of November 25th 1972 (won by Belgrave). The North Surrey League was born in October 1962, so this season is the 11th. The league champions table looks like this:- 1962/63 - Walton A.C. 1963/64 - Walton A.C. 1964/65 - Hercules A.C. 1965/66 - BELGRAVE HARRIERS 1966/67 - BELGRAVE HARRIERS 1967/68 - BELGRAVE HARRIERS 1968/69 - BELGRAVE HARRIERS 1969/70 - BELGRAVE HARRIERS 1970/71 - BELGRAVE HARRIERS 1971/72 - BELGRAVE HARRIERS Impressive isn't it? But, as we feared last season, chalking up an eighth consecutive title is going to be a tough task. The new, powerful Aldershot, Farnham & District team will be difficult to beat, and with two matches behind us they are already proving their strength. In the opening fixture on our home ground we were well clear of our old rivals Hercules Wimbledon A.C. but in turn were ourselves soundly beaten by the Aldershot/Farnham men. It seems that this defeat may have been the tonic we needed, for at the second match at Lloyd Park, excellent packing gave us an 85 point win and we pushed ourselves into an overall lead of 26 points. We need every one of our best men out for the remaining two fixtures if we are to be sure of continuing our run of league victories. POSITION AFTER TWO FIXTURES. 1. BELGRAVE HARRIERS .... 406 pts 2. items.s: Sad to say he's on his way Farewell to Tony Binda, who left on December 10th to return to his birthplace Jamaica, with hopes of seeing him at future Commonwealth and Olympic Games. December 10th was a sorry day for Belgrave. That popular runner Tony Binda left these shores to return to sunny Jamaica, his birthplace, and rejoin his parents now living in Kingston. He will be sorely missed for his cheeky wit and of course his excellent running. Tony is beginning to blossom into a really good athlete and as long as he is able to maintain his interest in a country not renown for longer distance running, we can almost certainly look forward to seeing him at Commonwealth and Olympic Games to come, wearing the black, gold and green of Jamaica. Will he return to us? Well, fifteen years in Britain must have made its mark upon him and he still has some relations here. We can only hope. Anyway, we wish you luck, Tony; don't forget to keep in touch. sad to say he's on his way... see page 39 Tony Binda Tony Binda left for Jamaica, his birthplace, on December 10th 1972, after fifteen years in Britain Tony Binda Tony Alan Black Alan Black took the back-cover photo of Tony Binda Commonwealth Games Olympic Games Jamaica Kingston Britain

items.sum: Countryman's cross-country column previewing the Surrey County championship at Morden Park, recalling Belgrave's County win 43 years earlier (labelled start-line photo), noting the loss of Tony Brien, Tony Binda and John Phelan, Lionel Mann's travels, team manager Bill Lucas (pictured with Surrey's 1971 winning team at Leicester) and the Kent trio of Fairclough, Kerr and Geoff North.
items.s: COUNTRYMAN'S JOTTINGS Countryman's cross-country column previewing the Surrey County championship at Morden Park, recalling Belgrave's County win 43 years earlier (labelled start-line photo), noting the loss of Tony Brien, Tony Binda and John Phelan, Lionel Mann's travels, team manager Bill Lucas (pictured with Surrey's 1971 winning team at Leicester) and the Kent trio of Fairclough, Kerr and Geoff North. The first of the big cross country championships is the Surrey County event, to be held at Morden Park on January 6th. We are well overdue for a win. Our last seven performances read 1,1,2,2,3,2,2. Five years without Surrey gold is a famine indeed, so what are the prospects this year? Well, John Bicourt has not fully recovered from the bout of hepatitus which he suffered on his return from the Olympics, and Bill Weller is expecting to undergo and extensive course of dental treatment at that time. As they were 6th and 13th last year they will take some replacing. Fortunately, Bob Smith and Jim Rimmer are going very well and Trevor Hart should repeat his 20th place of last year. Leading us home, we hope, will be Gerry North with his regular place inside the first ten. It will be a tough fight for gold this year. My picture opposite shows the start of the County race of 43 years ago which Belgrave won from Surrey A.C. and S.L.H. The winner was our own Bert Footer, and three others joined him in the County team. Les Cohen (then Ashcombe A.C.) also made it. How close will we get to that in 1973. In the front row of the line-up can be seen the famous Laurie Weatherill, Jimmy Green (later Belgrave and managing editor of Athletics Weekly) and George Tolley, who went on to become President of the E.C.C.U., S.C.C.C.A., S.C.A.A.A. and the Surrey County A.A.A. It was a sad loss to British Athletics when George died suddenly only last month. We have suffered a severe blow in the loss of three of our leading runners in recent weeks. TONY BRIEN, who was our first man home in last year's National, is now resident at Kansas University, U.S.A., TONY BINDA, a fast improving Junior with tremendous potential has returned to the West Indies just as he was beginning to show the form to get amongst our senior scorers, and JOHN PHELAN is our third loss, having returned to Ireland after finishing his studies at St. Mary's College. However, in his case, we hope he will make the trip for the Southern and National. Another likely to have to travel for our major races is Lionel Mann. Lionel, a chef in the Queen's household, is presently being groomed for a principal position and this necessitates his working in Switzerland and France for lengthy periods. Fortunately, he has now regained full fitness and looked very lean and sharp on his recent return from the Alps. In Paris at the moment, he is most keen to get back for the big races. Whatever our runners do in the Surrey County race next month we are assured at least one place in the team. Yes, I mean the team manager. This position has been held for several years now by Bill Lucas and my picture shows him with Surrey's winning team at Leicester in 1971 which he managed to engineer during his year as Surrey County President! This season he takes the County team to Leicester once again - can he repeat the feat? Tony Fairclough and Bill Kerr now live within about six miles of each other in the Gillingham/Sittingbourne area. Nearby, of course, is Geoff North who was actually seen watching a race recently - though it was difficult to tell whether it had any effect on him! Is it possible that this formidable trio will form a training pack this winter and then let themselves loose on an unsuspecting world next Spring? Countryman 3rd [illegible]HOMPSON (SLH); 4th L. items.sum: Light-hearted Sunday Times piece comparing Bob Beamon's and Pat Matzdorf's world records with the jumping power of the flea and the click beetle, illustrated with a cartoon of a flea on a victory podium.
items.s: FLEA POWER Light-hearted Sunday Times piece comparing Bob Beamon's and Pat Matzdorf's world records with the jumping power of the flea and the click beetle, illustrated with a cartoon of a flea on a victory podium. FLEA POWER Bob Beamon's long jump and Pat Matzdorf's high jump - world records at 29ft 2½in and 7ft 6¼in respectively - are fairly feeble feats when compared to a flea. If a flea were a man, we discover in the British journal Nature, he could leap clear out of a stadium. In fact, size for size, an Oriental rat flea can high jump 275ft and long jump 450ft. "Although fleas," write Nature's flea-watchers, "have lost their ability to fly, they have retained and modified several important features associated with a winged mode of locomotion and incorporated them into the jump mechanism." Which is to say, the flea doesn't rely on muscular strength at all, but cocks and locks itself back on a store of spring like energy in its jumping legs before it lets fly: its peak acceleration is 140 times the force of gravity, which is 14 times the acceleration that would cause a man to black out. That rules out the application of flea power to athletics. In fact, if Nature magazine had scratched deeper they might have discovered, as a subsequent issue of New Scientist did, that another bug is a few jumps ahead of the flea. The click beetle, it seems, accelerates at 380 times the force of gravity when it has to flip over from flat on its back. (Sunday Times) Bob Beamon Bob Beamon long jump world record 29ft 2½in Pat Matzdorf Pat Matzdorf high jump world record 7ft 6¼in

items.sum: Philip Gee's review of the track and field team's season: third places early on, then four straight Southern League wins for third of twenty-five clubs, the Brockman Trophy, and a plea for members to answer selection.
items.s: TRACK & FIELD Philip Gee's review of the track and field team's season: third places early on, then four straight Southern League wins for third of twenty-five clubs, the Brockman Trophy, and a plea for members to answer selection. TRACK & FIELD A season which started quietly and somewhat disappointingly, with third places in our first two Southern League matches, gradually gathered momentum and we finished by winning the last four league matches. This effort placed us third out of the twentyfive clubs. In between these victories we also won the Brockman Trophy which was an extremely acceptable feather in our cap. It was very noticeable that as the season progressed and our results improved that the team spirit (something that is often looked upon as a joke but which is nevertheless an essential ingredient of success) improved and with it the willingness of members to turn out and "double up" if necessary in our important matches. If this spirit and determination can be continued next year then there is no reason why we cannot resume where we finished and win the Southern League. It would be difficult and indeed unfair to pick out anyone for special mention because our success was due to everyone who competed during the year. However, I would like to welcome back after periods of absence Jim Vivian and Charlie Gillett both of whom turned out regularly thereby adding strength to the team. Finally an impassioned if somewhat hackneyed plea. It would be a great help to all those concerned in trying to field a team if all members who are notified of selection to compete in a meeting made an effort to turn up or at least to let their sectional secretary know if they are not available.. There is nothing more detrimental to team spirit than a member not turning up either due to careless oversight or the opinion that he need only compete if he feels like it. items.s: SOUTHERN LEAGUE DIV. 1 Final Result Final 1972 Southern League Division 1 table (Belgrave third) with reports and results of Belgrave's wins at Epsom on August 12th and Bournemouth on September 16th 1972. SOUTHERN LEAGUE DIV. 1 Final Result AUGUST 12th 1972 - EPSOM. This match was a very important one for us to win as three of the other four clubs were all close on our heels in the league. Once again we had a strong team, the only change from our previous league meeting at Luton being that our "one man team" Snowy Brooks who has been invaluable in these meetings was wisely not hurdling as he was leaving for Munich the following week. John Martin deputised in both hurdle events and did a great job, especially in the 400m hurdles. Steve White and Jim Vivian, who we were very pleased to see back on the track this year, both completed sprint doubles and Charlie Gillett won both the 400m hurdles and the 400m 'B' race. Perhaps the most exciting race of the day was the 4 x 400m relay which we narrowly won, thanks mainly to an excellent anchor leg (51.1) by Peter Carton who had earlier won the 800m. Our Field section once again had a successful afternoon with Rodney Heward-Mills, Glyn Ratcliffe and Snowy Brooks all making notable contributions. We were never headed during the afternoon and ran out comfortable winners by a margin of 16½ points. RESULT: SEPTEMBER 16th 1972 - BOURNEMOUTH. With only eleven on the coach (including two officials and two wives) there seemed little chance of continuing our success of the previous three league matches even though a number of people were travelling down to Bournemouth under their own steam. A number of key men were missing because of holidays including Steve White, Peter Carton and Reg. Hopkins who have all been instrumental in our run of success but once the meeting was under way it soon became clear that we were not the only club affected in this way. Our opponents included Exeter who were lying third in the league with the same number of points as us but with a better points average and we were obviously keen to beat them if we could. After our usual sound start in the 400m hurdles by 'Snowy' Brooks (just returned from Munich) and Charlie Gillett we were never headed throughout the afternoon. Almost everyone ran, jumped or threw in more than one event including Charlie Gillett (400m H, 400m, 4 x 100m and 4 x 400m) Arnold Bentt (110m H, long jump, pole vault, high jump, triple jump and 4 x 100m) and of course our usual one man team "Snowy" (400m H, discus, shot, 4 x 100m and 400m). All in all it was a great effort by everyone concerned and we deserved our victory although I think most of us were just a little surprised. RESULT: Position in each match Match pts League pts 1. items.sum: Report and results of the World Veterans meeting in Cologne, 13-16 September 1972, where Laurie O'Hara won the 5,000m, Clive Shippen took steeplechase silver and John Bromley was fourth in the 10 km road walk.
items.s: O'Hara wins world vets. title Report and results of the World Veterans meeting in Cologne, 13-16 September 1972, where Laurie O'Hara won the 5,000m, Clive Shippen took steeplechase silver and John Bromley was fourth in the 10 km road walk. O'Hara wins world vets. title SEPTEMBER 13th - 16th 1972 - COLOGNE Showing his usual flair and a speedy finish, Laurie O'Hara demolished the field in the 5,000 metres final at the World Veteran's meeting in Cologne. Third, was Geoff Warren (Australia) who ran in the Vancouver Commonwealth Games of 1954, and fifth our own Clive Shippen. It was unfortunate that the 10,000 metres and marathon should be held the same day as this diluted the field. There were at least six other runners who could have made the first six. None, however, would have matched Laurie who not only won his heat with ridiculous ease but two days previously won a 5,000 metres against Dave Power and Geoff Warren (Australia) and Bill Allen (Canada). Clive ran one of his hardest races for many years when he finished 2nd in the 3,000 metres steeplechase on the second day of this five day meeting, splitting two Australians. Our third Belgrave representative was John Bromley who travelled solo and camped out, all for the privilege of tackling the 10 Km road walk. He beat all the opposition he had reckoned on, but three Swedes appeared and took first three places. However, the medal awards were gold, silver and four bronze so Belgrave did well for medals. 100m (Over 60yrs) 1. J.Williams (former Belgrave) 13.0 1. L.O'Hara (BEL/GB) 15:02.4 2. items.sum: Editorial recording with sorrow the death of Alf. Harley and introducing the tributes to him in this issue.
items.s: COMMENT Editorial recording with sorrow the death of Alf. Harley and introducing the tributes to him in this issue. COMMENT It is with great sorrow that we have to record the death of Alf. Harley, a man who worked tremendously hard for his Club and athletics in general and who in return was held by all who knew him in high regard. Whatever the event, Alf. Harley always seemed to be there and it is almost impossible to visualise Belgrave's future functions without his dignified presence. The tributes to him have been many and included in this gazette are personal memories of those who have worked alongside him for many years and those who knew him only comparatively recently, some in length and some extracts from letters. All make plain the fact that in the history of Belgrave Harriers there has never been a greater man and there probably never will be. Alf. Harley Alf. Harley death recorded; tributes in this issue

items.label: March 1973
items.sum: Club news notes: Alf Harley's and Syd Roberts' funerals, poor turn-outs at the Surrey Junior and Youth championships, Belgravians marshalling the South of the Thames race, members abroad in India and Australia, Surrey club amalgamation rumours, the club's membership at the end of 1972, the walker Fred Rickards' career, Ernie Duffett, Sandy Law closing his shoe business, John Cope, Wilf Wesch, Carl Lawton's marriage to Barbara Inkpen and the Wrench family's new daughter.
items.s: GRAPEVINE Club news notes: Alf Harley's and Syd Roberts' funerals, poor turn-outs at the Surrey Junior and Youth championships, Belgravians marshalling the South of the Thames race, members abroad in India and Australia, Surrey club amalgamation rumours, the club's membership at the end of 1972, the walker Fred Rickards' career, Ernie Duffett, Sandy Law closing his shoe business, John Cope, Wilf Wesch, Carl Lawton's marriage to Barbara Inkpen and the Wrench family's new daughter. GRAPEVINE When ALF HARLEY departed from us in January it was requested that no flowers should be sent to his funeral. Donations instead were to go to the Mount Vernon Hospital where Alf spent his last days. Spontaneous contributions were received from all quarters of the Club and we were able to send a cheque for £38.00 to Mrs. Harley for forwarding to the hospital. Alf's funeral was held on Monday 15th January at Brakespeare Crematorium, Ruislip - the same day as the funeral of our other Past President, SYD ROBERTS, which was held at St. Annes on Sea, Lancs. Although the majority of mourners were at Ruislip - 90 attended - the thoughts of all Belgravians were also with Syd on that cold and wet January day; a black day indeed for Belgravians. Are the County championship events losing their appeal? This years Surrey Junior and Youth races at Morden Park certainly seem to indicate that things are not all they ought to be. In the Youth race only three teams managed to close in but the Junior race was even worse - not one complete team made it to the finishing funnel. The South of the Thames Senior cross country race was held on Wimbledon Common towards the end of January and it was good to see so many Bels out to help mark the course and act as pointsmen. Which ever way one turned,it seemed, familiar figures were there armed with flags to guide the 300 odd runners around the course. News from Delhi, where RANJIT BHATIA has been nominated a member of the A.A.F.I. Committee to prepare plans for the reorganisation of athletics in India. He has also managed to persuade the A.A.F.I. to send two men to compete in the 1973 Maxol Marathon and is in fact going to concentrate on the marathon himself this year. Even further afield, in Australia, MICK HARVEY (21, Mount Street, Coogee, N.S.W. 2034) and MARTIN ELLIOTT (13, Forest Way, French's Forest, N.S.W. 2086) both seem to be settling down to Sydney life. They live a mere half hours drive apart and who knows, this note may well encourage them to get together for a training session. Could we yet see an antipodean section of Belgrave being formed. " A shake up for Surrey athletics? " cried a headline in the "Surrey Comet" of February 3rd, and rumours of club amalgamations are in the news again, this time between Surrey A.C., Walton A.C. and Epsom & Ewell H. The article went on to say that this could result in Surrey's first (?) 'super-club' and that both Surrey and Walton are suffering from declining membership and saw amalgamation as a possible solution. Latest gossip, however, hints that Epsom & Ewell H., already 400 strong and doing well, are not really interested. We await developements with great interest. At the last count, taken at the end of 1972, it was found that Belgrave Harriers had 453 members on the books, comprised of 327 seniors, 29 juniors, 15 youths, 48 boys and 34 honorary members. Let us hope that many of our swelling band of boys will stay with us through to senior status, strengthening our Junior and Youth Sections on the way. Although meeting on the sad occasion of Alf Harley's funeral, Jack Goswell was very pleased to see FRED RICKARDS looking so well and hearty and defying his 73½ years. They last met in the mid-50's when Jack looked after him and his pupil George Checkley in his last walk in Club colours (was it the Birmingham Outer Circle 25 miles or the Leicester Mercury 20 miles race) and Jack well remembers his belief in 'rice pudding'. Fred joined the club in January 1924 and during the years 1924/39 he won the Police Barking to Southend Walk no fewer than eight times. His very distinguished career also included - 1930 Norwich to Ipswich 42 miles,1st in 7:11:48; 1931 and 1933 Guildford Cup 50 kilos, 1st; member of winning team in the National 50 kilos 1934/5/6/8. Fred moved from the Slough area some years ago and now lives at 19, Davids Avenue, Palm Bay, Cliftonville, Kent, and how well the sea air must suit him. He would be pleased to hear from his old friends and walkers, particularly from TOMMY GREEN a great friend of his. How about it Tommy? He did travel to Southampton some time ago to look you up but had the old address and was unsuccessful. Tommy's address is believed to be 19, Consort Road, Eastleigh, Hants. So Fred, pleased to see you again and trust you keep looking so fit and well, and hear again from your old friends. Another who wishes to be remembered to his old friends is ERNIE DUFFETT. He and his wife are now living at 42, Springfield Court, Church Village, Pontypridd, S.Wales and are thoroughly enjoying themselves down in West Wales. Ernie is the Secretary of the local Senior Citizens Club and hopes to hold that office for as long as he was Running Hon. Sec. for the Bels - 25 years! He passes on his best wishes and says that he is with us in spirit if not in person. The end of an athletic era draws to a close as ex-Belgravian SANDY LAW closes up his shoe making business to move to Eastbourne. For many years athletes have gone to Sandy's shop in Revelstoke Road, Wimbledon for a pair of hand made to measure running shoes, possibly his most famous customer being Roger Bannister, the first man to run a mile in under four minutes. Unfortunately in today's world individual manufacturers like Sandy find it increasingly difficult to compete with the mass production of shoes by the giants of the sports shoe business. Former Belgrave quarter miler JOHN COPE, who helped us to many inter-club wins in the days of Harry Shields' track captaincy, was recently appointed Deputy Chief Industrial Relations Officer by the London Transport Executive. The ubiquitous WILF WESCH is now Manager of the Sport Hotel Adidas at 8522 Herzogenaurach, Beethovenstrasse 6, West Germany. The luxurious hotel is equipped with facilities for a real sportsman's holiday. Wilf and Anne hope to be visiting England again shortly but in the meantime extend a warm invitation to Belgravians who are promised "an extremely comfortable stay". Congratulations to CARL LAWTON and best wishes to BARBARA INKPEN on the occasion of their marriage on March 10th. Let us hope that being married to a Belgravian, and a real 'case'at that, will not affect Barbara's international career as a high jumper. More congratulations are due, this time to PETER WRENCH and his wife ANN. Ann has recently given birth to a daughter, their second child. Rumours that Peter is only doing so well at work because he named his son Robin after his boss Lord Rubens are quite untrue. items.label: March 1973
items.sum: Harry Shields' tribute to the late Alfred Harley, recalling his funeral, his devotion to the club, his 26 years as Secretary, 44 years of service and two terms as President, old members from the 1930s and his own memories of Alf.
items.s: ALFRED A. HARLEY Harry Shields' tribute to the late Alfred Harley, recalling his funeral, his devotion to the club, his 26 years as Secretary, 44 years of service and two terms as President, old members from the 1930s and his own memories of Alf. ALFRED A. HARLEY Harry Shields writes:- When the Vicar who was to officiate at the cremation telephoned for some details and to ask what I considered Alf's greatest characteristics, my mind went to my schooldays in which we learnt extracts from the Bible, more particularly that piece which includes, " and the greatest of these is Charity". In the new English Bible, in the First letter of Paul to the Corinthians, Chapter 13, I note this now reads:- "Love is patient; love is kind and envies no one. Love is never boastful, nor conceited, nor rude; never selfish or quick to take offence; does not gloat over other mens sins, but delights in the truth." The other quotation which came to mind was:- " Life is made up, not of great sacrifices or duties, but of little things, in which smiles and kindness and small obligations given habitually, are what win the heart and secure comfort ". Those of us who were able to attend the funeral of this great "Belgravian" could not fail to be impressed with the splendid and thoughtful "Oration" given by the vicar outlining Alfred's career and many qualities. His devotion to his Club, Belgrave Harriers. Administrative qualities so thoroughly and competently carried out in the whole spectrum of athletics. His outstanding career during the War years with the R.A.F. and the human understanding he displayed. The high regard in which he was held by his firm and business colleagues and the esteem of other organisations to which he belonged. Above all the love he had as a husband and father. In the September 1970 edition of the "Belgravian", Clive Shippen wrote a splendid "Spotlight" to mark the end of Alfred Harley's second term as President of the Club in recognition of his 26 years as Secretary and 44 years of service to the Club. Those members who read this "Spotlight" cannot fail to have been inspired by the unique qualities it portrayed and that the "Epitaph" of his passing must surely be "It is well finished". Looking round at the large number who paid homage at his funeral, there were many from Athletic Bodies, from his firm and other organisations in which he held high office, but it was clear that first and foremost he was 100% Belgravian, in its full sense with no sectional bias. There were many whose presence I missed, but knew they had written wonderful letters to Alf's wife and family. The regard with which the Club is held by his family is only second to that held by Alf himself, and I have been asked to express their deep thanks for the support and many kindnesses they received during his illness. All age groups of the Club were represented but I especially noticed those from Alf's earlier days, in the 1930's, Ken O'Kell, Bill and Frank Webb, Tom Carter, Tom Morrell, Albert Shaw, Tom Cotton, Tommy Scrimshaw and many others. I wondered at the thoughts going through their minds and how Alf would have loved to be there, shake their hands and have thoughts similar to my own. Tom Cotton, who, in the pouring rain at Shepperton camp, gave an exposition lasting many hours warning us younger members of the wiles and wickedness of women. Ken O'Kell for his enormous enthusiasm in introducing new members. Frank and Bill Webb for their comradeship on those wonderful all day strolls over Ranmore and Leith Hill, with Frank no matter what the weather, emerging debonair as ever. Tommy Scrimshaw for his outstanding athletic career and tussles with the great Tommy Hampson at Stamford Bridge. To each and everyone, Alf's memories would be of the great times we had and the pleasure from each others company, the arguments we had and above all the enormous team spirit for the Club to succeed. For myself the outstanding memories of Alf are peace. Sitting on the banks of the river Fal, listening to the lap of the waves, watching the sunset, waiting for the Ferry to take us to the other side. Resting on Rinsey Head, near an old Cornish Tin Mine, in beautiful autumnal warmth and sunshine, watching the sea-gulls and shag-greens on the rocks, enjoying the colour of the heather and bracken and, except for the noise of the sea and birds, complete quietness and solitude. I am sure these reflect the qualities deep inside Alf, the love of comradeship, beauty and serenity. His passing will leave a large gap in many of our lives and his memory will always be with us. An influence, impossible to evaluate, is how he helped to develop many of our lives. He was educated at the Upper Latymer School, Hammersmith when many of us had to leave school at 14 years to find our way through life. His inspiration was the first experience many of us had to carry out administrative duties and service to our fellows. Much of any success we may have later achieved emanates from his example. As well as I knew Alf it was not until his funeral that I learnt he was a "Freeman of the City of London". Such was his humility. It all brings to mind that lovely song:- "If I can help somebody as I pass along then my living will not be in vain". Our deepest condolences go to his wife and family and we thank the Supreme Being for the opportunity of enjoying his comradeship and the benefit of his talents. Alfred A. Harley ALFRED A. items.sum: Gordon S. Doubleday's tribute to Alf Harley, whom he met at the Rising Sun in the thirties, recalling his club offices, R.A.F. war service, two terms as President, committee work and character.
items.s: A.A. Harley Gordon S. Doubleday's tribute to Alf Harley, whom he met at the Rising Sun in the thirties, recalling his club offices, R.A.F. war service, two terms as President, committee work and character. When I turned up at our old mid-week training headquarters, the "Rising Sun", Ebury Bridge Road, in the thirties I was greeted by a tall red-headed fellow and welcomed to the Club. Thus began a friendship which was sadly ended by the death of Alf. Harley. Alf believed that amateur sport played a part in our lives, his chosen sport was athletics, and the club of his choice - Belgrave. Not only was he an active athlete, first as a runner then as a walker but he was also Walking Hon. Sec., Hon. Editor of the "Belgravian" and on the Committee. He was obviously a man of great administrative and organising talents and these were unstintingly given both to Belgrave and other athletic organisations. He had a deep admiration for what people like Bob Ricketts, Jimmy Belchamber, Oscar Horwood and many others had done to make Belgrave Harriers one of the strongest clubs in the country. Not only were our teams bringing championship honours to the Club but our administration and organisation were on a sound basis. He threw himself wholeheartedly into anything associated with the Club - a Social or Dance would find him there, if a few banded together to go to a "show" in town there he was. He was a great believer in the all-day Sunday stroll and was one of the regulars of a group of Belgravians who would tramp many miles over tough country in the Home Counties. These strolls sometimes extended into week-ends at youth hostels, indeed many of his holidays were spent with a Belgrave party. Expressing his ideas and thoughts came easily to him whether written or spoken, one of his favourite topics being the future well being of the Club. We know that his views were sincerely held, and he in turn always respected other peoples views. The Second World War saw the majority of members doing some form of National Service and Alf joined the R.A.F. where his administrative gifts were put to good use. He rose to the rank of Squadron Leader. He maintained close touch with the Club by corresponding with those at home and when the war was over he was soon back in his job of General Hon. Secretary. In due course he was honoured by being elected an Hon. Life Member, a Vice-President then President. His election as President for a second term of office is unique in Club history. It must have been one of his proudest moments when as President for the second time Alf and his wife Nancy greeted members and guests at the 1970 Annual Dinner. He was on many committees right up to the top levels of athletic administration and thus he had an unrivalled knowledge of both athletes and clubs, and his opinions on Committee were always closely listened to. When he retired from active participation he would invariably be found judging or doing some other important job. In fact we can say that for nany years no Belgrave event or committee meeting would be complete without him. He was known to many as Mr. Belgrave. On a personal plane he was universally liked, a word for everybody, a laugh, a joke, or, if needed, a word of sympathy when the occasion arose. He was a representative of a large firm of printers and travelled a good deal and picked up a wide knowledge of all sorts of subjects and could hold his own in conversation whatever the topic. By encouraging others he played a large part in the Happy Club we are proud to be members of. Let us hope that the work and enthusiasm of Alf Harley will be as much an inspiration to others as was the inspiration of those whose example Alf so faithfully admired and followed. There are many who feel that they have not only lost a fellow Belgravian but also a warm and loyal friend who radiated sincerity and good fellowship. Gordon S. Doubleday Alf. Harley Alf. Harley runner then walker; Walking Hon. Sec., Hon. Editor of the Belgravian, committee member; R.A.F. Squadron Leader in the Second World War; General Hon. Secretary; Hon. items.sum: Frank Simmons' short tribute to Alf Harley, whom he first met in the winter of 1935, praising his wisdom and fairness in committee.
items.s: A.A. Harley Frank Simmons' short tribute to Alf Harley, whom he first met in the winter of 1935, praising his wisdom and fairness in committee. Many words will have been spoken and perhaps many written more eloquently than my written respects towards Alf Harley. I first met Alf in the winter of 1935 and was, as a young man, deeply impressed by his desires and sound reasoning on behalf of Belgrave Harriers. Having been on many holidays with Alf, walking over many parts of England, I feel that I got to know him well. To listen to his reasoning and wisdom made me realise what a great Club personality we had. A person with a gentle but strong approach to various subjects, his wonderful ability to calm slightly heated discussions and to guide committees upon a good path to decisions, his democratic insistance that even the newest or the youngest should be allowed to air their views, made him into one of the Great Belgravians. I am proud to be able to say with many more, "I knew Alf Harley". Frank Simmons Alf Harley Alf Harley Alf Harley Alf Frank Simmons Frank Simmons first met Alf Harley in winter 1935 England

items.label: March 1973
items.sum: Peter Hilliar's tribute to Alf Harley, recalling joining the committee in 1966 at Alf's suggestion, succeeding him as General Hon. Secretary in 1970 and Alf's help and knowledge.
items.s: A.A. Harley Peter Hilliar's tribute to Alf Harley, recalling joining the committee in 1966 at Alf's suggestion, succeeding him as General Hon. Secretary in 1970 and Alf's help and knowledge. It is particularly difficult to realise that Alf Harley is no longer with us in Belgrave. He was a veritable embodiment of all that the Club represented and stood for and his untimely death has left us with a gaping wound which will be difficult to plug. My first experience of Alf in action came when I was elected to the Belgrave Committee in September 1966. I had written to him a few months previously on a matter of club finance and although I was probably unknown to him at that time he had replied with his customary courtesy and in great detail. It seemed to me that no matter was too trivial to engage his interest. At that time, he suggested that I should stand for election to the Committee at the following A.G.M. I was immediately impressed by his confident handling of Committee Meetings, not to mention General Meetings. What is more, he had a tremendous memory and a passion for detail that none could surpass. I never remember seeing him flustered at any time and the greater the odds against him the greater his confidence. You may recall that I was bold enough to volunteer to succeed Alf. as General Hon. Secretary in September 1970. After all, it seemed to be all so easy with Alf in the hot seat. I was soon to find out that it was by no means as easy as I had imagined but my transitional year was greatly assisted by Alf's second spell of presidential duty. He was always willing to give a helping hand and I can well remember his "little notes", which served to remind me of club business I might otherwise have missed. Needless to say, the notes sometimes amounted to four or five pages. Given Alf's immense breadth of knowledge on all facets of amateur athletics, it might be supposed that he was unapproachable but nothing could be further from the truth. He was always only too pleased to sort out a point of legal or administrative detail and to assist a less experienced colleague who might otherwise have given way to panic. Even after he had retired from the Committee "top table", which he had occupied for some thirty-odd years, he was to be seen at Committee and Club athletic meetings through thick and thin and I cannot remember having seen him absent from two in succession. I consider it a great privilege to have served the Club at the same time as a man of Alf's calibre. I feel we shall not see his like again but Belgrave will be able to take advantage of the tremendous volume of work he put in for the Club. Peter Hilliar Alf Harley Alf Harley General Hon. Secretary until September 1970; second spell as President; on the Committee "top table" for some thirty-odd years Alf Harley Alf Alf. items.sum: Extracts from letters about Alf Harley from Bob Glover, Ernie Duffett, Edmund P. Donovan O.B.E., Harry Hare, Ranjit Bhatia and Ron Goodman, A.A.A. General Committee Chairman.
items.s: A.A. Harley Extracts from letters about Alf Harley from Bob Glover, Ernie Duffett, Edmund P. Donovan O.B.E., Harry Hare, Ranjit Bhatia and Ron Goodman, A.A.A. General Committee Chairman. ".....Although not being one of his closer friends I have always respected him and felt he was a great part of Belgrave. It seems so tragic that many other members cannot use our Club as something a little more than just an athletic club....." Bob Glover "..... I well remember Alf and myself kicking about with a rolled up paper ball on the wharf down at Tower Hill during our lunch hour in the City. My deepest sympathy to his wife and family....." Ernie Duffett "..... He was the man who rekindled my interest in the Club after the war and during the last fourteen years that I have been coming home regularly, Alfred was one of the first people I contacted upon my arrival in London. We would have a drink and lunch together and he would bring me up to date on the doings of the Club. His passing has left a void I will find hard to fill....." Edmund P. Donovan O.B.E. "..... There is no doubt that of all Belgravians he has been truly "the greatest". I easily recall his first introduction to the Club and the early days and meetings in his company. His intense interest, from the very beginning, to all its activities, indicated to me that he would make great strides towards an administrative career. There is so very little that I could add to what has been expressed, so well, by so many, of his sterling qualities. " Harry Hare "..... Alf was one of the first people I got to know at Belgrave Hall in 1957 and I am sure his loss will be really felt in athletic circles this winter. He was typical of the stalwarts behind the club athletics set-up in England who, through their quiet and dedicated approach manage to keep athletics going....." Ranjit Bhatia "..... After a Belgrave dinner to which he had invited me a few years ago, I referred to "Lord Harley of Belgrave Hall, raised to the peerage for his services to athletics". Of course that was said in the fun of an after-dinner speech but I meant the sentiment and still do...." Ron Goodman Gen. Committee Chairman A.A.A. items.label: March 1973
items.sum: Reg Hopkins' tribute to Alf Harley, headed by a Kipling quotation, on what he learnt from watching Alf at work on committee and hopes to pass on to young people.
items.s: A.A. Harley Reg Hopkins' tribute to Alf Harley, headed by a Kipling quotation, on what he learnt from watching Alf at work on committee and hopes to pass on to young people. If you can walk with Kings and yet keep the common touch Rudyard Kipling. As we go through life we meet many varied types of people. Some come into our orbit and pass without any apparent effect upon us. Others with some special quality have a much greater influence. It is not always possible to analyse what these qualities are but we all recognise them when we are in the presence of someone who has them, and we listen carefully to what they may have to say, knowing it will be of value. Such a person was Alf Harley. Watching Alf at work on committee or indeed at any other time we learnt a tremendous amount about how to conduct our affairs and at the same time glean much about human relationships. Alf was a living symbol of the democratic way of life. In my work with young people it is my earnest hope that what I have learnt from him, I can in some way pass on to them and like the proverbial stone in the pond, the reverberations will go on and on, perhaps the best memorial of all. items.sum: Carl Lawton's review of the walking section's winter season, covering the Open 7s team results and the form of individual walkers.
items.s: WALKING Carl Lawton's review of the walking section's winter season, covering the Open 7s team results and the form of individual walkers. An 80% success was the result of the Open '7's with wins in the Luton, Belgrave, Cambridge and Met. Police races. Our only unfortunate error was in the Enfield but we still managed third. All this was achieved without any individual win and purely on team effort. Our highest placing came from Carl Lawton with third in the'Cambridge'. Len Duquemin, John Moullin and Ray Middleton together with Carl were our ever consistant team despite an attempt by Allan Callow to split things in the 'Cambridge'. Other consistant performances during the winter came from John Hall and Tom Cook. John for his consistant appearance and Tom for his consistant non-appearance. John progressed erratically and it was not until January that he began to smell 56 minutes. Since then he has meandered rather but if more time could be spent in races concentrating, he would improve beyond recognition. Martin Bennett was another to star midfield with some excellent performances being thrown in. His best efforts were generally produced when he arrived late for race. Changing behind the fence at Imber Court and running down Enfield High Street at 2.26pm to mention just two. John Dunsford had his days as did Dave McMullen, in between his complaints about his performances, despite his gold G.L.C. medal. Ray Hall began to regain his fitness but a stomach virus put paid to that. Len Evans, now prominent in Belgrave colours, showed that he could be reliable as one of our reserves in the summer season. Bernard Eglington made the long trip down from North Wales for the Belgrave Open '7'. Bob Picton showed just a little of what he could so easily be capable of in the Met. Police '7' and Bob Carter and Doug. Fotheringham were generally oblivious but present. John Bromley went into hospital for an operation in January and is now on the road to recovery and full fitness one hopes. There is still life in the old dog yet, especially with those veteran's prizes looming. Johnny Morris and John Keown could not decide as to which of them was the most unfit. The appearance of Eric Stroud could bring a bit of depth to our long distance side as could Paul Wiltshire to our sprint team. Pat Duncan did manage to put on a set of gear and compete in club races although questions were asked as to who the friend was under his shirt. Welcome appearances were made by Percy Wilson and John Johnson, both of whom have suffered serious problems during 1972. As to what the summer will bring in the way of results, we will wait and see, but with the Bels team still looking strong and with some promise in depth, we should be able to carry on the normal pattern. Since October we have had nobody disqualified which is especially promising with the new walking definition to be brought in to being at the end of August or there abouts. items.s: Narrow win in Cambridge 'Open' Report and result of the Cambridge Harriers Open 7 miles walk at Bexley on 9 December 1972, won by Belgrave on team points, with a note on John Dunsford's 5th place in the London Business Houses 7 miles at Wembley. DECEMBER 9th - CAMBRIDGE HARRIERS OPEN 7 MILES - BEXLEY. A cool but dry day, which made a change from recent weather, was prevalent for the Cambridge Open. The competitors were already lining up to start as Ray Middleton casually made his appearance in his car, horn blowing furiously. Fortunately, due to the Bels efficiency, he was ready to start with the others in under two minutes. Carl Lawton surprised all by making a sprint start and actually led for a mile before slipping back to 4th. Shaun Lightman took the lead after 3 miles and was never headed whilst Carl retook Amos Seddon for 3rd. Leicester packed their first three in nine but we powered in by one point with our usual scoring four despite the return of Allan Callow, and Ray Middleton leaving the road at one time to water the flowers. John Hall walked as though he was dragging his feet or had forgotten to take off his Fell boots. He was almost caught by Dave McMullen and Ray Hall. Bob Picton it seems is getting less fat and more fit, maybe he is aiming to do well in the 'Garnet'. Team: 1. BELGRAVE H 34pts; 2. Leics.W.C. 35pts; 3. Camb.H. items.s: DECEMBER 26th - BOXING DAY HANDICAP MEETING - BATTERSEA PARK. Report and result of the walkers' Boxing Day 3 miles handicap at Battersea Park on 26 December 1972, won by John Hall. A mammoth turnout for the Boxing Day meeting unbeknown for many years was seen at 11pm on a pleasant but chilly morning. Twelve walkers lined up to battle amongst themselves and the Christmas spirit and all but one got away on schedule. Odd man out was John Moullin who was discovered hiding in the changing rooms. Cecil Gittins was first away followed by a stream of strollers all complaining that they had been badly handicapped. Last away was Carl Lawton who definately had been 'done'. After the stipulated 3 miles, John Hall was first over the line, just pipping Jonathon Dunsford to the post. Third, not far behind would have been Carl Lawton but he still had a lap to go. However, this position went to Stuart Bennett with the rest of the field strung out over a lap. John Dunsford was sweeper up. 1. J.Hall 23:15 2. J.L.Dunsford 27:44 3. S.Bennett 28:11 4. items.s: NOMADS OPEN '10' Report and result of the Nomads Open 10 walk at Redditch on 6 January 1973, where Carl Lawton was second and Belgrave led an unofficial team result. JANUARY 6th 1973 - REDDITCH. An unfortunate technical fault rules out the possibility of Belgrave competing as a team in the Nomads '10' at Redditch. However, our lads turned out bravely on a cold day. The course which is rather flat was slippery and muddy in parts due to its location around an industrial site. Tolley and Court took an initial lead, opening up quite a gap but Court later managed to make a break to win comfortably. Len Duquemin and John Moullin were up in the thick of it in the first six for the whole race and at five miles Smallwood was disqualified leaving three Bels in six. With a mile to go Carl Lawton began to come into the picture and from his 6th place, gallantly won after losing valuable time at the start due to a road side conference, he moved through to 2nd by the finish, passing Adams in the last 200 metres. Ray Middleton was our 4th man but to no avail, despite having a clear points victory over Leicester. Unofficial Team result: 1. BELGRAVE H 25 pts; 2. Leicester 42 pts 1. R.Court (Nomads) 74:24 2. items.s: LEICESTER BEATEN AGAIN IN POLICE '7' Report and result of the Met. Police Open 7 walk at Imber Court on 13 January 1973, where Belgrave beat Leicester W.C. by two points for the team prize. JANUARY 13th 1973 - IMBER COURT. Two hundred and four starters lined up to compete in the Met.Police Open. Slightly fewer finished - apparently even less than should have done. A battle evolved between five competitors; Flynn, Lightman, Tolley, Court and Lawton. This group later split, with Flynn and Lightman breaking away to finish in that order. Court strutted in 3rd with Tolley and Lawton just behind. Positions of the previous week were reversed with John Moullin getting the verdict over Len Duquemin. Novice Ray Middleton finished well down the field but despite this setback we were still able to take the team by two points. As per usual it was a fast race, enabling John Hall to come in exactly on 56 minutes. Dave "I'll never break the hour again" McMullen only had 2 minutes 44 seconds to spare and Len Evans, Martin Bennett and John Dunsford also were under the hour. In 96th position was former Belgravian, now resident in Australia, G.Townsend, taking a brief holiday over here. Team:- 1. BELGRAVE H. 50pts; 2. Leicester W.C. 52pts; 3. Enfield 67pts. 1. items.sum: Jack Goswell describes the late Harry Churcher's collection of 133 walking medals, which Mrs. Churcher has offered to the club, and asks about one unidentified medal.
items.s: Harry Churcher's Medals Jack Goswell describes the late Harry Churcher's collection of 133 walking medals, which Mrs. Churcher has offered to the club, and asks about one unidentified medal. The Club have been pleased to accept the kind offer of Mrs. Churcher of the late Harry Churcher's medals and have agreed to hold them in trust during her life time, after which they will become the property of the Club. After collecting the medals one Saturday afternoon, I spent the rest of that evening and the following day collating and putting them together into their various club categories. Harry's great career was spotlighted in a previous 'Belgravian' but one realises more the length and greatness of this career when dealing with these medals. Space does not permit a full length copy of the list but they start with a 1931 Belgrave H. Junior Walk Championship 1st gold medal and move through the years to a 1933 A.A.A. 2 miles on to a total of ELEVEN A.A.A. championship medals up to 1951, 31 Surrey County A.A. medals 1933/52, 12 Counties Athletic Union medals 1935/1951, 14 Southern C.A.A.A. medals 1933/1952, 8 L.B.H.S.A. medals 1937/1952 - all over 2, 7 or 10 miles, also 20 Belgrave H."Junior", 2 and 10 miles championship medals 1931/1952 11 Polytechnic H "Kinnaird" team and individual medals 1938/1951, even 1 Surrey Walking Club medal. This gives some idea of the scope of his career, the total being 13 gold plus 4 almost certain gold, 52 silver and the rest various metals bringing a total of 133 medals. There was one puzzle I could not solve, One medal, not engraved, almost certainly gold and with a coat of arms and the motto "SINE LABEDECUS". I believe it is a medal from another country. Any ideas? As one realises this collection is rather valuable and the Committee are now deciding how best to use them. They must be taken care of and preserved as a memento of a great athlete and Belgravian. items.s: LAWTON WINS 'MURPHY SHIELD' Report and result of the Belgrave 10 mile walking championship (Murphy Shield) at Wimbledon on 20 January 1973, won by Carl Lawton, with handicap result and team match against the Metropolitan Police. JANUARY 20th 1973 - WIMBLEDON - BELGRAVE 10 MILE CHAMPIONSHIP. A tough battle was prevalent throughout this race with an early breakaway group of Lawton, Duquemin, Moullin and Callow, although Allan Callow fell of the back on the first laborious lap around the hills. The remaining three battled on with the lead being shared at intervals. Carl Lawton, on the second lap, began to fade but held on up the hills. On the last lap Len Duquemin took the lead on the downward section but could not hold on during the last climb and thus it was Moullin and Lawton who passed the church together. Nearing the Common Lawton managed to make a getaway and held on to his lead to the finish. Further back Middleton was walking his early season "quiet" one and John Hall was turning in another personal best. Handicap Result: 1. items.s: JUNIOR '5' GOES TO MARTIN BENNETT Report and result of the Belgrave Junior 5 mile walking championship (Tommy Green Olympic Cup), held with the senior 10 miles and won by Martin Bennett. BELGRAVE JUNIOR 5 MILE CHAMPIONSHIP. This race was held in conjunction with the Senior event and the Junior contenders for the"Tommy Green Olympic Cup" matched strides for five miles with their elders. As has been the case over recent months, Martin Bennett held his own fairly comfortably. He was, however, a little worried by newly signed Paul Wiltshire but still managed to win clearly. Bob Carter was 3rd ahead of last year's winner Bob Whitehead. 5th and 6th positions were filled by the youngsters of the Club Jonathon Dunsford and Stuart Bennett who were told to race between themselves and not against the others. Apparently they did this to start with but found themselves passing others on the way round the Common. They finished together completing a time well inside"six in the hour" schedule. These two lads if carefully nurtured could bring great reward for themselves in a few years time. 1. M.Bennett 41:20 2. P.Wiltshire 42:24 3. R.Carter 45:39 4. R.Whitehead 46:15 5. S.Bennett 48:41 6. items.s: G. L. C. '10' Report and result of the G.L.C. 10 walk at Battersea Park on 10 February 1973, where Belgrave won back the team trophy. FEBRUARY 10th 1973 - BATTERSEA PARK. This race, on paper, was much more promising than the "Garnet" had looked. If all went well Belgrave would have no difficulty in winning back the team trophy. In a field of ninety a leading bunch of four broke away leaving Lawton in 6th position with Ray Middleton and John Hall backing up. Four laps gone and Carl Lawton, who was by no means walking up to his usual standard, began to suffer but held on to his 6th. Ray Middleton came in 10th followed by John Hall with Dave McMullen (dare we say a sprightly 52) being 4th man to bring home the team to a comfortable win. John Dunsford was not quite as fit as he has been and could not catch McMullen over the closing stages. Paul Wiltshire put up a distinguished time and to quote one of the judges, "could be very good if he will get his arms right". Doug Fotheringham for the second week led home Eric Stroud, although Eric was walking better than his "Garnet" performance. Team:- 1. BELGRAVE H. ; 2. Surrey W.C. ; 3. Enfield. 1. items.s: A 5th consecutive win in Basingstoke 'pot-hunt' Report and result of the Basingstoke Open 10 walk on 17 February 1973, Belgrave's fifth consecutive team win there, plus Allan Callow's 3rd in a 20 km race at Croydon. FEBRUARY 17th 1973 - BASINGSTOKE OPEN '10'. A change in the weather brought warm sun to the road upon which Belgrave were to repeat their annual pot hunting session. From the start Roy Court went to the front and stayed there over the tough undulating course to win in a record time. Carl Lawton, performing much better than during his G.L.C. turn-out the previous week, also finished inside the old record. John Moullin and Len Duquemin were close to Carl on the turn at 5 miles and held on to finish in that order. Steyning were allowed some thoughts of high placings for eight miles with Ray Middleton sitting back but then he powered through to 5th place. John Hall walked a rather sleepy sort of race and never got going but John Dunsford delighted in turning the tables on Dave McMullen again. Ray Hall, not too fit at the moment,was our 8th man. COUNTY 10 MILE CHAMPIONSHIPS. HAMPSHIRE. Len Duquemin turned in a stormer in the Hampshire '10'to win convincingly and beat John Moullin into the bargain. Held on the usual short downhill course, Len won in a sub 75 minute clocking. 1. L.Duquemin (BELGRAVE) 74:31; 2.J.Moullin (BELGRAVE) 75:47 SURREY. Meanwhile, over on the steep hills of Croydon in the over distance Surrey '10', Carl Lawton was on to a hat-trick. He won by a minute from Peter Selby who had beaten him by two minutes at Battersea two weeks earlier. Ray Middleton failed to make the start due to his car breaking down north of Croydon. Belgrave just failed to retain the team title by a mere point. Dave McMullen and Ray Hall walked their way back into the county team and Eric Stroud turned in a commendable performance on the tough course. items.s: GRAND REUNION Photograph and notes on the reunion, at the Veterans' Dinner and Dance, of Belgrave's mile medley relay team of 40 years earlier, who presented a plaque to Charlie Speechley. At the Veteran's Dinner and Dance recently a grand reunion of the Belgrave Mile Medley Relay Team of 40 years ago took place. Left to right. DICKIE LAW (220y). Aged 59, retired Sub-Chief of Bournemouth Fire Brigade, now Fire Consultant to Ministry of Works. Ex-President of Bournemouth AC. JACK WILLIAMS (220y). Aged 62, civil servant, took up Veteran Running after a 32 year rest. British (over 60) sprint champion 1971 and 1972 and double gold medallist in the over 60 sprints at both the Veteran Internationals at Crystal Palace and Cologne last year. ERNIE JARVIS (440y). Aged 67, retired publican, probably the fastest man "out of the holes" in the late 1920's. TOMMY SCRIMSHAW (880y). Aged 62, ex-international who ran so many times for Great Britain with the great Tommy Hampson, gold medallist at the 1932 Olympic Games. Jack last saw Dickie a few days after he had joined the Bournemouth Fire Brigade and then didn't see him again until he had retired. The other chaps hadn't seen each other in 40 years. To mark the reunion they presented their old club mate CHARLIE SPEECHLEY with a plaque in admiration of his courage and sportsmanship. Left to right. DICKIE LAW (220y). JACK WILLIAMS (220y). ERNIE JARVIS (440y). TOMMY SCRIMSHAW (880y).
