Report and results of the National 20 km walking championship at Victoria Park on 12 May 1973, won by Roger Mills, in which Belgrave regained the team title from Sheffield; with a full-page photo of the winning team. BELS REGAIN NATIONAL 20 Km. MAY 12th 1973 - VICTORIA PARK. Walking in a way so dominating it was not a matter of which team would win the National 20 kilometre championship at Victoria Park, East London, but which four Belgravians. On a warm day and a flat course, a fast start was prominent with Len Duquemin, John Moullin and Allan Callow all in the first 25, and Ray Middleton a few places lower. By the 5 km point Carl Lawton had moved into the picture from the rear of the field. A large group was leading but the Bels were strongly pulling back places and by 10 km we had 5 men in 20. Len was still first Bel with John, Allan, Carl and Ray in that order. By 15 km the leading group had split and was left with Roger Mills, Jake Warhurst and Bob Dobson contesting. The Bels retained their dominance although the positions had changed to Len, Carl, John, Allan and Ray. With a lap to go of the 6½ lap course Carl got stomach cramp and had to concede 7 places. However, Ray came through to pass John who had already been passed by Allan. So finally, a win for Roger Mills with our own Len Duquemin finishing 11th with the next four Bels in 12th, 14th, 15th and 18th positions. The title was regained from Sheffield and Carl was not in the medals. All told we had a modest 12 starters, partially due to the Barking-Southend event the following day. John Hall placed 31st with John Dunsford and Dave McMullen well up. Ray Hall was forced to retire but Bob Picton and John Keown completed the distance. Waving the lantern rouge for Bels was Pat Duncan. Teams:- 1. BELGRAVE H 'A' 44 pts; 2. Sheffield 51 pts; 3. Southend 96pts 21. BELGRAVE H 'B' 385 pts. items.sum: Harry Shields' impressions of the National 20 km walk at Victoria Park, praising the Belgrave officials and helpers and the team's packing.
items.s: Harry Shields' view :~ Harry Shields' impressions of the National 20 km walk at Victoria Park, praising the Belgrave officials and helpers and the team's packing. Harry Shields' view :~ The warmth and atmosphere of a walking championship is difficult to describe. It is different to a cross-country or athletic meeting, the comradeship is something quite its own, with the taste only acquired as a result of deep knowledge of each other. A little late in arriving, as I walked across to the venue at Victoria Park, how lovely it was to see the Belgravians in their usual prominent roles in the organisation. Jack Goswell as Master of Ceremonies, in all matters concerned with recording and producing results, ably abetted by his wife Joan. Although no one is indispensable, their absolutely unique service in producing complete duplicated results to all competitors must surely be irreplaceable. Dignified Frank Jarvis with his white mane as Competitors Steward and tying up loose ends, Gordon Doubleday personifying the solemnity, wisdom and calmness befitting a Grade I Timekeeper, Harold King a respected Judge and Jean Middleton in her effervescent role of selling programmes and all other matters by which to coerce money from pockets for the good of the Sport. The whole was capped in the person of our President, Clive Shippen, whose style and good-will was appreciated by all. What of the race ? "Dog bites man", is not news. "Man bites dog", is news. Similarly "Belgrave again wins Championship" is not news. The only difference, we had no one challenging for individual honours, but our team packing was superb. MAY 18th 1973 - PADDINGTON - BRITISH RACE WALKERS CLUB INVITATION. Sponsored by Charringtons, this race proved to be a highly popular event with 18 starters and cycle racing being carried on around the outside of the running track. items.s: News note that Cliff Roffey is working as an accountant at Kericho in Kenya and still running to keep fit. CLIFF ROFFEY is now living at Kericho in Kenya where he is working as an accountant for Brooke Bond Liebig Kenya Ltd. He still runs through the tea plantations or round his garden to keep fit and plays squash and tennis once or twice a week but doesn't get much chance to see many athletic meetings as Kericho is 170 miles from Nairobi which is the centre of athletics in Kenya. During his six weeks leave last year he met Bob Taylor during a Bournemouth track meeting but doesn't expect to return to the U.K. for good for some time. items.s: YOUTHS & BOYS - Reg's report: Junior Hon. Secretary Reg Hopkins's column welcoming the big turnout at the opening Norbiton meeting and urging juniors to support fixtures and aim for the AAA 5 Star Award. YOUTHS & BOYS Reg's report: How very exciting it was to see such a great turn out of members for the opening meeting at Norbiton. It seemed quite like old times to see so many claret and gold vests on display; the enthusiasm for each event was so much more keen when one of our own Bels were taking part. This is just what we need to build up Club spirit and with this encouragement we will soon be winning County Championships again. So keep your eye on the fixture list and support your Club whenever you can. If you can't find your own way to wherever the meeting may happen to be, give me a ring (my number is on the inside front cover of this mag.) and I may be able to arrange transport. Keep attacking those personal bests and don't forget that all your performances can count towards the A.A.A. 5 Star Award. There were 635,000 winners of the award in 1972 and from these the very best have been selected to form a national squad for specialised all-year-round training. They are reckoned to be the internationals of the future. Could 1973 be your year ? Reg Hopkins, Snr. Junior Hon. Secretary Reg Hopkins, Snr. Reg Hopkins, Snr. Junior Hon. items.s: MEET STEPHEN WALTERS Profile of young Belgrave runner Stephen Walters, his school, training, start with the club and hopes for organised coaching for juniors. MEET STEPHEN WALTERS Whenever [illegible] [illegible]ave a Youths or Boys fixture Stephen's cheerful countenance is certain to be present. He used to play soccer for his school and in fact had a trial for Crystal Palace F.C. but now his first sport is athletics and four times a week he makes his way to the Tooting or Crystal Palace tracks for a training session. Probably this will be his last year at Henry Thornton School at Clapham Common and at the moment he is intent upon a career in the Civil Service. He came into the Club getting on for a year ago when he met our General Hon. Secretary, Peter Hillier, at Battersea Park. He also competes for the Oxford and Bermondsey Boys Club whilst younger brother Michael has also become a Belgrave stalwart. Like many of our youngsters, Stephen has no favourite event as yet and is content to attempt whatever is going until he finds what suits him best, although his performance in the Youths and Boys race preceding our '5¾' championship last March opened quite a few eyes and it is obvious that he will be a great asset to our Senior middle distance teams in a few years if his interest is sustained. Stephen does feel that we tend to lose some younger athletes through a lack of planned coaching and would like to see something set up on a regular basis whereby those interested in similar events can train together in a squad. Interests outside running include 'pop' music and going to disco's. items.s: MEET PETER NORTH Profile of 16-year-old new member Peter North of Southfields, a Wandsworth School pupil, Air Training Corps sergeant and would-be 800m runner. MEET PETER NORTH " I've always enjoyed watching athletics and wanted to compete myself. I couldn't find Hercules Wimbledon A.C.'s headquarters, so I joined Belgrave...." Perhaps this is not the most auspicious way to gain new young members but whatever, pleased we are that Peter North made his way to Belgrave Hall in October 1972 and signed on. Peter is 16 years old, lives at Southfields and is a pupil at Wandsworth School (whose colours are identical to our own). Up to now he has only done cross country and road running and has become a familiar figure on the Thursday night "burn-up" around Raynes Park but now that the track season is with us, he is looking forward to trying his hand at 800 metres. He is a member of three years standing in the Air Training Corps and holds the rank of Sergeant. This summer Peter will be going on a gliding course and will be studying for a provisional gliding licence but apart from all this, is in the process of attempting the Duke of Edinburgh's Award (silver). A busy lad, you might think but we have not finished yet. He enjoys shooting and belongs to a .22 rifle club as well as making the odd trip down to Bisley to fire .303s with the ATC. items.sum: Instructional piece setting out the competition rules for the long jump, covering trials, the take-off board, run-up marks, failures and measurement.
items.s: know the rules — LONG JUMP Instructional piece setting out the competition rules for the long jump, covering trials, the take-off board, run-up marks, failures and measurement. know the rules — LONG JUMP (a) The competition may be decided in either of the following two ways - the conditions should, if possible, be printed on the programme and must be explained to the competitors before the competition begins: (i) Each competitor being allowed from three to six trials; or (ii) Each competitor being allowed three trials and the three to six best competitors being allowed three more trials. (b) Each competitor shall be credited with the best of all his trials. (c) The take-off shall be from a board the edge of which nearer to the landing area shall be called the "scratch line". If a competitor takes off before reaching the board, it shall not for that reason be counted a failure. (d) The distance of the run is unlimited. No marks shall be placed on the runway, but a competitor may place marks alongside the runway. No competitor may place, or cause to be placed, any mark beyond the Scratch Line. (e) If any competitor touches the ground beyond the scratch line or scratch line extended with any part of his body, whether running up without jumping or in the act of jumping, it shall be counted as a failure. Note: "Ground" includes any form of "No jump" indicator. (f) (i) The measurement of the jumps shall be made at right angles from the nearest break in the ground in the landing area made by any part of the body of the competitor to the "scratch line". If in the course of landing, a competitor touches the ground outside the landing area nearer to the scratch line than the break in the ground to which the measurement of the jump would have been made, such jump shall not be measured but shall count as a failure. (ii) The distance shall be measured to the nearest ¼ inch (1 centimetre) below the distance covered, i.e. fractions less than ¼ inch (1 cm.) must be ignored. If calibrated measuring equipment is used its accuracy must be checked with a steel or fibre-glass tape; otherwise a steel or fibre-glass tape should be used and the part of the tape showing the distance jumped must be held at the scratch line. (g) The employment of weights or grips of any kind is forbidden.

items.label: June 1973
items.sum: Harry Shields thanks the club catering committee for teas at the Southern Road Relay and the club 20 mile walk, reflecting on food, companionship and club tradition with quotations from George Borrow and Pepys.
items.s: A 'SALUTE' TO OUR CATERING TEAM Harry Shields thanks the club catering committee for teas at the Southern Road Relay and the club 20 mile walk, reflecting on food, companionship and club tradition with quotations from George Borrow and Pepys. A 'SALUTE' TO OUR CATERING TEAM After the Southern Road Relay on April 7th my admiration for the catering committee of the Club was without bounds. Following a five hours competition it was reasonable that those responsible for dispensing would be jaded, out of stock, impatient to get home. Not a bit of it, there were the ladies, charming, colourful and dispensing the needs of the inner man with tea, lemonade, rolls of various fillings, cakes, etc., all tastefully laid out, with a competence and pleasantness that would put many elite establishments to shame. Again the following Saturday, on the occasion of the Club 20 Mile Walking Championship, although a smaller fixture, there was the same treatment of mouth watering ham and cheese rolls, cakes, tea, etc. It was so unexpected, when experience over many years, partly due to the lateness that a 20 mile finishes, was to anticipate a cup of tea and even then only if made by yourself. How pleasant it was to sit, happy in the communal gathering, to reminisce on the afternoons happenings and to reflect that another afternoons sport had been successfully completed. On the way home, my thoughts led to the object of an athletic club. There have been many definitions but none contain those facets of friendship, hardships, fun, achievements, disappointments which mould the character of a club, from which is produced the tempered steel leading to the finished sportsman. George Borrows had the right idea, when he wrote early in the 19th century accounts of his many journeys. Before athletic clubs were thought of he wrote, "Wild Wales" and immortalised much of its beauty, describing paths traced by many club parties in their holiday wanderings. " There's night and day brother, both sweet things; Sun, moon and stars brother, all sweet things; There's likewise a wind on the heath, Life is very sweet brother; who would wish to die. " He was a great walker, teller of stories and companion, and if about today must surely have joined the "Belgrave Harriers". How he would have enjoyed a spin over the heath and common, and participated in his great love of food and talk after a hard days slog. The diaries of Samuel Pepys, 150 years earlier, show the same urge for refreshment and love of companionship after a strenuous day in the dock-yards on the nation's business. Our worthy catering section follow these traditions and fully understand the necessity of meeting these basic needs. They do much to revive the gastronomic feats of the 1930's, the Social Teas at the Hall, at Youth Hostels where we stayed and out-shone the best, our proven ability at inter-club meetings to out-play and out-eat whenever put to the test, the stories of cheese and onions eaten on the walls of Hampton Court Palace. These must be replaced by new memories, revived by splendid catering and social pow-wows afterwards. Who knows where it will lead and prowess it will awaken in all sorts of pursuits. Even if you were late that Saturday for work, thank you Brian, and all your helpers for their dedication and splendid eats. ROAD AND COUNTRY Laurie first in Veterans' "Southern" MARCH 4th 1973 - WOODFORD GREEN. Laurie O'Hara won yet another title when he was first past the post in the inaugural Southern Veterans Cross Country Championship held at Woodford Green's headquarters. John Baker was lucky in losing a shoe after a mile as, following the tail-enders after a short rest, he suddenly found himself in 12th position. All the earlier runners had gone off course. It did not take Laurie long to get to the front again and considering the circumstances all the club runners felt satisfied with their performances. It's a pity training stopped our so called faster Veterans from competing but after all training is more important than helping the Club to win a team title. J. V. IT'S LAURIE AGAIN ! MARCH 17th 1973 - WIMBLEDON - 5¾ MILES ROAD RACE CHAMPIONSHIP. The finishes down Lauriston Road in our 5¾ mile (9.2 km ?) races are becoming truly amazing these days. The autumnal non-championship race saw Laurie O'Hara and Bill Weller battling to the end, both recording the same time with Laurie winning by an eyelash. Now, with the "Wimbledon Cup" at stake in the spring race, Gerry North joined these two for the 'eyeballs-out' final 300 yards. Close as it was, with Laurie in the form he is these days plus his ever present devastating finish, it would have taken Superman to deny him another victory. John Baker, our Hon. items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of the eighth Southern Counties Road Relay, promoted by Belgrave at Wimbledon, in which Aldershot won and Belgrave were third, with a full-page photo of Peter Carton and John McNamara.
items.s: SOUTHERN ROAD RELAY Stage-by-stage report of the eighth Southern Counties Road Relay, promoted by Belgrave at Wimbledon, in which Aldershot won and Belgrave were third, with a full-page photo of Peter Carton and John McNamara. SOUTHERN ROAD RELAY A good TEAM effort by the Bels. Twelve noon. With whitewash arrows daubed on the road that very morning, pointsmen in their positions and the take-over area roped off, Belgrave Promotions Inc. had made their preparations well and the eighth Southern Counties Road Relay Race held at Wimbledon was ready to roll. Each year the traffic becomes that little bit worse so this time it was decided to slightly alter the course, thus avoiding a couple of the trickier junctions. The alternate long and short stages now measured 5 miles 334 yards and 3 miles 553 yards. STAGE 1: Peter Carton 24:37 (fastest). Once again Pete showed what a tough competitor he is. With the leaders constantly jockeying for the front position, he was always ready to cover any break-away and as the hills took their toll it developed into a battle between MacNamara (TVH), Faircloth (Croydon) and our man. As they approached the end of the leg Peter opened up and there was no one else in it. His time proved to be the fastest of the day by any of our long stage runners. STAGE 2: John Stow 16:04 (3rd fastest). The first of the short stages saw John setting off with Davies (TVH) haring after him. The "Valley" man swept past and went on to clock the fastest short stage time of the day but John was not put off in the slightest and brought us to the next take-over 23 seconds ahead of Hillingdon, now 3rd, and 32 seconds down on Thames Valley. No other Belgravian was to beat his time over the short stage. STAGE 3: Bill Weller 25:25 (8th fastest). Already it seemed the field was stringing right out but at the end of stage 3 Bill had cut half a minute off of TVH's lead only to see Hillingdon A.C. go even better, breaking through to the front with 13 seconds in hand. Cambridge H. and Cambridge & Coleridge A.C. both crept up and now 26 seconds covered the first five teams. STAGE 4: Trevor Hart 16:14 (2nd fastest). Carrying on the good work, Trevor got past Stevens (TVH) and made ground on Wainer (Hillingdon), all three of them increasing their lead over the next few clubs. Aldershot moved up to 6th after having made a bad start of 17th on the first leg but they were still over a minute down. STAGE 5: Lionel Mann 25:58 (12th fastest). Certainly no "cut and dried" race this, as TVH, thanks to Mike Davies, again hit the front whilst Hillingdon slipped back to 8th, never again to be in the hunt. Lionel kept Belgrave hopes high, closing on Davies again during the last mile of his stint. Local rivals Hercules Wimbledon came up to 5th with a fiery run from Briscoe. STAGE 6: Colin Pearson 16:41 (7th fastest). A grim looking Colin was faced with the prospect of holding on to our 2nd position and as he sped away from the take-over area Cambridge & Coleridge, Cambridge H., Hercules Wimbledon and Medway were hot on his heels less than half a minute behind. TVH fractionally stretched their lead but Colin fought magnificently and as he handed over to Gerry North with half the race now gone, he had pulled away from those behind. continued on page 43..... STAGE 7: Gerry North 25:15 (7th fastest). Traditionally the "names" begin to appear about here in the race and this day was no exception. Bernie Ford steamed through the field setting up the day's best long leg time and taking the dreaded Aldershot team up to 2nd whilst Malcolm Thomas, 1972 'National' Champion, took TVH even further away. Still, contrary to pre-race opinion, Belgrave were having a good day and although Maurice Benn (Cambridge H) also passed our Gerry, Beevor (Hercules Wimbledon) and Newble (Medway) couldn't do likewise. STAGE 8: Pat O'Connor 16:22 (2nd fastest). Pat scooted past Cambridge H. but Aldershot were also going well and TVH's 36 second lead began to rapidly dwindle. Soon the red and green colours of Aldershot headed the field for the first time as they got 26 seconds clear of the "Valley" with ourselves a further 22 seconds down. STAGE 9: John Phelan 24:54 (=4th fastest). John Phelan ran a "blinder" and pointsmen were to be seen leaping up and down with excitement as he closed up to within 4 seconds of TVH and maintained our 3rd position as Aldershot sank back to 4th and Hercules Wimbledon rocketed from 6th to 1st with a 24:24 clocking from Bob Holt. After 40 miles of racing, a mere 8 seconds covered the leading four teams. STAGE 10: Tony Fairclough 16:20 (2nd fastest). It took just 16 minutes and 20 seconds for Tony to prove that he is back into our 'A' teams with a vengeance, putting us back into 2nd spot. Hercules Wimbledon crashed so TVH again held the lead but with two stages to go we were beginning to sniff the medals. STAGE 11: Laurie O'Hara 25:11 (=4th fastest). Another change round in the positions and the red-headed Adams took Aldershot back to the front. Laurie gave his all, around the roads he knows so well from past '5¾'victories, fighting for every second that he could give to our anchor man Bob Smith. STAGE 12: Bob Smith 16:28 (5th fastest). The last leg. Bob looked as nervous as a kitten as he took over 9 seconds down on Fred Bell (TVH) and 27 seconds down on Fletcher (Aldershot). Bell attacked immediately and gained ground all the way round, with Bob desperately plugging away behind him. With a mile to go it seemed Bell would catch the leader and go on to win but he had made his effort and whilst Bob closed on him again towards the end, Aldershot went away to take yet another title. It was an excellent result from our point of view with every one of our team running well and confounding our critics. The race was over but our organisers were still in top gear. Result sheets had been posted after every leg and soon the official result was available to all. Now came Belgrave Promotions Inc.'s master stroke. The glorious sunny weather specially arranged for the event was now switched off and before you could say "Gordon Biscoe", cleansing rain had swept the last vestiges of whitewash from the roads. Copies of the official programme, autographed by the King of the 6th Stage - Colin Pearson, were later seen changing hands at 5p a time. - photo opposite by Ron Linstead. items.label: June 1973
items.sum: Stage-by-stage report by Colin Pearson of the National Road Relay at Derby on 28 April 1973, won by Birchfield, in which Belgrave finished 5th, with Belgrave stage times and the leading team placings.
items.s: 5th in NATIONAL ROAD RELAY Stage-by-stage report by Colin Pearson of the National Road Relay at Derby on 28 April 1973, won by Birchfield, in which Belgrave finished 5th, with Belgrave stage times and the leading team placings. 5th in NATIONAL ROAD RELAY APRIL 28th 1973 - DERBY. Leaving London at 7.30 am we drove up the M1 and after early morning cloud, the sun came out to stay for the rest of the day. Ideal for spectators, if not for the runners. The noon start saw 24 runners toe the line for the first long stage, a circuit of 5¾ miles. The course was a tough one. After 2 miles came an extremely severe mile long hill. Picture if you can the 'kiss of death' on our own 5¾ course laid end to end three times and you'll get an idea of what the lads were up against. Starting the ball rolling for us was Peter Carton. With his fine Southern Relay effort behind him we were hopeful of Peter coming in with the leaders. However, that was not to be, for Peter, although not sparing himself, was slightly below form and came in 9th, 40 seconds down on the leaders, Birchfield Harriers. Next off, on the first short stage was Trevor Hart. The short stage also took in the long hill and this apparently suited Trevor well, for he pulled up three places to bring us home in 6th spot having passed the Stoke, Hillingdon and Morpeth runners. John Bicourt took care of stage three, the second of the long legs. Not having raced recently, though, John was forced to concede two places so that we were now laying 8th. John seemed to find the hill a bit tough and had to give best to Stoke's Roy Fowler and Hillingdon's Tony Moore. Stage four was taken by Bob Smith, who despite giving his best, lost ground to Whitty of T.V.H. although he managed to overtake Beard of Hercules Wimbledon. Ahead an enthralling battle was taking place for race leadership between Stoke and Hillingdon. Whilst we were involved in an equally thrilling tussle with Aldershot, T.V.H. and Hercules. Bill Weller on stage five closed right up on Birchfield's Smedley to take us by our great pre-war rivals. On Bill's shoulder was Bob Holt who managed to get by after the long hill had been climbed. Bill was also overtaken by Derby's Mike Tagg but still kept us in place by picking off the Hillingdon and Sale runners. John Stow, recovering from tonsilitis, hardly treated stage six like a convalescent's outing for he took us up two places overtaking Bartlett of Birchfield and Collins of Hercules Wimbledon in the process. Next away, suffering from what seems is the Club's current affliction, was tonsil troubled Gerry North. Gerry did not let his discomfort worry him and running his usual gritty race he maintained our position and held off Dave Holt, who had taken over a mere 8 seconds behind him. Pat O'Connor took the eighth stage and was really on form bringing us home 5th and taking us to within two minutes of the leaders, who in race order were Tipton, Stoke, Birchfield and Aldershot. Early contenders Hillingdon had by now faded to 15th. John Phelan was on stage nine and although dropping places to Coventry and Aldershot, John left us still in contention for a place as only a minute covered 3rd to 6th spots, although Tipton and Birchfield were two minutes clear of the field. On stage ten Tony Fairclough took us past Smallheath and into 6th place once more, having to put in a determined effort to hold off Kirby of Cardiff. Meanwhile the leading position had changed again, the order now being Birchfield, Tipton and Stoke, the latter being two minutes down. Laurie O'Hara running stage eleven clocked fourth fastest of our long legs and went past the Stoke runner. Laurie was caught at the top of the hill by Hercules Wimbledon's Steve Badgery. Some thought that he would be able to hold on to Steve and pip him at the end with his famous finish but this was not to be for Steve drew away over the last mile. Laurie did well to keep the gap down to a mere 6 seconds. Lionel Mann took the twelfth and final stage which turned out to be the most exciting of the day. Lionel tore after Hercules Wimbledon's Tim Beagent and was on his shoulder after a mile. Beagent, however, after a more leisurely start managed to pull away to bring his team in 4th. Lionel managed to outsprint Goodfellow of Stoke to bring us in a praiseworthy 5th. It was slightly disappointing not to have been first Southern club home but there's still next year to come. items.label: June 1973
items.sum: Eve Stimpson's account of a country-and-western barn dance at Belgrave Hall with the Triumph Country Dance Band and the club's own "Swinging Jock Strappers" group.
items.s: the barn dance Eve Stimpson's account of a country-and-western barn dance at Belgrave Hall with the Triumph Country Dance Band and the club's own "Swinging Jock Strappers" group. the barn dance Wyoming comes to Belgrave Hall complete with check shirts, neck ties, bibs, braces and gingham dresses. What a night we all had dosey-do-ing and happy-hoe-downing to the music of the Triumph Country Dance Band which was melodius enough to get the room swinging and yet still be pleasant enough to talk. Old social nights were once again revived by the "Swinging Jock Strappers" led by Bill Couzens on the guitar. He was also the vocalist. Bill was strongly backed by "Fingers" Penny - the cigar puffing pianist from the deep south who had his glass of water rocking on the top of the piano in traditional style. A second Bill - friend of Gordon's (nothing like that) did sterling work on the banjo and he helped to keep Charlie Manning (Bass) in tune. Charlie is tone deaf like John Martin on his sally ack. symbols. Stewart Barrett's harmonica played the sweetest sounds, always coming in at the right time, unlike "Scrubber" Gordon on his wash-board who came in all the time on the assumption that he would be right some of the time. But as a compere he knitted the whole shambles together to make a very successful group and the grapevine now informs me that their next performance is being kept secret but I understand they are having talks with Lew Grade. It was so nice to see everyone so happy for the whole evening, with many familiar and unfamiliar faces having such a good time together even if they didn't know what they were doing in the way of dancing. Undeterred by their lack of ability the floor was always crowded and the bar relatively empty. This may have been because of the efficiency of our barmen in dispensing the drinks which were quickly whipped downstairs. Thanks Bill ( Couzens) for a lovely evening. When is the next one ? items.sum: Poem following a cross-country race from the start flag to the finish, signed with the pen-name Sem E. Serkel.
items.s: The Joys Of Cross-Country Poem following a cross-country race from the start flag to the finish, signed with the pen-name Sem E. Serkel. The Joys Of Cross-Country The flag is up, all eyes thereon, The flag drops, off they go Like a broad coloured ribbon, Some too fast, some too slow. A lengthened pattern now takes form As bustling rush calms down; Of some who to the front did storm, To stay have no renown. Past meadow and herd of cattle, Fields of green, plough of brown; In the lead the stalwarts battle, Plod the rise to its crown. The ribbon has become a thread A line of toiling men, The tail furthering from the head Now far from starting pen. The leader kept free of trouble, A ditch! One stride he took, Over stile, cross field of st[illegible]ble, Splashes through shallow brook. Others follow, plodding along Some back, their effort spent Some gather strength, running strong All with forward intent. By a path through a wood they run, 'twixt gaunt trees bare of leaves Flickers the light of Winter's sun; Scent of mould on the breeze. Out to open country they come, Across meadow they go, Down by orchard of slumb'ring plum And flight a startled crow. There ahead on distant hills brow Forward supporters stand, "Here they come, they're coming now" Says a voice of this band. On and nearer comes the leader, Plodding hard on the rise, Past bushes and tree of cedar, Heeding not the crowd's cries. To the top comes the leader strong, Not far distant he sees The finish and the waiting throng, In meadow clear of trees. Steady he runs with no one near Through funnel to the end Sounds of ovation to his ear, His title he did defend. Running hard comes the second man, Another on his heels Putting in everything he can Fronts as the other reels. So they finish, some fast some slow, Muddied from head to foot, Moistened brow and exertion's glow, All tried, none can dispute. Sem E. Serkel Sem E. Serkel Sem E. Serkel apparently a pen-name

items.s: 'VETERIS' Boxed notice announcing Veteris, the new quarterly magazine of the Association of Veteran Athletes edited by Clive Shippen, with subscription details. 'VETERIS' " Veteris " is here. A new athletics magazine published quarterly by the Association of Veteran Athletes and edited by our own Clive Shippen. Its 56 pages hold a wealth of information for the veteran athlete the world over; articles from the U.S.A.; news from Canada, Australia, New Zealand; results of meetings; a foreword by Dr. Roger Bannister; ranking lists; it has the lot. The number of copies already sent overseas is phenomenal and it would seem that its place in athletic literature is already assured. Of special interest to Belgravians is the spotlight on Laurie O'Hara in the first edition. Those who wish to subscribe to this new venture should write to Clive at 24 Fryston Avenue, Coulsdon, Surrey. Rates including postage are:- U.K. £1.00 per annum, Overseas £1.50 per annum. items.label: September 1973
items.sum: Editorial lamenting the International Olympic Committee's decision to drop walking from the Olympic programme, and urging members to attend the A.G.M. on 20 September.
items.s: COMMENT Editorial lamenting the International Olympic Committee's decision to drop walking from the Olympic programme, and urging members to attend the A.G.M. on 20 September. COMMENT The decision of the International Olympic Committee to drop Walking from the Olympic Programme is a shattering blow to those who are involved in this branch of athletics. In Belgrave Harriers we feel it particularly keenly, for over the years our members have proved themselves to be amongst the best walkers in the world and they have Olympic medals to show for it. Yes, the 'Games' do need pruning but the events to be axed should be the team events which are nothing more than nation against nation, directly in contrast to the Olympic ideal. Is it too late to do anything about it? The British Race Walkers' Club is not taking the decision lying down and is doing all it can to stir up some action and welcomes any helpful suggestions which should be sent to C. W. Fogg, Metropolitan Police Training School, Hendon, N. W. 9 . The Notice of the Annual General Meeting, to be held on Thursday, 20th Sept., is to be found on page 4 of this gazette. Your Committee hopes that you will make the effort to attend if you can, for if you have any criticisms or observations to make, this is the time to do it. C. W. Fogg C. W. Fogg contact for suggestions on the Olympic walking decision Olympic Games Hendon British Race Walkers' Club

items.sum: Short note on "Snowy" Brooks's hurdles wins and sprinting at the National Championships of Barbados, including a doubtful 10.7 for 100m.
items.s: Short note on "Snowy" Brooks's hurdles wins and sprinting at the National Championships of Barbados, including a doubtful 10.7 for 100m. "Snowy" Brooks competed in the National Championships of Barbados with considerable success. He won both hurdle races with 15.9 and 56.0 and also reached 4th place in the 100m final with 10.9. His time in the heat of the 100m was an astounding 10.7 (equalling our existing Club record) but "Snowy" doubts the authenticity of this as he thought he was some way down on the first two who clocked 10.6. items.label: September 1973
items.sum: The President's column (signed Clive Shippen) looking back on his year of office and the deaths of Alf Harley, Syd Roberts and Percy Wilson, with notes on coaching helpers, John Bicourt's steeplechase season, a pre-World War I club photograph, the Belgrave Hall facelift, the Merton open day and an old photo of Ernie Duffett.
items.s: PRESIDENT'S PARS The President's column (signed Clive Shippen) looking back on his year of office and the deaths of Alf Harley, Syd Roberts and Percy Wilson, with notes on coaching helpers, John Bicourt's steeplechase season, a pre-World War I club photograph, the Belgrave Hall facelift, the Merton open day and an old photo of Ernie Duffett. PRESIDENT'S PARS With my year of office almost at a close I would like to thank all those officers, members of Committee and the many other Belgravians who have made the year so enjoyable and, indeed, so successful. Although I was present at most of our activities during the year there were several that I missed due to fixture clashes or outside pressures and I can assure you that it is most disappointing to miss any Belgrave turn-out when in the "Chair". Unfortunately my year of office was irretrievably marred by the loss of a man I greatly admired - Alf Harley. Alf's death left a vacuum which will take a long time to fill, and your Committee has missed the wise counsel he so often gave. As President, I discovered just how much Alf did on behalf of the Club, for when he had gone the many things we had all taken for granted for so long were suddenly left undone, and on more than one occasion we fell down on our responsibilities. The loss of our Past President, Syd Roberts, so close on that of Alf Harley, struck a double blow to the Club and filled me with disillusionment - my term of office being only 3 months old. But 3 events did bring me a great deal of pleasure. The R.W.A. 20 kms. at Victoria Park where our team packed in for a great win. The National Road Relay at Derby where our twelve shocked the opposition by more than holding their own against star-studded teams to finish a magnificent 5th. And then there was the meeting we held at Wimbledon Park Track for 60 or more unattached colts and boys. Such enthusiasm. Such dedicated work too by so many Belgravians who gave their day to the event. There were many other occasions also where one witnessed the tremendous amount of work put in by our officials - work so necessary to keep our Club strong and thriving. It has been a joy to work with them all and Belgravians can rest assured, their Club is in good hands. Just as the beginning of my term was a sad memory, so it was near the end too. Percy Wilson lost a long and brave fight against illness and died in July. He will be remembered, alongside brother Joe, for his many appearances at walking fixtures, his regular manning of sponging stations on the Brighton Road and particularly for his work with youngsters. As another year approaches with its untold fortunes, and misfortunes, I am proud to have had the privilege of leading you through the eventful Club year of 1972/73. Thank you. Coaches, helpers - anyone! That's what we need down at Wimbledon Park Track on Sunday mornings between 10.30 and 12.00. Our recent coaching day for unattached youngsters has stimulated a steady flow of new members local to Wimbledon. About 20 have been appearing regularly and Philip Gee, Bill Couzens and Alan Mead have been bearing the brunt of looking after these lads for 1½ hours. Measuring throws or jumps, rough timekeeping or just controlling and helping groups of lads is something many of our inactive members could do. Their help is needed and it is a job I am sure they will enjoy. By such small beginnings are coaches made. Can you help? If so, contact any of the abovenamed trio or contact me direct. What a fine season JOHN BICOURT has been having. Now established as an international choice, John has only had Hollings and Davies to contend with amongst U.K. 'chasers. But the three of them have had some fascinating struggles to register a 1973 U.K. best. Each in turn held the mark and then John went to Norway, lost narrowly to Moravcik of Czechoslovakia but had the great satisfaction of hearing his time given, not only as a 1973 U.K. best, but as a U.K. record! Or so it seemed. A rapid revision of times left John just inches away from the National record A bitter disappointment, but he has regained his 1973 lead and is only the third Briton (after Andy Holden and Dave Bedford) to break 8:30. Well done John. continued on following page ....... Club records are particularly sparse between the years 1887 and 1914, so any information relating to that period is particularly interesting. We should all be very aware of our history and traditions, and members would be doing the Club a service if they passed on any information they feel to be of value. If old cuttings or photo's have a special sentimental value then they will be returned after a sight by the writer. The photograph reproduced here is one of our few pre-World War I groups and features; R.W. Ricketts, E. Gordon, E. Adams, C. Cook, R.W. Best, J.B. Belchamber, H. Brown, H. Parker, O. Horwood and R. Savage. Can anyone identify any others? Visitors to Belgrave Hall this last few weeks will have noticed the expensive looking facelift it has been given. Well it would have been expensive all right but for Arthur Bruce, our Chairman of the Building Sub-Committee. We live in an age of very high maintenance costs and Arthur decided that a bit of 'do-it-yourself' was called for. He organised a rota of working parties over a 7 week period. The Hall was washed down, made good, re-decorated and the floor sanded and sealed. Needless to say it was Arthur and just a handful of members who gave up a lot of their time, and our thanks is due to them and any others who helped out when they could. Not only was the work successful but the efforts of Arthur and his team saved the Club a great deal of money. Belgrave Harriers went into the publicity business at Ravensbury Park on Saturday, June 23rd. An Open day for the Borough of Merton's sports clubs was held and our stand and display was the best on view - but then I'm biassed! Charlie Manning was behind the successful stand, despite many late changes of plan imposed upon him, and Bill Lucas made our demonstration go with a swing with his lively commentating. Your President was the first to be pulled out in a "devil take the hindmost" race which was eventually won by Gerry North. Trevor Hart and Alan Mead won the paarlauf and two teams of our colts and boys fought out a relay. To cap it all Carl Lawton demonstrated how easy it was to walk two laps of the grass "track" leaving a heap of struggling, moaning runners walking (?) in his wake. Our next show-piece (static only) will be at Morden Park on Merton Show Day, August Bank Holiday Monday (27th). You can't keep a good man down! It was only 3 years ago that I reproduced a photo of Ernie Duffett (Dec.1970) showing him in some pretty good company - he was 3rd in the Surrey County C.C. of about 1928. Well here he is once more (see opposite page) - and 3rd again! Showing a novel form of drop finish, Ernie (111) fails to catch No. 1 and the winner (53) L.E.Hope of Shaftesbury who won this handicap mile in 4:25. The occasion was an S.L.H. meeting at the Oval in the late twenties - a venue where that small group of enthusiasts back in 1887 decided to form a club called Belgrave Harriers. items.label: September 1973
items.sum: Harry Shields's obituary of walker Percy Wilson, who died in his 61st year after 30 years' service to the club as helper, organiser of feeding stations and coach of young walkers.
items.s: R.I.P. PERCY WILSON Harry Shields's obituary of walker Percy Wilson, who died in his 61st year after 30 years' service to the club as helper, organiser of feeding stations and coach of young walkers. R.I.P. PERCY WILSON My mind is filled with many thoughts in an endeavour to do justice to the memory of Percy Wilson who died in his 61st year after a long and distressing illness. The 30 years service he gave to the Club is filled with acts of kindness and example. He was never a Champion or an Officer but more in the tradition of a Sergeant, whom Wellington in his Peninsular Campaigns, leading to great victory at Waterloo, so well described as the back-bone of his army. His remarks were:- " The ideal sergeant is not easily found and when found is invaluable, he can be relied upon never to connive at others faults, but to use tact to get his wishes carried out. He has to be a meritorious man whose personal example is the means of swaying actions. He demonstrates by example and his reward is the benefit of popularity by receiving loyal and intelligent help instead of mere obedience. No mercenary motive actuates his conduct and whose hands are never soiled with the gifts of an inferior." My first experience of Percy and his inseparable brother Joe was when I forsook running to take up Walking. They took me under their wings and instilled in me the love and comradeship of the sport. Many others, including subsequent champions, have similar reason to be grateful for their early advice and encouragement. In discussion after the Cremation, it was said he was a natural coach, of unselfish dedication and without thought of reward or thanks. This is indeed true. Examples to indicate his sterling character readily come to mind. (a) The organisation of the Annual Boys Brigade Events at St. Magdelene's Church, Earlsfield, which attracted some hundred boys in graded walking races. It was apparent that most of the cost of the awards and other expenses came from Percy's pocket. (b) The London to Brighton Walk - during recent years he organised the Earlswood Common Feeding Station and accepted responsibility for many of the supplementary refreshment points on the road. (c) His ready help in all running and walking events either as a pointsman or to man a feeding station. On 100 mile walk and runs his cheery encouragement with a drink or a sponge during the long hours, no matter what the weather conditions, were acts of pure dedication. His own career as a walker was not insignificant. He was a "Centurion" i.e. one who has walked 100 miles in under 24 hours. The number of London to Brighton and other long distance walks he has completed must bear comparison with any. The events in which he has taken part for Belgrave and his second claim club London Vidarians must be astronomical. His full capabilities as a walker were never seen because of his pre-occupation of help to others. The loss of Percy is another of our great stalwarts gone. His service was different to that of Alf Harley and Harry Churcher but still one which brought lustre to the Belgrave Harriers and the whole of race walking. It is astonishing that he was not put forward as a "Vice President" or "Life Member" of the Club. Probably I should take the blame for this omission. His cremation was attended by representatives of the London Vidarians and the R.W.A. (Southern Area), while the affection in which he was held by his family was evident. It upset me considerably in scanning the 47 floral tributes not to see one from the Club. In these days of Inter-Flora surely there can be no excuse. To such a man the only fitting epitaph is, "It is well finished". Our deepest condolences to Joe, and all his family and relations. Harry Shields The late Percy Wilson (left) with his brother Joe. Gold Award in the steeplechase, with the Gold Award standards and his four international 3000m steeplechase results of June-July 1973. TRACK & FIELD JOHN BICOURT: our greatest ever track-star? Some superb running has come lately from John Bicourt. Last season he gained the A.A.A. Silver Award and this year he has already qualified for the Gold Award - the highest that the A.A.A. can offer. The standard for this is 8:33.0 in the 3000 metres Steeplechase so John's 8:26.6 recorded in Oslo is well under. items.s: SOUTHERN COUNTIES CHAMPS. Report and Belgrave-relevant results of the Southern Counties A.A.A. Championships at Crystal Palace on 22-23 June 1973, where Rodney Heward-Mills won the club's only medal (triple jump bronze) and John Stow ran a 1500m personal best. SOUTHERN COUNTIES CHAMPS. JUNE 22nd/23rd 1973 - CRYSTAL PALACE. Eight Belgravians ventured into the Crystal Palace arena to compete in the Southern Counties A.A.A. Championships. Although lacking in numbers they achieved a fair measure of success. Rodney Heward-Mills gained our solitary medal with a 15.54 triple jump but Steve White only just missed in an exciting long jump competition in which 2 centimetres covered 2nd to 5th places. Stevie was pushed down to 4th with an inferior second best leap, having already managed 6th place in a good 200m final the evening before. Track Vice-Captain Charlie Gillett improved on his best times for 1973 in the 400m flat and hurdle races and looks as if he could go faster still. After setting a target of around 3:52 for the season, John Stow is going to have to think again. On the Friday night he qualified in the 1500m with an excellent personal best of 3:51.1 and then improved again in the final to equal John Bicourt's best, thus continuing their keen rivalry. John Bicourt says that he can go a bit faster yet but on this occasion he understandably found the exertions of a 5000m race too much after his run in Warsaw the previous day and he was forced to retire. 200m: 1. items.sum: Report of the Southern League match at Crawley on 30 June 1973, where Belgrave, joint leaders beforehand, were beaten by a solid Met. Police team and finished second on the day (headlined as a slump to 4th in the league), with the 'A' and 'B' string results.
items.s: Bels. slump to 4th in League Report of the Southern League match at Crawley on 30 June 1973, where Belgrave, joint leaders beforehand, were beaten by a solid Met. Police team and finished second on the day (headlined as a slump to 4th in the league), with the 'A' and 'B' string results. Bels. slump to 4th in League JUNE 30th 1973 - CRAWLEY. Going into this meeting the position at the top of the Southern League was extremely tight. Windsor, Slough & Eton AC and ourselves shared the lead with 10 league points and 268 match points each and Cambridge Harriers were 3rd with 10 league points and 267 match points. The opposition at Crawley was not expected to be as strong as in our previous matches but with a couple of our lads competing abroad and some unable to make it for other reasons, we slipped up and found ourselves beaten by a solid Met. Police team. Cambridge Harriers went on to win their meeting so the lead, temporarily one hopes, has been wrested from us. Young Reg. Hopkins gave a glimpse of his all round ability with a first ever 400m hurdles run of 58.6 whilst Charlie Gillett, who has yet to lose a Southern League one lap event this year, took the 'A' race. Steve White and Mick Marshall had the 100m/200m pretty well sewn up, and Charlie and Phil. Gee were first past the post in both the long sprint races. Our Track Secretary, Philip, is hitting good form every time out and in the 1600m relay, which proved to be the most exciting race of the day, he took the 'Claret and Gold' through the tape after our team had a mediocre start, with a 50.4 'split' time. John Stow shocked everyone, including himself, with a 51.7 circuit in the same race. No brilliant performances this day on the field although our 'heavy boys' put in some good all-round work and Steve White again picked up top points in the Long Jump. Dave Roberts, competing in our league team for the first time, had the misfortune to fall very heavily in the 110m hurdles due to a knee injury. In spite of this he pluckily ran through to get his point, and it is just these odd points which count in a competition as close as this. continued on next page... ..... continued 1. Met. items.s: CLUB CHAMPIONSHIPS Report and results of the 1973 Belgrave Club Championships at Hurlingham on 7 July 1973, with over sixty competitors, highlighted by "Snowy" Brooks, Charlie Gillett, John Stow and John Martin. CLUB CHAMPIONSHIPS JULY 7th 1973 - HURLINGHAM. The 1973 Club Championships proved to be quite a successful affair with over sixty competitors, plenty of officials, good weather and a fair sprinkling of onlookers. Only a few hours after he had stepped off the jet from Barbados, "Snowy" Brooks was making his mark on the meeting with a good shot putt win in a personal best distance. Perhaps coming down from high altitude helps field events men too. He also equalled the Championship Best Performance along with Mick Marshall in the 100 metres. Charlie Gillett finished a metre or so down in this but turned the tables when it came to the two longer sprints. An 800 metre/ 1500 metre double was scored by John Stow who was untroubled over either distance. John Martin, resplendent in brand new javelin boots, beat his best distance with the 'spear' and if we can keep him off the beer and encourage him to concentrate on this event he is going to throw further still. Great throwing too from Peter Crosbie who although only a Youth, does a pretty good job with the senior implement. Ivan Beaumont (a Boy) and Steve Walters (a Youth) also fancied their chances and took on the Seniors, putting up a couple of quite respectable performances and neither of them a long way down on the senior standard. Juniors are a bit scarce these days, giving our Youths the chance to have a go at the medals. Toby Staff equalled his best in the 800 metres and then took the 400 metres for good measure, whilst the 100 metres was a 'Crosbie Brothers benefit'. Our irrepressible Boys and Colts turned out in force and David Didino in the older age group looked most impressive with a 100 metre win in 13.5 and then twice improving the Championship Best in the High Jump. Appeal for volunteers to take over as the club's Honorary Starters from Arthur Penny and George Chantler, with guns, licences and training supplied by the club. WHO is going to start our races next season ? We have had long and valuable service from Arthur Penny and George Chantler our Honorary Starters but both of these gentlemen are adamant that it is time someone else took over. Guns, licences and training if necessary will be supplied by the Club. Don't just read this and then forget about it. If you would like to continue to help your club now that your competitive days are over, please step forward at the A.G.M. items.s: League Record for Steve White Report of the Southern League match at Redhill on 28 July 1973, won by Belgrave to move back to equal first overall, with Steve White setting a Southern League 200m record of 21.6, and the 'A' and 'B' string results. League Record for Steve White JULY 28th 1973 - REDHILL Cliff Temple, writing in the "Sunday Times", has league athletics weighed up just right: "You are not only trying to score points yourself, but also to cheer on your most harmless rivals if they are pushing your most dangerous ones down the field. It's not just a case of 'We won' - it is 'We won, and they were only 5th which counts'. " So it was at Redhill and close though it was, the final positions were just as we needed - Bels 1st, Windsor 2nd and Cambridge Harriers, the league leaders before this match, 3rd. We moved back to equal 1st overall although Oxford City's match point score is superior to our own. The standard at this meeting was very high and yet we came through with honours. Steve White was in brilliant form, breaking the Southern League 200m record and equalling our own Club mark with 21.6. Unfortunately our sprinters suffered a set-back when Mick Marshall, after doing well in the 100m, TJ and LJ, "pulled" a hamstring in the 'B' 200m and had to step out of the relay squad. Philip Gee filled the breach admirably and we again took maximum points in both relays. Young Reg Hopkins, fresh from his 4th place in the AAA Junior Decathlon, looked most impressive over 2nd leg in the 4 x 400m. As usual Glyn Ratcliffe and Eric Barker scored well in the heavy-weight section although Glyn, now taking a keen interest in the technique of hammer throwing, found he could not stay in the circle with three turns and failed to register a throw. Seasonal bests came from Philip Gee in the 400m, during which he reached 200m in close to 23 seconds which would have been a personal best, and from Alan Mead in the 800m where the whole field of ten runners got under 2 minutes. 1. items.s: SPOTLIGHT on CLIFFORD 'SNOWY' BROOKS Profile by A.R.M. of Olympic decathlete Clifford "Snowy" Brooks: his background, Royal Navy service, joining Belgrave, decathlon progress, his 1972 season and Munich Olympics for Barbados, with statistical notes of his best performances. SPOTLIGHT on ........... CLIFFORD 'SNOWY' BROOKS Turn up at the start of any of our main track fixtures and you are certain to see the muscular figure of Olympic Decathlete Clifford "Snowy" Brooks, limbering up for the early events. Hours later as the meeting draws to a close he will still be there, holding together a relay team, having competed non-stop on the field and track throughout the whole match. A great deal of our success is owed to this prolific points scorer who is one of the most popular personalities in the Belgrave team and athletic circles in general throughout the Southern Counties. Everyone seems to know "Snowy" whether they be an international woman discus thrower or a lowly 800 metre runner. Talking to him in the restaurant after a session at the Crystal Palace is like being in the centre of a whirlwind as back-chat and banter flies back and forth between him and all and sundry. He was born on 19th August 1944 at Camberwell and for most of his life he has been more or less based in the South London area. Athletics for him was a once a year affair at school - the school sports day. He was not particularly good, showing probably just as much ability in football and cricket but towards the end of his days at St. Luke's Secondary Modern, Kingston-upon-Thames, he did run in a few races for Kingston Athletic Club. In 1960 he signed on with the Royal Navy and until 1971 he served as a steward on board the anti-submarine frigate HMS Plymouth and the aircraft carriers HMS Victorious and HMS Hermes. Life in the navy was enjoyable and his travels with the "grey funnel line" gave him the chance to see a good deal of the world, particularly the Far East and the Mediterranean. During a spell at home, he decided to have another dabble at the sport of athletics - perhaps he would even do a bit of training. It was good fortune that during a visit to Battersea Park track he renewed his acquaintanceship with Ben Lulham who had been the mainstay of Kingston Athletic Club. At that time the club had recently wound up its affairs with some of its members joining Surrey AC and others, including Ben's remarkable squad of sprinters, coming to Belgrave. Cliff Brooks became a Belgravian. Almost immediately he made his presence felt by winning three Club Championships and in the "Belgravian" of November 1964 it was reported... " A new face of great promise was that of C.T.Brooks whose performances of 5'2"/20'9¾"/38'6" in the three jumping events were on sheer natural ability. " Being at sea much of the time meant that most of his training consisted of weight lifting which he had to do in a narrow space below deck in between the fuel tanks, with barely enough room to swing a "cat". His enthusiasm was not to be daunted and in 1965, with his all round ability, he made the natural progression to the ten-in-one-event, the Decathlon, competing as a guest in the R.A.F. Championships. By 1968, influenced by his training companion Great Britain international and fellow navy athlete, Peter Gabbett, "Snowy" was beginning to make real progress. Sometimes this progress was to our dismay, for the following season we lost one of the premier trophy meetings - the "Ryder Trophy" at Southampton - to the Royal Navy by just eight points. Fifteen points were scored for the RN that day by an athlete wearing a tracksuit with the name "Snowy" emblazoned across the shoulders! The Belgrave Club Record for the Decathlon was by now his own, and in his final year with the navy in 1971, he won the 400m hurdle championship in a RN record which still stands of 55.1 and in the same season was placed 3rd in the Inter-Services 400m hurdles and 2nd, behind Gabbett, in the RN Decathlon. He now exchanged his sailor's uniform for another, that of the armoured division of Securicor. Life now took on a different routine, one that involved an almost daily trip, winter and summer, to the National Recreation Centre at Crystal Palace, training with four or five other decathletes. A considerable amount of his sessions were still with the weights and he is quite proud of his best lifts, although he asserts that a weight lifter of his body weight would be able to do far better. continued on following page ....... Statistical notes: Height 5'11¼". Weight 13st.2 lbs. Best performances - 100m/10.7, 200m/22.6, 400m/49.8, 600m/1:24.0, 800m/2:08.0, 1500m/4:47.0, 400mH/55.1, 110mH/15.7, Shot/13.74m, Discus/40.06m, Jav/43.38m, HJ/1.86m, LJ/7.06m, TJ/12.21m, PV/3.27m, Decathlon/6389 pts (100m/11.2, LJ/6.86m, Shot/12.45m,HJ/1.72m, 400m/50.7 - overnight score 3558 pts - 110mH/16.0, Discus/33.18m, PV/3.10m Jav/42.02m, 1500m/4:50.8). Weight lifting bests - Military Press/200lbs, Snatch/198lbs, Clean/251lbs, Clean and Jerk/245lbs, Deadlift/550lbs. Spotlight continued His best season yet followed in 1972 with an unexpected win in the Surrey County 400 metre Championship, representative honours for the Amateur Athletic Association and Southern Counties A.A.A., and 7th place in the A.A.A. Decathlon where he amassed 6389 points, his best score to date. This moved him up to 11th on the British Ranking list for the event and meant that he had improved our Club Record by 986 points since he first took it over. All this, of course, was crowned by his selection to represent Barbados, the birth-place of his father, at the Munich Olympic Games. Munich was the experience of a life time. The facilities and stadium were superb and in the athletes' village language problems were soon overcome and a friendly atmosphere prevailed. "Snowy" particularly enjoyed meeting the U.S. Decathlon team and Bill Toomey, winner in the Mexico Olympics and World Record Holder. The competition took place on 7th/8th of September and as he was not expected to excel in this company, he found himself quite relaxed and admits to having felt a lot more nervous prior to a Surrey Championship. His overnight score was on a par with that during the AAA Championship and there were hopes that he would again improve his best but trouble struck during the pole vault. He found himself unable to get in a clear vault - not surprising when you consider that the starting height was around his best ever. He decided at that point to retire from the competition, and watched as the mighty Nikolay Avilov of the Soviet Union crushed the best all rounders in the world to win with a World Record score of 8454 points. What of the future? His progress since 1967 has been relentless but in an event where skill in so many different areas is necessary it takes a long while to reach ones best, so who knows what mark he will eventually attain. An obvious target for the time being is 7000 points but as long as he continues to improve, "Snowy" will keep up the daily grind, aiming higher and higher. A.R.M. Cliff hands the baton to another up and coming decathlete - Reg Hopkins - during a 1600 metre relay. items.h: FROM THE BELGRAVIAN 25 years ago... and 40 years ago...
items.sum: Reprints from 1948 (Belgrave second to Surrey W.C. in the R.W.A. National 20 Miles at Sudbury yet taking the Nijmegan Shield) and from 1933 (W.A. Rice's social notes on the club dance at Queensberry Hall).
items.s: FROM THE BELGRAVIAN 25 years ago... and 40 years ago... Reprints from 1948 (Belgrave second to Surrey W.C. in the R.W.A. National 20 Miles at Sudbury yet taking the Nijmegan Shield) and from 1933 (W.A. Rice's social notes on the club dance at Queensberry Hall). FROM THE BELGRAVIAN 25 years ago... R.W.A. NATIONAL 20 MILES CHAMPIONSHIP, SUDBURY. May 8th 1948 ........... Our teams were supported by what must be the biggest crowd of Club members and friends ever seen at a road race. Our Road Captain, Charlie Churcher, surprised most people by not adopting his usual get-a-way method and the opening stages of the race were unusually slow. Later on, however, Charlie developed stomach trouble and was obliged to fall back. About the same time Colin Sutton had trouble with his shoes and lost a lot of ground. In the centre of the field, however, our Vice-Captain, Jack Bidgood, was doing some excellent work holding together about half a dozen of our walkers which no doubt had much to do with the ultimate result of the race. On recovering from his trouble, Colin Sutton battled bravely on recovering position after position and eventually caught up on Jack Bidgood and Co. Charlie, however, had continued to drop back and with our friends, Surrey W.C., holding two places in the first five, a win for us seemed out of the question. Eventually our lads finished in a procession with five consecutive placings from 18 to 22 and backed up by George Bentley, Joe Wilson and Joe Coleman, we succeeded in taking the Nijmegan Shield with our eight walkers in the first 48, an excellent performance on which all are to be congratulated. 1. G.B.R.Whitlock, 2:52:7 , 18. H.G.Clayton, 19.J.C.Bidgood, 20. C.F.Sutton 21. C.E.Churcher, 22. A.Readman, 32. G.Bentley, 33. P.Sapcote, 45. J.Wilson 48. J.Coleman, 65. G.Doubleday, 74. G.Boddington, 76. S.Spencer, 96. G.Oliver, 100. F.Tasker, 106. A.Pink. 1. Surrey W.C. 56 pts; 2. BELGRAVE HARRIERS 78 pts. and 40 years ago... SOCIALLY SPEAKING....... (W.A.Rice writes) .....Our first dance was held at the Queensberry Hall, South Kensington on Saturday, October 21st and was well attended. I noticed Len Rollins looking very M.C.-ish, dancing with that air of detached boredom which characterises the really good dancer, as distinct from the plebian, chance-to-the-luck-and-the-girl's-good-temper enthusiasts [illegible]ke ourselves. Incidently, I declare his waves are becoming more natural week by week. I also espied Harry Shields setting a new fashion and carrying a tightly clenched handbag under one arm. Whilst admitting that there may have been special circumstances, I hardly think this is a fashion likely to catch on among our members. H.E.Footer seemed to have put the cares of captaincy aside for one evening and I understand that on this occasion the moral to be preached was " Don't do as I do, etc. ". Several of our champions (past and present) were there, including A.Penny, F.Stroud, T.H.Scrimshaw, J.Tosh, J.Crilly, and the proportion of Club members present was very gratifying. ......... .....Our next event is a Social on November 4th, at Wimbledon. There will be the usual dance in the evening, and I have heared whispers that some of the natural talent, with which the Club abounds, will be in evidence during the evening. Those who remember Castor and Oil making their bow last year will remember how enjoyable this mixture can be, so roll up in your hundreds. Come along to tea and stay on for the dance and fun in the evening Charlie Churcher Charlie Churcher Road Captain 1948; 21st R.W.A. items.sum: Humorous comments set beside newspaper cuttings about Belgrave's talks with Merton Council over a headquarters site and President Clive Shippen denying a move to Wimbledon Park.
items.s: CUTTING COMMENTS Humorous comments set beside newspaper cuttings about Belgrave's talks with Merton Council over a headquarters site and President Clive Shippen denying a move to Wimbledon Park. CUTTING COMMENTS During the past nine months, Belgrave Harriers have been wooing Merton Council. You mean the blonde in the typing pool? - Guilty. Bels asked the council to find them a headquarters site Does this mean the trustees have sold Belgrave Hall for an astronomical figure? - Confiscate their passports. and in exchange they would contribute a substantial sum—amounting to several thousand pounds. We don't remember seeing a large amount on the last Balance Sheet. By the way, have you seen the Treasurer lately? In the meantime, however, the newcomer had been approached by members of Belgrave Harriers. Our Track Officials show great Club spirit. They should be awarded their Club Honours Badge for devotion to duty. Belgrave president Clive Shippen this week denied any decision had been taken to switch Belgrave's track headquarters to Wimbledon Park. At one time most of our members used to train at Tooting. However, clubs like Selsonia, Herrne Hill and South London Harriers, are based there. This raises an interesting point. Is Clive a double agent for SLH? Or is he a talent scout for Selsonia Ladies AC? Now that's a job we would like. Sporting, sorry, spotting the talent in Selsonia. items.s: 'LEICESTER MERCURY' Retained for 5th Year Report of the Leicester walk on 26 May 1973, won by John Moullin with Ray Middleton 2nd, as Belgrave kept the 'Leicester Mercury' trophy for a fifth year. WALKING 'LEICESTER MERCURY' Retained for 5th Year MAY 26th 1973 - LEICESTER. Belgrave went to Leicester for their annual Midland pot-hunt with the usual strong team, although two weak links were the absence of Allan Callow (racing in the Isle of Man over 20 miles) and the uncertainty of Carl Lawton being able to last the distance. All went well for the Bels from the start with Len Duquemin an early leader. By 5 miles John Moullin was clear and he was never headed to the finish. Ray Middleton finished an easy 2nd closing the gap between himself and John over the last 5 miles. At the 8 mile point it was Bels 1,2,3,4 but this fell to pieces soon after when Eric Crompton came through for 3rd and Carl made an emergency stop. By 17 miles Carl had got back up to 4th with Len Duquemin 5th, however, at this point he tired drastically and recorded 24 minutes for the last 2 miles to finish 11th. John Dunsford was our fifth man with John Bromley and Bob Picton walking the last few miles together. 1. BELGRAVE H 17 pts; 2. Leicester 43 pts; 3. Met. W.C. 60 pts. 1. items.s: Goswell Throws Fit ! Light-hearted report of a 3 km evening walk at Battersea Park on 23 May 1973 with 38 walkers, won by Carl Lawton. Goswell Throws Fit ! MAY 23rd 1973 - BATTERSEA PARK. A quiet evening race was envisaged as Jack Goswell arrived to assist in the 3 km walk. However, on discovering that John Bromley had transported half the Police Cadets from Hendon over to Battersea for the race, he concluded that he had better disappear. Gentle persuasion followed and Jack re-emerged exclaiming profusely that his results board would collapse under the strain of 38 walkers. Despite this, all was concluded satisfactorily with a win for Carl Lawton from Peter Hodkinson of Cambridge Harriers. items.sum: Harry Shields' report and results of the 54th R.W.A. 20 miles championship at Ewell on 16 June 1973, held in tropical conditions, where Belgrave were second team to Sheffield United Harriers and Carl Lawton fourth.
items.s: 2nd IN R.W.A. 20 MILES Harry Shields' report and results of the 54th R.W.A. 20 miles championship at Ewell on 16 June 1973, held in tropical conditions, where Belgrave were second team to Sheffield United Harriers and Carl Lawton fourth. 2nd IN R.W.A. 20 MILES JUNE 16th 1973 - EWELL. Apart from being the oldest and most cherished of the R.W.A. Championships, the 20 miles is that which requires a most careful balance of speed and stamina. No pity is given to those who mis-judge the course or weather conditions. To be with the leaders, an average speed of 7½ miles per hour must be maintained with turns of pace to match and break those around you. This 54th annual competition was held in tropical conditions, surpassed in memory only by the grey-beards, with "Ah ! You should have been in the 50Km at Preston, or in the 'Brighton' of 1953 when the tar melted and the only encouragement was imaginary hallucinations of oases, like those described by desert explorers, to spur you on your way". These were this championship's conditions and how soon the "sheep" and the "goats" were sorted out. On an approximately six lap course, indiscretions taken soon showed themselves. Our first grievous loss was that of Allan Callow, who after leading our team for some time, found the conditions too much, and dropped out. This eliminated us from the"Nijmegan Shield" for the Club with the first complete team, which until recent memory, was a trophy held by us for many years. It was a point of honour that outside the four scoring men, the others should encourage and prop up any in distress to make certain all finished, and many are the tales that could be told. The tenacity of Dave McMullen, D.Hall and John Dunsford showed this spirit and the pity was that E.Stroud could not be included in the team and rewarded for his fine walk. The championship was well fought, both individual and team. Although much the stronger team over the last 5 miles we lost to Sheffield United Harriers by a margin so small that it was only necessary for one of our first three men to catch and beat the man in front in order to win. items.label: September 1973
items.sum: Question-and-answer profile of junior walker Martyn Bennett, holder of the Olympic Cup, covering his training, interests, ambitions and best performances.
items.s: MEET MARTYN BENNETT Question-and-answer profile of junior walker Martyn Bennett, holder of the Olympic Cup, covering his training, interests, ambitions and best performances. MEET MARTYN BENNETT Martyn is one of Belgrave's leading Juniors and the current holder of the'Olympic Cup' - our 5 mile Junior Championship. Q. Why did you take up walking? A. I don't really know. I suppose it came as a natural progression from doing a few minor school walks to joining Belgrave and eventually concentrating on it as my premier sport. Q. What training do you do? A. Winter: Rugby training Monday to Friday and a match on Saturday morning. Race Walk on Saturday afternoon. I did no real walking training during last winter save for races on Saturdays. Summer: Sunday- 14 miles slow in Richmond Park. Monday- 2 miles slow and 5 miles fast. Tuesday- 5 miles including sprints. Wednesday- 5 miles slow. Thursday- 8 (increasing by 2 each week) x 400 metres in 1:45-1:50 with 1:10 rests. Friday- 2 miles slow. Saturday- race or rest. My summer training has proved less effective than I hoped and at the moment I'm doing a lot of circuits and weights in preparation for the oncoming Rugby season. Q. Any other interests? A. All sports interest me and I'll have a go at anything. Rugby and Cross-Country occupy me during the winter but I'm not much good at either, though I enjoy both. Music, Pubs (though I don't drink much) and books seem to occupy most of my spare time but for the past year I have managed to put training before these in terms of importance. Q. Aims and ambitions? A. Unfortunately I am one of those people who have tremendous ambitions but who rarely realise them, mainly through lack of effort on my behalf. Athletically, I had hoped to walk in an Olympics but now a group of sensationalist and twisted showmen, hypocritical to the Olympic spirit, have deprived me and every other Junior race walker of one of the major reasons for remaining in the sport. Outside of sport, I hope to go to university next year and get a degree, probably in history. Q. Best performances? A. In terms of time my best performances have been at Crystal Palace in the spring of this year where I did a 14:16 3km and a 24:28 5km. I suppose my three sub 58:30 seven mile races during the winter were my most satisfactory, as they all came as a bit of a surprise to me (and to everyone else I think). Martyn Bennett Martyn Bennett leading junior walker, holder of the Olympic Cup (5 mile Junior Championship); bests 14:16 3km and 24:28 5km at Crystal Palace; three sub 58:30 seven mile races MARTYN BENNETT Martyn Olympic Cup Richmond Park Crystal Palace

items.sum: Instructional piece setting out the competition rules for the high jump, from raising the bar to what counts as a failure.
items.s: know the rules - HIGH JUMP Instructional piece setting out the competition rules for the high jump, from raising the bar to what counts as a failure. know the rules - HIGH JUMP (a) The uprights or posts shall not be moved during the competition unless the Judges consider the take-off or landing ground has become unsuitable. Such a change shall be made only after a round is completed. (b) Unless such details are specified on the programme, the Judges shall decide the height at which the competition shall start, and the different heights to which the bar will be raised at the end of each round. The competitors shall be informed of the details before the competition begins. (c) A competitor may commence jumping at any height above the minimum height and may jump at his own discretion at any subsequent height. Three consecutive failures, regardless of the height at which any of such failures occurs, disqualify from further jumping. n.b. The effect of this rule is that a competitor may forego his second and third jumps at a particular height (after failing once or twice) and still jump at a subsequent height. (d) Even after all the other competitors have failed, a competitor is entitled to continue jumping until he has forfeited his right to compete further and his best jump shall be recorded as the winning height. (e) The employment of weights or grips of any kind is forbidden. (f) A competitor may place marks to assist him in his run up and take-off and a handkerchief or similar object on the cross-bar for sighting purposes. The distance of the run is unlimited. (g) All measurements shall be made perpendicularly from the ground to the upper side of the cross-bar where it is lowest. A steel or fibre-glass measure should be used. Any measurements of a new height should be made before competitors attempt that height. In the case of records the officials must check the measurement after the height has been cleared. The height shall be recorded to the nearest ¼ inch (1 cm.) below the height measured, i.e. fractions less than ¼ inch (1 cm.) must be ignored. n.b. Judges should ensure, before commencing the competition, that the underside and front of the cross-bar are distinguishable and that the bar is always replaced in a similar manner. (h) A competitor fails if he - (i) In the course of a jump dislodges the bar so that it falls from the pegs; or (ii) Touches the ground or landing area beyond the plane of the uprights without first clearing the bar; or (iii) Takes off from both feet.

Belgrave Harriers '20' 21st July 73 We apologise for the poor quality of these prints - which might have been - had the film passed through the camera, but as the 'bard' said in the prelude to 'Henry V', "Upon your imagination draw full reign". WOW! Here is the incredibly beautiful Marion Dew - talking to that equally beautiful Geoff North!! The Orgy Because of the embarrasing nature of this, the names have been omitted, but some familiar (faces) should be immediately apparent. Nerve Centre Olly Beard (H/W) keeps a watchful eye on Clive Shippen and Charlie Dabbs, manipulating the results. Herc./Wim. Member from a rather insignificant local Club, Ian Blakey. Sorry, his hair is a bit of a mess but we didn't give him time to get it done. Bwana Gordon Biscoe anticipating the next crisis which never came. Oasis A unique photo this - Ken Stimpson (Senior Belgrave 'Sponger') hard at work with his faithful assistant Ron 'Tinker' Langheim. Family Group Extreme left, the suave (a lady's choice not mine) Bill Lucas - Referee. Next to him is 'The Thin Man' Charlie Jones, and looking like the benevolent Colonel Saunders of Kentucky Fried Chicken is Harry Shields (minus the goatee. Just visible the scholarly Gordon Doubleday. * EDITORS NOTE. Isn't this a stupid page -Belgrave is for strong limbed,healthy minded lads-I'll check on this contributor and see if he's fully paid up. items.s: JUNE 3rd 1973 - MANCHESTER - MAXOL MARATHON. Short report of three Belgrave runners finishing the Maxol Marathon in Manchester. JUNE 3rd 1973 - MANCHESTER - MAXOL MARATHON. Three competitors from Belgrave took part in this international studded Marathon which started in St. Peter's Square and finished at Manchester United's football ground.
