items.label: June 1974
items.sum: Profile of sprinter-hurdler and rock-music writer and broadcaster Charlie Gillett, from his Teesside youth and Cambridge running to joining Belgrave via Battersea Park, his 'Honky Tonk' radio programme and his views on athletics.
items.s: SPOTLIGHT on .......... CHARLIE GILLETT Profile of sprinter-hurdler and rock-music writer and broadcaster Charlie Gillett, from his Teesside youth and Cambridge running to joining Belgrave via Battersea Park, his 'Honky Tonk' radio programme and his views on athletics. SPOTLIGHT on .......... CHARLIE GILLETT "Come on Charlie. Come on. Come on." The cries of encouragement from Charlie Gillett's wife Buffy and children Suzy, Jody and Ivan, have become a regular feature at our league meetings. And more often than not that encouragement is rewarded as Charlie powers round the 200 metre bend and notches up another five points for Belgrave Harriers. To the track and field team he needs no introduction, and those with an interest in rock music will certainly have heard of the name of Charlie Gillett before now. Charlie was born in Lancashire on 20th February 1942 but grew up in the town of Stockton-on-Tees in Durham. His only recollections of his schooldays at Grangefield Grammar School involve athletics. As a youngster he became a member of Billingham Synthonia AC who numbered amongst their members the famous names of Howard Payne and J.H.Metcalf. Most of his races in those days were handicap events over any distance from 100 yards to 1 mile and these races used to attract athletes of all standards. You might well have found Ron Hill standing on the scratch mark. In fact after the Rome Olympics the New Zealanders Peter Snell and Murray Halberg toured Britain and whilst up in the North East they also toed the line with athletes from the Durham area. In 1961 Charlie left Teesside to go up to Cambridge University and his immediate aim was to get into one of the sports teams - not necessarily athletics, for he was prepared to tackle cross-country, rugby, anything. He ran for the University team of Alverstone AC, trying to find the weakest point of their track team so that he could lever his way in. Each week before a fixture, the names of those selected would be posted in the window of a local sports shop and on one occasion as Charlie eagerly scanned the list he picked out his own name - as second string quarter-mile hurdler. He immediately made his mark by running that race in 59.8, anyone who could beat one minute being classified as "a born hurdler". His ambition now was to beat 50 seconds for the quarter-mile on the flat, after all, he had clocked around 51 seconds as a 17 year old. Training long and hard his times crept down but that barrier just would not be broken. Every week he ran fifty-point-something and one afternoon he even raced three times over one lap only to have the watches stop at 50.2 - 50.6 on each occasion. 1964 was a good year for Charlie. He won the British Universities 440 yard championship in ..... yes, fifty-point-something-else, and by now he had met Buffy and they moved to Bristol. His training slackened off but he was selected to run for the Northern Counties A.A.A. in a relay and it was something of a revelation to find that his relay split was 49.8. And then in an N.C.A.A.A. match against the American Brigham Young University he reached his goal with 49.5. He was astounded, for on virtually no training he had attained what had hitherto seemed impossible. His outlook on athletics immediately changed - athletics is for enjoyment. Now he was off to the United States of America. He had toured there a couple of years previously, and after visiting places like New Orleans and El Paso his already keen interest in music was intensified. At Teachers College Columbia in New York his athletics came to a stop. "How anyone ever does any sport in New York I don't know. There just seem to be no facilities what so ever." Returning to London in 1966, he took up a teaching post at Kingsway College for Further Education. He found it tough going and eventually left this career in 1969. About this time Penguin Education asked him to contribute towards a book about sport entitled "All In The Game", and whilst driving across Chelsea Bridge he had noticed a running track down between the trees. He had vowed to call in there when he had a little more time so why not combine the writing with a return to running as well? A little jogging at Battersea Park track and the next step was to approach a by-stander and enquire," Do you know of a club round here?". Well, as the by-stander was Bob Taylor the reply was obvious, and after a three year lay off, Charlie was back on the track. His first event was the long hurdle race again in the Cecil Fry Trophy Meeting at Ilford. He reflects, "I was running quite contentedly around the final turn when four or five guys I'd never seen before suddenly started shouting and urging me on. Wow! These people take it seriously, I thought, so I finished as hard as I could." His time was 55.6 and by the end of the season he was down to 54.4, a personal best and Club Record. Charlie is deeply involved in writing for the music papers and broadcasting, and his book "Sounds of the City", a history of music since the 1950's was put out by Sphere Publications in 1970. Occasionally he appears continued on page 33. Right: Charlie sets out on another 200m. His best times are 200m/22.6, 400m/49.5, 400mH/54.4. SPOTLIGHT ON CHARLIE GILLETT continued from page 21 on "chat-shows" on TV, for whenever there is anything to be said about contemporary music, Charlie Gillett is the man to say it. His programme "Honky Tonk" on Radio London on Sundays at 12 noon has been on the air for over two years now and is a favourite with those who love good rock music. The thing Charlie likes most about athletics is the competitiveness. He likes nothing better than to get out on the track and run as hard as he can. Fitness is really just an incidental. What does bother him is the generally poor presentation of the sport. He comments, "Buffy isn't really interested in sport but she likes to come to an athletics meeting and enjoys it for it's variety of events. There must be many more people who would become interested if only it could be put over to them in the first place." Belgrave Harriers he regards as a pretty good set-up which is efficiently run, and he particularly appreciates the advice given by Frank Simmons during Sunday morning sessions (before he has to dash off to the studio and "Honky Tonk" that is). One weakness though, he feels, is the fact that we are an all male club. As he says, "It's nice to see that some people take along their girl friends and wives to watch the meetings but it could be better still with a ladies section." items.s: It's North again in '5¾' Report, result and photo of the club 5¾-mile handicap road race at Wimbledon on 16 March 1974, won by Gerry North, with Michael Manning taking the handicap prize. ROAD RUNNING It's North again in '5¾' MARCH 16th 1974 - WIMBLEDON. The turn-out for this race was a little bit healthier than for some of our Cross Country Championships this year although still below those we have had in former years. "I'm only just getting fit so I'm not taking it seriously", but Gerry North never could resist a challenge and once again, after running the best part of the race with the leading group, turned it on at the end to grab the verdict from Lionel and Laurie. John Stow pleased himself and the selectors for the Southern Relay with a very fine run after his gradual return to form in the latter part of the cross country season. It was also good to see Danny Wiseman back from wherever it is he disappears to in the winter. It's a pity we don't have his talent around more often on the country and road. Junior, Simon Holmes, got up into the respectable half of the field and Michael Manning, a youth, brought comfort to those of us looking for some new Belgrave talent with a splendid first time run in this event. Michael earned himself the handicap prize and the recognition of being a must in our future teams. + short course. Handicap:- 1. M.Manning 26:18; 2. R.Dixon 27:04; 3. L.Mann 27:11. INTERNATIONAL VETS' 10km On Sunday May 19th in Paris, a 10,000m road race for Veterans was held as a curtain raiser to the World Veterans Marathon. A team of Bels made the trip but the race turned out to be a bit of a fiasco when half the field went off course and took a short cut. Clive Shippen, running in 18th place before the disaster, found himself 92nd at the finish, although by the same token Fred Paget did come up to 39th. Only the first five runners of the original leaders managed to get back to the front, amongst them Laurie O'Hara who was only narrowly defeated. Belgrave did not appear in the official result but after unofficial calculations placed 3rd behind German and French teams. 1. A.Ida (WG) 38:15; 2. L.O'Hara (BELGRAVE) 38:19; 3. items.s: Canterbury '6' Report and result of the Canterbury 6 on 20 April 1974, where Gerry North was third and Belgrave lost the team race to Invicta by one point. Canterbury '6' APRIL 20th 1974 A departure from our normal routine at this time of the year, it was decided to run this one to give some of the team competition between our own 12 stage relay and the National. As it was, it turned out to be a very pleasant afternoon with Belgrave getting back amongst the 'pots' after the recent lean spell. The course was ideal with only a small amount of traffic in the early stages. The rest of the race was run in quiet country lanes and the service roads of an orchard in full blossom. Whilst in the terms of a well-known soap advert, one could hardly call a bunch of steaming runners "beauty cradled in fragrance" it made the suffering that much more pleasant. A return to form Gerry North was only just held off at the end by a younger element from Invicta, a club to be reckoned with next year when some of their new signings become first claim. Trevor Hart, also back in form, ran himself into a long stage for the National Relay and Pat O'Connor did a typical "run through" at the end. With Tony Fairclough suffering from a heavy cold and joining the supporters, it was left to a still far from fit Bill Kerr, straight from a decorating session at home and still with paint in his hair, to complete our scoring team. He was rewarded with his share in the 'pots'. As the results show the team places were very close and in spite of two recounts, demanded by the captain and team manager respectively, we still had to be content with second place to Invicta by one point. 1. items.s: NATIONAL ROAD RELAY Report and Belgrave leg times from the National Road Relay at Sutton Coldfield on 27 April 1974, where an under-strength Belgrave finished 17th. NATIONAL ROAD RELAY APRIL 27th 1974 - SUTTON COLDFIELD In recent years Sutton Coldfield's reputation has done little to commend it to our hearts and this year was no exception. It did nothing for our health! nothing for our runners! and nothing for our prestige! After a pleasant drive up by car, the weather broke and the start coincided with the downpour which we have now come to expect. This seemed to set the seal in the race as far as any Southern club was concerned. Any ideas they may have had of breaking the Midland stranglehold on this race were soon washed away, as the results show. It is true we were not at full strength, missing Laurie O'Hara, due to work and domestic commitments, and John Bicourt who was in South Africa. Unfortunately, Pat O'Connor and Bill Weller were both suffering with minor ailments which caused them to run below form but, having made due allowance for all these reasons, we were still some minutes behind the leaders although everyone tried their best. It is probably best summed up by a comment made at the time - "We are not just up against good club competition, with the likes of Dave Black (Smallheath H.) and Brendan Foster (Gateshead) around it's world class competition". This, of course, once again highlights our need for good new blood in the team, but on a brighter note, it was great to see Peter Carton back in the team (which I hope will now be permanent) and showing something like a return to form with our second fastest short leg of the day. items.label: June 1974
items.h: Bill Weller Leads Belrave To Victory
items.sum: Report and result of the Chichester to Portsmouth 16-mile road race on 11 May 1974, won by Bill Weller as Belgrave took a third successive team victory.
items.s: Bill Weller Leads Belrave To Victory Report and result of the Chichester to Portsmouth 16-mile road race on 11 May 1974, won by Bill Weller as Belgrave took a third successive team victory. Bill Weller Leads Belrave To Victory MAY 11th 1974 - CHICHESTER TO PORTSMOUTH 16m ROAD RACE One of the few point to point races left, this has long been an established fixture in the Belgrave calendar. This turned out to be our third successive team victory, only this year we went one stage further in providing the individual winner also, namely, Bill Weller. Although the start was somewhat delayed by the non-appearance of the Mayor of Chichester, the official starter, once under way the field lost no time in settling down as they set out for Portsmouth in spring sunshine and a headwind. After the first mile a leading bunch of about seven had already formed, including Bill Weller, Lionel Mann and Trevor Hart with Pat O'Connor showing signs of becoming detached. At eight miles, Bill and Lionel had drawn away from the rest of the field by some 30 to 40 yards but with Trevor in close attendance with the chasing group. Around 12 miles Bill was out on his own and Lionel, having been caught, was tucked in behind Dugdale of T.V.H., Trevor was having a private battle with Chris Haines of Blackheath some 30 seconds behind whilst Pat was having a similar struggle with Ian Wilson, also Blackheath, some distance further back. Thus the procession entered Portsmouth with Bill coming home a clear winner, Lionel just unable to regain second place, and Trevor in spite of some anxious queries along the route as to "where's Pat! - where's Pat!" completing our scoring team. Pat, in spite of a bout of sickness near the end, still managed to get himself into the individual prizes, which was very convenient, as Bill's mother, delighted at his success after several attempts, had not only provided some tremendous vocal support for the team along the road, but I think was about to take up a collection on Pat's behalf as she didn't like to think of him being left out! Eddie Thorp provided another good 'back up' run, as he has done so many times for us this year, whilst George Piddington scored a convincing victory over John Baker.- There's no need to be too smug about this though George, for if only we could convince John to stick to the shorter distances, which we all know he's better at, then you'd have problems - (Still, with 1:54:50 for 16 miles you must have them now, I should think! ) 1. items.label: June 1974
items.h: THE SAGA OF TEN THOUSAND MUTTERS
items.sum: Humorous first-person account by 'Thumper', a cyclist-turned-runner, of preparing for and running a 10,000 metres at Battersea Park track on 22 May 1974 despite a sore foot.
items.s: THE SAGA OF TEN THOUSAND MUTTERS Humorous first-person account by 'Thumper', a cyclist-turned-runner, of preparing for and running a 10,000 metres at Battersea Park track on 22 May 1974 despite a sore foot. THE SAGA OF TEN THOUSAND MUTTERS There is an old Polish proverb that goes "Never tell the devil too much of your mind", so when I just happened to mention up at the Hall that I was going to have a go in the 10,000 metres, a deathly hush fell about, heads turned and eyeballs cracked round in their sockets. I ventured to add that "10,000 metres was just a nice round number and I wanted to get a time", and I was with friends again. As you all know, us cyclists know how to train hard and race hard, so I worked out a training schedule and a diet sheet, and stepped up my evening runs on the Embankment. On Saturday afternoons I ran my utmost and I even did a few press-ups before "brekkers". But Easter was now upon us and we were away on our bikes, touring the West Country. Up hill and down dale, in all we covered about 300 miles but no running for about three weeks. So straight into running again and on one of the evening five mile runs on the Embankment my left foot started to hurt on the instep. Now us cyclists never get this sort of trouble so I got all the advice I could and bathed it in hot water, cold water, hot water, cold water, rubbed it, strapped it, massaged it, cussed it, cursed it, kicked it, spat on it and after all this careful treatment it slowly got better. I was way behind with my training and I missed the 'Ten' in the Park which I was going to use as a training run. Anyway I placed sponge rubber in my shoes and after a little rest started running again but very gently and I figured about 40 minutes for this 30 minute event as I wanted to run inside my limit. So on the evening of 22nd May we were at Battersea Park track warming up. We lined up and were away. A few laps and the race settled down into a pattern, the fast runners in front and the not so fast behind (good thinking). After a while my mind settled down too .... ten laps gone... I think I'll go rock climbing for my holidays ... those power station chimnies are straight .... Laurie's going well .. must fill the scooter tomorrow .... Linda Manning is quite nice looking .... pity Charlie is such a good runner .... a real good dinner tonight ... Laurie's going well, and it was five laps to go. I started to make my move but my left foot was beginning to hurt again and soon it was all over. I enjoyed the experience if enjoyed is the right word. A year ago I did not even run. So after a couple of gulps of power station fumes I was trotting round, working out my toxins. Now the moral of this little story is, "always take note of Polish proverbs", and as a footnote, the Thumper Fan Club may be interested to know that at the time of writing my left foot is better but both legs ache like hell! THUMPER Thumper THUMPER pen-name; cyclist who took up running a year earlier; ran 10,000m at Battersea Park 22 May 1974 Laurie Laurie running well in the 10,000m Linda Manning Linda Manning Charlie Charlie Embankment West Country Battersea Park

items.s: YOUNG ATHLETES Round-up of the young athletes' section, highlighting new club marks in the field events by Peter Crosbie, Albert Ryan, Mark Shippen, Ivan Beaumont and the shot putters. YOUNG ATHLETES Great things are happening amongst the younger element in the Club. In each age group records are being broken and several of our youthful members are on the verge of joining Martin Scott, a Junior, in representing Belgrave in full blooded Senior competition. Particularly pleasing is the fact that so many of these new marks are being set on the field, an area which has been neglected in the past. Peter Crosbie, for example, launched the Javelin out to 53.87m in a meeting at Camberley. This broke the Youths Club record set 17 years ago and he has subsequently sent the Senior implement over 49 metres. Albert Ryan is another with a powerful arm action, promising great things with the Discus. Down in the Boys section there is an even greater state of flux. Whilst Mark Shippen has been setting a worthy Club best in the Pole Vault, at a height which must be considered for Youth and Junior records as well, Ivan Beaumont has been pushing out the Triple Jump 'frontier'. The results of the Friday night weight sessions have made a dramatic impression in the Shot where many lads have virtually doubled their last year's performance, with Martin Munro leading the field. David Warren is the 'Samson' of the group. There can't be many boys of twelve years old who can do six military presses with a 60lb bar. items.s: The Night Of The Gladiators Bill Couzens on the Boys' Friday-night weight and circuit training sessions at Belgrave Hall, with the best circuit-training times. The Night Of The Gladiators Belgrave Hall can rest in peace at least until September when "they" are back. Yes, the pulling, heaving, pushing, gasping, struggling, gritting of teeth, Friday night training for Boys is over for the summer break. Some twelve to fifteen boys have attended these sessions continuously for five months and from learning to lift the weights correctly, they have progressed rapidly in technique and strength. The weight training is followed by circuit training where four exercises finishing with a short sprint are carried out one after the other against the stopwatch, and the fastest times of the evening are keenly sought after. Finally hand-ball gives a lighter side to the evening although not a game for the faint hearted, especially the referee. items.sum: Profile of 14-year-old Michael David Bailey of Vauxhall, a Boys sprinter and middle-distance runner coached by Frank Simmons with ambitions in the steeplechase.
items.s: MEET DAVID BAILEY Profile of 14-year-old Michael David Bailey of Vauxhall, a Boys sprinter and middle-distance runner coached by Frank Simmons with ambitions in the steeplechase. MEET DAVID BAILEY Michael David Bailey favours athletics to the exclusion of all other sports. He ran well in his school races last summer and went on to represent Kennington School in the district championships over 1500 metres. David, as he prefers to be called, then heard about Belgrave Harriers from a friend and lost no time in turning up at Battersea Park one Sunday morning. This rangy youngster from Vauxhall has not looked back since. Several times throughout the winter he performed well over the 'country' and now that the track season is with us again and with the careful guidance of coach Frank Simmons, he has revealed a turn of speed in the sprints that has already caught a few Seniors unawares in training sessions. As he is now 14 years of age this will be his last season in the Boys age group and he hopes to do well in the Surrey Championships at Motspur Park where he has entered the 80 metre hurdles, 200 metres and 400 metres. His immediate aim is to improve on his best 200 metres (26.8) and 1500 metres (5:00) and to this end he trains three times a week with the occasional extra run in the early morning. But it is the steeplechase that figures in David's long term plans, and if the enthusiasm and potential he has already shown are anything to go by, he will be making his presence felt in this event in a few years time. items.sum: Report and Belgrave results from the Surrey County A.A.A. Championships at Motspur Park in May 1974, with county titles for Martin Scott (Junior long jump), Peter Crosbie (Youth javelin) and Mark Shippen (Senior Boys pole vault).
items.s: Three Surrey Champions Report and Belgrave results from the Surrey County A.A.A. Championships at Motspur Park in May 1974, with county titles for Martin Scott (Junior long jump), Peter Crosbie (Youth javelin) and Mark Shippen (Senior Boys pole vault). Three Surrey Champions MAY 14th/16th/18th 1974 - MOTSPUR PARK - SURREY COUNTY A.A.A. CHAMPS. This was one of our most successful Surrey Championships for a long time, with a Champion from Belgrave in each of the age groups. Peter Crosbie retained his Youth Javelin title although he was a little disappointed with the distance and Albert Ryan excelled with 2nd place in the Discus. In the youngest group, the Senior Boys, it was really pleasing to watch Mark Shippen tackle the Pole Vault with a maturity beyond his thirteen years. He survived early difficulties at the lower heights and after getting the uprights moved back a few inches went on to exceed his best training height (this was his first competition) by some 50cm. His winning vault of 2.65m would not disgrace any Southern League Senior! Mark will still be eligible for the same age group next year. continued on following page .... SURREY A.A.A. CHAMPIONSHIPS continued .. Ivan Beaumont put in some good jumping and his 11.15m in the Triple Jump beats the Club Senior Boys record set 13 years ago. Over 400m, David Bailey in only his third attempt at the distance including the heats, set up a worthy personal best of 58.6 and was unlucky not to get amongst the medals, coming through strongly in the finishing straight. Martin Scott's performance in the Long Jump was remarkable. His second leap carried him 7.13m beyond the take-off board - a personal best, Junior Club record and 12cm better than the previous County Championship best performance. Two jumps later he improved again to 7.17m, a distance which puts him 8th in the United Kingdom so far this year. His 49.7 for 2nd place in the 400m final seemed quite commonplace after that, inside the old County record as it was. It is obvious that Steve White's Junior Club mark of 49.4 is in danger. items.label: June 1974
items.sum: Reprint from Runners World, with a short club introduction, profiling Belgrave member Tony Brien's running career and his NAIA cross-country title at Marymount College, Kansas.
items.s: AN IRISHMAN IN KANSAS Reprint from Runners World, with a short club introduction, profiling Belgrave member Tony Brien's running career and his NAIA cross-country title at Marymount College, Kansas. Stories of wonderful times by Tony Brien have been filtering through from the United States. Times like 13:29 for 3 miles followed half an hour later by 8:29 for 2 miles in a relay, both races indoors on the boards. The following article appeared in "Runners World" in May and gives some idea of what our member at Marymount College has been up to. AN IRISHMAN IN KANSAS by Skip Olsen If you've heard of Marymount College it has probably been because of Tony Brien. Marymount is in Salina, Kansas, and has an enrollment of about 600. Tony Brien is from Ireland. He is the NAIA cross-country and indoor two-mile champion, but perhaps his biggest accomplishment since coming to the United States was his fourth place in the AAU cross-country. When Brien decided to come here, he didn't know of Marymount himself. Two friends from Ireland, brothers Phil and Liam Ryan, had persuaded Tony to join them at Cal Poly in Pomona. Brien arrived only to find the school had filled its quota of foreign students. The Ryans contacted Tom Rupp, a former Poly coach who had gone to Marymount. Rupp said sure, send him along. How often does a school of 600 in Kansas come across an almost-Olympian? At 18, Brien had been good enough to make the Irish team for the international cross-country championships. His competitive running had only started when he was 17, having evolved from his soccer playing. The soccer team ran 6 - 8 miles three days a week at a track club's facilities. The club's coach talked Tony into running for its youth team, and his running career blossomed quickly after that. It wasn't without hitches, however. "Due to severe attacks of tendinitis and shin splints," Brien says, "I have never been able to train continuously for a long period of time." He didn't have another injury-free period until almost three years after he ran the cross-country international. "In the spring of 1972, I remained free of injury long enough to train for the Olympic trials in the marathon. I ran twice a day for four months (99% LSD*) and built my mileage up to 180 a week. I finished fourth in 2:18:45 (my previous best was 2:46). The first three went to Munich." At the time, Brien was working as an air traffic controller in the British Air Force, and he says,"the shift work was not conducive to hard training. So when I was offered an athletic scholarship in the States I jumped at the chance to be able to train harder plus gaining the benefits of travel and a college education." He tried to train harder when he got to Kansas in late 1972, but the tendon problems cropped up again. Tony placed 20th in the NAIA cross-country race as a freshman. Last track season, he began to come around. He ran a 29:18 six-mile at the Kansas Relays. The same weekend he did 2:26 in the meet's marathon. A week later he had a 2:27 marathon at the Drake Relays. Again he was having tendon troubles - hardly a surprise considering the heavy schedule of races. (Brien himself says he prefers only to run a hard race every two months or so, with the others being easier and used as training sessions.) By the fall, 22-year-old Tony was back in the best form of his life. He won all but three races, losing only to Australian Garry Bentley (NCAA College Division champion from South Dakota State), Kenyan Mike Boit, and US Olympians Frank Shorter, Doug Brown and Jeff Galloway - these three in the AAU. Brien had lost to Boit by 15 seconds in an early season race. They met again at the NAIA, this time on Marymount's home course in Salina. Tony says he was hoping to place "in the top three". But after the first mile, he felt he could win. That first mile was run in 4:16! Boit ended up falling after two of the five miles and coming in 11th. The fall may or may not have changed the outcome. At any rate, a tailwind of 30 miles per hour pushed Tony across the line a comfortable winner in a course record time of 23:42. * LSD for the uninitiated means Long, Steady, Distance work. items.sum: Look-back column recalling Alan Sexton's 1949 junior sprint titles and, from 1934, Arthur Penny's Empire Games six miles win and the Club Championships at Battersea Park.
items.s: from the 'belgravian' 25 years ago Look-back column recalling Alan Sexton's 1949 junior sprint titles and, from 1934, Arthur Penny's Empire Games six miles win and the Club Championships at Battersea Park. from the 'belgravian' 25 years ago The Senior and Junior Surrey County Championships, with one or two exceptions, were held at Motspur Park on June 4th 1949 when the Club did quite well and the result of the Club's coaching methods was clearly seen. Alan Sexton performed a double in winning the 100 and 220 yards and in the latter event he set up a new county record of 22.7 secs. S.C.A.A.A. Junior Championships at Cambridge - July 9th. Sexton won his heat in 24.1; Tebbutt won his heat in 24.6; Picton, Marshall and Rae were each second in their heats. Sexton beat Marshall in the second round in 23.6; Picton won his second round in 23.9. Final: 1. A.Sexton 23.0 4 x 110 yards relay 1. Belgrave 43.5 (Sexton, Marshall, Tebbutt, Rae). A.A.A. Junior Championships at Birmingham - July 29th. In the 220 yards Alan Sexton won his heat in 22.8 secs. and the final in 22.1 secs., a new junior record. and 40 years ago There is only one way to commence this issue of our Journal ( July - August 1934 ) and that is to extend our heartiest congratulations to A.W. Penny upon his magnificent win for England in the Six Miles event at the Empire Games. It is no exaggeration to say that every one of us shares in the pleasure which Arthur undoubtedly feels, and it is our very sincere hope that this coming Cross Country season will find him National and International Cross Country Champion....... ........ Fine weather favoured the Club Championships held at Battersea Park on August 11th, and a number of sound performances were witnessed, even if there was nothing of a really exceptional character. The mile was looked upon as one of the "star" events of the afternoon,. and a good field including our Empire Champion, Arthur Penny, lined up for the start. Joe Flower led the field for a lap at a pace which suggested he had no intention of completing the distance - a suggestion which, of course, was soon confirmed. This left Allum, Shaw and Ring together. In the closing stages, last year's race was repeated, Allum again winning by a small margin from Shaw. Ring continued his wonderfully improved running by taking the third medal, and Penny finished fourth. Fifteen walkers contested the 2 miles championship, and from the starting shot Brown led, with Harley on his heels for 200 yards. Joe King the Sussex Champion, then came into second position and so the race finished, with Don Brown never in any danger of being caught, although the time was fully three-quarters of a minute slower than his best. E.S.Stimpson, 18½ years of age, showed style and ability in taking the 880 yards handicap. He should develop into a Club Champion, with maturer years. items.s: Club Honours Board Letter from Clive Shippen appealing for donations towards a Club Honours Board of Senior Championship successes, carrying a plaque in memory of Alf Harley. Dear Belgravian, Following A.A.Harley's untimely death last year your Committee considered various proposals for commemmorating the unique service rendered to the Club by this fine Belgravian. It was eventually decided that a Club Honours Board featuring Senior Championship successes was not only something that a club of our stature merited anyway, but it would be particularly appropriate for carrying a plaque in memory of Alf. who took such an interest in the history of our club and its many team successes. During Alf Harley's 46 years of membership he was twice President, Honorary Secretary for 26 years, Editor for 9 years and Walking Secretary for 10 years, and thousands of Belgravians enjoyed the benefits of his selfless devotion to the Club. There are many, I am sure, who would wish to be associated with this project by contributing to the cost of the board (approximately £270). The fund has already been launched by the Past Presidents, Vice-Presidents and Life Members of the Club but its success depends also on General membership. Subscribers will be notified of the unveiling date and acknowledged in the December "Belgravian". Your donation, however small, will be gratefully received by:- Clive Shippen (Past President) 24, Fryston Avenue, Coulsdon, Surrey. Alf Harley A.A.Harley died 1973; 46 years a member, twice President, Honorary Secretary 26 years, Editor 9 years, Walking Secretary 10 years A.A.Harley Alf. items.label: September 1974
items.sum: Editorial on the new all-weather jumping surfaces at Battersea Park, the lack of facilities in south-west London, and athletics as a sport open to anyone.
items.s: COMMENT Editorial on the new all-weather jumping surfaces at Battersea Park, the lack of facilities in south-west London, and athletics as a sport open to anyone. At last Battersea Park athletic track can boast some all-weather surfacing. Well, on the jumping areas at least. The long jump run-up was put down by Dunlop and the high jump area has been laid with a substance developed in the United States and completely new to this country. In the few weeks that these areas have been in use there has already been a noticeable increase in the standard of jumping and in the number of those who wish to jump at Battersea track. There appear to be no plans afoot to resurface the entire track or to enhance the pole vault and throwing areas. Apparently there is also a problem in safely housing the high jump landing bed, for at the present the only vandal proof store is on the other side of the Park, and this means that it is not always available for use. All this is a great pity because the whole south-western sector of London is very much a barren wasteland as far as the athlete is concerned. He or she must travel to West London Stadium or the Crystal Palace to use the most modern athletic facilities. On the credit side, the groundsman at Battersea has intimated that during the winter months when he is less busy he will cut down the remains of the old pole vault 'mound'(at present inhabited by a nest of rats), so that at least that site will be ready should any developments arise. On a slightly different tack, a TV programme some weeks ago highlighted the problems faced by youngsters in south-west London. The main point made was that there is nothing for them to do and nowhere for them to go, not even for a kick-about with a football. The fact that a large park exists in Battersea with football pitches, tennis courts and an athletic track, not to mention a fun-fair, riverside embankment and gardens, seemed to be totally ignored by the programme. However, it must be admitted that these amenities are not available on winter evenings, and if a scheme could be got off the ground to develop a sports centre that would be open all year round in all weathers, a great deal would have been done to alleviate the problem. It would certainly also give athletics the chance to exploit an area of London that is virtually untapped. Our sport has a great advantage over others in that it can be practised by almost anyone who has the determination to get up and have a go. Bear in mind the incredible performance of the man at our league meeting at Exeter who, with only one leg, won the high jump with a leap of 6'0"! Whatever one's sex or shape or size, there is an athletic event to be tackled and even if one is never likely to become a world-beater there is the pleasure of measuring improvements, inch by inch and second by second. Given the facilities athletics can be a real glamour sport, attracting many more than the comparative few who now take part. Battersea Park West London Stadium Crystal Palace Exeter

items.label: September 1974
items.sum: Club gossip column: Ted Stimpson's operation and career, Richard Moody's naval tour, Wilf Wesch judging at Hamburg, the death of Hall caretaker Tom Savage, Leo Coy's ranking lists, John Martin leaving the AAA Championships, births in club families, and short notes on Gordon Biscoe, Dennis McKeown, Paul Whitby, Henry Martin, Paul Williamson and Lionel Mann's Civil Service Marathon win.
items.s: grapevine Club gossip column: Ted Stimpson's operation and career, Richard Moody's naval tour, Wilf Wesch judging at Hamburg, the death of Hall caretaker Tom Savage, Leo Coy's ranking lists, John Martin leaving the AAA Championships, births in club families, and short notes on Gordon Biscoe, Dennis McKeown, Paul Whitby, Henry Martin, Paul Williamson and Lionel Mann's Civil Service Marathon win. • TED STIMPSON recently underwent an operation in Wimbledon Hospital and is now out and about again. He was pleased to see a number of Belgravians who visited him during his short stay in hospital. Ted, a Past-President, is one of those who do a great deal for us, lending a hand at track, country and road fixtures. He also plays a large part on our social side and for many years has organised the Club's Annual Dinner - an event which few, if any, clubs can equal. In 1939 he led our cross-country team home in the "National" at Manchester to score our second team win (the first was in 1935), and as fourth man home gained an international vest. After war service he gained another E.C.C.U. winning team medal at Sheffield in 1948. Over recent years he has enjoyed a weekly spin over the Common, and is a regular attender at Committee meetings; he also represents us on the Middlesex County A.A.A. Committee. • RICHARD MOODY, now a Surgeon Lieutenant in the Royal Navy, is off on an enviable tour of duty this winter. He sails from Plymouth on September 17th on board HMS Achilles, a Leander Class frigate, as Medical Officer for a group of ships. Ports of call will be Gibralta - where he hopes to take part in the race to the top of the rock, Cape Town, Mombasa, Mauritius - for Christmas, and Singapore. Richard will be back in the UK next summer. • We had a representative at the International Walks at Hamburg in May, the Chief Judge was our Vice-President and Olympic representative WILF WESCH. • Many years ago when Belgrave Hall was St. John's Hall it was looked after by a Mr. and Mrs. SAVAGE. With the passing of time the Hall became ours, the dear old couple passed on and the good work was carried on for a number of years by their son TOM. We are sorry to learn that Tom died recently in Wimbledon Hospital. For a good many years he cleaned up at the Hall and served us with refreshments, and we mourn the passing of an old friend. • LEO COY has taken over the job of recording the United Kingdom's Club Ranking lists for the National Union of Track Statisticians. Let us hope that the performances of Belgrave athletes will make his task that much more enjoyable. • The scene was the A.A.A. Championships. The world record holder and ex-world record holder were engaged in a seven-foot-plus duel in the high jump and three leading American pole vaulters were also in action. ".... Cheerio blokes, I'm going now...." JOHN MARTIN our field events captain was actually leaving right in the middle of such excitement. It has always been said that the call of true love is strong. Poor John must have it bad! • For two years now PETE SUTTON has been unable to run because of a chipped bone in his foot but it's nice to see him regularly at the Hall on a Sunday morning, keeping in touch even if he can't get out for a jog. • There seems to have been a population explosion in Belgrave circles recently. PETER and MARGARET HILLIAR and DON and JENNY MacLEAN are hearing the patter of tiny feet ... again. Spectating at the Club Championships was none other than our 800 metre record holder DAVE COCKS with two year old daughter ELIZABETH. Dave and his wife CHRIS (ex-Selsonia) are both well and have recently had another addition to their family - a son GRAHAM. PAM and JOHN DAVIS, another Selsonia Ladies AC/Belgrave partnership, are also doing their best to keep the Club stocked with thoroughbreds, and seven weeks after the arrival of another bouncing boy, Pam was out jogging again. • A few raised eyebrows were in evidence from visiting officials at the Club Championships when GORDON BISCOE regarded the new all-weather long jump run up and said with tongue in cheek, "Looks good. Should be alright when they get the cinders down on top of it!" • DENNIS McKEOWN has been away in Belgium for two months racing on his bike with some success. He looks forward to donning his running shoes again in the near future. • Hurdlers beware! PAUL WHITBY begins a post graduate physical education course at Madeley College this autumn. Hopes to be super-fit next season. • Making a welcome appearance at our last Battersea track meeting was the incredible HENRY MARTIN who has probably been a member of more athletic clubs than he has had training sessions. Now running in the colours of Hercules Wimbledon, his come-back run over 200 metres was his first race on the track after four years of injury problems. • PAUL WILLIAMSON is off to Norwich and East Anglia University where he will be studying history and art. • Congratulations to LIONEL MANN upon winning the Civil Service Marathon Championship held in conjunction with the Poly A.A.A./R.R.C.marathon. items.sum: The President, Charles Manning, thanks the many members and families who quietly help run the club, its Hall, bars, socials and fund-raising.
items.s: Consideration .... The President, Charles Manning, thanks the many members and families who quietly help run the club, its Hall, bars, socials and fund-raising. .... is probably the word I'm looking for - it's this that makes administration so much easier. It's when someone goes beyond the line of duty, often without being asked, to put themselves out to help our Club. I'm not referring to the Carters, Biscoes, Bakers and Couzens of our Club who frequently receive the accolades they deserve, but to the man often overshadowed. Someone like Pete Sutton who sweeps out the canteen and committee room, someone like Joe McDonald who at the hint of a suggestion is so eager to please, or Fred Paget washing up and running a bar. And talking of bars - Dennis MacManus, Jack Carter and Stuart Barrett - we couldn't have done without them. These are not just words, without them we could have put up the shutters as far as socials were concerned. Brian 'T' Gorman and his efforts have given heart to our training from the Hall. Colin Pearson, an active athlete, has rolled up his sleeves to the most foul but necessary cleaning work. Arthur Penstone, always busy - Bert Stroud with his wife and kids, whether it's in the canteen or standing on corners directing runners for four hours at a stretch and still smiling. To mention one lady makes others immediately spring to mind. Pat Mead, never an observer, always involved, the track people know how much and all who read this magazine owe her thanks. Evelyn Stimpson, mainspring in so many ventures, grafting away with needle and thread or paintbrushes or pottery, forever helpful and understanding. Margaret McMillan and her great efforts at the Bazaar - Sue Coy - Mary Crookes and Stephanie Langheim - have all pitched in with their positive contributions. Gwen Couzens and Bill's Mum at the Jumble Sales. My own Mum, not Yidisha but a continuous source of lucrative ideas and help. And Linda, my bossy daughter, who as I write is making papier mache piggy banks for the Merton Show - her involvement with tea making, distributing leaflets, selling programmes, running raffles, etc., is total. I thank you all - missed some? Of course. The bloke what never made a mistake never made anything. To those, please accept my apologies. And to you all, cited or not, thank you - thank you very much. CHAS. MANNING, President. Chas. Manning CHAS. items.sum: Profile of sprinter and jumper Steve White, who joined Belgrave in 1965, with his representative honours and an interview by Alan Mead about his training, motivation and views on Belgrave's future in the Southern and National Leagues.
items.s: SPOTLIGHT on .......... STEPHEN WHITE Profile of sprinter and jumper Steve White, who joined Belgrave in 1965, with his representative honours and an interview by Alan Mead about his training, motivation and views on Belgrave's future in the Southern and National Leagues. Steve White became a member of Belgrave Harriers as a 15 year old in 1965, introduced by Tony Brooks. Immediately, those connected with the track and field side could not help being impressed by the slim youngster who trained with purpose from the very beginning, who seemed to know exactly what he was about, and who exuded the calm confidence of a future champion. Nearly a decade later, Steve could be said to be the man at the heart of our team. It's not just that he nearly always wins for us, it's the way he does it with assurance and flowing style, perhaps three or four times during an afternoon. He lives at Oxford and in spite of the travelling involved, always turns out for the Club in league and cup matches. On one occasion this year he had gone down to Brighton for the weekend yet still visited Mayesbrook Park in East London to spearhead our team. Another time, representative honours had been gained by him but there was no easing up for the event as he staunchly carried the claret and gold for us just the day before. Representative honours include the A.A.A., Southern Counties A.A.A., Surrey A.A.A., Berks/Bucks/Northants/Oxon., and he gained a junior international vest in matches against France and West Germany in 1969. Steve was 3rd in the English Schools senior 200 metres in 1968, 2nd in the junior A.A.A. 200 metres championship in 1969 and a finalist in the senior A.A.A. 200 metres in 1973. He has sprinted faster than any other Belgravian and only John Mitchell has leapt further. Honours are not confined to the sports field, however. At Tulse Hill School he was Deputy Head Boy and has been President of Oxford University Athletic Club. The following questions were put to Steve recently by Alan Mead and give some insight to the motivation of this quiet, great Belgravian. Alan: What made you choose athletics as your main sport? Steve: I suppose I enjoyed the personal success of athletics. It was good to win at football of course but there it's a team success, athletics gave me a lot of personal confidence. Also, I preferred the loneliness of the training, it seemed more purposeful and there was a greater sense of progress than in the team games. This is not to say I spurned company, not that I didn't enjoy team games. It was just that if I was going to take something seriously then I had to devote all my self-centred attention to it; football etc., was an enjoyment, athletics became more fundamental. There was, moreover, the sheer aesthetic pleasure of running well and being fit. A: Are any other members of your family involved in sport? S: I think my father used to play football in the Army, otherwise not. A: How often did you train when you started running and jumping? S: I started at primary school when I was 9 but that didn't involve much training, I just ran when the district sports came along. I can remember going to Sunday morning training at Tooting Bec prior to the local cub pack's sports - we really were very keen. I didn't start training seriously until I was 14 - about 5 days a week. A: What other sports did you take part in at Tulse Hill School? S: Soccer, basketball, cricket for my first two years until athletics began to intrude. A: A basketball player I once encountered said you were known as "wonderboy" as you were a good all-rounder. S: It makes me sound like some "All American Boy" cartoon character. I hope nobody called me this, but I certainly was actively involved in three major sports, captain in two of them (athletics and basketball) and particularly successful in athletics, and my successes were well paraded by the school authorities. I suppose it did make me popular and it meant that I got to know a great many people whom I would never normally have spoken to, and they me. For a great many boys at Tulse Hill prowess at sport was more admirable than any other ability. A: Did you receive any coaching at school? S: I did receive the regular coaching from school masters until I had some success and showed some promise. I was then singled out for more privileged attention and given more detailed schedules and so on. Then, when I joined Belgrave, there was Dave Ansell who was one of the finest long jump coaches in the country. (I think Derek Cole and Alan Lerwill have missed him since he went North - we all owe a lot to Dave). Then in my fourth year at school, Dick Wyer arrived to teach P.E. and he has been friend and 'coach' ever since. A: Where did you train at that time? S: At school, where gymnasium and weights facilities were excellent, plenty of encouragement too; Brockwell Park and Herne Hill track. A: How much of your early success was due to sheer ability? S: I honestly don't know because I was training relatively seriously relatively early and therefore never permitted myself to rely for long on natural ability alone. However, I did win races at primary school, at district level and at holiday camps. I suppose actually that natural ability was important and also a contributory factor in my choice of athletics as my main sport. I've tended to be a bit philosophical in my answer to your first question - sheer natural ability was important. A: What ambitions did you have in those days? S: In the short run to win the English Schools (I'm still upset that I never did); to win a junior international vest; to pass my exams ('O' and 'A' levels) - this above all else. In the long run to win the Olympics, of course! and to go to University. A: What were your achievements in sport in your Tulse Hill days? S: Early on in soccer; in my second year we won the Ewell Trophy and London Grammar School Cup (we were the best team in London that year). I was playing for a Sunday club side which perennially won league and cup. Until I started to play in the 1st eleven, I honestly think the team I was playing in lost no more than 10 matches. That probably had little to do with me but it was marvellous to play in such successful teams. In basketball I played for London Schools. In athletics I won the London Schools Intermediate long jump in 1967, 3rd in the English Schools senior 200 metres 1968, 2nd A.A.A. junior 200 metres, junior internationals against France and West Germany 1969. A: When did you go up to Oxford and what were you reading? S: October 1970; Politics, Philosophy and Economics. SPOTLIGHT ON STEVE WHITE Continued.......... A: How did you make your mark in the athletics team? S: I actually went up to Oxford assuming I would have no trouble getting into the athletics team and quite honestly I didn't; the standards were not particularly high and anybody who had success at school was eagerly welcomed. A: When did you become President of Oxford University Athletic Club? S: In 1973 for academic year 1973-74. My term ended in May this year after the Varsity match. Julian Goater is the present President. I was Hon. Sec. in 1971-72 and have been on the committee in one way or another ever since. A: You graduated in 1973, how is your post graduate course going? S: Fairly laboriously at present. I spent much too much time being President of O.U.A.C. last year and now spend hours in the library catching up and trying to find a thread for a thesis. I must admit I'm looking forward to finishing and leaving the academic environment. A: What do you hope to do after this? S: "Something in the City". Actually I really don't know specifically, but probably something allied to my subject (Economics). Perhaps Government Economic Service or Bank of England. I do fancy working for the U.N. or something like that but they usually require experience in business or government first. I really don't relish the prospect of becoming an urban commuter with mortgages and gas bills. Perhaps I'll work for 'Shelter' or 'Child Poverty Action" - the irony of that would be that I probably couldn't afford to find accommodation myself. This might all sound a little flippant but I'm not too concerned about my future (I think my wife's more concerned!) and I'm confident I'll do something worthwhile and enjoyable. A: When did you meet your wife? S: I met Jean in 1968. We were married in 1972. A: How does Jean view your athletic career? S: With benign tolerance. A: What moments stand out in your athletics? S: My worst moment is being knocked out of the English Schools 200 metres in 1969 when I had the fastest time in the country to date and was favourite - I really wanted to win that. I was really pleased on beating Cambridge by a record margin this year, not because the Varsity Match is a prestigious match nowadays, not primarily because of anything I did personally, but because it was such a magnificent team performance and there was a real sense of club spirit. That was a wonderful reward for all the tribulations I experienced as President throughout the year. Other than this I felt totally elated to break 22 seconds for the first time and 24 feet and also 50 seconds for 400 metres. I've run abroad for Lambeth, Great Britain and O.U.A.C. and I've enjoyed every trip. A: Have you met many athletic "personalities"? S: David Hemery once in the showers at Crystal Palace. Alan Pascoe is a "good bloke". Both he and Hemery, I've noticed, are prepared to give encouragement to youngsters, to interrupt their own sessions to say a few words. I really admire such humility in such greatness. But I have met many people in athletics and quite honestly, whether they've been "personalities" or not hasn't really been significant. A: Do you prefer jumping or sprinting? S: It depends whether I am jumping or sprinting well. Though I do find it more difficult to train for jumping because of lack of company and coaching at Oxford; it's easier to get out and run. A: Have you realised your athletic ambitions? S: I do worry about improving and I do still want to obtain an international vest. But I'm not obsessed with this particular ambition. I will do all I can to achieve it but if I fail I will find satisfaction in the knowledge that I have tried rather than disappointment in failure. More important is to enjoy athletics here and now, and I do, so I have no reason to complain. Doing the O.U.A.C's President's job made me approach the sport from a new direction, and as I have said, creating a club spirit and helping the rest of the team gave me a great deal of enjoyment and satisfaction. I'm sure it is the most worthwhile thing I have done at Oxford. A: How long will you continue to compete? S: For as long as I enjoy it. I suspect that when I start work, it might be a case of for as long as I can find the time. A: Would you be satisfied with competing at a lower level? S: I often wonder whether my enjoyment of athletics derives from my success. I believe it might. In which case if I cease to be successful I shall cease to enjoy athletics and therefore pack it up. However, my criteria for success might change, I might regard myself as successful if I am fit at 30 and so continue to do athletics even though I am no longer winning. I hope I shall do some sport when I am older. I'm certainly not doing it for the glory and nothing else. It's 1969 and Steve White, fastest junior in Britain with 21.[illegible], wins the Southern Counties A.A.A. junior 200 m. in 21.8. Photo: Ron Linstead. SPOTLIGHT ON STEVE WHITE Continued.......... A: How often do you train and what type of training do you do? S: Six days per week, winter and summer. Weights three times per week in winter, twice per week in spring and once in summer. I get coaching/advice from Dick Wyer, otherwise I just work things out for myself. I train mainly at Iffley Road track and sports hall or on college playing fields. My sessions are very flexible and varied to avoid boredom. I usually try to concentrate on one particular aspect of technique per session, leg drive, arms or whatever. I do repetition work over 60, 70, 120, 150, 200, 300 metres and always try to keep the quality high, even in snow. This isn't easy but I prefer This approach to doing, say 10 x 300 metres with 30 seconds recovery in about 45 seconds. Anything above 38 seconds for a 300 metres is poor for me. I do a lot of supplementary work, stretching, hopping, bounding, weighted belts, etc. In fact, I spend one whole session a week doing this sort of thing in the winter. Weights: I mix pyramid work, in which I go for maximums (215lbs. clean, 210lbs. bench press, 600lbs squat), with light, fast repetitions in order to facilitate speed of contraction and avoid feeling cumbersome. In general I try to fulfil set tasks but never by strain and unnecessary pain. Relaxation is fundamental, enjoyment is absolutely essential. I couldn't become an athletic metronome. I like to think that what I am doing requires some thought and some grace. A: Do you play any other sport now? S: This year no. Last year I played football but at present athletics is my sole sport. A: What other interests do you have? S: Theatre, Literature, the papers, dinners with friends, weekends with friends, a few pints, my wife (not in that order'.). A: Do you have any regrets about being so involved in athletics? S: Believe it or not I've always taken pains to avoid being involved in athletics to the exclusion of all else. So athletics is just one, albeit important, of the things I do. I don't regret any part of my athletics career. It has enabled me to meet many people, it's given me self-confidence, self-control and so on, and of course I've enjoyed the glory and respect of others. A: What are your views on Belgrave Harriers? S: I think Belgrave's first priority must be to win the Southern League and gain promotion to the National League. This has become an increasingly difficult task and will continue to become more difficult. We shall, if we are not careful, become a club firmly entrenched in the Southern League with little hope of improvement. This will arise because good athletes, and promising athletes, will be attracted to the better competition they will find in the National League. The situation is therefore cumulative, the existing strong clubs will grow stronger and the provincial league clubs, competing with these National League teams in recruitment, will grow weaker until some equilibrium position is reached. The final result might be that clubs relegated from the National League will be too strong for provincial league clubs and therefore will be promoted back to the National League the following year; the population of National League clubs therefore remains fairly stable over a time. I wouldn't like to generalise too much in this respect. There are and will be provincial league clubs who will rise to National League standard and prosper. As examples of these we have Borough of Enfield, Essex Beagles, Metropolitan Police, Oxford City A.C., in the future perhaps Windsor, Slough and Eton and Haringey. But these clubs all have special characteristics not possessed by Belgrave: (i) a single readily identifiable area from which to recruit, very often with no competing clubs in the same area (Oxford City, Metropolitan Police, Windsor, Slough and Eton), (ii) a tartan track which has provided a focal point to the club, which is why I rate the prospects of Haringey and Windsor rather highly. Belgrave, on the other hand, has a catchment area which stretches over the whole of South London and competes for recruitment with many other South London clubs. Although Belgrave Hall provides some sort of focal point it benefits mainly cross country and road runners and anyway its attraction must be weakened by having club members so diversified geographically. This makes it difficult for a large percentage of the club to get to and train at the Hall at the same time. I would therefore include Belgrave (potentially, if not yet) with clubs like Herne Hill Harriers, South London Harriers, Surrey A.C., Queens Park Harriers, Hercules-Wimbledon. All these clubs hardly inspire hope for the future and appear, if anything, to be on the wane as far as competitive results are concerned. I am informed that Belgrave has the athletes - if only they would turn out'. - I have been told this since the Southern League was formed. Belgrave, I was assured, were still a great club, just wait till next year, and if only so many athletes weren't on holiday or in the army and posted elsewhere, or else just couldn't be bothered, we would win the Southern League easily. I think we are still deluding ourselves. In the last Belgravian we were congratulating ourselves for being the best club in Surrey. How can we honestly regard this as a success when we still haven't won the Southern League. And if we do regard this as a success then I think our standards are ashamedly low; how can we, in all conscience, encourage a promising youngster to join us when all we can offer is success in Surrey, surely if we are interested in his development we would rather prefer to divert him to Thames Valley Harriers or Croydon Harriers or Enfield where he would find better competition. I think that if we are still potentially National League calibre, all those holidaymakers and couldn't be bothered athletes should be pressed to turn out now, because if we wait we will not even have the expectation of good results, the current athlete will have retired and the good youngster will have gone elsewhere. But if the malaise is more fundamental, as it probably is, then we must look for more fundamental solutions. I would favour amalgamations. There are too many clubs in South London. Talent is diluted too thinly and consequently good athletes are condemned to Southern League competition indefinitely. I think that serious consideration should be given to a more rational athletics set-up in South London so that we can eliminate petty squabbles between clubs about who uses which track and who has prior claim on a local youngster. I appreciate that there will be serious opposition to such changes. Many of the South London clubs are the oldest in the country and have long and admired traditions. Also Belgrave Harriers has one of the finest social set ups of any athletic club with its dances and socials and club magazine. I recognise all this and would hate to see it jeopardised. Moreover, the Southern League isn't such a bad league. In some ways, it is preferable to the National League as you compete against different clubs each time out and the atmosphere is more relaxed. Again I accept this and have personally enjoyed the Southern League a great deal. However, unless there is some attempt to win the league and to get into the National League one of the most fundamental drives of athletics is denied - the will to win. If this is missing in Belgrave, and we don't want to get into the National League, then we might as well become a successful social club and forget about athletics. Finally, if we did have bigger clubs and a Belgrave team in the National League, it would still be possible by some adjustment to the existing rules, to run 'B' sides in the provincial leagues. Thus you have a club catering for all levels of ability and providing a means for the athlete who ceases to be good enough for the National League to continue with his athletics with the same club at a lower level. I am sorry for the length of this answer, but it really has been frustrating getting nowhere in the Southern League over the years; I'm afraid nothing less than winning or coming second will give us access to the National League. The alternative is not encouraging. It's 1969 and Steve White, fastest junior in Britain with 21.[illegible], wins the Southern Counties A.A.A. junior 200 m. in 21.8. items.sum: Road Running and Cross Country Secretary Gordon Biscoe regrets last season's results and low turn-outs and announces a new points competition for road and cross country members, with its scoring rules.
items.s: ROAD AND COUNTRY Road Running and Cross Country Secretary Gordon Biscoe regrets last season's results and low turn-outs and announces a new points competition for road and cross country members, with its scoring rules. As the records now show, our cross country and road performances last season were not very exciting to say the least. Second place in the Surrey C.C.Champs. and the performance in our own 12 stage road relay being probably our proudest boast. As has now been stated many times it is important that in the next few seasons we must find new talent to take over from some of our more 'ageing' members, either by developing them through our junior ranks and/or from recruiting new members. However, apart from our need for new stars what was perhaps more disappointing last season was the general low turn-out at all levels in just normal inter-club events as well as Club championships. Due, it appears, generally to apathy and the non-desire to travel to away matches in preference to counter attractions! In order to give a new look to some of our traditional fixtures and maybe inject a little incentive, a bit more club spirit and teamwork once again, it has been decided for the coming season to introduce a points competition This will cover a number of selected races which will be indicated in the forthcoming fixture list. The basis of this competition is not new and has, in a similar form, been run effectively by one of our Surrey rivals for some years. The rules of the competition are detailed below and it is intended that for this season (Sept - April) it will be treated as a pilot scheme and depending upon its success any modifications needed will be made for following years. The prize for this competition will be to the value of £10 and of the winners own choosing. Other prizes may be awarded as is felt necessary. It should be noted that this competition in no way affects handicap prizes or medals etc awarded for any individual Club championship. May I request that all cross country and road runners help to make this scheme a success but more than this, that in the coming season they will endeavour to make Belgrave a success, especially when selected for representative teams. (Special dispensation will be arranged for those gaining international representation!!) ROAD RUNNING AND CROSS COUNTRY POINTS COMPETITION. Points will be scored as follows: 1. In any designated inter-club match open to all members, a) the first 12 members to finish - 6 points. b) the next 12 members i.e. 13 - 24 - 5 points. c) the next 12 members i.e. 25 - 36 - 4 points. d) the remainder who complete the course - 3 points. 2. In any Club championship, a) members whose positions in the championship are within the first third of the total number of starters. - 5 points. b) members within the second third - 4 points. c) the remainder who complete the course - 3 points. 3. All members actually coming under starters orders in the races designated, irrespective of whether finishing or not, will score 1 point. 4. For acting as a recognised official, course marker or pointsman - 2 points. The competition is open to all junior and senior members, both first and second claim. In the case of road relays, points will be awarded as in (2) above except that times will be considered instead of positions. In the event of any dispute the decision of the Belgrave Committee will be final. GORDON BISCOE Road Running and Cross Country Secretary. items.h: WE WIN OUR OWN & SURREY 20 MILE ROAD RACE
items.sum: Report and results of the Belgrave Open 20 Mile Road Race at Wimbledon on 20 July 1974, won by Bob Atkinson of Cardiff, with Belgrave winning the open team race and the Surrey Championship team race; the text spells Stuart Barratt and the results S.Barrett.
items.s: WE WIN OUR OWN & SURREY 20 MILE ROAD RACE Report and results of the Belgrave Open 20 Mile Road Race at Wimbledon on 20 July 1974, won by Bob Atkinson of Cardiff, with Belgrave winning the open team race and the Surrey Championship team race; the text spells Stuart Barratt and the results S.Barrett. JULY 20th 1974 - WIMBLEDON - BELGRAVE OPEN 20 MILE ROAD RACE. On a hot and humid afternoon and without a single Belgrave vest in our scoring team (is this a record?) we won the open team race from Cardiff and T.V.H., and the Surrey County team race from Epsom & Ewell and Croydon In fairness to our scoring men, however, it was probably just as well that they wore the lightweight white string vests rather than the heavier club vests since in common with other competitors they were denied the refreshment station we should have had along the Kingston by-pass as there were simply insufficient helpers for us to man it. With the aid of helpers from Mitcham and Hercules we managed to have sufficient (just!) pointsmen and helpers. The Club is indebted to the few regular helpers who did turn up. D.Patterson of T.V.H. led at 5 miles by 13 seconds from Bob Atkinson (Cardiff) and Bill Weller, and by 10 miles had increased his lead to 76 seconds. However, by 15 miles Bob Atkinson was in the lead by 14 seconds from Bill Weller who was in turn 44 seconds up on Patterson. Lionel Mann and Pat O'Connor were running strongly well up the field and although Atkinson increased his lead to win and the second Cardiff man D.Jones was 4th, Bels. ran out winners by 5 points. Bill Weller won the Surrey race held in conjunction with Pat O'Connor 2nd. With Stuart Barratt in support we just won the Surrey team race by one point. All in all a good afternoon for our runners but an embarrassment to a club of our size that we had to rely on outside help for one of our major promotions of the year. items.sum: Round-up of Belgrave runners' performances in road races from April to July 1974, including the Isle of Wight Marathon, Hanwell Carnival 5, Horsham 10 and Lionel Mann's win in the Bedfordshire 10 mile championship.
items.s: ROAD ROUND-UP Round-up of Belgrave runners' performances in road races from April to July 1974, including the Isle of Wight Marathon, Hanwell Carnival 5, Horsham 10 and Lionel Mann's win in the Bedfordshire 10 mile championship. In the Maidenhead 10 miles, back in April, Lionel Mann was well up the field with 5th place in 53:29. Stuart Barrett just missed the hour with 60:12 (56th) and George Piddington clocked 67:31 (67th). The Isle of Wight Marathon is always a tough event. This year's race in May took place on a very hot day when only the first 21 beat 3 hours. Paul Pringle's 2:53:58 (16th) was excellent. George (52nd) reached the finish in 3:56:47 having taken 68 minutes for the last six miles! You can't keep old George down though. Nine days later he lined up with Lionel and Trevor Hart for the Aldershot 6-miler. Lionel (2nd) and Trevor (3rd) had a close race, finishing only 4 secs. apart with 31:52 and 31:56. George (41st) completed the team with 40:22 and gave us 4th place just missing the prizes by 1 point. What a lad he is! Another week goes by and on June 1st George picks a very hot day for his annual pilgrimage to Hull, to fly the Belgrave flag in a 20 mile road race. Only the first two home beat 2 hours and our man was timed at 2:34:11 (32nd). Bill Weller, limbering up for the Belgrave '20', led home our team in the Hanwell Carnival '5' with 24:50 (3rd). Pat O'Connor wasn't far behind - 26:09 (10th), and the Bels. closed in 2nd team behind Shaftesbury H. On the same day the Fleet '4' gave Derek Crookes 21:45 (31st), George 23:53 (51st) and Ron Langheim 31:09 (64th) the chance to flex their muscles. Good to see you competing again Ron - at least it made a pleasant change for George to have another Belgravian behind him for once!+@'+ June 23rd, and over at Grays in the Thurrock 10 mile race Bill paced out a respectable 49:51 (4th). He gained another 4th with 66:59 on July 7th in the Welwyn Half Marathon, won by Kirkham of Coventry. Pat 70:48 (16th), Lionel 71:41 (21st) and Doug Maughan 77:15 (62nd) gave us another 2nd team place behind TVH. Sweet revenge came for Pat O'Connor in the Horsham '10' when he beat Trevor Hart who had gained an earlier victory in the Chichester to Portsmouth race. Pat was 12th in 52:55, with Trevor 53:39 (15th), Paul Pringle 58:57 (46th), Stu' Barrett 63:11 (77th), the ubiquitous George 65:05 (87th) Don Bonsor 65:29 (89th), and we finished 4th as a team. The following day, June 14th, Lionel waged a lonely battle against mainly Luton United runners to win the Bedfordshire 10 mile championship. He finished 26 secs. clear of the field in 52:19. Glen Haszard who recently joined us and comes from New Zealand, ran in conditions more suited to his homeland when he tackled the Chigwell '10'. In 80F degrees over a very hilly course he pulled through the field well in the second five miles to finish in 61:03 (22nd). Doug. Maughan finished 27th in 61:48, hot and tired. items.label: September 1974
items.sum: Light-hearted tribute to Hon. Treasurer John Baker, aged 50, who covered 30 miles around Richmond Park in an Esso sponsored run/walk raising £138 for a kidney machine for Charing Cross Hospital.
items.s: HEROIC RUN BY JOHN BAKER Light-hearted tribute to Hon. Treasurer John Baker, aged 50, who covered 30 miles around Richmond Park in an Esso sponsored run/walk raising £138 for a kidney machine for Charing Cross Hospital. John Baker, our 50 year old Hon. Treasurer, has been the butt of many a jest regarding his un-athletic appearance. Looking like an emaciated version of West German international Harald Norpoth, he lurks near the back of our road and country races, eagerly waiting to pounce like death upon any runner who should get within his range. The writer will remember to his last days the terror that struck him one murky Saturday in mid-winter. In the gathering dusk on the last lap of the Club '10' he entered the woods with all strength rapidly failing and John Baker behind in full cry. The wail of the banshees could be heard, the harsh panting of tortured lungs getting closer and closer ... until ... he could struggle no more, and he too fell prey to the grey ghost of Belgrave. We in Belgrave know that beneath John's fragile frame burns a determination that is matchless but one can well imagine the disbelief expressed by his fellow employees at Esso - "What, you a runner!" . Well, they are regarding John with awesome respect now. You see, a sponsored run/walk was organised by the Esso folk, to raise money to buy a kidney machine for Charing Cross Hospital. John had no problem in gaining sponsors, for after all, surely a bloke like him wouldn't last a mile! The event took place around Richmond Park, a favourite haunt of our hero. After 30 magnificent miles he wanted to go on and on but Mrs. Veronica Charles, one of the organizers, insisted that John called it a day. He was tired but was in no trouble with his health and doubtless he could have gone on all week. No, it was his poor sponsors that needed protection. They had already been skinned to the tune of £138 by John's efforts and if someone hadn't stepped in they would be working off their debt for another year! One sour footnote was that one of his sponsors refused to pay up on the grounds that he just did not believe it. Great work John. ARM John Baker John Baker Hon. Treasurer, aged 50; covered 30 miles in an Esso sponsored run/walk round Richmond Park, raising £138 for a kidney machine for Charing Cross Hospital John Baker John Harald Norpoth Harald Norpoth West German international Veronica Charles Mrs. Veronica Charles one of the organizers of the Esso sponsored run/walk ARM ARM Belgrave Club 10 Esso sponsored run/walk Richmond Park Charing Cross Hospital

items.sum: Walking section notes on the summer season: veterans' team placings, Belgrave's improved standing in the 'Nationals' table, Bob Farley leaving for Saudi Arabia, and news of Allan Callow and Dave De Bondi.
items.s: WALKING Walking section notes on the summer season: veterans' team placings, Belgrave's improved standing in the 'Nationals' table, Bob Farley leaving for Saudi Arabia, and news of Allan Callow and Dave De Bondi. The summer season has passed and left behind its mark of success and failures. Without doubt much of the credit for placings in some of the races must go to our 'veterans'. John Bromley gave us 2nd team in the Leicester Mercury, Dave McMullen, 2nd team Lambeth, and Bob Farley, winning team Hastings to Brighton. We pulled up well to be 2nd team in the National 50km after a bad one in the '20'. However, despite our bad ones, we have moved up in the 'Nationals' table from last year's position but this was due to our turning out a team in the Junior Championship last October. With now three active walkers in each age group, Junior and Youths, plus two in the Boys, there is every hope of having teams in this year's 'Nationals' at Chelmsford in October. On a farewell note, Bob Farley is off to Saudi Arabia for a two year term as a University Lecturer. Bob, who had a quiet period as a result of a knee operation, has fought back well to regain his team position in the longer races. This again leaves our team depleted, especially following Allan Callow's departure mentioned in the previous issue. News from overseas indicates that Allan has settled in to his new abode and Dave De Bondi is changing status at last. He is marrying a physiotherapist who one hopes will speed Dave up.
