items.label: December 1974
items.sum: New President Ray Hall's letter to members setting out his plans to improve Belgrave Hall, link with schools, draw in local talent and raise money to put the club back among the top clubs.
items.s: FROM THE PRESIDENT New President Ray Hall's letter to members setting out his plans to improve Belgrave Hall, link with schools, draw in local talent and raise money to put the club back among the top clubs. Dear Belgravian, Thankyou for electing me your President for 1974/5. We are without doubt coming to the crossroads as a club; please always remember we can only go forward or back, we cannot stand still. The world is forever changing but with the exception of league athletics and the demise of trophy meetings and open handicaps, British athletics has changed little over the last 30 years. Opposition has grown to the traditional sports of soccer, rugby, cricket and athletics. The new generation of tennis, squash, swimming, hockey, golf, judo, table tennis and possibly the fastest growing of them all - badminton, are gaining from the change in the social climate, and are providing strong competition for the newcomer to sport and the school leaver. During the past 15 years these new popular sports have received impetus from the new sports centres provided by local government around the country with their swimming pools, squash courts and indoor facilities for other sports. In this country, with its weather, we must give these sports an advantage over athletics for at least six months of the year. The questions are, how do we counter attack to meet the opposition? How do we provide for the change in people's outlook and expectations? First improve the facilities at Belgrave Hall; we have at present out-line planning permission to build a second floor after inserting a steel frame. This would be the first major alteration to the Hall for 20 years. Then, the ladies facilities could be improved, and a larger refreshment area be provided. Without doubt, people would look forward to coming to Belgrave Hall in any weather, and we would not have the sad sight of a dozen women waiting outside in the cold for their husbands or boy friends. Perhaps following on from this we could have a ladies section and family membership We need to sell ourselves to the schools in our area, that means the whole of south west London and north Surrey. The recent enquiry in 'Athletics Weekly' into why school athletic champions left the sport was enlightening but also proved that ability needs something extra to motivate it. The wastage is frightening and disappointing. We must provide a link between school and club, the problem here being that with 50% of teachers changing schools every year, the liaison must be kept going at all times. It is not a one year job, it is every year. The talent (athletic of course) is available in our catchment area because Surrey is the champion county or region in the country. But the competition between clubs for these athletes is fierce, and in the end, this strength is fragmented between many clubs. Just think how many clubs are within ten miles of Belgrave Hall. This makes the Surrey clubs too small to compete with the Birchfields and Cardiffs, not only in physical size but also in financial stature. If and when we can provide the facilities and management, the youngsters will come. I mentioned the number of clubs within ten miles of us. The number of these may be 12 with two walking clubs. That is far too many for the area. It means some will not survive or will have to merge with other clubs. Let them be driven to us by our improved facilities. These ideas or thoughts of a madman need several things, the main item being money. The financial side is the problem, because in my crystal ball I can not see further expenditure by government departments on the assistance of sport. Also, sponsorships will be declining with the present lack of cash in industry. So if support is not coming from official sources, we must motivate ourselves to raise the money. That needs your support in all Club activities and the selling of draw tickets and football tickets. Also, it wants your shoulder to the wheel, your backing. We must become Club spirited, not a group of individuals. The Club has good facilities but they must be made better to become the best in the South. The main question at all times, how fast can we run to put Belgrave back amongst the top clubs? Only time will tell. RAY HALL PRESIDENT. Ray Hall RAY HALL President 1974/5 Belgrave Hall south west London Surrey Birchfields Cardiffs

items.label: December 1974
items.sum: John Keown's report of Ray Middleton setting new World Best distances and times for 6, 7 and 8 hours, 40 and 50 miles in an international 8 hour track walk at the New River Sports Centre, with a table of old and new records and the leading six placings.
items.s: MIDDLETON SETS WORLD BESTS John Keown's report of Ray Middleton setting new World Best distances and times for 6, 7 and 8 hours, 40 and 50 miles in an international 8 hour track walk at the New River Sports Centre, with a table of old and new records and the leading six placings. Down the last 70 years many Belgrave walkers have by their deeds on the track and road carved a permanent place for themselves and the club in the history of race walking. One of these walkers is Ray Middleton who over the last 15 years has by his great performances both at home and abroad kept the name of Belgrave to the fore. On Sunday September 29th in an international 8 hour track walking race at the all-weather track at New River Sports Centre, White Hart Lane, London. Ray crowned all his previous performances by establishing new World Best distances and times for 6, 7 and 8 hours, 40 and 50 miles. The previous records had been set by H.W.Whitlock (Met. WC) on October 5th 1935. Harold, now 70 years old, was present on this occasion as walking judge. Ray, one of the great masters of the art of race walking, gave a majestic display of fast controlled walking. Few competitors can match the confidence which Ray has in his own ability or the faith which other walkers and officials have that he is always in control of a race. During the first three hours or so when John Lees (Brighton & Hove) opened up a gap of about 600 metres on the field, the faint hearted amongst us were comforted by the fact that many spectators who included a number of very knowledgeable walkers and officials said, "Don't worry, leave it to Ray, he knows what he is doing". How right they were! As Lees began to slow up a little after passing the 20 miles mark Middleton, who was now going through each lap in about 2m15s, relentlessly closed the gap between them until at 25½ miles he went into the lead and pressed onwards to victory, setting on the way five new walking records. His walking throughout the 8 hours was faultless Although his lap times did vary during different stages of the race from 2m05s to 2m25s, his average time was just inside 2m15s. Carl Lawton, our other competitor, began steadily, passing 10 miles in 5th place, 20 miles in 4th place and 25 miles in 3rd place. At this stage we had high hopes that both Belgravians would lead the field home, as Carl was moving confidently along some 2m40s down on Ray. But his luck was not to hold for as Middleton began to take command of the race Carl had a reoccurence of some leg trouble which has plagued his racing career recently with the result that he was forced to slow up and eventually retire shortly after passing the 50km mark. Just after 9.30am on the Sunday morning, 16 walkers, including the two Belgravians and one each from France, Holland and Ireland, were sent on their way. Although the weather was fine an overcast sky kept the temperature below average for this time of year. Ray began with a couple of fast opening laps of 2m03 and 2m00s before settling down to lapping at around 2m09s. His only complaint about the organisation was the fact that he could not hear the timekeepers. At 10,000 metres he was leading the field by only one second with a time of 53m04s. Shortly afterwards John Lees, Brighton's Trans-America Record Holder, went into the lead and gradually drew away from Ray and the others. There was a marked difference in the styles of the two leaders. John with his very straight legged action, chopped stride and aggressive arms across the chest, gave the appearance of a walker in a great hurry, whilst Ray, with his longer stride and fluid body movements, looked comfortable and more graceful. Lees was almost a minute ahead at 10 miles which he passed in 1h24m56s. During the next 10 miles the leader gradually lapped the rest of the field. He lapped Ray just after the 20 miles mark which he reached in 2h50m59.2s (Middleton 2h53m02.6s). For another mile or so the gap between the two leading walkers continued to widen. Lees now began to tire and slow up a little whilst Middleton continued to reel off one lap after another in 2m15s During the next four miles he rapidly made up ground on the Brighton man. The 25 miles mark was passed by John in 3h37m35.6s and Ray in 3h37m59.6s. Another lap or two and the Belgravian was in the lead and well on his way to smashing Whitlock's 40 year old records. Each lap now took Middleton further and further away from Lees until he lapped him before they reached the 30 miles mark. Time at this point were 4h23m21s against 4h26m20s. A check at 35 miles showed that Middleton only required to cover the next 5 miles inside 56½ minutes in order to break the 40 miles record. This he did by the wide margin of over 10 minutes. From this point on, to the end of the 8 hours, one record after another fell to Belgrave's walking postman When the race, which was sponsored by Nicholas Laboratories the makers of 'Accolade', was 6 hours old the sky darkened and it looked as if a thunder storm would make the last 2 hours very difficult for both competitors and officials. After an anxious 20 minutes the heavy clouds dispersed temporarily and the weather remained fine until the last 5 minutes of the race when it rained. Good performances came from a number of other competitors. Lees held 2nd place until 42 miles had been reached when Ken Harding (Royal Sutton Coldfield WC) who had walked a beautifully judged race took over. These two walkers retained their respective places until the end. During the last half hour a great battle developed between Charlie Fogg (Enfield) and the young Frenchman Alain Moulinet for 4th place. In the end the veteran Enfield International won the duel by finishing 223 yards ahead of his rival. Four competitors were inside the old record at 6 hours and 40 miles whilst three were inside those at 7 and 8 hours, and 50 miles. 1. R.Middleton (BELGRAVE) 53miles 352yds; 2. K.Harding (R.Sutton Coldfield) 52mls. 649yds; 3. J.Lees (Brighton) 51mls. 1353yds; 4. C.Fogg (Enfield) 51mls. 1040yds; 5. A.Moulinet (France) 51mls. 817yds; 6. P.Selby (Surrey WC) 50mls. 1482yds. items.sum: Treasurer John Baker thanks Charlie Manning for raising £1,162.27, notes the year's profit of only £43 and urges members to sell more AAA draw tickets and support fund raising such as the Merton Show stall.
items.s: A word from your Treasurer— Treasurer John Baker thanks Charlie Manning for raising £1,162.27, notes the year's profit of only £43 and urges members to sell more AAA draw tickets and support fund raising such as the Merton Show stall. We must thank Charlie Manning for his efforts in raising £1,162.27 during his term as President and also those who helped in the various activities. The few members who remembered the date of the A.G.M. and attended will already know that the profit at the end of the financial year was £43. It will be seen therefore that we either continue fund raising on a large scale or cut our spending. One way of bringing in funds is to sell at least twice as many AAA draw tickets as we do now. With our large membership a sum of £200 could be collected but members just cannot be bothered. At the time of writing Ron Langheim is very confident that last year's figure will be passed but I hope that next year you will make an even greater effort. The Merton Show was a success in as much that we had plenty of help and made £144.97 profit. This would have been exceeded if more bottles had been donated by members. Let's have more support next year if the committee decide to run a stall at the show. Remember, the money you spend will have to be raised or taken out of your own pocket. The decision is yours. JOHN BAKER John Baker JOHN BAKER Hon. Treasurer Charlie Manning Charlie Manning raised £1,162.27 as President Ron Langheim Ron Langheim AAA draw tickets Merton Show Merton

items.sum: Walking Secretary Carl Lawton's notes on Ray Middleton's late-season revival, injuries, young walkers coming through, the National Young Athletes championships and the London - Brighton team placing.
items.s: WALKING Walking Secretary Carl Lawton's notes on Ray Middleton's late-season revival, injuries, young walkers coming through, the National Young Athletes championships and the London - Brighton team placing. Not to give a mention of Ray Middleton's success in August and September would be a travesty, despite coverage elsewhere. His Hastings, Brighton and 8 Hour performances were all produced after he had virtually packed up as a result of his poor showing in the National 50km. Ray's motto could well be, "perseverance pays". John Moullin is still not back in training, at the time of writing, after hospital treatment for a back injury. As a result we are now relying on up and coming hopefuls including Richard Tanner. Apart from our 100% strength team, individually some excellent performances have been produced by Richard and John Hall. Richard has won one of the police cadet championships and was in our Luton 2nd team, together with Alan Lucas, competing as a team member for the first time. The result of the National Young Athletes championships were quite promising in the Youth section, although with a little bit more effort we would have been placed. With time Desmond Bennett and Cliff Woodward will prove worthy of their standing and we could have an exceedingly strong junior squad. One of the downfalls, if it could be called that, occurred in the London - Brighton where, due to Dave King not having an attendant, we were forced into 2nd place with the same points as winners Brighton. We surely must have someone within our ranks willing to ride a bicycle to Brighton for a day out! items.sum: H.S.'s account of the storm-hit 49th London to Brighton Open Walk on 7 September 1974, won by Ray Middleton from Carl Lawton, with Belgrave second to Brighton & Hove on the last-man count in the team race.
items.s: a belgrave one-two H.S.'s account of the storm-hit 49th London to Brighton Open Walk on 7 September 1974, won by Ray Middleton from Carl Lawton, with Belgrave second to Brighton & Hove on the last-man count in the team race. SEPTEMBER 7th 1974 - THE 49th LONDON TO BRIGHTON OPEN WALK - 53 MILES. Shakespeare must have had premonition of this year's Brighton when he opened 'Macbeth':- "When shall we three meet again, In thunder, lightning or in rain." I met our President Elect, Ray Hall, who was looking after Carl Lawton, with his car windscreen wipers working double speed to clear the rain and a howling south-west gale, blowing the walkers to the gutters. After leaving Gatwick the rain ceased but the wind increased in ferocity to the extent that on the many open stretches, the competitors staggered as though drunk in battling against its force. My admiration for Ray Middleton and Carl Lawton is boundless. They went to the front shortly after Gatwick (28 miles), Carl having a slight advantage. Ray, whose consistency over a great number of years makes him legendary with Tommy Green and other names of the past, then took over in his powerful, rugged style. His strength enabled him to pull away to win in an excellent time, while Carl, showing the tenacity of a true top-class man finished an easy second. The awe inspiring seas at Brighton, up-rooted trees on our way home and the state of my garden were convincing evidence of the worst conditions I have ever known. It was also the first occasion that I can remember us having the first two. In the team race we were equal on points but lost on the position of our last man. H.S. 1. items.sum: Short historical note recalling Paul Khlopin, a Russian former cross country runner who was in Belgrave's winning 1934 London - Brighton Walk team.
items.s: Short historical note recalling Paul Khlopin, a Russian former cross country runner who was in Belgrave's winning 1934 London - Brighton Walk team. Nowadays we take Russian long distance walkers for granted and indeed their performances command the admiration and respect of the walking world. Russian walkers are, however, no new phenomenon. Going back to the 1934 London - Brighton Walk, one of the members of the winning Belgrave team was Paul Khlopin, a Russian. Formerly a cross country runner he took to walking. He was powerful, walked with determination and was a popular club member. Paul Khlopin Paul Khlopin Russian; member of Belgrave's winning team in the 1934 London - Brighton Walk; formerly a cross country runner London - Brighton Walk

items.s: CHIPPENHAM TO CALNE H.S.'s report of the Chippenham to Calne walk on 12 October 1974, won by Carl Lawton by 24 seconds with Belgrave 2nd in the team race. OCTOBER 12th 1974 - CHIPPENHAM, WILTSHIRE. The visit to this lovely part of Wiltshire was rewarded by a splendid autumnal day. The trees and white horse on the hills were a joy with their colouring of gold, red, bronze which makes England a paradise for tourists. We had a team of five in this ever popular walk, with Jack and Joan Goswell responsible for compiling the results. In the rush for the first mile Carl Lawton kept slightly behind the leading bunch, then on reaching the open road challenged for the lead to draw steadily away to win by 24 seconds. In a number of ways Carl reminds one of Stan Vickers, tall, long striding, superb arm action, yet there is a difference. Perhaps Stan walked with more of a killer determination and Carl with a steadier determination. Sufficient that their elegance of styles are rewards in themselves. We finished a creditable 2nd in the team race and it was good to note John Hall in a forward position, promising well for the future. Our President took an active part. H.S. 1. C.Lawton 43:29; 2. items.label: December 1974
items.sum: George Piddington's humorous account of the mix-ups before Ray Middleton's radio interview at London Broadcasting, after Ray went to Radio London by mistake.
items.s: ray's a laugh George Piddington's humorous account of the mix-ups before Ray Middleton's radio interview at London Broadcasting, after Ray went to Radio London by mistake. ✰ The Ray Middleton Radio Interview ✰ I had arranged to meet Ray outside the Aldwych tube station at 5.45pm. Leaving the car at Havant, I decided to travel up to London during the day by train as I was eager to do some training at Battersea Park. All trains seemed to be running at any time other than the times that they should. Anyway I did an hours training and was surprised to find the dressing room at Battersea full of cab drivers. Further travel to Tooting was also chaotic with more rail delays and buses running in groups of fours. By now I had a sense that something was going to go wrong before the day ended I booked to the Aldwych only to find that the station was closed due to staff shortage. A dash down from Holborn, Kingsway and I was outside the Aldwych by 5.40pm. It was beginning to rain and I had no coat! Six o'clock arrived but no Ray, and knowing he's a reliable bloke I guessed that something had gone wrong. A 500 yard sprint along Fleet Street took me to the studio of London Broadcasting, with the time now 6.10pm and the programme due on the air between 6.30pm and 7.00pm. After leaving a description of Ray I told the producer that I would make a relay dash to and from the Aldwych to see if I could find him. Without my knowing, Ray had gone to Radio London in Oxford Street! He was welcomed in at 6.00pm and after about 20 minutes they decided that he was not at the right place. "We have a five minute programme, but only to give the horse racing results ", said an official. Ray eventually realised that it was London Broadcasting that he wanted, and with the clock approaching 6.30 he ran up and down the middle of Oxford Street with his hands in the air, trying to get a taxi. Alas, they were all at Battersea. Eventually he managed to get one. In the meantime I was making my third return trip from the Aldwych, and by now was very desperate. I had just arrived back at the studio at 6.50pm and was met at the door by a secretary who said, "Quickly. Follow me. You are wanted." I sighed with relief to see that Ray had made it right on the line! Afterwards he looked at me and said, "What do you want to do now George?" "I don't know about you, Ray, but I could do with a couple of pints" I replied. And so we adjourned to the nearest pub where we laughed it off. Parting a little later I thought that's the day over. But no, my 8.50 train from Waterloo was cancelled - shortage of staff! GEORGE PIDDINGTON Ray Middleton Ray Middleton interviewed on London Broadcasting after first going to Radio London by mistake Ray Middleton Ray George Piddington GEORGE PIDDINGTON GEORGE PIDDINGTON George Aldwych Havant Battersea Park Tooting Holborn Kingsway Fleet Street Oxford Street Waterloo

items.label: December 1974
items.sum: Thumper's ghost story of a snowy night run in 1962 when he was joined along the Embankment by a pack of old-time runners talking of Dorando and the London Olympics, only to find his own footprints alone in the snow.
items.s: PHANTOM FOOTSTEPS Thumper's ghost story of a snowy night run in 1962 when he was joined along the Embankment by a pack of old-time runners talking of Dorando and the London Olympics, only to find his own footprints alone in the snow. "It's been snowing", cried the girlfriend with a yelp of glee. "That won't stop me" I replied, and with a clunk of the front door I was out, thumping down the streets. Soon I was onto Prince of Wales Drive and with long, lanky strides the yards were eaten up. This was back in 1962. I had taken up running for the first time to get fit for the runs organised by cycling clubs. The snow was only an inch deep but it was bitterly cold and I had plenty of gear on. The cold weather had driven everyone indoors and although it was only nine in the evening there was not a soul to be seen. I felt fit. As I ran through to Nine Elms Lane, the moon had wisps of striated snow cloud across it making it look weird. There was a deep, dark stillness everywhere, with just a touch of mist coming up from the Thames. There I was alone on the London roads and with a good firm step I reached the Albert Embankment, on to Lambeth Palace and over Westminster Bridge. Left and along to Millbank. The beads of sweat felt cold on my face. There was not a car to be seen, just grotesque shadows cast by the embankment lights. Gosh! It felt creepy, anyway I was on my way home now but what was that! Clip clop ... a horse and cab trotted by. Funny, I kept on going but weariness was beginning to tell. What was that chap doing on the corner with that flame on a stick? All these lights are electric. I moved along the Grosvenor Road, still alongside the embankment. There was a murmur of voices and I looked back to see a large pack of runners catching me fast. There must have been about 30 of them. Before I knew it they were up with me. "Hallo young fellow, out for your evening trot" called one "Keep going" cried another, and we all sped on to the Chelsea Embankment. Now I had seen runners before but not all running in step with arms going back and forth like pistons on a great locomotive. All were dressed in long white shorts and floppy vests, and leaning slightly forward with eyes fixed well ahead, their feet hardly seemed to touch the ground. "What club?" someone said. "Bellevue Cycling Club" I replied. "Damn contraptions, keep to horses" came the reply. The chatter was on and off. "Dorando did well in the London Olympics, real stout fellow, what!" "Corned beef and penny a pint beer, that's the stuff tc train on" .... We flew over Albert Bridge at a speed that was almost sprinting. Gosh these blokes were fit. It was like running with a pack of guards officers. On up to the gates of Battersea Park and then I peeled off. "Cheers", I cried. "Cheerio fellow" came a reply. I pottered home in a daze flopped in through the door and sank into a chair. "Done too much again" said Judy. She had a box of chocs. opened and the cushions arranged on the floor. I took off my shoes and started thinking. "The last Olympics were not in London", I said. "No, Rome", said Judy, her mouth full of chocolate. A horse and cab... a lamp lighter... corned beef.. penny a pint beer... runners all in white, running like guardsman. I put on my shoes and hobbled back to Battersea Park gates. There in the cold,clear,crisp snow was a sight that made my blood run cold, my legs go to jelly and my knees knock together like two stones in a tin can .... just one set of runners footprints - MINE! Pearson, C.Manning and Mead being warned that any more arguments over the points allocated to them and they will have points deducted, more darstardly tactics were used. One Thursday night as the pack swept along a dark alley, the leading runners suddenly split, leaving Charlie Manning to run smack into a post at full tilt. A medical check up revealed severe bruising but no cracked ribs. Yes, it's going to be murder at the tail end of the club'10'. items.s: from the 'belgravian' 25 years ago and 40 years ago Look-back column recalling Bill Webb's re-election as President and the club 5 miles cross country handicap in 1949, and a 1934 match against the 2nd Scots Guards at Wimbledon fought out between the Webb and Patience brothers. 25 years ago ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING, OCTOBER 8th 1949 ....... Once again our popular President, Bill Webb, was elected to the premier office of the Club and this was received with unanimous acclamation. CLUB 5 MILES C.C.HANDICAP, OCTOBER 29th 1949 ..... The individual winner was Bill Lucas, and he finished full of running, and was followed home by Chas. Walker and Jack Brown. Mick Porter and Lew Bush also ran well as did J.H.Braggington, who is a first season runner over the country. The winner of the handicap was R.T. (Bob) Taylor, who is 20 years of age, and looks like developing into a real find for the Club. As he was once a member of the Poly., it looks as if Poly's loss will be our gain. and 40 years ago NOVEMBER 17th 1934 Cecil Penny on "brotherly love" and, in passing, our match v. 2nd Scots Guards at Wimbledon. ...... Did I hear such remarks as "A snaky piece of work" emerging from the babel of voices after the match versus our ever-welcome visitors? How brotherly! Now, now, fellows! You must hand it to the veterans this time! To be placed first in a race of any description figuring on our fixture list, is a praiseworthy performance, and I believe I am correct in stating that this was Frank's first win in a cross-country race for the Club, so, sarcastic youngsters, hold your peace! The race itself was not unduly exciting. Several of our visitors were prominent at the start, but principally due to lack of training, they soon fell back and the race resolved itself into a friendly battle between the brothers Patience (who led for a considerable way) and the Webb brothers, with the result as shown. =1. items.sum: Young athletes' notes on AAA 5 Star award certificates and badges, Belgrave's entry into the Young Athletes League next summer, and the new format of the Boys and Youths competition.
items.s: YOUNG ATHLETES Young athletes' notes on AAA 5 Star award certificates and badges, Belgrave's entry into the Young Athletes League next summer, and the new format of the Boys and Youths competition. In the last issue of the 'Belgravian' we published a list of all youngsters who had qualified for an award under the AAA 5 Star Scheme. It is still not too late to apply for your certificate and don't forget, a badge is available as well for 25 pence. Apply to Leo Coy,40 Jedburgh Street, London SW 11. for your certificate and if you want the badge as well, enclose a postal order for 25 pence. You will be pleased to know that Belgrave will be entering the Young Athletes League next summer. All meetings will be held on Sunday afternoons and will cover every event - relays, hurdles, hammer and pole vault as well as the normal events. If you want to make the team now is the time to get training. Bill Couzens will be pleased to see you at the Friday night circuit and weight sessions at Belgrave Hall, 6pm. The Boys and Youths competition will be held in a different format next year. There will still be eight events as before from which the competitors best five performances will count. However the events will be made up as follows:- 100m, 400m, 1,500m, 80m hurdles, Shot, Javelin, Long Jump, High Jump. The events will take place early in the season on one weekend (Saturday afternoon and Sunday afternoon), further details to be advised. Once again the Boys events will be on a handicap basis. items.s: SHANKS AND DANPURE FIRST HOME FOR BELGRAVE Report and results of the KLG Open Boys cross country races at Putney Vale on 6 October 1974, where Simon Shanks and Richard Danpure were first Belgrave finishers and 10-year-old Philip Headley was 19th in the under-14 race. OCTOBER 6th 1974 - PUTNEY VALE - KLG OPEN BOYS C.C. RACES. With 20 boys turning out in rainy, cold conditions, this was one of our best ever forays to the KLG races over the other side of the Common. In the younger section, Simon Shanks steamed round the course to be first man home for Belgrave, five seconds ahead of Martin Cain who had the bad luck to miss the start and set off some 100 metres in arrears. Most outstanding however, was the mighty Philip Headley who at 10 years old in a race for under-14's finished an incredible 19th of the 70 starters. Another to excel was John Searle. As a team, we were 4th, just out of the prizes. Richard Danpure spearheaded our 14 - 16 team which really consisted of shorter distance track men. items.h: Meet Martin Munroe, Simon Shanks and Andrew Byrne
items.sum: Profile of three young New Malden members, Martin Munroe (printed Munro in the text), Simon Shanks and Andrew Byrne, their schools, weekly training and sporting achievements.
items.s: Meet Martin Munroe, Simon Shanks and Andrew Byrne Profile of three young New Malden members, Martin Munroe (printed Munro in the text), Simon Shanks and Andrew Byrne, their schools, weekly training and sporting achievements. Three youngsters who have shown early promise in their athletics are Martin Munro (13), Simon Shanks (12) and Andrew Byrne (11). They live in New Malden and originally met at Corpus Christi School although Simon and Martin now attend Beverley School. Simon was the first to join Belgrave Harriers early in 1973, and it wasn't long before the other two followed his lead. At Beverley there is plenty of opportunity for Simon and Martin to exercise their talent with cross-country races and athletic matches nearly every week. They both play rugby, Martin for the school, and when one tots up their sporting efforts each week it looks quite impressive, with Tuesday their only non-active day: Sunday/cross-country with the Club, Monday/circuit training at school, Wednesday/1½ mile run, Thursday/3-4 mile run, Friday/the famous Friday night weight and circuit sessions with Bill Couzens at the Hall, Saturday/race! Andrew has become an exciting prospect during the 1974 season, improving on all his previous performances with ease. He captains his school soccer team, playing at centre-back, and is also a member of the district side. That's not all, for he has represented his school at cricket and, particularly of interest to us, placed 2nd in the Kingston District Sports in the long jump. All three lads really enjoy their athletics with Belgrave but would very much like more inter-club competition on the track, preferably of the league variety that some of the other local clubs enjoy. Also, the chance to tackle events such as the hurdles, which have not been available up to now. items.label: December 1974
items.sum: C.E.M.'s report on the club's fund-raising and promotional stand at the Merton Show, which survived rain and vandalism to make a net profit of £143.97, with thanks to the helpers.
items.s: THE MERTON SHOW C.E.M.'s report on the club's fund-raising and promotional stand at the Merton Show, which survived rain and vandalism to make a net profit of £143.97, with thanks to the helpers. The participation of your club in the Merton Show had been envisaged for some time. We had an exploratory presence at the 1973 show and an evaluation of the most lucrative fund raising scheme at our Bazaar. Planning was simple. Booking under cover stand space, we took two units, one for fund raising and the other (to placate those who thought we were a good social club with an athletic interest) was for the promotion of Belgrave Harriers. Prizes were put up, Hoopla was made, display panels set out, scaffolding was organized, transport arranged and an appeal was made for bottles for the bottle stall. We had such an overwhelming response for this appeal that we only had to purchase £53 worth to make a show commensurate with a club of our calibre! Our involvement gathered momentum and a full days work on Sunday left us all prepared for a 9 o'clock start on holiday Monday. Now another element crept in - the weather. It bucketed down from early morning. With high winds and a little vandalism, marquees and tents flapped with torn panels. However, our spirits rose with the numbers of people coming in. The rain gave way to fine weather and things began to look up. After lunch it was all systems go and Belgrave took on the mantle of buskers extraordinary with waves of people flocking to our stall.until we wearily called it a day at 7 o'clock in the evening. It was possible only because of John Baker and Carl and Barbara Lawton, rolling up 4,000 raffle tickets and putting them into straws, Gordon Biscoe, Ron Linstead, Jean Manning with daughter Ann, her sweet voice in contrast to brother Chris whose dulcet tones did nothing for fellow helpers, Linda, wanting to do everybody's job and absent for lunch (about 4 minutes - she couldn't stay away from all that money), Johnny Morris and son and the man of the year Ray Hall. Let us not forget Tom Carter (transport), Evelyn Stimpson (facia), Arthur Penny (scaffolding) and the ever present Bob Taylor. It was a great effort that payed off - and it paid off to the tune of £241.30 gross to give us a net profit of £143.97. That's teamwork. Imagine what we could do as a club. C.E.M. C.E.M. C.E.M. items.sum: Report of the 87th Club Dinner and Dance at the Worcester Hotel, Worcester Park, on 23 November, welcoming Ray Hall as President, with the Tommy Green Cup to John Bicourt, a special award to Ray Middleton, and Roger Mills among those present.
items.s: Dinner and Dance Report of the 87th Club Dinner and Dance at the Worcester Hotel, Worcester Park, on 23 November, welcoming Ray Hall as President, with the Tommy Green Cup to John Bicourt, a special award to Ray Middleton, and Roger Mills among those present. Even by our normal high standards the 87th Club Dinner and Dance, held for the first time at the Worcester Hotel, Worcester Park on November 23rd, welcoming Ray Hall to the Presidential office, was a tremendous success rated by many as the best they can ever remember. The six course meal was superb, the service faultless and the rooms magnificent. Well done Ted and Evelyn Stimpson - organisers supreme. Official guests were His Worshipful the Mayor of the London Borough of Merton, Councillor B.N.Clifford, and Chief Superintendant E.M.Pitts of 'V' division whose long suffering constables put up with the traffic chaos when we hold our Belgrave '20' and road relays. In fact our local copper, Joe Hilsom, was a special guest. Many's the time he has stood on Copse Hill for up to 4 hours, holding up the traffic for our races. A more jovial chap you could not wish to meet. John Bicourt was awarded the Tommy Green Cup once more, for the best performance by a Belgravian during the Club year ending 31st August, this time for his 4th place in the 3,000 metres steeplechase at the Commonwealth Games. A special award was made to that stalwart Ray Middleton for his World Record breaking performance in the Accolade 8 Hour Walk. The spontaneous and warm applause that greeted Ray came straight from the hearts of all in attendance; it was a moving moment. Stephen and Peter Crosbie, two of our most promising younger athletes, .... continued at the foot of following page DINNER AND DANCE continued..... attended thanks to the munificence of Mrs. Hampshire who once again provided two tickets in memory of Jack Hampshire, one time Junior Secretary. And amongst others present, Roger Mills, whose heroic efforts in reaching the finishing line at the Rome European Games after a punishing 20 kilometres were witnessed by millions on TV, and were rewarded eventually with the silver medal. A marvellous evening. May there be many more at the same venue Ray Hall Ray Hall welcomed to the Presidential office Ted Stimpson Ted organiser of the Dinner and Dance (printed 'Ted and Evelyn Stimpson') Evelyn Stimpson Evelyn Stimpson organiser of the Dinner and Dance B. items.sum: Short report on the three Belgravians in the 1974 London to Brighton Running Race on 29 September: Bill Weller 24th, Glenn Haszard 69th, and Paul Pringle retired.
items.s: Short report on the three Belgravians in the 1974 London to Brighton Running Race on 29 September: Bill Weller 24th, Glenn Haszard 69th, and Paul Pringle retired. Three Belgravians were in the record field of 93 in this year's London - Brighton Running Race, Sunday 29th September. The weather was very good and Bill Weller, who normally likes a long steady run on a Sunday, decided that a bit of company might help him go a bit further. He finished 24th in 6:20:21 not far outside first class standard. Glenn Haszard, our member from New Zealand, finished 69th to gain a R.R.C. certificate to say that he did the journey in 7:44:35. Our other starter, Paul Pringle, had to retire before the finish, a great pity as we know how hard and conscientiously he trains. Congratulations to Bill and Glenn, to run to Brighton is a feather in anybody's cap. Bill Weller Bill Weller 24th, London to Brighton 1974, 6:20:21 Bill Weller Bill Glenn Haszard Glenn Haszard member from New Zealand; 69th, London to Brighton 1974, 7:44:35, R.R.C. certificate Glenn Haszard Glenn Paul Pringle Paul Pringle retired, London to Brighton 1974 London to Brighton London Brighton New Zealand R.R.C.

items.sum: C.S.'s report and full result of the club's Autumnal 5¾ miles road race at Wimbledon on 21 September 1974, won by John Bicourt from Laurie O'Hara, with Charlie Henn winning the handicap.
items.s: bicourt takes '5¾' C.S.'s report and full result of the club's Autumnal 5¾ miles road race at Wimbledon on 21 September 1974, won by John Bicourt from Laurie O'Hara, with Charlie Henn winning the handicap. SEPTEMBER 21st 1974 - WIMBLEDON. With a 16 months long track season just behind him, which culminated in the European Games at Rome and the Coca-Cola meeting at Crystal Palace (8:31.2) the previous week, John Bicourt let down his hair at Wimbledon on 21st September and drove his sun tanned body through some good old English rain to score a clear win in the Autumnal 5¾ miles road race. It was unusual to find poor weather for this race, especially rain. Unusual too to see the likes of Gerry North, John Stow and Trevor Hart spectating rather than racing. Our new President sent 34 starters on their way, and a mile later a rather leisurely-paced group of eight led the field. Black, O'Connor, Pearson, Bicourt, O'Hara, Weller, Jardine and Coy. Quite surprising to see the latter two still there, but after the second lap of the Common they were 150 metres down; the front six still together. Down Copse, Bicourt and Black forced the pace shoulder to shoulder and at the bottom John went clear, only Laurie O'Hara going after him. Alan Black had had it. Three hundred metres back Doug Jardine also attacked Cambridge, having just re-passed Leo Coy, and looked to be on a personal best if he could master the hills. Bill Laws had led the rest of the field but now had to give way to Pringle, Crookes and young Michael Manning. At the'kiss of death'Bicourt was eight seconds clear but O'Hara was still pushing him hard. Two hundred metres back Bill Weller had won a 10 metre gap over Pat O'Connor. Fully aware of Laurie's finish, John made sure that he kept well enough clear to avoid any last ditch battles and cruised home looking very composed, though he said afterwards, "that was my hardest race of the year" - which should be a comfort to Laurie. The steady start, and the conditions, ruled out spectacular times though Doug Jardine still did a personal best and showed just what he could do with the right application. It was surprising that he didn't gain a handicap award but Paul Pringle and Charlie Henn chose this day also to run exceptionally well and thwarted him. Derek Crookes (what a fighter he is) and Michael Manning also had fine runs - and at the rear of the field "M" force (C.Manning, Maclean, McDonald and Mead) did the dirty on our Treasurer. No doubt he will get his revenge! C.S. Handicap: 1. C.Henn (7:45) 26:15; 2. M.Best (9:30) 26:41; 3. P.Pringle (5:45) 26:49 1. J.Bicourt 28:24 2. L.O'Hara 28:32 3. W.Weller 29:03 4. items.label: December 1974
items.sum: Track secretary Alan Mead's call for Belgrave members to put the six Southern League matches and qualifier first in 1975, thanking Philip Gee, reviewing Leo Coy's 1974 league points statistics by event, and naming the new track and field captains and officials.
items.s: TRACK AND FIELD Track secretary Alan Mead's call for Belgrave members to put the six Southern League matches and qualifier first in 1975, thanking Philip Gee, reviewing Leo Coy's 1974 league points statistics by event, and naming the new track and field captains and officials. Before going any further I must tell you that I have thanked Philip Gee on your behalf, for the two years hard labour that he has put in as Track Secretary. To manage a team whilst training and competing as well is tough and we are in his debt. Now for the crunch! Browsing through some '74 league statistics put together by Leo Coy, the weaknesses in our side become apparent. Our sprint relay teams collected an amazing 97% of the possible points available to them, with the longer relay gaining 87%. Top individual events were the 200m (87%) and 100m (80%). Long jump, 400m, shot and both hurdles were in the 60-80% range - very respectable. 800m and upwards plus hammer, javelin and pole vault not so good with 50-60%, and high jump (47%), discus (38%) and triple jump (37%) proving the lowest. It's not really bad but it is not the overall performance of a team on it's way up. Incidently, let us not decry the efforts of anyone who has competed for us. I know only too well what it is like to garner a measly one or two points at the tail end of an 800 metres, knowing we need more. Regularly in the "Belgravian" you will have read such phrases as: "Who knows where we are going?" and "How does Belgrave rate as a club now?". Steve White in the last "Spotlight" hit the nail right on the head with: "...unless there is some attempt to win the league and get into the National League one of the fundamental drives of athletics is denied - the will to win.". OK, the point has repeatedly been made. NOW IS THE TIME FOR THE ACTION TO BEGIN. I want you to give me your wholehearted support on seven occasions next year - six league matches plus the qualifying competition. Two tough clubs, Essex Beagles and Met. Police, have been promoted up to the "Nationals" but with the Haringey and Windsor teams growing ever stronger, and the rejuvenated South London H and unknown Royal Navy sides joining our regular rivals in the premier Southern League, things are not going to be any easier. If we pick up any other trophies next year they will be welcome but they will be incidental. It's those league matches we must concentrate on. Of course by it's very nature, athletics tends to encourage individualism but team competition and tactical racing can be just as exciting and rewarding. On league days we must compete as a team, every member playing his important part and every member appreciating the role taken by others. It doesn't matter whether you aim to peak next summer for the Bodmin 120y Handicap, tossing the caber at the Knotty Ash Games, or the A.A.A. 5000m. Do so by all means but keep those league dates clear. League days must be TEAM DAYS. If you have the remotest chance of being selected, don't go out hammering 20-milers during the preceding few days - I might be dialling your number as next reserve on the list on Thursday or Friday night. If you have a big event coming up, how about offering to drop down a distance for a sharpener, because if Brendan Foster can run for Gateshead Harriers over 800 and even 400 metres, anybody in Belgrave can do similarly, and will earn the respect of their club-mates in doing so. Already I have approached several of our likely middle-distance team members, and all seem keen to get to grips with the competition. Steve Crosbie, now triple jumping almost 14 metres in training (over 45 feet), has promised his support. We have launched an appeal, published in many of the South London newspapers, for "big men" to take up a field event and come and join Belgrave. Youngsters, David Didino for example, are beginning to make their mark, and it is even rumoured that Arnold Bentt is going to train this winter. Sprinters? - you've done us proud for many seasons - no retirements now, please! continued on following page .... I have two admirable "bully-boys" to help me get things going, Philip Gee (Track Captain) and Colin Pearson (Track Vice-Captain). On the Field Bill Couzens will be Field Events Secretary once more, backed up by Snowy Brooks Contact Bill Couzens or myself whenever you feel the need (our addresses and phone numbers are on the inside front cover of this magazine). We care about Belgrave Harriers and we are certain that you do too, and look forward to seeing you in action in the arena next season. Oh! and one more thing, a special note to those who are studying away from London. If necessary we will help you with travelling expenses (the Hon. Treasurer will wince when he reads this) and we can arrange to put you up for the weekend as well. items.sum: Decathlon news: Snowy Brooks's club record 6707 points for second in the Scottish AAA Open Decathlon at Meadowbank and his win in the Southern Counties AAA decathlon, plus the first decathlons of Youths Ronnie McCrossen and David Didino.
items.s: decathlon news Decathlon news: Snowy Brooks's club record 6707 points for second in the Scottish AAA Open Decathlon at Meadowbank and his win in the Southern Counties AAA decathlon, plus the first decathlons of Youths Ronnie McCrossen and David Didino. It seems that a decathlon tradition is being forged in Belgrave Harriers these days, headed of course by Snowy Brooks. Reg. Hopkins,Jnr. has firmly established himself and two more youngsters who have made auspicious beginnings in the event are Youths Ronnie McCrossen and David Didino. Up at Meadowbank on August 24th/25th Snowy Brooks continued his quest for 7000 points with yet another Club record in the Scottish AAA Open Decathlon Championship. His second day total of 3025 points was his finest ever, the highlight being a PB throw in the javelin. The longjump, high jump and hurdles also gave him his best figures for 1974 and he finished up in 2nd place overall with 6707 points, behind M.Corden (Sheffield) 6943 and ahead of L.Spencer (Sheffield) 6228. - For the record: 100m/11.2, LJ/6.81, Shot/13.18, HJ/1.86, 400m/51.6, 110mH/16.3, Discus/37.24, PV/3.40, Javelin/49.94 1500m/5:01.9. The Southern Counties A.A.A. competition took place at Crystal Palace the following weekend, August 31st/Sept 1st,with heavy rain on the second day. As stated in the 'AW', the senior competition "was comfortably controlled by the popular Snowy Brooks". He won by 163 points from C.Young of Worthing scoring 6577 points. Ronnie McCrossen and David Didino, both Youths, with the latter only in his first year in the age group at that, showed great courage in tackling their first decathlon competition - the S.C.A.A.A. Junior Championship. All implements used were of senior men's specifications. Ronnie's 3748 points equals the figures set by Reg. Hopkins in his first competition at exactly the same age, a coincidence that points to a bright future and gives him a share in the Youths Club record. One can't help thinking that David Didino will improve on this mark, however. His 3106 points were notched up without the benefit of a pole vault score and he must have a full minute to come off his 1500 metres with a little training. items.label: March 1975
items.sum: Editorial marking fifty years since W.H. Hare produced the first Belgravian in April 1925, quoting its opening lines and reflecting on the gazette's role in club comradeship.
items.s: COMMENT Editorial marking fifty years since W.H. Hare produced the first Belgravian in April 1925, quoting its opening lines and reflecting on the gazette's role in club comradeship. Half a century has now gone by since W.H.Hare produced the first edition of the Club's gazette in April 1925. The opening lines of "The Belgravian" No. 1 read: "It has long been the desire of many of those of our members mostly concerned with the management and welfare of the Belgrave Harriers that we might have a periodical publication whereby the activities of the Club could be more closely presented to our members and friends thus increasing their interest and developing the feeling of good comradeship which is so great a part of the Club's objectives." Now, 50 years on, surely we can say that those original aims have been attained and kept to. The gazette's publication, thanks to successive Editors, has added much to our athletics and it is more than coincidence that nearly all of Belgrave's major club successes have come since that first issue. Of course, no one would claim that the regular appearance of "The Belgravian" has been directly responsible for any of our past triumphs, only individual determination and effort can cause that. But it has helped to provide us with heart. It has drawn us together and given us that comradeship during our competitive years and after, from which success can spring. Long may it continue to do so. W.H. Hare W.H.Hare produced the first edition of The Belgravian, April 1925

items.label: March 1975
items.sum: Club gossip column with news of members' health, visits, an engagement, a new Grade I timekeeper and Life Members and Vice-Presidents elected at the AGM.
items.s: grapevine Club gossip column with news of members' health, visits, an engagement, a new Grade I timekeeper and Life Members and Vice-Presidents elected at the AGM. grapevine You can't keep the COLEMAN family away from a Belgrave Open Walk. JOE was scudding around the course on a motor cycle and it is good to see him about again and doing the important job of judging. Brother LEN made the journey from Northern Ireland and was promptly snapped up to do some recording. Whilst waiting for the tail-enders to finish Len had to say something so he gave an account of how he beat Joe in a A.A.A. Seven Mile Championship in the thirties. Making a welcome visit south over the Christmas period was JOHN BLAIR-FISH who led our small team home over at Blackheath. On Boxing Day he teamed up with his brother PETER and sister to enter the Chipstead Pram Race and finished a worthy second behind one JOHN THRESHER. Veteran walker LEN EVANS has been in hospital for an operation and it was good to see him around at Imber Court on the day of the M.P.A.A. Open Seven. He looked remarkably well and no doubt when he's given the OK he will be in action again. STAN DAVIES is now living at Haverhill (Suffolk) and is hoping to get in touch with WILL SPENCER who is also retired in that County. They used to enjoy Saturday runs with FRANK WEBB and Co. Several visitors managed to call in to CHARLIE SMART's home and see him before Christmas. He is progressing reasonably well after his illness and is determined to throw away those walking sticks eventually. - Might be an idea to hold on to them Chas., you're going to need something to prop you up if you get through all that Christmas booze too quickly. A nice thought from the "Dukes Joggers" was to present him with a book about antiques. Congratulations to CYRIL GITTINS on becoming a Grade I Timekeeper. Although his first allegiance is to Queens Park H he rarely misses one of our Battersea meetings where his services are of great value to us. He is also an active walker (and runner, when the occasion arises!) and serves on a number of committees. We are pleased to learn that HARRY HATHWAY is making good progress after a successful operation on his hip. He takes regular walks and hopes to be timekeeping again this summer. In our last issue it was stated that Harry was not a member. This is not so as in addition to being an S.L.H. stalwart he is also a Belgrave member. Our apologies to you Harry together with our best wishes for your continued progress. REG. HOPKINS (young Reg that is) and JACKIE are to be congratulated on their recent engagement. Jackie faithfully supported our track and field team at each league event last season, even travelling down to Exeter. We look forward to renewing her acquaintance this summer and issue an invitation to all other girl friends and wives to come and support the team. Whilst on the subject of the Hopkins family, we must mention how pleased we are to see SUSAN jogging at Battersea Park on a Sunday morning, a much prettier sight than brother Reg. Everyone will be pleased to know that HARRY SHIELDS continues to make progress and a recent check-up showed a marked improvement. Not only do we see him at various meetings but he is always doing a job and although retired from work he has found many new interests. You just can't keep chaps like Harry down. At the A.G.M. last autumn LAURIE O'HARA and GEORGE PIDDINGTON were elected Life Members whilst BERNARD MERRY, STEVE WHITE and ALAN MEAD became Vice-Presidents. items.label: March 1975
items.sum: President Ray Hall's interim comments after five months in office, appealing for helpers at the Merton Show stall, criticising poor cross-country turn-outs, explaining the E.G.M. on raising subscriptions, and (continued on page 19) noting the Merton clubs' choice of Clive Shippen for the Sports Council and the 100 x 1 Mile Relay at Crystal Palace.
items.s: FROM THE PRESIDENT - INTERIM COMMENT President Ray Hall's interim comments after five months in office, appealing for helpers at the Merton Show stall, criticising poor cross-country turn-outs, explaining the E.G.M. on raising subscriptions, and (continued on page 19) noting the Merton clubs' choice of Clive Shippen for the Sports Council and the 100 x 1 Mile Relay at Crystal Palace. FROM THE PRESIDENT - INTERIM COMMENT Most of you know I work in the Stock Exchange, where pessimism and euphoria go hand in hand, so after five months as President I would like to pass a few comments or observations. The work of the Club seems to fall on a certain few people, some elected officers and others who are always available when called upon. But these willing workers are rarely thanked or named or remembered by the members in general. When I mentioned that I would appeal in the 'Belgravian' for the future commitments of the Club, the census of the workers was, "You're wasting your time." But I cannot believe a club of our size and ability has such apathy. There must be many members who could or would help if asked. For the past several years we have taken space in the Merton Show. This takes place in Morden Park. Last year we raised over £100 profit with a bottle and jar stall. This year the show will take place over two days, Sunday August 24th from 12.00 to 18.00hrs and Monday (Late Summer Holiday) 25th from 10.00 to 18.30hrs. (the times are in the modernists idiom). So those few I mentioned earlier will have to give up their whole weekend and holiday because the stall will have to be erected on the Saturday. If you can assist in any way, help with transport, give bottles or jars, help erect or spend a little time behind the counter, perhaps you will give half a day to help. Please get in touch with John Baker or myself. Don't leave it to those few I've already mentioned. Personally, I was disappointed (or would the word disgusted do?) at our turn-out for the South of Thames Senior at Swindon. Only three competitors turned out and they were outnumbered by Belgrave Officials, six if I'm included. The excuses were pathetic and one wonders whether the work involved is worth it. You must give, in return for the work done, some enthusiasm and support. Belgrave cannot live on history. The team spirit must come from the grass roots. In my heart I feel so sorry for Gordon Biscoe who works so hard and gets very little support. Please apologise to him for letting him down. The first feelings I had were to write an obituary for the cross country section. Even support for the Southern has dropped (only seven in the senior race) and it could be that we will find ourselves in division 2 of the Surrey Cross Country League at the end of next season. Gordon was not the only one to have little support. Clive Shippen sent out 60 cards concerning a league fixture for the youngsters - two turned out! Included with this 'Belgravian' is the notice of an E.G.M., to vote on the proposal to increase the subscriptions. We, like all organisations, are suffering from inflation. Just think of the increases in costs of electricity gas, water, rates (two minutes silence please) that will be coming during the year. We as a Club must be half a step ahead of the game. In the past few weeks the Club has booked tracks for the summer season and some of the charges have risen by 60%. Also in the near future it is hoped to improve the facilities at Belgrave Hall. At present the Building Committee are working on proposals and costs and these will be put before the Main Committee soon. It's agreed by everybody that our money should be spent on our main asset Belgrave Hall before anything else. I don't agree with a Past President who I heard to pass the remark,"If you improve the Hall it will be used only by a few old runners on Saturday afternoons." That remark was destructive and not constructive. We must look forward and not back. But the Club must at all times be financially viable. To the reader I will ask one question. "Do you personally in any way support fund raising within the Club (i.e. football tickets etc.). Sorry if I made you blush. If you don't agree with my comments come along on April 21st and state your reasons. Come and stand up and be counted. continued on page 19 ........ From The President ..... In this magazine we would like to re-introduce photos again but costs have to be kept under review. It is still the best club magazine, good value included in your subs. We are indebted to our Editor Alan Mead. Now to better things. An historic meeting took place towards the end of 1974 The major clubs in Merton met to discuss the local borough's request for an athletic representative on the newly formed Sports Council. After an informative meeting, the clubs agreed on Clive Shippen. What made the meeting interesting was that it was the first ever held between the three clubs and all agreed that it should be the first of many. It is a fact that all the clubs believe there should and will be mergers of clubs but no one person seems to have the answers on how it should be done. Please note the following date in your diary - June 29th - for the 100 x 1 Mile Relay at Crystal Palace. You will have to beat me to get in the team Perhaps we could have qualifying races for the scrubbers. Alan Mead is the man for information. Any comments or protests about what I've written - you may telephone me at Leatherhead 76264. RAY HALL President. items.label: March 1975
items.sum: Chas. Manning's tongue-in-cheek attack on Gordon Biscoe's cross-country points competition, proposing a handicap-based scheme, followed by an Editor's note with a mock points formula.
items.s: points Chas. Manning's tongue-in-cheek attack on Gordon Biscoe's cross-country points competition, proposing a handicap-based scheme, followed by an Editor's note with a mock points formula. points Its time to chase a new leader. "Biscoe must go". As the instigator of the most abortive attempt to get runners out by the introduction of a points competition this was a hoot. It was the sloppiest bit of legislation dreamt up by a bloke whats got marbles instead of the usual grey stuff in his head. It makes the the Social Contract look like it was iron law. Its another sop to the good runner at the expense of his inferiors. Now, this is how it should be done. Fairly to give everyone an equal chance. The season starts with the Yacht '3' and/or the '5¾'. Bill Lucas produces, in his inimitable and efficient (forget Peter North) style a handicap for nearly every Bel who's still warm. This list needs simply to be divided into three equal sections. Secondly the number of races; let's say for example 10 are nominated. Then, the first third start the season from scratch - the middle third are given 1 point per race, i.e. they start off with 10 points. The third group are given 2 points and consequently start off with 20 points. All this means everyone starts off on equal terms. I would suggest that a further point per race be given to all Vets. and a bonus of 5 extra for me because I thought of it. As far as administration goes it simply means that the handicap number is added on the big table that has to be prepared anyway from the first race. That's it. So Gordon, make way for a more virile,dedicated, far-seeing man such as Doug. Maughan or John Plummer. Get in an unselfish worker like Doug. Jardine or Jim Rimmer. What's wrong with the intellectual talents of Paul Pringle and why can't Eddie Thorp or Alan Black display their talents of leadership? Remember - you've got a bloody good Vice-Captain. Doesn't he deserve better? CHAS. MANNING Editor's Note: (i) Charlie Manning 'sat in' on the planning stage and when reminded about it replied that Gordon had just bought him a drink and that had completely upset his concentration. (ii) He'll never beat me anyway. (iii) A far better system would be to use the following simple formula on each competitor's record at the end of the season: Points = R(1+AO/(2H+3Cr+4C))+5S-0.1P Where R = No. of races in competition. A = Average position up the field expressed as a percentage i.e. if you were 3rd out of 12 score 75% O = No. of times officiated in the last 12 months. H = No. of handicap prizes gained during current season. Cr = Creep factor. No. of times seen pandering to Bill Lucas or Gordon Biscoe. C = No. of times carded during season but failed to turn up. S = Star rating - ranging from 10 for McDonald, McMillan, Glover,etc. to 0 for Pearson O'Connor and North. P = Potential. Charlie Manning CHAS. MANNING Vice-Captain (implied); wrote the piece CHAS. items.sum: Two short notes: veteran Chas. Henn's mismatched shoes for heavy going, and thanks to Bob Taylor for a winter of cross-country course marking.
items.s: Two short notes: veteran Chas. Henn's mismatched shoes for heavy going, and thanks to Bob Taylor for a winter of cross-country course marking. Veteran CHAS. HENN continues to run well over the country, year after year. One of the secrets of his success is now out, however. Contrary to normal advice about mixing cross-plys with radials, Chas. has been wearing studs on one foot and ripples on the other when the going is heavy! As the cross country season draws to a close we must thank BOB TAYLOR for another winter of course marking. This onerous task, carried out in inclement weather as often as not, goes largely unrecognised by most of our runners. When travelling up to the Hall for the afternoon's race it is worth remembering that Bob is already out on the Common setting out the flags. And long after the winner has crossed the finishing line and the winter evening closes in, he will still be at work gathering up the markers. Chas. Henn CHAS. HENN veteran cross-country runner CHAS. items.label: March 1975
items.h: from the 'belgravian' 25 years ago and 40 years ago
items.sum: Reprints from April 1950, when Belgrave Hall became the club's freehold property, and from 1935, when Belgrave won the English Cross Country Championship at Beaconsfield with 97 points.
items.s: from the 'belgravian' 25 years ago and 40 years ago Reprints from April 1950, when Belgrave Hall became the club's freehold property, and from 1935, when Belgrave won the English Cross Country Championship at Beaconsfield with 97 points. from the 'belgravian' 25 years ago APRIL 1950 OUR OWN HEADQUARTERS ..... It is said - "that he who plants an avenue of trees, cannot, in the nature of things, hope to enjoy them in their grandeur" - but it was a very happy occasion and a most gratifying result to the labours of all Belgravians responsible for it, when our popular Hon. Secretary told the Special General Meeting held at Belgrave Hall on Thursday, March 16th, that Belgrave Hall was now our own freehold property. What many of us years ago dreamed of, even dared to think possible, has now been achieved. To Harry Hare, the originator of the idea, and others too numerous to mention, who helped to make it possible - we say - fervently - thank you, and we know they feel fully repaid for their efforts. They now hope that the wheels of officialdom will not turn too slowly and that in the near future we shall obtain a permit for rebuilding a Hall that will be a fitting and lasting monument to the greatness of Belgrave. Then, and not till then, will they, the men who achieved so much, so unselfishly, sit back and observe complacently - the dream that finally came true. and 40 years ago THE ENGLISH CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP, BEACONSFIELD, 1935 ....... A fortnight previously we had surrendered our Southern title to Surrey A.C. and whilst we had plenty of confidence that this result would be reversed, and that Salford would have to yield to us this time, we were not so optimistic as to think that Birchfield, holders for the previous seven years with eight internationals entered in the team, would be humbled and forced into fourth position! However, we anticipate. Let's start at the beginning. Two hundred and ninety-five runners thundered from the starting pens, and in the first 50 yards Shaw and Shields had nasty falls over two prostrate Ealing men. They picked themselves up and had all the field before them. The first lap of one mile was soon covered, and then out into the country on the first lap of three miles of fast, undulating park land, with our boys fairly well placed. At four miles we had another view of the runners. Jim Ginty was fourth at this point, and our other men all seemed to be weighing up their opponents and running strongly. An attempt to get an idea of the scoring was doomed to failure owing to the speed at which the men passed. We could see, however, that Surrey A.C.'s sixth man was behind our eighth. Salford had three men prominent, but where were the others? Birchfield seemed well beaten even here. Currie the Midland champion, had retired at 1½ miles, and they had two men in the first bunch, the rest nowhere! However, we have been deceived before by the wearing of white vests and so were not unduly jubilant. At seven miles it was obvious that, bar accidents, victory was ours. Ginty had fallen back a little and was running with Bert Footer, Dan Patience being a few yards in the rear - all in the first 25 places. Over the last lap many places were gained, our Taylor-Shields-Carter trio, in particular, pegging back many opponents. In the last mile our boys gave all they had, and we had the remarkable scoring sequence of 11th, 14th, 15th 18th, 19th, 20th places. It must have been a proud moment when Bert Footer realised that one of his greatest ambitions had come to pass, and that he had led home a Champion team- not by a narrow,fluky margin - but with 56 points to spare. 1. Belgrave H (Footer 11, D.Patience 14, Ginty 15, Taylor 18, Carter 19, Shields 20) 97pts; 2. Salford H 154pts; 3. Surrey AC 156pts. A.A.H. items.s: Richardson shows us how Report and full result of the Club 7½ miles cross country championship at Wimbledon, won by second-claimer Bob Richardson with Gerry North retaining the club title, plus the handicap result and a worry about the lack of young runners. Richardson shows us how DECEMBER 14th 1974 - WIMBLEDON - CLUB 7½ MILES CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. In heavy conditions that slowed down this year's times, second-claimer Bob Richardson won our 7½ mile race at a canter from Gerry North who sustained a heavy fall but nevertheless retained his championship. Fine running came from Colin Pearson who gained his first ever Club championship medal over the country. Also outstanding were John Davies and young Simon Holmes, whose steady and regular training over the past few months is beginning to pay dividends. New member John Dudman was another to run well, opening his account quite promisingly. A close handicap win went to Alan Mead who, amidst the mud, managed to rise above his regular rivals. Whilst not wishing to detract from the performances of our older runners, amongst whom are some of the best veterans or near veterans in the country, the dearth of fresh young blood must be remarked upon. It is a situation difficult to remedy and not auguring well for the future. H'cap: 1. A.Mead (14:30) 40:31; 2. S.Holmes (8:00) 40:32; 3. J.Davies (7:30) 40:50. 1. R.Richardson 43:28 2. This race will also incorporate the Road Runners Club Championship and takes over from the famous Maxol Marathon. items.s: 'Something In The City' Report of the City of London New Year road races, where Belgrave won the 10 miles team race on aggregate times led by Bill Weller and Laurie O'Hara, and Chris Barber won the Open 1 Mile. 'Something In The City' JANUARY 1st 1975 - CITY OF LONDON NEW YEAR ROAD RACES. We have always had members associated with the famous "Square Mile", and with New Year's Day a public holiday we saw some of our members in action there. The Road Runners Club promoted an Open 10 Miles Road Race over a seven lap course and shortly after one o'clock the race was on. Bill Weller was with the leaders over the early stages with Laurie O'Hara consolidated in fourth place. As the second half of the race proceeded P.Flavel (Oxford City) and J. Jones (Windsor, S & E) drew away and dead-heated in 50:03 with Bill following them in 26 seconds later. Then over a minute of waiting for Laurie who was an easy fourth in 51:54 - nearly a minute ahead of the fifth man. So we had a good foundation for the team race, three to score, the race being decided upon aggregate times. The team was completed by Doug. Maughan who finished 44th in 58:14. and this made us winners from Woodford Green (who, incidentally, would have won if the points system had been used) and Havering AC. It was good to see a good clubman and persevering runner like Doug. getting amongst the awards. Laurie had a second visit to the prize table (the presentation took place in the Jolyon Restaurant in London Wall) for the Veteran's Prize. We also had a bonus in the Open 1 Mile. Our Manchester member Chris Barber won from a very "classy" field in a fine 4:06.7 - a great start to the New Year, in which we hope Chris will make many successful visits to the South. FOOTNOTE: A.A.A. Rule 106 has been modified to allow organisers to decide a team race on the basis of team aggregate times but the normal points system is to be used unless the organisers have made it clear to everyone concerned that the time system is to be used. =1. items.s: Mitcham 25km ~ Herbal Tonic ! Report and result of the Mitcham 25 kilometres road race, won by Keith Penny, in which Belgrave won the Jim Peters team trophy led by Bill Weller in fifth, while Croydon took the six-to-score Fry Trophy. Mitcham 25km ~ Herbal Tonic ! JANUARY 11th 1975 - MITCHAM. Mitcham used to be famous for its lavender and other herbs. Nowadays, particularly if you run in the Mitcham 25 kilos (15 miles plus). you are more likely to get a whiff of petrol with a dash of diesel. So, a fine afternoon plus a Belgrave team win gave us all a tonic on January 11th. Over 100 runners faced the starter and after a couple of miles Laurie was hammering it out with men of much more tender years, however, he eased a bit and by 10 kilos the race was taking shape. Bill had settled nicely into fifth place (31:42) with Laurie and Pat running strongly together a few places later. Our other lads were all going steadily further down (mindful that there was also a trophy for six to score). At 20 kilos (roughly 3 miles to go) positions were much the same, but Eddie Thorp had to pull out owing to a toe injury. The winner was Keith Penny (Cambridge H) in 77:56, followed by European Games Marathon representative Bob Sercombe (Newport H) in 78:22. Bill held on to fifth position and Pat pulled away to finish ninth, two places ahead of Laurie. A convincing team win, 16 points to 41 (Croydon H) and 47 (Ranelagh H). However Croydon beat us for the Fry Trophy (six to score). Incidentally, the main team trophy is named after one of the marathon "greats" - Jim Peters. Laurie once again had a recall to the table for the Vet's Prize. Our others enjoyed their run on such a fine day and we look forward to seeing them and others on what should be an even finer day for our own Open 20 Miles. G.S.D. 1. K.Penny (Camb.H) 77:56; 2. items.sum: Light-hearted account of the Duke's Round The Bridges handicap race at Chelsea, won by John Thresher from Doug Maughan and Alan Mead.
items.s: The Duke's 'Bridges' Light-hearted account of the Duke's Round The Bridges handicap race at Chelsea, won by John Thresher from Doug Maughan and Alan Mead. The Duke's 'Bridges' One evening back in the autumn, the classic Duke's Round The Bridges Race was held over the 2⅝ miles Chelsea Bridge - Albert Bridge circuit. The race is a yacht handicap open to all those who run at the Duke of York's Barracks, Chelsea, and a more unlikely bunch of cripples assembled at the north end of Chelsea Bridge for the start would be difficult to imagine. Homeward bound commuters halted spellbound as the hobbling, limping competitors warmed up, each making a desperate last minute attempt to influence the handicapper. Once off, however, they tore down the Embankment like the wind, and as the field reached the coloured lights of Albert Bridge, twinklingly reflected in the dark Thames below, our Belgrave heroes - McDonald, Plummer, 'Boofer' Bruce, etc. - could be seen bounding along like young gazelles. It all ended in victory for John Thresher whose storming finish up the Chelsea Bridge slope gained him the top prize - an ultraviolet lamp suitable for the treatment of 'injuries'. Doug Maughan was second and Alan Mead, who says he is trying to mould a handicap career on that of past master Dudley Gordon, took third. Times and handicaps? Ah! That would be telling. items.s: It's Gerry in worst ever conditions Report and result of the club 10 miles cross country championship on Wimbledon Common, run in flooded conditions and won by Gerry North, with John Dudman taking the handicap. It's Gerry in worst ever conditions JANUARY 18th 1975 - WIMBLEDON - CLUB 10 MILES CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Our course is generally reckoned to be fairly easy but for this year's ten mile championship the conditions on the Common were the worst anyone could remember. Bitterly cold rain fell throughout. The open stretch out to the windmill was flooded and over by the cemetery was a sea of mud. Water cascaded down the hill by the windmill, the Avenue was completely submerged and worst of all the quarter mile finish to each lap along the horse ride was literally knee deep in water and thick black mud. Times of the leaders were up to six minutes slower than normal and of the 29 starters only 21 finished. In conditions like these no one can stand up to Gerry North, the complete cross country runner. Colin Pearson had another excellent run and it was good to see Doug. Maughan up the field again. John Dudman improved again to take the handicap but really congratulations should go to every man who finished. H'cap: 1. J.Dudman (15:00) 58:09; 2. L.Morris (13:00) 60:23; 3. items.s: All Time Record for Belgrave Report deploring that for the first time Belgrave could not start a team in the South of the Thames senior cross country championship at Swindon, with only three of 18 entrants turning up. All Time Record for Belgrave JANUARY 25th 1975 - SWINDON - SOUTH OF THAMES SENIOR C.C.CHAMPIONSHIP. Our current trend in enthusiasm, or lack of it! hit a new time low on January 25th at Swindon for the South of the Thames Championship when for the first time in living memory we were not only unable to complete a team but could not even get one to start! The sorry tale is that of the 18 names entered and a potentially good team only three runners bothered to make the trip. Of course there were the usual quota of 'good reasons' and excuses but even considering that the South of the Thames is not now the attraction it was, over 300 runners from other clubs managed to start! The offenders may care to reflect that six Club officials plus the President's wife managed to get there and that the non-appearance of a team resulted in approx. £11.50 being wasted as part cost of hiring a coach and entrance fees. My thanks to those who did turn out and keep our colours flying. G.I.B. 27. P.O'Connor; 133. D.Maughan; 173. J.Dudman. P. O'Connor P.O'Connor 27th D. Maughan D.Maughan 133rd J. John Blair-Fish's fell running record for the tail end of last season was 5th in the Glenurquhart Highland Games (3 miles/ 500 feet); 22nd in the Ben Nevis race (10 miles/4,400 feet) with 1hr 45mins., 18 minutes and 5 places better than last year in spite of suffering from tonsillitis; and 22nd again in the Langdale Fell Race (15 miles/ 5,500 feet) in 2hrs 33 mins His running this winter has not been confined to pure country, for against country and road runners he won the Edinburgh University race up Arthur's Seat, Holyrood Park.
