items.label: March 1975
items.sum: Review of the Surrey Cross Country League Division 1 season in which Belgrave finished fifth, their worst ever, with the final league positions.
items.s: Surrey C.C. League Division 1 Review of the Surrey Cross Country League Division 1 season in which Belgrave finished fifth, their worst ever, with the final league positions. Surrey C.C. League Division 1 A most disappointing season ended with Belgrave down in 5th position, our worst ever, only 7 points down on Hercules Wimbledon but 100 points adrift of the top three clubs. 1971/72 was the last occasion when we won the league, in fact that was our sixth successive victory. Aldershot, Farnham & Dist A.C. who were second that year took over the following season and have not been headed since, whilst the Bels have slowly sunk - 2nd, 3rd and now 5th. Hercules Wimbledon have also begun to wane and their 4th position is their lowest since 66/67 and 62/63 when they were also 4th. The Hercs. won the event in 64/65. Walton have had a reasonable season after a spell in Division 2 since 1971. They are the only other winners of the league (in its first two seasons 62/63 and 63/64) and after returning to Division 1 this season have held on well just 77 points short of our own score. Clubs of the moment, however, are Croydon and South London H., both creeping up gradually over the last few years. For Herne Hill H. it is time to face relegation again, although with their hordes of excellent youngsters, when they come back it could be with a bang. Meanwhile, have we touched bottom or will we continue the downward trend - next year will tell. 1. Aldershot, Farnham & Dist 875 2. Croydon H 1,123 3. South London H 1,341 4. items.label: March 1975
items.sum: Humorous account of the Tuesday night 7 mile 'By-pass Run' training handicap from Belgrave Hall, won on the line by Stewart Barrett, with Bernard Merry judged handicap winner.
items.s: RUNNING WILD Humorous account of the Tuesday night 7 mile 'By-pass Run' training handicap from Belgrave Hall, won on the line by Stewart Barrett, with Bernard Merry judged handicap winner. RUNNING WILD "OK it's 6.15, we can't wait any longer." ".... Got your numbers, time-keepers ready?" "We're off!" The usual wisecracks come thick and fast as we leave Belgrave Hall. Never mind the ebb and flow of Belgrave's cross country/road fortunes, the REAL action takes place on a Tuesday night on the 7 mile 'By-pass Run' returning via Cambridge Road and the 'Kiss of Death'. Invariably, heading the dozen or so runners who set out is Brian " I feel terrible" Gorman. Just let anyone get within a foot of him and he'll flinch and surge away again. It has been likened to touching a worm with a lighted cigarette. But let us continue. Cannily plugging away in the middle of the bunch as the early jockeying for positions takes place, 'Boofer' Bruce can be seen, shepherding along his latest handicap springer. A mile out, along Parkside, and John Wasbrough makes a break taking Eddie Thorp with him. He'll come back. A car pulls up at a side turning waiting to get out into the main road. "Round the back, always round the back, its much safer" cries a suddenly concerned Brian, as he leaps across in front, floodlit for a moment in the headlights. Those who did go round the back now have to work like stink to make up a 6 yard deficit. Tibbett's Corner approaches. Will we go under the subway tonight? A sudden movement by anyone now and we'll all be darting across through the streaming traffic. But no, under we go. That's the last major road crossing and if we can only keep going at least we'll get back alive tonight. Up the other side and Bernard Merry's silhouette can be seen ahead. The crafty devil went over the top after all and now he has sneaked a 50 yard break, up with John. It's eyeballs out now as we tear down Roehampton Vale at what is a suicidal pace for most of us, down past K.L.G. The early leaders come back and as Brian sweeps by, his rolling head turns for a second and he smiles charmingly at John, whispering "Die you ?@+:@, die!" At Robin Hood Gate all hell is let loose for here begins the one mile flat out effort for those who are still in contact, all along the by-pass to the footbridge. The pace is always hottest here because Colin Pearson is probably doing 'strides' on the playing fields, and he'll see how good we look. The pack is now strung out over a good 1½ miles but tonight those at the back get another chance to catch up because John Stow has to be peeled off the side of a bus shelter after running into it at full speed. Left at Fuller's Garage and soon Cambridge Road is being tackled. Only 'Boofer' and Stewart Barrett now cling leech-like to Brian but he puts in another surge. "Go get the swine, Stew!" Up the hill and along the Ridgway the battle rages until sprinting past the 'King of Denmark' Stewart just gets ahead and holds it into the Club hall. They burst through the door and Brian has to shake Stewart's hand in congratulations amidst the roaring laughter of those sane enough to avoid going out with this 'pack'. It's not over yet though. 'Boofer' is 3rd but who will get tonight's handicap? Runners continue to stagger in for another 20 minutes. Poor Gerald Collins. It was his first Tuesday run from the Hall... "And my last!" he gasps. Eventually the general consensus of opinion is that Bernard should be handicap winner for the week ahead of Peter North. Will they have enough strength left to turn out for the Club on Saturday though? Still that's not important, it's preparing for next Tuesday's dice with death that counts. The cross country/road running secretary sits in a corner head in hands. items.label: March 1975
items.sum: John Keown's history of Belgrave walkers in the London to Brighton walk from 1897 to 1974, covering individual medallists such as Tommy Green, Norman Guilmant and Ray Middleton, the Club's team wins, and tables of Belgrave individual medal winners and winning teams and hopes for a clean sweep at the 50th Surrey Walking Club race in 1975.
items.s: BELGRAVE AND THE 'BRIGHTON' John Keown's history of Belgrave walkers in the London to Brighton walk from 1897 to 1974, covering individual medallists such as Tommy Green, Norman Guilmant and Ray Middleton, the Club's team wins, and tables of Belgrave individual medal winners and winning teams and hopes for a clean sweep at the 50th Surrey Walking Club race in 1975. BELGRAVE AND THE 'BRIGHTON' JOHN KEOWN writes On Saturday 6th September 1975 Surrey Walking Club will promote their 50th Open London to Brighton walking race. Amongst the starters will be a number of Belgravians who will strive to uphold the proud tradition which Club walkers have established over this historic course since the turn of the century. In 1897 Polytechnic Harriers organised the first Open Brighton Walk. There were 37 starters. The only Belgrave entrant was W. Poole who finished 7th in 9hrs. 38mins. 45secs. Six years later Club Hon. Secretary H.A.Smith finished 6th in 9hrs. 33mins. 08secs. in an Open Brighton promoted by the Hairdressers A.C. To the modern walker the 'Brighton' of those far off days would seem very strange. Leading the field was a trap containing the timekeepers, closely followed by the baggage wagon known to all as the ambulance cart. A further horsedrawn carriage called a brake was used to convey the judges. All the competitors were surrounded by hordes of cyclists who both helped and hindered their progress by acting as pacemakers and adding to the difficulties of walking on a rough dusty road. Surrey Walking Club, who had since their formation in 1899 held a number of time trials for club walkers over the Brighton course, decided in 1919 to promote an open race from Big Ben to Brighton sea front. With the exception of the war years 1939-45 this race has been held every year since, during the month of September. All the great British long distance walkers and many of those from abroad have competed in this race, including Olympic medallists Tommy Green, Harold Whitlock, Lloyd Johnson, Don Thompson, Norman Read and Abdon Pamich. Although the course has down the years followed the same general route from Westminster to Brighton, various changes to the road such as the construction of Gatwick Airport have meant that the length of the race has varied from just under 52 miles to just over 53 miles. Right from the start Belgrave walkers began to make their presence felt in 'Brighton' races by taking 3rd individual place in 1920, 21, 23 and 24 through J. Bellchamber, J.H.Allen, J.Miles and E.A.Wall, and providing the winning teams in 1921 and 24. Further encouragement was given to take part in the race when in 1923 Bob Ricketts presented the "Belgrave" Cup for a Club Long Distance Walking Championship to be held in conjunction with the Surrey W.C. Open Brighton. Jimmy Bellchamber, the Club's first great long distance walker, finished 2nd in the Brighton and Back race in 1921 in 20hrs. 53mins. 35secs. and so became our first Centurion. In 1927 Tommy Green, who later won the first Olympic 50 km Walk, began to carve a permanent place for himself in the history of the 'Brighton' when he finished 2nd to the 21 year old Italian Giani in 8hrs. 26mins. 44secs. and led the Club to victory in the team race. Two years later he recorded the first of his four wins and again led Belgrave to victory. During the 1920's Belgravian J.N.Thomas, who began his race walking at the age of 44 with North London Harriers, became the first walker in history to finish three successive Brighton and Back races. In 1930 Tommy Green broke Harold Ross's 1909 course record of 8hrs. 11mins. 14secs. by 8 minutes and 19 seconds. But for the sheer force of the wind and rain he encountered during the last 2 hours he would have broken 8 hours for the 'Brighton'. A year later Tommy again won the race with a time of 8hrs. 05mins. 43secs. just 2 minutes and 48 seconds outside his own record. Ross's record was beaten for the third time in 1932 when 25 year old J.H. Ludlow of Derbyshire Walking & A.C. clocked 8hrs. 01mins. 06secs. Tommy Green was an early pacemaker but the effects of his strenuous efforts at the Los Angeles Olympics soon told on him and he fell away to finish 3rd. A year later he was back in winning form with a victory in 8hrs. 01mins. 19 secs. Belgrave completed a hat trick of wins in the team race (now four to score) in 1932, 33, 34. On 23rd/24th June 1933 A.G.White finished 3rd in the Brighton and Back with a time of 20hrs. 48mins. 16secs. Before the 1930's were over two more individual medals were won by Club walkers; by F. Bentley in 1934 and F. Rickards in 1937. Both finished 3rd. Rickards also led the Club to victory in the 1937 race. On 7th September 1935 Harold Whitlock (Metropolitan W.C.) broke the 'Brighton' record and became the first man to beat 8 hours for the course which had been slightly shortened because of the reconstruction of the road at Bolney. His time was 7hrs. 53mins. 50secs. Harold won gold medals in the 50 km Walks at the 1936 Olympics and 1938 European Games. After the Second World War Belgrave walkers slowly re-established the Club as a force to be reckoned with over the Brighton course. In 1950 the great A.J.Stirling Wakeley, who a year later won the Brighton and Back in 18hrs. 46mins. 00secs., led the Club to their first post war victory in the team race. Two years later 128 walkers, the highest number ever to compete in the 'Brighton', faced the starter. Despite the fact that the Club had 13 starters we could only finish in 4th team position. The following year Norman Guilmant took Belgrave's first individual medal since 1937 when he finished 2nd. In 1954 the Club rounded off a triumphant season by taking both individual and team honours in the 'Brighton'. Norman walked a finely judged race to win by 2 minutes after 21 year old Don Thompson had led for 45 miles. Don, surely the best known British walker ever because of his famous triumph in the Rome Olympics 50 km Walk, scored the first of his nine wins in 1955 (eight in successive years). He broke the course record in 1956 with a time of 7hrs. 44mins. 52secs. and again in 1957 when he established the current record of 7hrs. 35mins. 12secs. Behind him Belgravian George Checkley was second in 1956 and 3rd the following year. The Club won the "Edward Knott" Team Shield in 1956, 57 and 58. George Beecham who was a scoring member of each of these teams later went on to collect four more first team medals. He was 4th in the 1958 race with a time of 8hrs. 37mins. 46secs. Belgrave's score of 13 points for four walkers in 1957 was the lowest on record. In this race Harry Shields finished 10th and outside the scoring four. Two years later he won the "Harry Preston" Cup which is awarded to the first veteran to finish the race. london to brighton walk BELGRAVE INDIVIDUAL MEDAL WINNERS * New course record of 8:01:06 established by J.H.Ludlow (Derby) in 1932 london to brighton walk WINNING BELGRAVE TEAMS Started 1919 No race 1939 - 45 The 1960's were great years for the walkers who wore the claret and gold. Although they failed to produce any individual winners they won the team race on six occasions, finished 2nd twice and 3rd once. They also won five individual medals. R.C. 'Ray' Hall, our Club President, finished 2nd in 1963 Ray, who was 3rd in 1959, won the Stock Exchange 'Brighton' in 1962 with a time of 7hrs. 58mins. 33secs. thus becoming the fourth walker in history and the first Belgravian to cover the course inside 8 hours. Third place in the open race went to Dave King in his first 'Brighton' in 1964 and to Pat Duncan in 1967 and 68. An American, G. Klopfer walking as an individual in Belgrave colours finished 3rd in 1969. Ray Middleton ensured that the 1970's began on a high note for the Club when he became the fastest ever Belgravian over the historic Brighton course by clocking 7hrs. 50mins. 47secs. when finishing 2nd to Shaul Ladany (Israel). He also led the Club to their 20th win in the team race with a score of 13 points, equalling their previous lowest team score of 1957. In the next two years the Club finished 2nd in the team race. Belgrave only started four walkers in the 1973 'Brighton' and for the first time in the long history of this event the Club failed to finish a team. Despite the worst weather conditions for many years Belgrave bounced back to the top in 1974 when internationals Ray Middleton and Carl Lawton took 1st and 2nd individual places and the Club tied with Brighton & Hove A.C. on points in the team race but lost first place because the latter's fourth scoring man finished nearer the winner. Down the years since W. Poole finished in the first Open London to Brighton race many Belgravians have followed in his footsteps. Some have only completed the distance once, others many times. The challenge which this Blue Ribbon event presents has ensured that all our long distance walkers, stars and others, have wanted to tackle the race at least once. Fifty Belgrave walkers have done so since 1946. Leading the table of 'Brightons' successfully completed since the last war are John Keown with 16 (consecutive); George Beecham with 15; Joe Wilson, Harry Shields and Bernard Eglington with 12 each; Gordon Doubleday with 11 (2 before the war) and Johnny Morris and Dave King with 10 each. Belgrave and the Brighton ----- The success of the Club down the years in the 'Brighton' is only partly due to the efforts of our walkers. Little would have been achieved without the encouragement and support of a gallant band of helpers who ensured that the individual needs of each walker were continually catered for between Big Ben and Brighton seafront. Many Club members, and families and friends of members, have acted as helpers to each successive generation of walkers. Without their aid and encouragement there would be no Brighton success story. They provided the support necessary to enable Club walkers to give of their best. Unfortunately in recent years this support has been on the decline. What a finish Belgrave walkers could write to the Club's success story over 50 years on the Brighton Road if on 6th September 1975 they could take all the individual medals and the team title! An impossible dream? Given that all our distance walkers are fit and available to compete and that there are no top class foreign competitors, that dream can become a reality. Ray Middleton and Carl Lawton are capable of repeating their successes of 1974 whilst John Moullin, absent through injury from the last 'Brighton', can grab 3rd place and give the Club the additional strength necessary to take top honours in the team race. Ray, given the right conditions, has the ability as he recently proved in the Accolade International 8 Hour Walk to break Don Thompson's 1957 course record of 7hrs. 35mins. 12secs. h. m. s h. m. s items.label: March 1975
items.sum: Treasurer John Baker explains the Special General Meeting on subscriptions, chases unpaid subs, repeats the bottle appeal for the Merton Show stall and notes Norman Dewberry's omission as Assistant Treasurer.
items.s: A word from your Treasurer— Treasurer John Baker explains the Special General Meeting on subscriptions, chases unpaid subs, repeats the bottle appeal for the Merton Show stall and notes Norman Dewberry's omission as Assistant Treasurer. A word from your Treasurer— Each of you will be receiving with this issue of the magazine an invitation to attend a Special General Meeting on April 21st to discuss subscriptions. As everything we use has steadily increased in cost it is inevitable that members will have to pay more. Even so, the senior subscription at £5 per year will still be small compared with other sports. There are a number of members who have not paid the current year's subscription and in some cases the previous year's. They will find a subscription reminder in the envelope and I hope they will return it with their subs before June 30th. To issue reminders costs the Club money and also my time. Elsewhere in the magazine you will find my request for bottles for our stall at the Merton Show. Remember what Charlie Manning said after last year's show in which the sum of £146 was raised. "That was a good team effort, just think what we could have done as a Club". I noticed that Norman Dewberry was omitted to be shown as Assistant Treasurer in the last issue. Subs. can be paid to him at Belgrave Hall on a Saturday afternoon. JOHN BAKER John Baker JOHN BAKER Hon. Treasurer Charlie Manning Charlie Manning commented on last year's Merton Show stall which raised £146 Norman Dewberry Norman Dewberry Assistant Treasurer; takes subs at Belgrave Hall on Saturday afternoons Merton Show Belgrave Hall

items.label: March 1975
items.sum: Walking Secretary Carl Lawton's notes on the walkers' improving prospects, newcomer Martin Lewin, returns from injury, Alan Lucas's return to Australia, second place in the Garnet, Brighton finishers omitted last issue and the National 20 miles in the Isle of Man.
items.s: WALKING Walking Secretary Carl Lawton's notes on the walkers' improving prospects, newcomer Martin Lewin, returns from injury, Alan Lucas's return to Australia, second place in the Garnet, Brighton finishers omitted last issue and the National 20 miles in the Isle of Man. WALKING With the turn of spring and a New Year, our prospects are not now as bleak as they were six months ago. The new member to our ranks Martin Lewin has quickly transformed into an 'A' team star, giving John Hall a nudge in the process and helping us to team placings in the Cambridge Open, Met. Police Open and the Garnet. John Moullin has made a welcome return after six months lay-off and hopes to be back in form by the National 10 miles. Even Bob Picton has made his reappearance as has Len Evans, in spectator capacity, after an operation. Richard Tanner and Alan Lucas have both been consistant performers over the last few months and it is with regret that Alan has now returned to Australia. We extend our thanks to him for his services over the last nine months. Despite our new team, we regret to announce the failure to win the Garnet, due to misfortune. John Bromley was involved in a car accident, now recovered, and John Hall automatically disqualified himself by finishing 3rd in the Scottish Championships last year. However, we were still good enough for 2nd with Alan Lucas, Richard Tanner, Martin Lewin (who deserved a medal for determination) and Martin Yates as the four. It was an oversight in the last issue of the 'Belgravian' that no mention was made of Johnny Morris, John Keown and Eric Stroud, all of whom competed in the notorious 'Brighton' and hence doubled our number of finishers of the year before. Looking to the future, the National 20 miles will be held in June in the Isle of Man. Travelling details will have to be arranged in advance so please give it some thought as it will involve a long Saturday. items.sum: R.C.H.'s report on the Garnet Cup junior 10 miles walk at Slough on 1 February 1975, where Belgrave, led by Alan Lucas in 4th, finished second team behind Brighton & Hove, with full results.
items.s: Lucas leads Garnet Cup Team R.C.H.'s report on the Garnet Cup junior 10 miles walk at Slough on 1 February 1975, where Belgrave, led by Alan Lucas in 4th, finished second team behind Brighton & Hove, with full results. Lucas leads Garnet Cup Team FEBRUARY 1st 1975 - SLOUGH. Through the wet winter, the walking section have held high hopes of winning the Garnet Cup for 1975. This race is junior by status. But hopes don't win championships. Luck helps but from Belgrave's point of view this disappeared the week before the race. Third place in a minor Scottish Championship ruled John Hall ineligible, a car accident put John Bromley on the side lines (delighted to see he's recovering from his injuries), the Irish had a demonstration so Doug. Fotheringham and Bob Carter were left behind in London to keep law and order. Go west young man along the M4 to Slough. The Belgrave team was a mixture of youth and experience. It still had a chance to win on this mild February day. Every one of the five Belgravians walked as well as could be expected on the day, our leading man being Alan Lucas. This likeable Australian walked his best race in our colours, always fighting his way through the field, finishing 4th and just one place short of his honours badge. A very solid performance and we are sorry to see that he is returning home soon but are pleased to have known him. Our next man, Bob Tanner, has that old Belgravian theory that you must win every time. To go home from a race without a prize or a medal is sacrilegious. Feeling the after effects from his police cross country training, Bob faded a little in the middle of the race but fought back with great determination to finish 8th. His police colleague Martin Lewin, our third man, was suffering from a virus infection but he fought all the way, even suffering several attacks of sickness during the race. A very fine performance in his first ever ten mile race. I believe that with normal progress Bob and Martin can become Belgrave's next walking internationals. The other member of the scoring team was Martin Yates. He walked his best race in our colours and with a little more class racing he could develop into a good walker. These four received their first championship medals for second team and they were ably supported by Bob Picton making a comeback. R.C.H. 1. C.Fisher (Enfield) 78:37; 2. D.Johnson (Brighton) 78:40; 3. items.sum: Obituary by G.S.D. of walker Joe Scamell Senr., a member since 1925, who died aged 74 at his home in East London on 4 December.
items.s: JOE SCAMELL, SENR. Obituary by G.S.D. of walker Joe Scamell Senr., a member since 1925, who died aged 74 at his home in East London on 4 December. JOE SCAMELL, SENR. We are sorry to record that Joe Scamell, Senr., whose illness was mentioned in the last 'Belgravian' , died at his home in East London on 4th December. He was 74 years old and joined the Club in 1925 - almost 50 years of membership. He was a member of our walking teams for a number of years and helped us to many a win in Open races. As a measure of his individual performances he won a First Class A.A.A. Standard over the old Two Miles Championship and gained a Middlesex County vest (Middlesex was a very strong walking county in those days), he also held the Club Record for our five mile course. With the passing of years he continued to turn out for the Club and if the speed wasn't still there the style was and it was obvious that much of his earlier success was due to his fine style. He was by nature quiet and reserved but travelled to Battersea or Wimbledon (quite a journey in those days) to compete and enjoy the company of the Bels. He would invariably stop for a handshake after the finishing line was crossed, such was the warmth of his character. We have, not so long ago, seen Joe, his son Joe,Junr. and grandson Michael competing in the same race - three generations! He was an inspector in the Electrical Industry by trade, before he retired. The family received many letters of sympathy from people in the Club, and, amongst the tributes was one of red and yellow chrysanthemums from the Club. The gratitude of his family has already been conveyed to us for the many words of kindness received. G.S.D. Joe Scamell, Senr. items.label: March 1975
items.sum: Harry Shields' profile of walker Carl Lawton, born 1948 in Shaftesbury, covering his rise since 1967, his 1974 successes, his Commonwealth Games selection, his wife Barbara Inkpen and hopes for a women's section.
items.s: SPOTLIGHT ON CARL LAWTON Harry Shields' profile of walker Carl Lawton, born 1948 in Shaftesbury, covering his rise since 1967, his 1974 successes, his Commonwealth Games selection, his wife Barbara Inkpen and hopes for a women's section. SPOTLIGHT ON CARL LAWTON Carl was born in January 1948 and hails from the Dorset town of Shaftesbury which he left at the age of 19 to seek fame and fortune in the great world. This gives our first clue to his remarkable determination, partly hidden by a genial smile and the somewhat hesitant and shy manner which beguiles the tenacity which he adopts towards a job to be done and to his enormous athletic ability. One cannot use a question and answer technique with him. He is the exponent of expediency and those who have known him from the time he joined the club have more than a suspicion that especially in his early days money was tight. Yet rather than admit this he would cycle and walk enormous distances to a race meeting and still produce performances from 3,000 metres to London - Brighton that, given a points value, would make household names of the past seem small by comparison. Only Ray Middleton could compare. Yet this man is still only 26 years old and at the threshold of his career. He fits into his working life an active administrative interest in the Club as a committee man,captain, walking secretary and one who steps in and does any job he sees wants doing. On race days he sorts out teams and gives out numbers in spite of the tension that must be present when he knows that the success of the team and the Club depends on his own performance. He is someone I am proud to know. Ray Hall relates the story of speaking to Carl, in August 1967, dejected after being "pulled" in the Brockwell Park 5 miles. He had previously won the Duke of Edinburgh Gold Medal for walking. From this time the ugly duckling became a swan of immaculate style. His performances from a time of 57 minutes 33 seconds in the Belgrave Open of 1967 to the present day have been of steady and continuous improvement. Last October he won the Chippenham - Calne 6 mile race in a time only beaten in the Club by Stan Vickers during the year he won the European Games. During 1974, apart from magnificent performances at shorter distances, he was 2nd in the Hastings - Brighton, 2nd London - Brighton, 1st Leicester 'Mercury' 20 miles, 1st Southern Area 10km track walk, 2nd Surrey 10km and 1st Surrey 3,000 metres. In all the National Championships, which with one exception, we either won or were placed, he was the king-pin together with his buddy Ray Middleton. Amidst all this activity he has managed to court and win for his wife Barbara Inkpen, the first woman to have a high jump of over 6 feet ratified as a British Record. In many ways she has Carl's characteristics and is a delightful person. They never brag when doing well or complain when things are difficult, and are two grand people who deserve well of life. The performance that has given Carl his greatest pleasure was his 3rd place in the Commonwealth Games Trial in which he set a new Club Record of 2 hrs. 34 mins. 44 secs. and was selected to represent his country in New Zealand. Training for him is a matter of instinct, using the time he has available. My own hope is for him to have stability at work and that he continues to make use of his enormous ability with credit to his country, his club and himself. With the exact opposite of my thinking of yesteryear, I hope that Barbara, together with our President's wife and many other ladies who do so much for the Club, can bring pressure for a women's section for Belgrave Harriers. Somehow I think that Carl and our President see hopes in this direction rather than amalgamating with other men's clubs. items.label: March 1975
items.sum: Peter Crosbie's account of a residential Southern Counties coaching course at Crystal Palace Sports Centre on 27-29 December attended by himself and three other Belgrave boys.
items.s: southern counties coaching course Peter Crosbie's account of a residential Southern Counties coaching course at Crystal Palace Sports Centre on 27-29 December attended by himself and three other Belgrave boys. southern counties coaching course On the 27th - 29th December three boys and myself attended a residential coaching course held at Crystal Palace Sports Centre, staying in the comfortable hostel especially built for this purpose. The course catered for Senior Boys up to the Junior Men's age group and covered all events. The events pursued by the four from Belgrave were: Triple Jump - Ivan Beaumont, High Jump - David Didino, 800 metres - Richard Danpure, and myself - Javelin. The nucleus of the course were the 'practical sessions', these were simply where everyone split up into their own events. In charge of the groups were some of the best coaches in the country. They gave good clear advice on all aspects of the separate events. The practical sessions were hard work but enjoyable. To back up the advice films were shown of the world's best athletes. A small competition was run, competing against those in the same event. It took the form of a heptathlon and the seven events were, 60 metres box test (running and jumping), standing long jump, standing triple jump, medicine ball throw and 800 metres. Prizes were given for the first three in each event. Overall the course is well worth going on. Apart from enjoying yourself, you also learn a lot about your event and other events and I personally recommend the course to any young athlete in the Club. On behalf of the boys who attended the Course I would like to thank the Committee for their generous support. items.label: March 1975
items.sum: Profile of fifteen-year-old Richard Danpure of Rutlish School, who joined in 1974, won the senior boys high jump and 800 metres at the Club Championships and attended the Crystal Palace coaching course.
items.s: MEET .. RICHARD DANPURE Profile of fifteen-year-old Richard Danpure of Rutlish School, who joined in 1974, won the senior boys high jump and 800 metres at the Club Championships and attended the Crystal Palace coaching course. MEET .. RICHARD DANPURE Fifteen year old Richard Danpure goes to Rutlish School and became a Belgrave Harrier in 1974 after his father met some of our members in our secondary headquarters 'The King of Denmark'. He plays rugby for his school along with fives, basketball and of course athletics. Soon after joining he began to make a name for himself by winning the senior boys high jump and 800 metres at our Club Championships, the former with a Championship Best Performance, and he went on to gain a A.A.A. 5 Star Award. He has had some advantage over other lads of his own age because of his above average height and weight but if he can continue to make headway when the others begin to catch up, then his success in athletics will be assured. Now training at the Hall three times a week with Tuesday and Thursday road runs and weights on Fridays, he has no real preference for events but looks forward to the coming Sunday track sessions and the chance to tackle any event he can to find out his best. He greatly enjoyed the residential coaching course at the Crystal Palace, although finding it hard work being the youngest person in the middle distance group. Most of his training on this course was repetition work over 150m/200m/600m and gave him some idea what real training is all about. He found himself so stiff after the first day that he could hardly move but would very much like to attend future courses if given the chance. Richard's object is to enjoy his athletics. He likes belonging to Belgrave with its tradition and friendly atmosphere and when it comes to 'ribbing' he gives as good as he gets from the likes of Colin Pearson and Chas. Manning. items.label: March 1975
items.sum: Field events and track secretaries' preview of the 1975 track and field season, covering the A.A.A. Decathlon date clash, coach travel to Portsmouth and Brighton, the end of the Brockman Trophy Meeting and appeals for inter-club support.
items.s: TRACK AND FIELD Field events and track secretaries' preview of the 1975 track and field season, covering the A.A.A. Decathlon date clash, coach travel to Portsmouth and Brighton, the end of the Brockman Trophy Meeting and appeals for inter-club support. TRACK AND FIELD The track and field season is again almost with us. Due to some confusion at National level the A.A.A. Decathlon Championship was arranged to take place on the same day as one of the league fixtures. You may well imagine the consternation this caused - the thought of a league event without Reg. Hopkins and Snowy Brooks! We immediately wrote to the powers that be, and, not entirely due to our own actions one feels, the date of the Decathlon was changed. Now for the bad news: it was changed to the day of the National League qualifying meeting which of course we must aim to reach. Further action is in progress. Travel to the matches at Portsmouth and Brighton will be by coach. With the price of petrol as it is, if we all go together it will be cheaper all round. Supporters will be more than welcome at all the matches, so if you are not in the team but would still like to come along, contact one of us a few days before each date. The final death knell of trophy meetings seems to have been sounded with the end of the 'Brockman', formerly one of the highlights of the season. Herne Hill Harriers have gamely fought a losing battle by promoting the Brockman Trophy Meeting in the face of declining interest in these type of fixtures. They feel the time has now come to call a halt and we are sorry to see it go. Please support our inter-club matches this year. We appeal particularly to those who do not regularly make the first team. Whatever your standard we can provide competition for you, so study your fixture card and especially note our home fixtures. If you still have not entered the Surrey Championships get in touch with us. We have the entry forms and will be pleased to hear from you. Good luck for the '75 season. BILL COUZENS Field Events Secretary ALAN MEAD Track Secretary Bill Couzens BILL COUZENS Field Events Secretary Alan Mead ALAN MEAD Track Secretary Reg. Hopkins Reg. items.s: Three club notes: Paul Williamson's training at the University of East Anglia and ankle injury, the successful January dance with the Jaguars organised by Colin Pearson, and pre-war police stalwart Bob Readman spectating at the G.L.C. Walking Championship. PAUL WILLIAMSON, now at the University of East Anglia, has been training up to 40 miles per week and is hoping to go really well over 400m and 800m this year. Unfortunately he sprained his ankle pretty badly in the Eastern Counties Championship at Peterborough and had to drop out after 6 miles. Nothing too serious we hope. Our dance in January starring the JAGUARS rock group was a huge success. Belgrave Hall was packed to its limit and the dancing was non-stop. A big thankyou to COLIN PEARSON for the organisation and may the Jaguars return again soon. Amongst the spectators at the G.L.C. Walking Championship at Battersea was one of our police stalwarts of the thirties and forties, BOB READMAN. A former Club 20 miles Champion, Bob also won police championships including one at National level. He looked very fit and after asking after old friends was off round the course with SYD SPENCER - did they sign on any new members as they used to in the old days? items.label: July 1975
items.sum: Editorial on recent accidents between road runners and motor vehicles, urging supporters, drivers and runners alike to take care on the roads.
items.s: COMMENT Editorial on recent accidents between road runners and motor vehicles, urging supporters, drivers and runners alike to take care on the roads. COMMENT A serious feature of road running in the last few months has been the number of accidents involving athletes and motor vehicles. On Easter Monday two separate races were struck by tragedy. After completing 25 miles of the Yorkshire marathon championship a competitor was hit by one of the cars following the race and was later detained in hospital with a broken leg and facial injuries. Meanwhile, in the Hartlepool '10', another received injuries - again caused by a supporters vehicle. Even worse, a Scottish international struck down last October is still paralysed. Near accidents at road races happen all the time. Supporters following by car should know better than to get entangled with the race but let us consider how those unconnected with the event react. When traffic is held up to let the runners pass there is always some driver who blasts his horn with impatience. More often than not there will be at least one other who insists on recklessly overtaking the field in the face of oncoming traffic when a few moments forbearance are all that are needed to keep everyone happy. It's no use the runner beating on the roofs of these cars as they pass. The only safe attitude is to keep close to the kerb, watch what is going on and run with care. But it must not be imagined that the problem is by any means one-sided. How many times does one see runners risking life and limb to cut off a few yards by running in in the centre of the road; ignoring pointsmen and crossing to the wrong side; skipping in between cars at junctions regardless of the danger? The fractions saved are worthless when balanced against the value of life and a whole body. Finishing the course by ambulance could mean being barred for life! Yorkshire Marathon Championship Hartlepool 10 Hartlepool

items.label: July 1975
items.sum: Club gossip column: Belgravians helping at the City of London Police relay, Reg Elson rejoining, the Threshers emigrating to Canada, Chris Manning's accident, Frank Jarvis in hospital, veteran walkers bound for Toronto and other news of members.
items.s: grapevine Club gossip column: Belgravians helping at the City of London Police relay, Reg Elson rejoining, the Threshers emigrating to Canada, Chris Manning's accident, Frank Jarvis in hospital, veteran walkers bound for Toronto and other news of members. grapevine How do the City of London Police manage to put on a four stage relay (each one a double lap of 1¾ miles) ? They leave it in the capable hands of DAVE DAVIES who enlists the help of a number of Belgravians. For this year's event in early March he had the help of GORDON BISCOE, JOHN BAKER, JIM HEATHFIELD, DENIS McMANUS and PAUL, and GORDON DOUBLEDAY; also present was timekeeper TOM REYNOLDS, a well-known figure at our open promotions. A welcome spectator at the Club 20 miles walking championship was REG. ELSON who joined us in the late twenties and was a regular member of our walking teams for a number of years. He had an array of old club photographs and programmes, and was armed with a camera to add to his collection He also used to play the saxophone at Club Socials. Reg has rejoined us as an Hon. Member and we hope that he will be a regular spectator at our events. JOHN and MAVIS THRESHER emigrated to Canada in April and have now settled in Regina, Saskatchewan. Our best wishes for a happy future go with them. John still remains our fastest ever miler - 4:02.1 - and 1500 metre record holder. CHRIS. MANNING had the misfortune to be involved in a car accident necessitating a lengthy stay in Epsom Hospital. Whilst wishing him all the best for a speedy recovery we feel that we must warn him of a threat uttered by JEAN now that she has to travel everywhere by bus. "You wait till he gets out - I'll break his other leg for him!" CHARLIE CHURCHER was recently spotted in New Malden. Although he has now retired from work he does the occasional odd job. Many years ago if there was a spot of decorating to be done at the Hall you would always find Charlie there. He still strolls around quite a bit with the inevitable pipe. Our Past President, FRANK JARVIS, had a recent spell in hospital for an operation and should by now be well on the way to recovery. Frank is a Past President of the R.W.A. and is immediate Past President of Surrey County A.A.A. Once again TOM CARTER has an active school of athletes at Battersea Park. As he strides it out from one side of the track to the other, stop watch in hand and urging on his charges, one wonders just who is the fittest. Three of our walkers are hoping to go to Toronto, Canada in August to compete in some veteran events, so good luck to DAVE McMULLEN, JOHN BROMLEY and JOHN DUNSFORD. EDMUND DONOVAN, our transatlantic Vice-President, is hoping to "come home" again in June. With the appearance of professional circuits he recalls old pro. meetings at Imber Court. There were running and walking events, the competitors being known as "pedestrians". Foot races alternated with whippet racing. It's good to see RICHARD LANGLEY training again. A very promising junior, he never completely stopped running, turning out for a jog every week or so. Now the bug seems to have got him again and after a few regular sessions he already shows signs of regaining fitness. Overheard at a track session: "You ought to get a season ticket to use Battersea track Jim, its much cheaper in the long run." To which came the reply, "No fear. I might get injured and not be able to use it!" items.s: Singing Laurie cycles home Laurie O'Hara finished second in a 25-kilometre veterans' race at Bruges in mid-June and won a bicycle, which he had to ride 13 miles home from the London boat. Singing Laurie cycles home At Bruges, Belgium in mid-June, Laurie O'Hara took on a field of 400 veterans over 25 kilometres. His training of late had been geared to 1500 metre running so he was well up at the start and he soon found himself in the lead. Loudspeakers on the pilot car relayed music to keep the competitors from being bored and as the race progressed Laurie found himself singing. Continuing to lead the race until about 13 miles, Laurie then had an attack of cramp but managed to keep going for second place behind the eventual winner a 2:22 marathon man. His problems had only just begun, however, for second prize proved to be a bicycle. Much argument eventually got him through the Customs and on to the boat with it but on arrival at London there was only one way to get the thing back to his home - mount it and start pedalling 13 agonizing miles. Laurie O'Hara Laurie O'Hara 2nd of 400 veterans over 25 kilometres at Bruges, mid-June 1975; prize was a bicycle Laurie O'Hara Laurie Bruges 25 km veterans race Bruges, Belgium London

items.sum: Report and full result of the Club 5¾ mile Road Race Championship at Wimbledon on 15 March 1975, won by John Stow, with Joe McDonald winning the handicap.
items.s: Stow wins 5¾m championship Report and full result of the Club 5¾ mile Road Race Championship at Wimbledon on 15 March 1975, won by John Stow, with Joe McDonald winning the handicap. Stow wins 5¾m championship MARCH 15th 1975 - WIMBLEDON. John Stow proved to be in good form for the approaching road relays and track season when he won the Club 5¾ mile Road Race Championship for the first time. Always around the front, he gained in confidence as the race progressed and eventually came home a clear winner by 15 seconds. Gerry North seems to be acquiring the habit of spending at least part of each Club race in a prone position. On this occasion he took a tumble over by the village with not a mile gone, and after picking himself up with a gashed leg and finding only a few runners behind him he manfully struggled back into the race. Simon Lloyd provided a shock for many. He joined the Club last summer and although we have not seen a great deal of him he has been steadily notching up around 50 miles per week. With hooped vest and pattering stride, Simon looked startlingly like one Allan Rushmer as he staked his claim for future runs in Belgrave colours. Returning to the Belgrave fold after a couple of years absence was Doug Brew and also prominent throughout were Leo Coy and Doug Jardine. Colin Pearson upset Pat O'Connor against the odds and Brian Gorman ('Don't put me in the relay team') had a remarkable run; but for most, onlookers and runners alike, the man of the race was Joe McDonald. Joe fought as only he knows how and was rewarded with first handicap prize and, more important, a victory over Chas. Manning. Handicap: 1. J.McDonald 26:15 (12:00); 2. L.Coy 26:17 (3:30); 3. items.s: Record run by Tony Brien Tony Brien set a new club marathon record of 2:17:20, finishing 12th of 2,051 starters in the Boston Marathon on 21 April 1975. Record run by Tony Brien The classic Boston Marathon was held on April 21st and in ideal conditions there were some sensational times. The race was won by Will Rogers (USA) in 2:09:55 and amongst the 22 competitors who beat 2:20 was Tony Brien, establishing a tremendous new Club Record of 2:17:20. Tony was 12th of the 2,051 starters. items.label: July 1975
items.sum: Humorous tale of Bill Laws being chased by a bear while running in a Swedish forest on a business trip.
items.s: A GRIZZLY TALE Humorous tale of Bill Laws being chased by a bear while running in a Swedish forest on a business trip. A GRIZZLY TALE A business trip to Sweden this spring gave Bill Laws the chance to sample cross country running Scandinavian style. Striding out over a carpet of pine needles he ran through the edge of the forest enjoying the peace and solitude. A deer browsed nearby and as Bill approached it moved slowly off into the denser brush. Then, from the direction of the deer's disappearance, shattering the tranquility, came a most hideous commotion. The undergrowth was torn apart and towering out into Bill's path came the grand-daddy of all bears, bellowing his disapproval of the human race and a certain Belgravian in particular! Now bears are mean. They can rip and tear and climb and swim ... and boy can they run. Another heart-stopping roar rent the air serving to wake our William from his shocked state, and with a turn of speed that could not have been matched by any but the legendary Wilson, he ran until his lungs were near to bursting. Yes he made it to safety but that was the only training session he did on the trip. After recounting the tale over a pint in the cosy surroundings of the 'Denmark' a wistful look came into his eyes and he muttered, "If only someone had a watch on me over that last mile .... it must have been a personal best." Bill Laws Bill Laws chased by a bear while running in Sweden on a business trip Bill Laws Bill William Wilson Wilson 'the legendary Wilson', invoked for his speed Sweden the 'Denmark'

items.label: July 1975
items.sum: Report and team result of the Belgrave/Southern Road Relay at Wimbledon on 5 April 1975, won by Thames Valley Harriers, with Belgrave Harriers 11th of 31 teams; includes fastest stage times and all twelve Belgrave times.
items.s: Thames Valley retain Belgrave Relay Report and team result of the Belgrave/Southern Road Relay at Wimbledon on 5 April 1975, won by Thames Valley Harriers, with Belgrave Harriers 11th of 31 teams; includes fastest stage times and all twelve Belgrave times. Thames Valley retain Belgrave Relay APRIL 5th 1975 - WIMBLEDON Belgrave/Southern Road Relay day, and once again the Hall bulged under the strain of holding nigh on 400 runners from 33 teams. Weeks of hard work from Gordon Biscoe culminated in another successful promotion although there was a complaint from Barry Jones of Hercules Wimbledon that for once we had not booked a fine day. As the afternoon grew colder, pointsmen and officials shivered in intermittent snow showers, and in these conditions Thames Valley Harriers came through the field well to win in a time 3 minutes faster than their last year's performance and only 4 seconds short of the record. The Bels reached home in 11th position - just about what should have been expected, although one somehow hopes for a miracle just because the race takes place over 12 stages and comparatively few clubs can maintain a top effort for that long. A closer look at the times however, reveals that each of our men put up a pretty solid performance, and with Messrs. Jardine, Lloyd and Coy all making the team for the first time, at least our Spring outfit had something of a 'new look'. Moreover, our team's final time was only 1:21 slower than last year when we led the race for three stages and eventually finished 5th. John Stow, '5¾' Champion for 1975, started out for the Bels. and clocking our fastest time of the day over the long stage, handed over to Jim Rimmer in 14th position in the middle of a line of runners with less than half a minute covering them. Aldershot were 12th, TVH 10th and Brighton & Hove, embarking upon a marvellous race for them, were 17th. Jim disposed of Blackheath and Shaftesbury on the first short stage with some spirited running, whilst Crawley AC, the leaders after one circuit, were rapidly overhauled by several clubs and began their decline to a final 31st. Presland took Aldershot into the lead on leg 3 but running even better was Standing (Brighton) who cut through the opposition to gain 2nd, only 8 secs. down, with 24:02. Gerry North, seemingly recovered from his fall in the '5¾', took us up past Feltham and into 11th place. Doug. Jardine found himself under attack from Blackheath's ex-international 'Kipper' Herring and the day's fastest short stage runner Barry Smith (Thurrock) who needed only 15:12 to scorch round the West Wimbledon hills. Grimly giving way to these two but no more, as the first of the afternoon's snow showers fell, our man handed over to Bill Weller. Up front, four minute miler Jim Douglas had eased TVH's black and blue colours into the lead with Aldershot still in contention 12 seconds behind. Brighton hit the front as stage 5 took its course and Bill Weller regained two positions for Belgrave at the expense of Portsmouth and Crawley athletes. From this point as large gaps began to open up in mid-field, we maintained 11th position until the end. Colin Pearson, as fit as he has ever been these days, ran our fastest short lap of 16:30 (equal 3rd fastest on his stage) to bring us to the half-way distance. Famous names came into the fray on lap 7 although team positions remained largely static. National Cross Country Champion Tony Simmons cut out a staggering 23:55 but only improved Luton's lot by 4 places - up to 13th but getting uncomfortably closer to our own reliable Pat O'Connor. Cambridge H slipped into 3rd through Keith Penny, TVH remained 2nd and still the men from Sussex kept the lead with Steve Ovett looking every inch the European Games 800m silver medallist and gliding up the sharp Wool Road incline as if it didn't exist. For Simon Lloyd it was his first time in the 'big time' and he stuck to his task well. Blackheath got by once more but he in turn put Thurrock behind Belgrave again. Meanwhile John Davies went into a good lead for TVH. On stage 9 Bob Holt shook things up for Hercules Wimbledon who had at one point languished as low as 20th. He went up 5 places and in the process passed John Phelan but once again the Bels held their ground as Blackheath slipped behind. Leo Coy continued as our 10th man on the road. How long is it since Belgrave had an Assistant General Secretary in the 'A' team? Leo had fought well for his place in the team and his reward was to run his lap without another runner in sight. Brighton had now begun to sag. They were 1½ minutes down on the 'Valley' and as their 11th runner set out he had the awesome sight of the course record holder limbering up to take over behind him in 3rd. Aldershot's Bernie Ford, a runners runner if ever there was, tore into the Brighton man's lead, took him, and then set about TVH, cutting their advantage from 2:33 to 18 secs! His time of 23:53 was the day's best. But Belgrave have their heroes too and Laurie O'Hara, chasing hard after Badgery of Hercules Wimbledon, took 34 seconds off of our rivals. And so to the last leg. Aldershot had left their final attack just too late and the 'Valley' came home 21 seconds to the good. Brighton were now in dire straits. Their last runner had failed to arrive and they pressed a reserve into service and gave him the unenviable task of salvaging 3rd place. His 18:50 might have been one of the slower times of the day but his efforts fully merited his 3rd team plaque as he gamely struggled round the course and just reached safety with runners fully two minutes faster breathing down his neck. As so often in the past, Alan Black was given the job of closing in for the Bels and he responded with our third sub-17 minute run of the day. items.label: July 1975
items.h: ARTHUR BRUCE CONQUERS THE COMRADES MARATHON
items.sum: Arthur Bruce's letter home from South Africa describing his run in the Comrades Marathon from Durban to Pietermaritzburg, finishing 401st of 1,500 starters in just over 8 hours.
items.s: ARTHUR BRUCE CONQUERS THE COMRADES MARATHON Arthur Bruce's letter home from South Africa describing his run in the Comrades Marathon from Durban to Pietermaritzburg, finishing 401st of 1,500 starters in just over 8 hours. ARTHUR BRUCE CONQUERS THE COMRADES MARATHON It's a Sunday and we are at Harrismith (next door to Ladysmith) after driving up from Zululand and it's bloody cold! We are quite close to the mountains on the reverse side. Well, it's over a week since the big one and I am pleased to report a successful run. Will bring back pictures, medal and newspaper cuttings. Everything went to plan the week before and I got out most days up to 10 miles especially running at altitude (6,800 feet) near Johannesburg. We went down to Durban by sleeper on Wednesday night which gave me two days at sea level. We hired a Volkeswagen and I had a good team seconding me with water, salt tablets and sponges. The start at Durban Town Hall at 6am was fantastic with television interviews although the field was cut to 1,500 starters as the novice entries were rejected (about 300). I started very slowly and fortunately it was fairly cool and I ran very much to schedule. Unfortunately Elsie lost me after seven miles because of the traffic pile-up. Imagine 1,500 runners each with a second in a car or on a motor-bike! The traffic was chaos although the police did a good job. I didn't see her again until I had covered 30 miles but I met a doctor who was running and who kept me supplied with glucose, salt tablets and water. We ran together for about 30 miles. I was very pleased to catch Doug. Sudbury of South London Harriers at 30 miles and I proceeded to beat him by 165 places ( half an hour). I was running well between 30 and 50 miles and taking refreshment every 30 minutes. Elsie was now in close attendance and I felt fine. At one stage I thought I would get a silver award for 7½ hours but started to get really tired at about 50 miles although I was still catching people. The last 4 km into Pietermaritzburg was rough but there was plenty of encouragement from bystanders. I even managed to catch somebody on the last lap on the track to record just over 8 hours, finishing 401st out of the 1,500 starters, tired but pleased. The first-aid tent looked like a battlefield afterwards. I felt OK until I sat down! When we drove back to Durban three hours later they were still finishing so I didn't do so bad. Nothing further than 10 miles now this year. Sunday I remained horizontal on the beach. You could tell everybody who had run on the 'Comrades', they were walking around like old men. On the Monday we drove up to Zululand for a wonderful week in the game parks. We walked 16 miles one day and viewed rhino, etc. at close quarters. Tomorrow we go to the Golden Gate National Park in the mountains, then back to Johannesburg and Pretoria where I'll get in a couple of jogs. Regards to all the lads - get ready for some training! Arthur Bruce ARTHUR BRUCE 401st of 1,500 starters in the Comrades Marathon, just over 8 hours; writer of the letter Elsie Elsie seconded Arthur Bruce in the Comrades Marathon Doug. Sudbury Doug. items.sum: Report and results of Southern League match 1 at Alexandra Park, Portsmouth, on 10 May 1975, where Belgrave were second to Ilford AC.
items.s: A fair start at Portsmouth Report and results of Southern League match 1 at Alexandra Park, Portsmouth, on 10 May 1975, where Belgrave were second to Ilford AC. A fair start at Portsmouth MAY 10th 1975 - ALEXANDRA PARK, PORTSMOUTH - SOUTHERN LEAGUE MATCH 1. The opening league match immediately provided the Bels with some stiff opposition. Ilford AC have been tipped as favourites for 1975 and in spite of not being at absolutely full strength they put together 135 match points to go straight to the top of the 25 clubs that contest the league. The Belgrave team still showed a few weaknesses with a couple of middle distance men unavoidably missing but these problems promised to be ironed out before the next match. It was on the field that our team looked most solid. Cliff Brooks, now Field Events Captain and temporarily forsaking the track to concentrate on the throws and jumps, led our strong men to some good scores. A double win from Steve White and Steve Crosbie in the long jump, a personal best vault from Reg Hopkins and very good shot putting from John Martin set an impressive standard that if maintained throughout the year should stand us in good stead. On the cinders we had four convincing wins with, of course, Steve White providing two of them in the sprints. John Bicourt led the 5,000 metres field home by a street and Leo Coy stormed down the final stretch to take the 'B' steeplechase. Newcomer Jim Evans showed a flash of great things to come in the 'B' 100 metres. Last away, he rocketed through the field and then just faded a little in the final 10 metres - a good performance, particularly as he has only just taken up the sport with a mere three weeks training behind him. Unfortunately Martin Scott again experienced hamstring problems but it was not too serious and hopefully he will be able to conquer that tenseness in his running and let the power flow. items.s: Note on the BAAB Decathlon incorporating the Southern Counties Championship at Crystal Palace on 3-4 May 1975, where Reg Hopkins scored 5650 and Cliff Brooks 6340 (the note calls Hopkins top Belgrave decathlete despite the lower score). In the first Decathlon competition of the year Reg Hopkins improved his best ever score to 5650 points with his outstanding mark being a long jump of 6.93 metres. The occasion was the BAAB Decathlon incorporating the Southern Counties Championship at Crystal Palace May 3rd/4th. Reg was 13th overall, 9th in the SCAAA competition, but still impressing that he is top Belgrave Decathlete and intends it to remain that way, Cliff Brooks scored 6340 points for 7th and 5th SCAAA. items.sum: Report and result of the club 10,000m championship for the Tom Carter Cup at Battersea Park on 21 May 1975, won by Laurie O'Hara for the sixth time.
items.s: O'Hara's sixth victory Report and result of the club 10,000m championship for the Tom Carter Cup at Battersea Park on 21 May 1975, won by Laurie O'Hara for the sixth time. O'Hara's sixth victory MAY 21st 1975 - BATTERSEA PARK - CLUB 10,000m CHAMPIONSHIP. With the report from the starter's gun, 23 Belgravians moved off to tackle the 10,000 metre Club Championship for the 'Tom Carter Cup'. A steady breeze ensured coolish conditions and a dry track, whilst the low evening sun made the lap-scorers' task just that little bit more difficult as they peered up the home straight. 'Moved off?' Well that would describe how the majority of the field set about the first of their 25 laps, but as far as Laurie O'Hara was concerned 'took off' would be nearer to the mark. As the tail enders entered the back straight for the first time, Laurie was already scooting past the dressing rooms looking for all the world as if he was putting in his finishing burst six miles too early. Lionel Mann was the only taker and it wasn't long before he too decided to let Laurie go it alone this year. Ere four laps were completed Laurie was lapping the back markers; and so it continued circuit after circuit until eventually only Alan Black was beaten by less than 400 metres. It was a good run for Alan over a distance at which we do not normally see him compete. Both Lionel and Gerry North looked fitter than of late, and, gaining a first class standard, Bob Smith made a most welcome return to the Belgrave scene. Who is going to put an end to Laurie's dominance in this event? In the last eight years he has only relinquished his hold on the cup twice, in 1969 to Bob Smith and 1970 to Lionel Mann, and the way he is going these days he could hold it a good while yet. items.sum: Report and results of Southern League match 2 at Wimbledon Park on 31 May 1975, where a weakened Belgrave team finished fourth but won the 4 x 100m relay.
items.s: League hopes crushed! Report and results of Southern League match 2 at Wimbledon Park on 31 May 1975, where a weakened Belgrave team finished fourth but won the 4 x 100m relay. League hopes crushed! MAY 31st 1975 - WIMBLEDON PARK - SOUTHERN LEAGUE MATCH 2. Belgrave faced three winning clubs from the first round in this crucial match at Wimbledon Park. Any of the clubs present could normally be rated as potential match winners but by a fluke they were all drawn together and some unlucky clubs worthy of better things were going to get less league points than they deserved. With Steve White and John Bicourt selected to compete at the British International Games on the same day our hopes took a tumble, and when sprinter Jim Evans became ill the day before the meeting all thoughts of winning had gone - it was to be a fight to avoid a real hammering. The afternoon opened on a high note when Reg Hopkins ran a brilliant 56.6 for a personal best in the 400m hurdles, gaining a clear victory. Paul Whitby immediately began to hand out the same sort of treatment to his rivals in the 'B' race until, leading down the home straight and desperately tired, he fell at the final barrier. It was a fall from which it seemed unlikely that he would recover but with badly cut legs he courageously managed to rise from the cinders and stagger on to the finish - still amazingly 2nd. These two again performed with distinction in the short hurdle race. Charlie Gillett, Martin Scott and Cliff Brooks covered for us in the sprints the latter notching up no less than seven individual performances plus a relay. Bill Kerr showed that Laurie O'Hara is not the only speedy veteran around with his 4:06 timing in the 1500m and Leo Coy improved his steeplechase again, getting closer to 10 minutes. Overall, however, our team slowly slipped beneath a tide of Windsor, Oxford and Aldershot vests. As the last events approached Herne Hill and the Bels were gripped in a struggle to avoid last place and as luck would have it, the relays gave us a chance to redeem ourselves slightly. Superb baton changing turned our sprinters, beaten in the individual events, into an unbeatable combination and they won by a full seven metres. Finally came the 4 x 400m, an event in which Oxford have not been beaten for several years. They are still unbeaten but the race was electrifying. In spite of good running from Philip Gee and Reg Hopkins we were 4th with two legs gone. Charlie Gillett then turned on a tremendous run. Closing a dozen metres, he took 3rd, then 2nd and coming off the last turn challenged for the lead. Martin Scott, not feeling at his best, also gave it the gun and although under severe pressure as the finish approached he kept 2nd and clocked 50.9 the same as Chas. Match Result: 1. Report and Belgrave results from the Surrey County AAA Championships at Motspur Park on 3, 5 and 7 June 1975, where Gillett, Hopkins and Whitby won titles and Belgrave retained the Surrey club championship. Bels retain Surrey Club Champ. GILLETT, HOPKINS AND WHITBY WIN COUNTY TITLES JUNE 3rd/5th/7th 1975 - MOTSPUR PARK - SURREY COUNTY A.A.A. CHAMPIONSHIPS. Full of confidence after his league outing the previous week, Reg Hopkins gave us our first win of the afternoon in the 400m hurdles. It is over the last 100m of any one lap race that Reg shows his strength and on this occasion he came through to outlean an Epsom & Ewell Harrier on the line. Paul Whitby equalled his best time in 6th place and when it later came to the 110m hurdles it was his turn to put down the Epsom man again. Neck and neck from blocks to tape, Paul just got there by the breadth of his whiskers! A win by Charlie Gillett over 400m gave the announcer the chance to give him some extra publicity, exhorting all to tune in to Charlie's "Honky Tonk" on Radio London. With the broadest of grins the Belgravian collected his trophy and took it off to be admired by the Gillett family. A best of 4:06.2 got Colin Pearson into the 1500m final and there he improved again to 4:05.5. John Stow ran a tactically perfect race. Running in the bunch but moving out and up whenever the current leader looked like breaking away, he reached 1200m with a crowd still round him. His all-out burst then devastated the field when they were least expecting it and as he raced away only Clive Thomas (TVH) could hold him. As expected, Thomas re-passed him in the home straight but John came home a clear second, beating several others who might have laid claim to the silver medal. The Club Competition is scored over all the Surrey Track Championships; and after Carl Lawton's winning walk and the performances of our relay runners and steeplechasers at the earlier meeting at Wimbledon Park, the Bels led the competition from start to finish. 200m: nq C.Gillett 23.5. 400m: 1. WHITE MAGIC Competing for the combined Oxford and Cambridge team against Harvard and Yale at Iffley Road, Oxford in June, Steve White again equalled his 200m club record of 21.6. At the same track in May he was clocked at 10.7 for 100m, another record equalling mark. Apart from Steve's windy 10.6 last year, four Belgravians share the 100m record: John Mitchell 1967 and 1969, Jim Vivian 1969, Cliff Brooks 1973, Steve White 1974 and 1975. items.s: Notes on Laurie O'Hara's 30:21.0 personal best in the Southern Counties AAA 10,000m at Crystal Palace, Doug Maughan's run there, and the club 3,000m championship won by O'Hara from Bill Kerr and Colin Pearson. What a great little runner Laurie O'Hara is. Running in the Southern Counties A.A.A. Championship 10,000m at Crystal Palace on April 16th he scored a marvellous 30:21.0 for a personal best. Anyone who is setting "pee-bees" as a veteran has got to be taken notice of - but a time like that is truly amazing. Laurie's position was 19th, the winner being Penny of Cambridge H in 28:49.8. Doug. Maughan was timed at 34:16.0 in 36th position, having clocked 16:35 a month earlier on the same track over 5,000m. The 3,000m Championship on May 14th gave Laurie the chance to churn out another good one - 8:31.0 - but this time he was followed by another Belgrave veteran who doesn't know when to give up. Bill Kerr ran 8:47 and right into the reckoning for subsequent team selection, beating Colin Pearson into the bargain. Colin nevertheless set his best ever time with 8:51. items.s: Bels bounce back Report and results of Southern League match 3 at Croydon on 21 June 1975, which Belgrave won to rise to 9th in the league, with Peter Crosbie breaking the club junior javelin record. Bels bounce back JUNE 21st 1975 - CROYDON - SOUTHERN LEAGUE MATCH 3. With three inter-club wins plus the Surrey Championships victory in the previous fortnight Belgrave's fortunes were waxing strong, and in the third league match we slammed the opposition by a wide margin to rise from 15th to 9th in the league table. For some weeks 17 year old Peter Crosbie had been on the verge of great things in the Javelin with a best of 53 metres, a Surrey Junior win, 2nd in the London schools and that l-o-n-g no-throw. The time was ripe for a legal 'big one' and it came at last with a throw of 54 metres plus. That pleased him greatly but as the competition drew to a close Peter launched an even better attempt, measured at 55.78 metres, beating our twenty year old junior record (incidentally set with a lighter implement anyway). Experimenting with a shorter run-up has paid dividends for Peter and once again he stays ahead of Olympic Champion Klaus Wolfermann's age/distance schedule, pinned on his bedroom wall. The obvious target now is 60 metres. Steve White again picked up maximum score in each of his events and he was backed up by Jim Evans, equalling his 11.3 best again, and Martin Scott who does us great service by regularly turning out and cruising below his best with that nagging leg injury. Cliff Brooks was in sharp high jumping form, near his best ever, and he too put out some good javelin throws. Our hurdlers and jumpers were devastating and with Leo Coy straight back off his holiday to compete, Lionel Mann gamely vaulting the barriers to fill a gap in our ranks, and John Bicourt offering his services after his trip to Lapland was cancelled, it was a good all-round effort. items.sum: Report and Belgrave results of the British Athletics League Cup match at West London Stadium on 22 June 1975, where Belgrave's second place behind Hillingdon took them into the semi-finals.
items.s: THROUGH TO BRITISH CUP SEMI'S Report and Belgrave results of the British Athletics League Cup match at West London Stadium on 22 June 1975, where Belgrave's second place behind Hillingdon took them into the semi-finals. THROUGH TO BRITISH CUP SEMI'S JUNE 22nd 1975 - WEST LONDON STADIUM - BRITISH ATHLETICS LEAGUE CUP. At last! Fourth in 1973, third in 1974 and now Belgrave have reached the BAL Cup semi-finals with a well fought second team place at West London. The mark of a good team is the ability to overcome the team problems that always arise and still do well. We certainly had the problems, for of our fifteen team members only two had not competed the previous day in the league, and after warming up for the 100 metres, Steve White, down for four events including relays, had to pull out with a knee problem. Only fifteen minutes after strolling into the arena Jim Evans was on the blocks for the 100m. With virtually no warm-up he did all that was asked of him and more, finishing 2nd behind the 10.7 of the Hillingdon runner and surely much closer to him than his 11.3 suggested. Early points were piled up by Reg Hopkins who placed 2nd over 400mH to Hillingdon's Shirley and then won the long jump. Alan Black cantered to an easy 5000m win and Paul Whitby again scored heavily in the high hurdles. With only two teams to qualify though, it was a close battle and Mitcham, Belgrave and Hillingdon (National League Div.1) took turns to head the race for points. Charlie Gillett chipped in with an emergency 400m as Martin Scott took on Steve's mantle in the 200m and both were on or near their seasonal bests. Equalling his previous day's 1.85, Cliff Brooks was again jumping well. John Bicourt's clear steeplechase win was followed by Laurie O'Hara's determined 10,000m run - what a hard way to score points and only the previous weekend he had been tackling 25km on the road in Belgium. Another mighty heave by Peter Crosbie kept us in contention and it all hung on the relays. We didn't have to win them but we did have to beat Mitcham. A false start by Martin Scott had spectators biting their finger nails but at the second attempt they were away and sure enough Brooks, Gillett and Evans chased Hillingdon hard and gained 2nd spot. Now the 4 x 400m. The National League club went away only to be disqualified as Mitcham and the Bels ran together for the first two laps. Charlie Gillett prised a gradually opening lead on leg 3 with an estimated sub-50 clocking and with Martin Scott to follow we made it! Our semi-final is to be held on Sunday, August 10th - venue uncertain as yet but possibly Crystal Palace, Cwmbran, Kirkby or Gateshead. items.sum: Walking notes covering the club's walking team prospects, Allan Callow's walks in New Zealand, Shaun Lightman's Leicester and Inter-Counties wins, and Ray Middleton's second place in the Southern Area 50km.
items.s: WALKING Walking notes covering the club's walking team prospects, Allan Callow's walks in New Zealand, Shaun Lightman's Leicester and Inter-Counties wins, and Ray Middleton's second place in the Southern Area 50km. WALKING The prospects of winning a National this year look rather bleak, with three down and one to go despite our progressive strength in depth. It has been extremely encouraging to have seen the turn-out in some of the recent races and being able to finish teams in the National 20 miles and the Vauxhall 10km on the same day. On January 25th Allan Callow competed in a 5,000m track walk during the New Zealand Games. He took the lead after 1 km but lost a shoe in the tightly packed bunch and after taking time out to replace it, clocked 24:09.2 for 5th. A week later, however, he gained his revenge by winning a 10,000m track event by over 2½ minutes with a time of 48:45.6. Shaun Lightman (Met WC) had an incredible weekend over the spring holiday. He won the Leicester Mercury 20 Miles on the Saturday, and then collected the Inter-Counties double at Crystal Palace on Sunday May 25th/ Monday May 26th with 45:08 for 10km and 12:45 for 3km. Carl Lawton was no less busy even if he didn't gain any wins when he followed up his 9th at Leicester with 4th 46:08 and 5th 13:24 at the Palace. L.Dick placed 11th in the 10km event with 48:38. Ray Middleton was placed second in the Southern Area 50km event at Basildon on June 21st. He recorded 4:50:15 behind Bob Dobson's 4:42. items.sum: G.S.D.'s report and results of the Southern Counties AAA 10 miles road walking championship at Selsdon on 22 February 1975, won by Carl Lawton with Belgrave second team on countback, plus the Middlesex Championship at Enfield won by Belgrave as a team.
items.s: Down Featherbed Lane G.S.D.'s report and results of the Southern Counties AAA 10 miles road walking championship at Selsdon on 22 February 1975, won by Carl Lawton with Belgrave second team on countback, plus the Middlesex Championship at Enfield won by Belgrave as a team. Down Featherbed Lane FIRST AND SECOND IN COUNTY 10m CHAMPS. FEBRUARY 22nd 1975 SURREY - SELSDON. This year's S.C.A.A.A. Ten Miles Road Walking Championship was held from Surrey W.C. headquarters at Selsdon. Our numbers were weakened by the absence of John Bromley, still suffering from the effects of an accident, but on the course to give support. As the field settled down to tackle the uphill slog to Warlingham they were led by Paul Nihill and Carl Lawton, then along past Chelsham and Farleigh to the half-way mark where Paul was opening up a lead. Dick Tanner and Ray Middleton were walking together in fourth place followed by a host of Surrey W.C. vests. Then came the rest of our team interspersed with more opposition vests. After a few twists and turns the road descended amidst some woods into Featherbed Lane and a long downhill back to a roundabout and a left turn to the finish. Nihill had come under the judges ban leaving Carl with a precarious lead on the popular Peter Selby (Surrey W.C.) which he maintained to the finish. Then a long wait - where were Ray and Dick? Were they lost? The resourceful Ray had asked a bus driver the way to the finish. Dick pipped him for third place, then came the Surrey W.C. hordes and we began to count the points. Could our fourth man do it? After a great effort Dave McMullen finished twelfth to give S.W.C. and ourselves 20 points each, Surrey gaining the day by the higher placing of their fourth man. Our President, hot-foot from the morning's jumble sale walked his usual determined and stylish race, and other stalwarts who between them have won many awards for us in the past, closed in. Congratulations to Dick on gaining his first county medal but what of Dave McMullen who added yet another to his tally. When asked how many county medals he had, he couldn't say, which isn't surprising as he won his first one in 1939. What a man! Many years ago Featherbed Lane was a winding lane which led to a road high up on the Surrey hills. Subsequent building operations are approaching it but the delightful name persists. Goodnight! items.s: National 20m Report and result of the National 20 miles walk on the Isle of Man on 14 June 1975, where Belgrave were fifth team, with a note on the reserves' team win at Luton. National 20m JUNE 14th 1975 - ISLE OF MAN. The first home National Championship to be held overseas. That was the prospect of the National 20 Miles. Belgrave ventured across the water with an 18 strong contingent - 11 walkers, 4 wives, 2 youngsters and 1 President, Held on a 4½ mile course in the late afternoon, the earlier part of the day being spent time-wasting, an uneventful race progressed with Bob Dobson (Southend) being the eventual winner. Bels first man home was again Ray Middleton who had passed a slowing Carl Lawton at 16 miles. John Dunsford followed and then John Hall (at last) dipped under 3 hours. P.B's were also produced by Bob Picton and Ron Day. In spite of all this we could only finish 5th team. The race was followed by a buffet supper and a long trip home after an enjoyable weekend. Meanwhile over at Luton our reserves were sweeping up in the Open 10km by taking first team place as well as fourth scorer Dave McMullen taking the Vets award. 1. R.Dobson (Southend) 2:36:26; 2.
