items.label: March 1976
items.sum: Humorous account of a Sunday training run in Richmond Park where an unknown runner, revealed as Steve Ovett, was chased down by 'Supergorm' Brian, with a footnote listing Ovett's achievements.
items.s: MY NAME'S BRIAN, WHAT'S YOURS? Humorous account of a Sunday training run in Richmond Park where an unknown runner, revealed as Steve Ovett, was chased down by 'Supergorm' Brian, with a footnote listing Ovett's achievements. MY NAME'S BRIAN, WHAT'S YOURS? LOCATION: RICHMOND PARK TIME: ONE BLEAK SUNDAY MORNING The day started as any other Sunday with an effusion of runners from Belgrave Hall laughing and chattering their way across Wimbledon Common to Robin Hood Gate prior to breaking up into smaller fighting groups in Richmond Park. The 'A' pack on commencing their climb up the Spankers Hill slope were joined by one unknown runner striding effortlessly in a faded blue track-suit. Other than exchanging a few witticisms nothing further was said although it became apparent that he was in no way discomforted by the pace. The pack, on reaching the Richmond Gate turn, were soon aware that here was no mortal man as he moved swiftly into a clear lead leaving the remainder of the pack struggling in his wake. But wait! All is not lost. Emerging from the pack like a thunderbolt came a figure - is it a man? is it a plane? No it's "SUPERGORM" in hot pursuit. Our hero was soon closing on the newcomer and quickly drew alongside as their breathtaking speed drew them clear of the labouring pack in their rear, and they were soon disappearing into the trees in the far distance. The silence was only broken by the words of our hero echoing across the valley. "MY NAME'S BRIAN, WHAT'S YOURS?" Of course Steve Ovett * ruminating over a cup of tea afterwards did say who was that old bugger matching strides with me - and of course we could have told him. 'Boofer' Bruce * 800 metre European Cup Winner 1975; four minute miler; 2nd in European Games at 18 years of age in 1:45.9; rated 10th in the world in '74 and 14th in '75; English National Cross Country Junior Champion '75........ items.label: March 1976
items.h: The City Road Races - New Year's Day
items.sum: Gordon Doubleday's report on the New Year's Day City road races, with Carl Lawton fifth in the three miles road walk and Laurie O'Hara winning the veterans' 10 miles.
items.s: The City Road Races - New Year's Day Gordon Doubleday's report on the New Year's Day City road races, with Carl Lawton fifth in the three miles road walk and Laurie O'Hara winning the veterans' 10 miles. The City Road Races - New Year's Day We were involved in two events of what is now becoming a regular meeting. The promoters have to keep an eye on the established races and with the county championships two days later there were no distance events for senior men. The first race in which we were concerned was the three miles road walk (invitation) and the field included many internationals. Our first man home was Carl Lawton in 20:53.6 (under 7 minute miles!) in fifth position. First home was Brian Adams (Leicester) in 19:57.6 followed by Olly Flynn (Basildon), Peter Marlow (Southend) and Roger Mills (Ilford) so Carl was in very good company. Richard Tanner was 22nd in 22:52.0, Mike Scamell (Newham) 24th in 23:00.0 and Ray Middleton 27th in 23:25.0. As Ray approached the finish one of the crowd called out "You want another 50 miles, Ray!" The biggest "field" of the day was the veterans' 10 miles which attracted about 70 runners. The starters gun appeared to be a signal for the rain. Luckily the spectators were able to get some cover whilst the drenched runners covered their seven laps. Our Laurie was always with the leaders and over the closing stages the O'Hara pressure was applied enabling him to gain a clear win in 52:26. In last year's race which was open to all Laurie was the first veteran home. Joe Dooley ran his determined race to finish in 30th position to beat the hour by four seconds. With New Year's Day 1977 being on a Saturday we wonder what the programme will be. Amongst the spectators was Jack Williams and his wife who had travelled up from Brighton. Jack still keeps fit and indeed looks it. items.label: March 1976
items.sum: Walking secretary's notes welcoming Jane Pritchard as the club's first female member, reviewing the winter walking season, plans for summer handicaps, and news of walkers overseas.
items.s: WALKING Walking secretary's notes welcoming Jane Pritchard as the club's first female member, reviewing the winter walking season, plans for summer handicaps, and news of walkers overseas. WALKING A new dawn on the horizon and a new challenge. Those ancient Belgrave corridors for so long a hideaway for the male chauvinist now echo to the sound of feminine charm as a result of the solid wooden doors being thrown open to all-comers. It was with great satisfaction that we noted that the first application for full membership from a female should come from an active walker. Jane Pritchard, already known to a few in the Club, will be displaying the Belgrave colours as of right during the coming season. Thus it is with hope that she and her compatriots will be known as 'one of us' and not a girl walker. On the less glamorous side we have now come to the end of the winter season. Success has not been easy to come by and for the first time in some years we did not win an open 7 mile team race. Although placed second on three occasions, we slipped to fourth and fifth in the Met. Police and Enfield races respectively. If, however, strength in depth is anything to go by it will not be long before we get back to our rightful position. Some of the turn-outs in recent months have been very encouraging although one must not be led into thinking that there is always someone else who will turn out if you don't. Carl Lawton continued his good early season performances by being placed in all the opens and winning the Belgrave race. We were unfortunately plagued with a spate of disqualifications from which the recipients, one hopes, will have learnt their errors. As was stated in the last issue of 'The Belgravian' we have a strong junior team 'on paper' but although we won the Surrey Walking Club promotion with five in twelve, we could not line a team up for the Chelmsford races in January. This situation is always unfortunate for those who have put in the effort to go and find themselves yet again walking as an individual. The winter season has slowly churned out some very good performances from some of the second string team, with Bob Picton showing the form that has been missing for a few seasons. Ron Day, in only his first season, broke the hour for 7 miles and is now producing good 10 mile times. Tim Thorogood has moved into senior ranks with incredible ease and is still only just eighteen. Jonathon Dunsford, who won his last race as a Youth at Chelmsford with only one day left in the age group, is now well capable of keeping up with those twice his age. On the more personal side it is good to see John Dunsford on the roadside, and in the middle sometimes when officiating, after his illness. Rumour has it that he is hoping to get back to work soon and start light training - handicapper please note. The rankings compiler in the last issue wishes to apologise to John Keown for the error in his 20 kilo's list. His time should have read 117:09 and not as printed. Finally, this summer we are returning to having handicaps with prizes in the three evening 3 km walks. An overall prize will also be awarded for the best three out of five races including the Club Championship 3 km at Motspur Park and the 10 km at Battersea. NEWS FROM OVERSEAS: Allan Callow is probably returning to these shores from New Zealand later this year and will be preceded by Graham Seatter, a leading New Zealand walker. Alan Lucas who graced us with his presence in 74/75 has now set up in the hotel business and misses those nostalgic cold evenings around Wimbledon. Also news of Dave De Bondi in Australia who has now bought himself a plot of land and is progressing in his house building ambitions. John Knifton has also written (he represents the U.S.A. regularly) informing of his exploits with dogs while out training. Carl Lawton Walking Secretary. items.label: March 1976
items.sum: Gordon Doubleday's report on the G.L.C. 10 miles walk championship in Battersea Park, where Carl Lawton won in a personal best and Belgrave took the team title.
items.s: London Pride Gordon Doubleday's report on the G.L.C. 10 miles walk championship in Battersea Park, where Carl Lawton won in a personal best and Belgrave took the team title. London Pride FEBRUARY 14th 1976 - BATTERSEA PARK - G.L.C. 10 MILES CHAMPIONSHIP. The former London County Council encouraged sport to the extent of promoting championships which included a Ten Miles Road Walk. When the authority was enlarged to become the Greater London Council the championships were continued and anybody who lives or works within their boundaries can compete. The walk has attracted leading walkers and clubs and we have in the past provided both individual and team winners. This year's event was held in Battersea Park on the 14th February, a dry but cold day, the course being five laps of the park with the first two laps lengthened. Right from the start Carl Lawton led the way from Paul Nihill (Croydon H.) with our other men well placed. We suffered an early mishap when Tim Thorogood came under the judge's ban. As the laps went by the leaders showed their class by pulling away from the rest but it was good to see our lads consolidating their positions. Over the last lap Carl powered his way to a fine win in 71 mins. 50 secs. - a personal best and a time few have beaten. His fine walking drew praise from all who were there. With individual honours decided interest became focused on the team title. Soon to arrive was Richard Tanner who has established himself as a regular scorer in our teams. John Hall gave us another solid performance (it must be the Brighton air!). Knowing that Ray Middleton was somewhere around we didn't have to wait long before our long-distance champion obliged to make us the first club with four men in. The points tally proved us winners. Of our others mention must be made of Ron Day who hasn't been walking a year but is developing a good sound style and improves every time out - proof of regular, dedicated and conscientious training. Our Newham A.C. member, Mike Scammell is another who is forcing his way to the front and will soon be a name to be reckoned with. So, with individual and team wins in this event Belgravians came away from Battersea Park proud to have collected a double victory in this London Championship. Gordon Doubleday 1. What a superb winter season Carl Lawton has had. Late news is that he successfully retained his hold on the Basingstoke '10' - winning by nearly three minutes in 74:59 with the Bels taking 1st team for the EIGHTH consecutive year. One week later he took the Southern RWA '10' in 73:58 and again excellent backing from the rest of the team - Richard Tanner 3rd, Ray Middleton 5th and Tim Thorogood 6th - meant that the Bels won the team title. As seen below Carl featured prominently at each of the recognised distances according to the UK Best Performers List for 1975 and with his latest form must be rated as a possible for the Olympics. items.label: March 1976
items.sum: John Thresher's letter from Regina, Saskatchewan, describing his family's emigration to Canada, the journey west, settling in, his running and cross-country skiing there, and the people and places he misses.
items.s: 'LETTER FROM CANADA' John Thresher's letter from Regina, Saskatchewan, describing his family's emigration to Canada, the journey west, settling in, his running and cross-country skiing there, and the people and places he misses. 'LETTER FROM CANADA' by John 'Alistair Cook' Thresher As we roll forward into another year, it seems an appropriate time to record some details of our life in the first eight months in a new country and to give some early impressions of the different life-style. We left London Airport on April 21st on a 747 Jumbo en route for Regina, in the heart of the Canadian Prairies. Our first stop was Montreal where we had planned to spend a day or two and collect our car, which we had despatched from London some five weeks earlier. However, Quebec and Montreal, as every Olympic fan will now know, have bad strike records. A longshoremens' strike ensured that our car could not be landed for an indeterminate period. It was necessary to replan the next 1,800 miles of our journey. Like the pioneers of less than 100 years ago, we decided to go by rail, on the Canadian Pacific Railway. Montreal is an exciting city. The old French quarter intrigued us particularly, with its historic old churches and official buildings and superb back-street restaurants so reminiscent of Paris. The modern buildings and underground shopping complexes are also very impressive. We travelled by rail to Toronto and stopped for two nights. It is a clean, bustling more modern city, dominated by the large bank buildings in the downtown area. We took a coach to Niagara Falls and were duly impressed by the incredible, awesome power of the water as we stood so close to the edge and clung on to the children for dear life! We met Derek Fernee briefly, who seems to have settled in well in Toronto and is enjoying life. The rail journey across Canada was an experience not to be missed. We had not realised before that the Canadian Pacific Railway had linked British Columbia in the West and the older parts of the East less than 100 years ago. Between Winnipeg and Vancouver lay 1,000 miles of grass land with the impenetrable Rocky Mountains beyond. The journey took 36 hours, but we were well looked after by the Dining car attendant (an ex-Blackpool fellow), and we had very comfortable accommodation. There was an observation car which was the favourite spot as we skirted the northern shore of Lake Superior, still covered in the remnants of the winter ice. We arrived in Regina at 5.30 a.m. on a wet Monday morning. I have since heard of a fellow who did the same and immediately re-boarded the train and didn't get out until Calgary, where he has lived ever since! Our furniture hadn't arrived and so we had to live in a hotel for a few days. Our house was ready, but empty, so like true pioneers we borrowed and hired necessities and decided to move in. Although it was then May, spring had scarcely begun and the temperature was slow to rise. I was soon out running through the park and round the lake which was flooded by the snow-melt. I was still being troubled by a sore tendon which had been aggravated by a ferocious bare-footed sprint down the Ridgway, S.W.20. against a certain Belgrave Olympian (did I say bare-footed?!!!). The first of many new friends we have made were an English couple from Feltham who have been here since 1965. Joe Turnham was a very useful half-miler and is the same age as myself. He even dug up a picture of Mitcham Youth's road relay in 1958 with us both fighting out the first leg! I ran in a 10 mile road race (my first ever) in 100°F in early July. I was desperately unfit and I really thought I was never going to make the finish for third and a silver pot (62 minutes, would you believe!). Since then I have run a few miles more and got reasonably fit by running most lunch times around the lake with scores of middle-aged joggers. The enthusiasm is incredible, the standards are abysmal - it suits me fine! Regina hosted the Western Canada Summer Games on its new all-weather Chevron track in August and it was the first time the public had seen a big track and field meeting. There were no outstanding performances by English standards, except by Diane Jones, the pentathlete, who could be a medal contender at the Olympics. I met Derek Boosey there, now a Canadian National Jumps coach. He is resident in Quebec but travels a great deal. I raced in September in Saskatoon in a 5 mile cross-country race and finished 21st out of 50 or so. This time the standard was much higher. Then, in October, I drove 500 miles to Prince Albert and back to run in the Saskatchewan cross-country championships. The temptation was a place in the first seven and a trip to the National in Vancouver. I finished a close-up 11th but was a little handicapped by not wearing spikes and as the race was run in five inches of snow and -2° C, this didn't help! Then the weather improved and I was running my 10 miles on Sunday morning in mid-November in shorts. The weather has been generally very good by Saskatchewan standards and I have kept running outdoors despite temperatures of -25° C and - 30° C (yes, that's 50-60° of frost!). Many days, however, have been only just below freezing and the air here is so dry it almost feels warm. My latest craze is cross-country skiing. I now make excuses not to run and go out on the ski-trails instead. It's very hard work if you attack it instead of cruising along, but as I become more proficient I can glide more and push less. I am hoping to be able to go on all-day excursions next winter, together with several other enthusiasts, with rucksacks on our backs. Mavis, Hannah and Neil seem to have adapted to the way of life, which admittedly is more comfortable and relaxing. We have more time together as a family and, talking of families, we are expecting an increase in June! My job has proved to be very interesting and rewarding. I have travelled extensively to Victoria, Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Ottawa, Toronto and Thunder Bay, sometimes by light 'plane or float 'plane.). The economy is very healthy out in the West, principally due to the abundant natural resources - wheat, oil, gas, potash and many other minerals and crops. Saskatchewan has tremendous potential yet to be realised and unemployment and inflation are very low by world standards. The population is under one million in a geographical area much larger than the U.K. The forests and lakes in the north are almost uninhabited, with no real roads. The fishing and hunting are unbelievable, as I found out on a thrilling fishing trip last year. Our summer weekends we spend at the "beaches" - unspoilt lakes with swimming from sandy beaches and fishing and boating facilities, all within a short car journey. We barbecue steaks by the shore in amongst the trees and this year we are going to invest in a large tent and canoe. Of course, we go through periods of nostalgia for family, friends, the English scenery, Chipstead, Wimbledon, Young's bitter, Belgrave Hall and Lauriston Cottage, The "Rawalpindi", Match of the Day, Fulham F.C. (I must stop before tears stain the page)! We hope to be back for a holiday in 1977 and to make regular visits in future. We would love to hear from anyone who has time to write and, better still, we would love to be visited. I shall be at the Olympics in Montreal this year and I hope to meet John Bicourt there. If there are any others who are going to make the trip, please let me know. John Thresher and family. Regina, Saskatchewan. January, 1976. items.sum: Track and field notes: Leo Coy's statistics of the 1975 league matches with lists of the club's point scorers (headed by Cliff Brooks' 122 points), then winter news of Jim Evans, Charlie Gillett and Brian Gorman and the season's new members.
items.s: TRACK AND FIELD Track and field notes: Leo Coy's statistics of the 1975 league matches with lists of the club's point scorers (headed by Cliff Brooks' 122 points), then winter news of Jim Evans, Charlie Gillett and Brian Gorman and the season's new members. TRACK AND FIELD Leo Coy has again been giving his slide rule a bashing, measuring up the statistics of the 1975 league matches. It's nice to see that the percentage of points in our previously weakest events - discus, high jump and triple jump - has risen tremendously. It comes as no surprise to learn that the 800 metres is now our weakest event whilst the long jump, both hurdle races and the three sprints and relays are far and away our strongest. Thirtytwo Belgravians made up our six teams and for the first time we provided a competitor for every single event throughout the entire season. Leo has also compiled a list of the point scorers EXCLUDING relays. As the sprinter and field event man has distinct advantages over the middle distance runner when it comes to scoring in more than one event per match, we show two lists below. It must also be borne in mind that a regular 'A' string competitor can appear in these lists below his 'B' string team mate for in the Southern League, a 5th place in the 'A' event scores less than a 'B' win. Nevertheless they make interesting reading and particularly highlight Cliff Brooks' staggering total of 122 points - over twice as many as the next man and more than the entire team scored in three matches! Figures in brackets indicate no. of relay runs. Points totals do not include relays. We look forward to Jim Evans' 1976 season with great interest. Last year, his first in athletics, he gave us some exciting runs improving as the summer wore on. A hard winter's training at Crystal Palace alongside international Steve Green (they share the same coach) has led to a couple of wins over 60 metres, timed at 7.0 and 7.2, the latter being a victory at Cosford over GB representative Aston Moore. In a race in January James was down to 6.8, just a shade behind Green who clocked the same time and ahead of Epsom's Paul Lavender (10.7 100m last year) and Herc. Wimb's John Gostelow. Surrey 400 metre champion Charlie Gillett is another to have put in a solid winter in a determined effort to raise the standard of our league 800 metre runs. Regular sessions with Brian Gorman of up to 8 miles including long strides' has done them both a lot of good. Veteran Brian suffers a lot of wisecracks but he is a changed character these days, rarely rarely turning training runs into races as was his wont. In fact he is running so well presently that he could make his mark on the track in the steeplechase. The track and field team has gained several new members since last summer. Martin Smith, a decathlete who knows what sub-50 400 metres are like, was previously a member of Crawley AC. He becomes eligible to compete in our teams in mid-summer and is aiming for a good 400 metre hurdles time - watch out Reg. Hopkins, Paul Whitby and Cliff Brooks! From Ghana comes 20 year old Ernest Obeng, an impressive sprinter who has recorded 10.8 for 100 metres in his home country, whilst another African, Lawal Bichi, prefers the longer distances and looks as if he has a lot of potential. At last we have some big young men taking an interest in the field events. Brian Marmion, one of our keenest young runners, has encouraged his two meaty brothers to become members and join the weight sessions at Belgrave Hall. Patrick is 20 years old and 6'4", whilst Philip is 18 and 6'1". They could provide a welcome boost to our throwing events. Junior Captain Adrian Cook has also been talent scouting and has signed up Roland Patten - just 16 years old and a delicate 14 stone. 1. C.Brooks 122 (6) 2. R.Hopkins 58 (3) 3. S.White 53 (7) 4. items.sum: Alan Mead's profile of Belgrave miler John Davies: his switch from football after injury in 1955, Stampfl's interval schedule, his 1956 and 1958 seasons against the world's best (including Billy Morton's Mile in Dublin, 1957), his marriage to the runner Pam, and his marathon running in the 1970s, with a footnote on Gordon Pirie still racing.
items.s: SPOTLIGHT on JOHN DAVIES Alan Mead's profile of Belgrave miler John Davies: his switch from football after injury in 1955, Stampfl's interval schedule, his 1956 and 1958 seasons against the world's best (including Billy Morton's Mile in Dublin, 1957), his marriage to the runner Pam, and his marathon running in the 1970s, with a footnote on Gordon Pirie still racing. SPOTLIGHT on JOHN DAVIES The crowd at Dublin's Lansdowne Road rugby stadium buzzed with anticipation. It was July 24th, 1957 and in sunny conditions over 28,000 had gathered to watch some of the great milers of the day in action and who knows, maybe witness a four minute mile run in Ireland. The excitable Irish brogue of Billy Morton, the meeting's famous organiser, came over the public address system further increasing the tension: "Will you all be coming out now for Billy Morton's Mile." Cheering shook the stadium as the competitors assembled for the start, amongst them Brian Hewson - Britain's future European 1,500M champion, Gordon Pirie - silver medallist in the previous year's Olympic 5,000M in Melbourne and world record holder over 3,000M, Ron Delaney of Eire - the Olympic 1,500M champion, and John Davies of Belgrave Harriers representing the A.A.A. Unfortunately the race was to take place on a spongy grass track so it was really expecting too much for anyone to beat four minutes but nevertheless as the gun was fired the Belgravian and John Cameron, also representing the A.A.A. went to the front and taking turns in the lead, they hauled the field round for the half distance in two minutes flat. Inevitably the pace slowed as the soft surface took its toll but again the crowd roared mightily as the high stepping Delaney, wearing the emerald green singlet of Eire went to the front and held on to the tape in 4:09.7. Hewson placed 2nd, a shade behind, with Pirie 3rd. Our man was not placed but once again had made his presence felt in a top class field. John was born on 25th July, 1931 and has spent the great majority of his life living in Pimlico, the heart of Belgrave country. He went to St. Peter's School in Lower Belgrave Street but unlike today's schoolboys, the pupils were not able to take part in any organised sport at that time due to the war and the constant threat of bombing raids. At 14 years of age he left school and went into the building trade to train as an estimator. Football now began to play a very important part in John's life. In the next ten years he progressed to playing for Wimbledon and Kingstonian and also spent a year on Tottenham Hotspur's amateur books. At 23, whilst playing inside forward for Kingstonian in February 1955, he received a severe injury to his right thigh that was to change his life. The injury necessitated a six week spell with his leg heavily bandaged, and by April when the bandaging was removed, the muscles of his leg had begun to wither. To build them up again he began to run regularly at Battersea Park track and there, of course, he soon met members of Belgrave Harriers and in particular the renowned athletic coach Franz Stampfl. His natural talent was immediately spotted by Stampfl: "If you train you could run fast!" Before long he was hooked on running and became a Belgrave member in May, 1955. On reflecting now, John says that taking up this sport was the finest move he made in his life. In the Club Championships of 1955 he ran in the 1 mile and clocked 4:27 for 3rd place behind Jack Brown's 4:23. Brian Hallowell, who was to become John's training partner and rival, placed 2nd. The club records for 880yds. and 1 mile at this time stood to R.T.(Bob) Taylor with 1:53.6 and Jack Brown 4:11.8. John returned to Kingstonian Football Club to play a few more matches but finally decided to concentrate on training for running. In October 1955, together with Brian Hallowell, he embarked upon Stampfl's schedule for milers, training mostly at the track at the Duke of York's Barracks in Chelsea's Kings Road, during the lunch hour. Stampfl, a strong advocate of interval training with the stopwatch, left for Australia at about this time but his ideas on training were all set out in his book "Stampfl on Running". John followed the schedules to the letter. Such training may seem slightly dated now after Cerutty, Lydiard and the like have shown other ways to train. Nevertheless, Stampfl's methods had produced 4 minute milers and there are still few athletes who would not be happy to attain such a standard. The schedule was as follows:- Mondays: 10 x 440yds. in 70 secs. during October reducing to 60 secs. by May. Interval between each effort 2½ minutes. Tuesdays: 5 x 880yds. 2:20 (Oct.) down to 2:00 (May) 10 mins. interval. Wednesdays: as Monday. Thursdays: 4 x 1,320 yds. 3:40 (Oct.) down to 3:15 (May) 10 mins. interval. Fridays: 6 miles steady. Saturdays: Cross country. Sundays: Rest. The intervals were regarded as the most important part of each session. A shorter rest than is necessary to bring recovery to a certain level would result in the work being too severe - a breaking down instead of building up and at worst non-completion of the session. On the other hand too much recovery and the session failed in its objective to gradually improve. By December things were really going well and John remembers Tom Carter shouting through the railings at the "Dukes": "You'll be burnt up by Christmas". The ¼ mile sessions came along a treat and the times floated down to reach an even 60 seconds by February but the ½ and ¾ mile sessions were found to be a lot tougher; the ¾'s still being stuck on 3:28 at the beginning of March. As those ¼ mile sessions were regarded as being the "rest days" between the days of really hard work, they were relaxed for a while to 65 seconds. Immediately the ¾ miles dropped to 3:21 and then 3:15 within two weeks. In April 1956 the season opened for John with a couple of wins in inter-club races, first over 1 mile and then over 880 yards in a time of 1:57.8. By May the end of Stampfl's schedule was achieved and time trials began to take the place of the odd session. During one of these lunch time trials, tailing Brian Hewson, John returned a comfortable 1:56 for the "half" and a A.A.A. official who had been watching was sufficiently impressed to tell him that he would try to get him into the forthcoming Whitsun British Games as a reserve for the invitation 800 metres. John subsequently received a stereotype letter addressed to "T.F. Davis" requesting him to attend the White City as reserve. He thought it would be a good idea to go along and stand in the dressing rooms alongside such great athletes as Iharos of Hungary and others of the international elite, and on the appointed day he arrived at the stadium and saw Jack Crump of the British Board. "I'm Davies, reserve for the 800 metres." "No you're not", said Crump, "You're running!". "No you've got it wrong, I can't race. I'm only here as a reserve" stuttered a suddenly aghast John. "You're running" said Crump firmly. And before long, far from rubbing shoulders with the stars in the dressing rooms, the Belgrave Harrier found himself down on the track lining up for his first proper race over 800 metres with the best two-lap exponents in Europe for company. There was the British Champion Hewson, Roger Moens the Belgian World Record holder for the distance, Sventgali of Hungary the European Champion, Mugosa of Hungary and three other fine runners. The "Belgravian" later reported: "Our boy was not intimidated by this array of talent and ran most creditably, challenging the leaders and finishing 5th in 1:52.3 which must be the fastest time ever by a Belgrave man at that distance." Moens was a clear winner from Hewson and Sventgali. Just to prove that it was not a flash in the pan, John was back on the White City cinders again two days later to record another sub 1:53 in a relay. Honours soon followed these remarkable runs. Representing the A.A.A. he raced to a 4:12.6 mile win in a match v Cambridge University at Fenner's grass track and on June 2nd, in windy conditions, he took the Middlesex mile championship at his first attempt. But Stampfl's training had not paid dividends for him alone. In the Cheshire Championships Hallowell won the 1 mile and also recorded 4:10.6 for a new club record. Trophy meetings were the top inter-club competitions at this time. John won the Heathfield trophy 880 yards in 1:55.9, attacking from the bell in the final after getting boxed in earlier in the afternoon during the heats. In the Brockman Trophy 1 mile, facing Boyd of Herne Hill and Woodford Green's Derek Johnson who gained an Olympic silver medal later in the year, John clocked his best time to date - 4:11.8 for 3rd with Hallowell, unable to find his customary finishing burst, 7th. In a whirlwind of competition throughout June and July he reached 5th place in the Southern Championships 1 mile (4:13,8 after a 4:14.8 heat the night before) and ran for the A.A.A. again v Kent. But the highlight was July 13th at the White City - The A.A.A. Championships for 1956. In the 880 yards he qualified for the final with 1:52.8, a Club Record which stood until David Cocks started chopping it down in the early 60's to its current 1:49.6. Some excessive buffeting in the final did not allow John to repeat the performance and hopes of a place were dashed. Brian Hallowell was back in good form in the 1 mile, not qualifying for the final but returning 4:11.2. Then came the Club Championships, and just a year after John's debut he raced off with the 880 yards trophy in 1:56.8 and later duelled with Hallowell in the mile, taking the lead with half a lap to go only to be repassed as they neared the tape. August saw Davies racing in Karlstadt, Sweden in an all-star 800 metres. A 52 second first lap pulled him through to 1:52.7 and 7th behind Audun Boysen of Norway (1:48.3), Dan Waern of Sweden (1:48.9) with another Norwegian and two more Swedes packed in between 1:50 and 1:52. Boysen, incidentally, still holds the Norwegian record at 1:45.9. Finally, this incredible first full season in athletics wound up with a victory in the Vancouver Trophy 800 metres, 2nd in the L.C.C. mile, an international 1,500M and a 1:55.8 relay leg on a cold damp night at Tooting Track as late as October 24th. It all seemed so simple. If he could do all this on one winter's training, all he had to do now was to increase the work and the 4 minute barrier was there to be beaten. So it was back to the schedule but make it tougher, double everything, 20 x 440 and halve the intervals. That was his first mistake. His second was to run on through a severe bout of flu' against a doctor's advice. Training became a struggle, the winter passed and in 1957 although racing in Dublin and Malmo, Sweden, he never really got near his previous year's form. The lesson was obvious. He had run worse on twice the training so in October '57 it was back to the schedule, carrying it through again to May '58 - and of course it worked! He regained his Middlesex Mile title and represented the A.A.A. against Cambridge again to clock his best ever mile of 4:10.6 equalling Hallowell's club record. Various wins in trophy meetings came his way and he returned a best half mile for the year of 1:53.4. Three performances which particularly stand out in John's mind were his wins in the Club Championships. He took the 880 yards ahead of Bob Taylor and Malcolm Robinson, the mile from Pat Newall and Ranjit Bhatia and the three miles, in 14:25, after sitting in on Newall for nearly the full distance. John Davies continued racing on the track for some years but never again really captured the sparkling form of 1956 and 1958. He began to race more on the road, turning out in Belgrave road relay teams, including the classic London - Brighton, well into the sixties. Whilst training at Tooting track in 1959 he met a certain girl from Selsonia Ladies A.C. running in the opposite direction. Pam and John married in 1960 and for these two setting up home together was not going to cramp their athletic style. Although he was not racing so much John was often encouraged by Pam to get out for a run. Often they would run together, around the "bridges" and as far as 18 miles on occasions. More often than not Pam was the first one to climb the 62 steps to their flat at the end of a run. Pam was at the height of her own athletic career and her tremendous record in the National Cross Country Championships must rate her as one of the best women distance runners ever: 3rd in 1963, 2nd 1964 then four successive wins in 1965,1966,1967 and 1968 followed by 2nd in 1969 before the birth of their first son Maxwell. They now have another son, Edward. More than a few Belgravians will remember Pam from their schooldays as she has taught Physics at Battersea County for some time. Looking for a challenge in another direction John began studying in earnest. Having left school at 14 he started tackling 'O' levels at the age of 30 and with that same concentration that was previously reserved for athletic training it was not long before he had gained 8 passes. All this time John's regular haunt was still the "Dukes" and around 1970 he fell in with George Betts, now 60 and one of the regular "Dukes Joggers". George encouraged him to have a go at the Finchley '20'. So in 1973 with a winter of long steady running, including a weekly Saturday run of 20 miles plus, John took on his first long race, completing the course in 2:07:59. Now he felt the almighty urge to take on the premier road race - the marathon. The long training runs were continued in fact his average mileage for the entire year was 44 per week and in October at the age of 42 he lined up for the Harlow Marathon. That race will long be remembered as it was the day Ian Thompson also made his marathon debut. John placed 142nd in 2:55:36 and later said: "You can run all your life but it's not until you've tackled a marathon that you realise you know nothing about running". It was the start of yet another challenge and since then he has run three more. In the same race in '74 he was down to 2:53, at Milton Keynes in the Road Runners Marathon in July '75 he became a Club Champion again with 2:52 and at Harlow last October the improvement was continued with 2:47.35 - a series of runs of which he is extremely proud. John admits to getting a lot more pleasure out of his running these days than he ever did on the track and recalls the terrible nerves that used to afflict him; the pain in the knee that would materialise on learning that Pirie would be running; having to turn away from Iffley Road track on hearing the self-assured voice of Derek Johnson. He now regards this as having been one of his shortcomings, something which took him some time to come to terms with; the belief that famous sportsmen were of a different breed and not just ordinary men. "Almost anyone can get to the top", John now says, "It's a matter of setting one's mind to it and really concentrating on it". Now at 44, John particularly enjoys those days when everything clicks and his running comes fresh, free and lithe. Those who run with him on a Saturday judge their standard of fitness by him, for when they manage to get a word in edgeways during his constant, cheerful chatter, they know they are improving. And there are still further targets ahead: - to beat the World Women's Best time for the marathon and to trounce Brian Gorman. Alan Mead Footnote: We learn from the latest issue of "The South London Harriers Gazette" that Gordon Pirie is also still running. He finished only 9 seconds behind the winner in the New Zealand Senior Men's Orienteering Championship and then immediately afterwards ran in the Veteran's race and won it. He has also been selected to represent New Zealand against Australia. The start of the Invitation 800m at the White City, Whitsun 1956. MacSweeney and present editor Alan Buchanan, and an article quoting Jack Bidgood. Congratulations... To "Race Walking Record" on the appearance of its 400th edition, first published in November 1941. It contains a fine article The "Record" Story by John Keown which starts with a quotation by the Chairman of the Southern R.W.A. (1941) our own Jack Bidgood. It was started by an active walker, the late Alf. MacSweeney (Highgate H) and the present Editor, Alan Buchanan (Brighton & Hove AC) is still very much an active walker. items.sum: Extracts from The Belgravian of 25 and 40 years earlier: C.W. (Ches) Walker winning the 1951 Surrey cross country title, and the 1936 Surrey, Southern and English cross country championships and the Brighton Relay win.
items.s: from the Belgravian... ... 25 years ago ... and 40 years ago Extracts from The Belgravian of 25 and 40 years earlier: C.W. (Ches) Walker winning the 1951 Surrey cross country title, and the 1936 Surrey, Southern and English cross country championships and the Brighton Relay win. from the Belgravian... ... 25 years ago SURREY COUNTY CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIPS.... Held at Coulsdon on January 6th from the SLH quarters, the race was across Farthing Downs... At the half distance J.W.Stone, the holder, was leading but Ches . Walker was close behind and, moreover, was running very easily, and it was obvious that unless Stone could get away from his opponent on the second lap of the country he had had it! This proved to be the case, and on the mile run home over the Downs Walker ran away from his rivals to win easily by about 150 yds. As this is his first senior championship race he is to be congratulated upon winning, and looks likely to be yet one more Belgravian to earn his English vest over the country. Our score of 41 pts was the second lowest score by the Club in this race .... our whole team in the first 28 places. (1st Belgrave H 41 pts - 1. C.W.Walker, 4. L.W.Herbert 5. J.Broughton, 9. C.L.Stokell, 10. J.Bromley, 12. J.H.Braggington - 2nd Surrey AC 156 pts, 3. SLH 162 pts) ... and 40 years ago THE COUNTY CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIPS.... The Surrey race, held at Epsom, provided us with our fourth successive win, and once again we supplied the individual champion (Arthur Penny). THE "SOUTHERN", SANDOWN PARK .... Proceedings started with the Junior race over five miles, and here we were delighted to proclaim one of our runners, Ted Stimpson, as winner. He ran a clever race, using his head as well as his legs, and in perfect style came away in the last mile to win comfortably ... Lucas, a newcomer, ran well in his first important race in our colours. THE ENGLISH CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP ..... Our team travelled to Alderley Edge, Cheshire on March 14th to defend our title of English Cross Country Champions but Birchfield carried too many guns for us on this occasion and regained the title ... Tom Carter had the distinction of leading our team home, and qualifying for the International team. Arthur Penny and Bert Footer were next home for us, one second separating them. (1. Birchfield 90 pts, 2. Belgrave H 112 pts - 12. C.T.Carter, 17. A.W.Penny, 18. H.E.Footer, 22. J.Ginty, 44. A.Allum, 50. S.Ring, 52. A.R.Shaw, 54. H.W.Shields, 68. A.Patience) BRIGHTON RELAY APRIL 25th 1936..... The Bels made more athletic history by winning this classic race for the third time in succession. Special mention might be made of Pat Parker, who fully justified our hopes of him; Tom Carter, who, although faced with the task of tackling an opponent who was out of sight when he commenced his stage, yet reeled off mile after mile in automatic fashion. He not only caught his rival but gave us a lead, which at this stage was the real turning point of the race. J.W. items.sum: Ron Langheim reports Belgrave finished third in selling 1975 A.A.A. Draw tickets, raising £182.40, and asks members to sell the 10p tickets for the 1976 Draw.
items.s: A. A. A. Draw Ron Langheim reports Belgrave finished third in selling 1975 A.A.A. Draw tickets, raising £182.40, and asks members to sell the 10p tickets for the 1976 Draw. A. A. A. Draw The 1975 A.A.A. Draw saw Bels finish in 3rd place in the race to sell the most books of tickets. Only the R.A.F. and Portsmouth A.C. sold more. I would like to thank everybody who sold books and made this a very profitable venture for the club. By selling 1368 books we made £182.40. Special thanks are due to Dennis Jones, John Dunsford, Mrs. Stow, Bill Couzens and John Baker who sold 300 books between them. Well done! The 1976 Draw sees a slightly different format with the tickets being 10p each instead of 5p. I don't see much of a problem here. I will be issuing books of tickets to you all and would ask everyone to sell them as soon as possible and not just leave them in the envelope and pop them behind the mantlepiece. So I will leave it to you to pull out all the stops - ask your neighbours, friends, parents and relations to buy a ticket. And don't forget to ring me or drop me a line when you need more. items.label: August 1976
items.sum: Editorial on John Bicourt reaching the Montreal Olympics but failing to make the steeplechase final, Carl Lawton's World Championship 50km walk selection, the surge of new members since women were admitted, and the coming Belgrave Hall extension.
items.s: Editorial on John Bicourt reaching the Montreal Olympics but failing to make the steeplechase final, Carl Lawton's World Championship 50km walk selection, the surge of new members since women were admitted, and the coming Belgrave Hall extension. Well, he made it. John Bicourt was as good as his word and he got to Montreal but disappointingly did not make the final. He has had a good season, his new found aggression first coming to the surface in Yugoslavia in May when he attempted to outrun the field. This aggressive attitude then carried him beyond the old British record in the 2000mSC (behind Staynings) and then to that marvellous 8:22.8 in Sweden - just 2 tenths behind the then British record for 3000mSC. It got him through the trials and into the Olympic arena but appeared to drain away with a couple of laps to go in the qualifying round when his "legs went". Congratulations to Carl Lawton who so narrowly missed the Olympic team for the 20km walk. At 50km, however, he was successful in gaining selection to compete for Britain in the World Championship, an event now taking the place of the missing walk at the Olympics. A look at the list of new members on the opposite page will show just how the decision to make Belgrave Harriers a club for men and women has had its effect. A veritable membership explosion! Add this to the emergence now of our youngsters, some of whom have been working away for two or three years with only small success, and the future is beginning to look a lot more exciting for the Club. Please note that as from November Belgrave Hall will be undergoing a dramatic face-lift with the extension of the upstairs floor and the addition of ladies changing rooms and showers. Please be patient in the event of any inconvenience. John Bicourt John Bicourt competed in the steeplechase at the Montreal Olympics, eliminated in the qualifying round; 3000m steeplechase 8:22.8 in Sweden, 2 tenths outside the then British record; ran inside the old British 2000m steeplechase record Staynings Staynings ahead of Bicourt in the 2000m steeplechase race in which both beat the old British record Carl Lawton Carl Lawton narrowly missed Olympic 20km walk team; selected for Britain in the 50km World Championship Olympic Games World Championship 50km walk Montreal Yugoslavia Sweden Belgrave Hall

items.label: August 1976
items.sum: Club gossip column with news of former and current members, including Beverley Shingles's marathon in New Zealand, the MacLean family joining, Bill Webb's heart attack, Reg Hopkins Jnr.'s wedding, Joe Wilson's judging grade and John Bromley's county walking selection.
items.s: grapevine Club gossip column with news of former and current members, including Beverley Shingles's marathon in New Zealand, the MacLean family joining, Bill Webb's heart attack, Reg Hopkins Jnr.'s wedding, Joe Wilson's judging grade and John Bromley's county walking selection. grapevine In 1965 Mike Shingles left these shores for the charms of New Zealand! It was interesting to read in 'AW' recently that Beverley Shingles, Mike's kiwi wife, placed 44th out of 308 starters in a marathon at Rotorua. Beverley, now 35, recorded 2:48:46, only 27 minutes behind the winner. - What about that John Davies? We note that the ladies of the MacLean family have signed up in force. Don MacLean always used to be most adamant that we should never have women members but recently he was heard to say: "My children can do what they like - they don't have to do athletics, they don't have to train but if they are going to join a club it's GOT to be Belgrave. John Thresher writes from Canada and sends his regards to all at the King of Denmark. He says that he eagerly awaits his Belgravian and other letters from home. Supergorm is now a local folk hero amongst the English runners in his area and he notes that Laurie O'Hara is still indestructible. Our Past President and Hon Treasurer for many years, Bill Webb, has recently been in hospital after a heart attack. Happily, Bill has made a great recovery and was present at the Club Championships. Our man in Cambridgeshire, Bob Barnes, recently suffered a collapsed lung shortly after moving house. We understand that he is making good progress. We also learn that an addition to the family is on the way. Our congratulations go to Reg Hopkins Jnr. and Jackie who were married on August 14th. Fancy picking the day of the AAA Championships. They will be setting up home near Crystal Palace so we can look forward to a super-fit Reg. next year. Television viewers who watched "The African Runners" in the Olympic Games series saw a face familiar to us in the early fifties - Franz Stampfl. He was Club Trainer for a while and recently has had an eye on the Kenyan athletes. Congratulations to Joe Wilson on becoming a Grade I Walking Judge. Even before he hung up his walking shoes Joe was putting something back into the sport and the Club, particularly with the youngsters. Joe's promotion shows the high regard which his fellow judges have for his capabilities. John Dunsford continues to improve and on June 9th he lined up for the 3,000 metre walk. We look forward to John finding his way back to his old form. In 1951 John Bromley narrowly missed a Surrey Vest (cross-country). Twentyfive years later his persistance was rewarded when he gained selection for the county team in the Inter-Counties 10 miles road walk held in conjunction with the R.W.A. Championship. A big thank you to Joe Coleman who motorcycled to York for the R.W.A. 10 miles championship and who was ready at the finish with welcome cups of tea for our lads as they finished. Chief Judge at this year's R.W.A. 20 Miles Championship was our own Harold King, a fine honour for an official who is held in high esteem by fellow judges and competitors alike. items.sum: Report on how Belgrave's application, prepared by Bill Laws and Arthur Bruce, won a Greater London and South East Sports Council recommendation for a £4,250 Sports Council grant to add ladies' changing and shower facilities at Belgrave Hall.
items.s: Great news for Belgrave Hall project Report on how Belgrave's application, prepared by Bill Laws and Arthur Bruce, won a Greater London and South East Sports Council recommendation for a £4,250 Sports Council grant to add ladies' changing and shower facilities at Belgrave Hall. Great news for Belgrave Hall project REGIONAL SPORTS COUNCIL BACKS LADY BELS. TO THE TUNE OF £4,250. The Sports Council's Grant-in-Aid Scheme has in the past attracted many requests from multi-sports clubs anxious to obtain funds for special projects. The rules of the Scheme require applicants first to clearly demonstrate that successful projects will provide improved facilities for several sports and second that the club or organisation concerned must have greater than local significance. It is the latter requirement which makes it particularly difficult for athletic clubs to obtain Grant-in-Aid from the Sports Council and it is believed that up to now no athletic club has been successful in obtaining financial support from the Sports Council. In the light of the known difficulties it was without a great deal of hope that the Belgrave Committee asked Bill Laws to produce documentation for submission to the Sports Council requesting finance towards modifying Belgrave Hall to provide proper changing and shower facilities for Belgrave's newly formed Ladies Section. The steps were carefully planned. While Arthur Bruce was preparing designs and obtaining budget quotations Bill was visiting the Sports Council finding out the rules for submissions. It immediately became clear that the submission would not be to the Sports Council itself but to the Greater London and South East Sports Council. It is the Regional Sports Councils who vet submissions and they meet every four months to consider applications following an initial screening process. Invariably the submissions are for monies considerably in excess of the funds available and it is the job of the Regional Councils to rank these and to 'draw the line' below which projects are referred for re-submission if desired. Many projects are rejected completely. The approved lists of projects are then submitted to the Sports Council by the Regional Sports Councils to make up a total U.K. portfolio supported by the Sports Council itself. Several discussions with officials of the London and South East Sports Council followed by a visit from senior officials to Belgrave Hall enabled the final case to be prepared. Two main themes were developed, the first arguing that the separate sections of race walking, track and field, cross country and road running constituted a multisport club. The second and most significant argument hinged around Belgrave's claim to have greater than local significance. Having two centres, one located at Battersea Park Track in the Borough of Wandsworth and the other at the Belgrave Headquarters in the Borough of Merton, clearly helped the case. A map of S.E. England showing the location of all Belgrave's members graphically illustrated how widespread is our membership and a final key factor was the increased opportunity for ladies in central London which the introduction of a Ladies Section will facilitate. The key meeting to discuss our proposals took place on June 14th and on the 21st June we received notification from the Greater London and South East Council that they had recommended to the Sports Council the Belgrave scheme be included for grant aid of £4,250. At the time of going to press final confirmation had not been received from the Sports Council but they traditionally support the recommendations of the Regional Councils. More information will be provided in the next edition of the Belgravian but all members will like to know that a working party headed by Arthur Bruce is already pressing ahead with plans for modifications to Belgrave Hall. Ken Stimpson has agreed to take charge of fund raising and has a mammoth goal of £4,000 to aim for. But more of this later - the story is just starting and represents an exciting opportunity for us all. Let the final words be from Colonel Garside, Secretary to the Greater London and South East Sports Council, who wrote "In recommending your project the Regional Sports Council is confident that it will make a real contribution to sport in your area". That's our intention - it's now up to all of us to turn this intention into reality. items.s: from the Belgravian ... 25 years ago ... and 40 years ago Extracts from The Belgravian of 1951 on plans to rebuild Belgrave Hall and of 1936 on acquiring the lease of St. John's Hall, Wimbledon, as the club headquarters. from the Belgravian ... ... 25 years ago 1951...... BELGRAVE HALL The new "House" Sub-Committee again crave your indulgence for conditions prevailing at the Hall. Every effort is being made to obtain the necessary licences for rebuilding. We ask, therefore, that you bear with us and hope that by the winter season of 1952 we will have reached at least part of our objective, i.e., completely rebuilding the Hall......... ... and 40 years ago 1936 ..... OUR WIMBLEDON HEADQUARTERS As we go to press, arrangements have almost been completed for the acquisition of the lease of St. John's Hall, Wimbledon........ .... It is hoped to add to the amenities of the Hall - which has of course been impossible in the past - and generally equip it so that we shall have a first class athletic and social centre for years to come. Our Committee are likely to have some late nights planning any alterations and developments that may be decided upon, and the co-operation of all members will be needed to ensure that Belgrave Hall (or whatever we decide to call our headquarters) is the success it deserves to be. Belgrave Hall St. John's Hall Wimbledon

items.sum: Report and full results of the 1976 Club Championships at Motspur Park on 10 July, with eight championship bests and three club records, including Ernest Obeng's 10.9 100m, Paul Whitby's hurdles and young athletes Jackie Carter, John Fernee and Matthew Cannon.
items.s: CLUB CHAMPIONSHIPS Report and full results of the 1976 Club Championships at Motspur Park on 10 July, with eight championship bests and three club records, including Ernest Obeng's 10.9 100m, Paul Whitby's hurdles and young athletes Jackie Carter, John Fernee and Matthew Cannon. CLUB CHAMPIONSHIPS JULY 10TH, 1976 - MOTSPUR PARK. The best Club Championships for years - that's how most members who were present viewed the 1976 meeting; and with eight Championship Best Performances, 3 Club Records, far more competitors than normal, glorious weather AND events for ladies, who would argue the point. One of our timekeepers was heard to remark afterwards, "it was the most attractive club meeting I can remember". Although in his case the presence of a bar and a pint of foaming amber liquid in his fist might have had something to do with it. Why on earth haven't we gone to Motspur Park before now - well done Fixtures Sec. John Martin for thinking of it. Star of the girls' sprinters was 15 years old Jackie Carter who won the junior ladies 100m. and the combined 200m. Anna Matthews recorded a very good time in the 2,000m. walk with S. Rook second and Jane Pritchard third. Carl Lawton, of course, was faultless in the men's 3,000m. walk and it's nice to have this event back in the meet. With injury still hampering him Jim Evans was unable to give Ernest Obeng a real fight in the men's 100m. but even without pressure Ernest sped to a time of 10.9, four tenths inside the previous championship best. Once again the 800m. provided plenty of excitement and we really must hand it to Colin Pearson who retained his title against strong opposition proving himself a worthy champion. Every time out now over the high hurdles Paul Whitby seems to produce a sparkling performance and this occasion's 15.8 took six tenths off from the championship best and was just one point slower than the club record he shares with Cliff Brooks. A commanding performance came from John Stow in the 1,500m where, out for John Thresher's record of 3:54.0, he ran a solo 3:55.5. Good running too from a speedy looking Stu' Barrett. Only three athletes contested the jumps but there were no easy victories. The Triple saw Steve Crosbie scrape home by a centimetre from Arnold Bentt but Reg. Hopkins had the advantage in the High and Long Jumps. As usual Cliff Brooks took the shot and discus and even had the audacity to approach within 36cm. of Peter Crosbie in the Javelin. There were two double victors amongst the juniors with the 100/200 going to Dave Bailey and Adrian Cook taking the 1,500m. and retaining the 800m. Mick Manning, last year's winner of the longer race found it a tough afternoon placing 2nd in the 1,500m after being shunted to 3rd in the two lap event by Peter North who startingly revealed some real fight. Two very good 15 year olds beat their elder brethren in the junior age group. John Fernee won the 400m in an assured manner, adding it to his Boys 800m and 100m titles (the latter in Club Record time) and Stephen Samson, who is just old enough to compete against seniors, clinched a place in the following Southern League match by clearing a magnificent 1.81m in the high jump. A couple of years back Sheik Wahab seemed so unco-ordinated in jumping and running that one would never have thought that he could succeed at athletics. This season he has taught us a lesson we should not forget - never underestimate anybody, particularly when they stick at it when the going is tough. Sheik's first win in a 100m at Chiswick this season surprised him as much as anyone else but now he has got used to the idea of winning - taking the boys high jump title at championship best performance height and running second to John Fernee in the sprint. On the other side of the coin we have the lad who at 13 years old has started off his athletic career with a bang. Matthew Cannon, having already reduced our Junior Boys record for 1500m by OVER HALF A MINUTE and added 24cm to the high jump mark, now added the 800 record to his tally - awe inspiring. items.sum: Walking section report by Richard Tanner reviewing a disappointing season, praising individual walkers and calling on the young walkers to come forward.
items.s: WALKING Walking section report by Richard Tanner reviewing a disappointing season, praising individual walkers and calling on the young walkers to come forward. WALKING This last season has been one of our worst for a long time, indicated by the fact that the club is now waiting, and often depending, upon its younger members to bring in the trophies. We have found ourselves 'pot hunting' this spring, very successfully I might add, and if you think that there is anything wrong with that - don't. The most important thing in the sport is to compete, the next is to win. I do not apologise for being critical. It is now the time for all of us to start putting in some hard training for ourselves and the club. Our performance against tough opposition, especially in the National Championships, has been disappointing partly due to non-appearance and injury but also lack of hard work. Individually, however, things have started to move; Carl Lawton just missed out in the Olympic trial and is forever holding the team together; Steve Sharp has become one of our most dedicated members and this is beginning to make a big difference to his ability and attitude; Tim Thorogood is also beginning to listen to sound advice and has become a necessary member of our team. Ron Day, with only a year's experience and a young 29 years old, has put in some creditable performances over 20 miles, and Richard Tanner also caused a few surprises by doing so well over the distance of 33 miles - against the advice of Ray Middleton who vows that his interest in the lad has finished. And of the 'old boys', their season of 'Hastings' and 'Brightons' is yet to come. I wish them all the best and expect them to win yet again. Well done those men who did so well in the 100 miles at Woodford! It leaves me to say that I want to see the arrival of our 'young promises' such as Morris, Bennett, Maxwell, Dunsford, Robson, Miss Jane Pritchard, Miss Anna Matthews and Miss Diana Cook bursting onto the scene. I look forward to a good autumn, to working with you and most of all to winning together. items.sum: Gordon Doubleday reviews Julian Hopkins's book "Race Walking", recommending it to walkers and other athletes.
items.s: Book Review..... Gordon Doubleday reviews Julian Hopkins's book "Race Walking", recommending it to walkers and other athletes. Book Review..... by Gordon Doubleday From time to time books have been written about Race Walking and they are mostly out of print or unavailable. Fortunately the gap is now filled with the publication of "Race Walking" by Julian Hopkins the National Coach. The cost is £1.25 for this well planned and well produced book. All aspects are dealt with and the author, who is an active walker, has gone to much trouble to produce it. As well as covering technique and style there are exercises, well illustrated by diagrams, and descriptions of the muscles, joints, etc. which play the essential parts in driving you along between 8 and 9 mph and retaining contact. There are model training schedules, hints on what to wear and how to plan your racing. The question of diet is dealt with comprehensively and this includes drinks and the timing of eating and drinking for racing. There are photographs too, including a "filmstrip" of the Russian Gold Medallist V. Golubnichy. For the competitive walker with serious intentions this book is surely a must. If its sales are followed by an improvement in our position in world walking it will have been well worth while. There is much in it to commend it to athletes other than walkers, so, runners and field events men get a look at it if you can - you might well pick up a hint or two. "Race Walking" is published by the B.A.A.B. and can be obtained from Peter Marlow, [address withheld]. The price (including postage) is £1.40. Gordon Doubleday Gordon Doubleday Julian Hopkins Julian Hopkins National Coach; author of "Race Walking" V. Golubnichy V. items.label: August 1976
items.sum: Walking report on the Southern Counties 10 miles championship in Battersea Park on 6 March 1976, where Belgrave took second team place behind Brighton and the juniors won team medals.
items.s: Two Seconds Walking report on the Southern Counties 10 miles championship in Battersea Park on 6 March 1976, where Belgrave took second team place behind Brighton and the juniors won team medals. Two Seconds MARCH 6th 1976 - BATTERSEA PARK - S.C.A.A.A. 10 MILES CHAMPIONSHIP. Our string of double wins came to a halt in Battersea Park on Sat. 6th March when we had the Southern Counties 10 miles walking championship. Although it was a bright day it was very cold. We were not at full strength with a number of absentees and Richard Tanner competing in the 10,000m junior event. After the first of the five laps Roger Mills (Ilford) was leading Carl Lawton at a very fast pace. Brighton vests were prominent then came John Hall and Ray Middleton and our next two men, one of whom would be our fourth scorer, were further back, Ron Day just having a small lead on Doug. Fotheringham - battling away as usual. Hopes of an individual win went as Roger drew away from Carl on every lap and he won with a sparkling performance. Carl held off fast finishing Shaun Lightman (Met. WC) to finish in a very good time although not as fast as his winning time in the G.L.C. race. John and Ray both gave sound performances to consolidate the team but it was obvious that Brighton would be the winners. Could we get a place? Ron provided the answer and his steadily improved walking brought him a second place team medal - after less than a year in the game! Ron is now finding himself in the most heavily populated part of the field, which will give him experience in picking off the opposition. It was good to see Joe Scamell out again. On his fourth lap he heard the patter of what were once tiny feet - his son Michael lapping him. Michael is now an established sub-80 minute man which must make dad a proud man. With an improving Steyning A.C. in third place we did well to split the "invaders" from Sussex. We always hope to have a good turn-out of club men in Battersea Park events and the finishing list will show how our others fared. The afternoon's programme was a full one with other events on the famous circuit. We saw our juniors hard at work and it was no surprise when we learnt that Richard was a good second,and, supported by the two Stephens Sharp and Bennett, we took first team medals. So we did get a win after all - one which points the way to future successes. items.s: National 20km Report and result of the National 20km walk at Southend on 15 May 1976, the Olympic trial in which Carl Lawton finished fourth, just missing Olympic selection. National 20km MAY 15th 1976 - SOUTHEND. With only four starters we could not expect much teamwise and in fact our final 7th place was higher than expected. For Belgravians, however, the main issue was whether Carl Lawton could continue his recent tremendous form and land a place in the Olympic team. In gusty conditions Flynn, Mills and Adams blasted it from the start whilst further back Carl steadily tracked Nihill who was making his bid for a fourth appearance at the Olympics. At the 15km point the early pace began to have its effect and drama set in as Seddon was disqualified and Marlow retired. With 2½km remaining, Mills began to sway about the road, Adams began to catch him but was himself overtaken by the Belgian DeJonkheere and Nihill. Fighting as hard as he can our man moved closer to that coveted Olympic berth as Mills collapsed with the finish just in sight. But Carl had given his all and the third Briton home, Adams, crossed the line 43 seconds ahead. Our congratulations to Carl for pulling out his best ever time in this Olympic trial and our commiserations too for coming so close to his goal. 1. O.Flynn (Basildon) 90:00; 2. items.sum: John Keown's account of the Woodford Green AC open 24 hours / 100 miles track walk at Woodford Bridge on 28–29 May 1976, in which Johnny Morris and John Keown completed 100 miles before both retiring at 101 miles, with results.
items.s: 24hrs — 100miles Track Walk John Keown's account of the Woodford Green AC open 24 hours / 100 miles track walk at Woodford Bridge on 28–29 May 1976, in which Johnny Morris and John Keown completed 100 miles before both retiring at 101 miles, with results. 24hrs — 100miles Track Walk MAY 28th/29th 1976 - WOODFORD BRIDGE. On the 28th/29th May Woodford Green AC promoted an Open 24 Hours Walk on the new all-weather track at Ashton Playing Fields, Woodford Bridge, Essex. This event incorporated a 100 miles race. Twentyfive walkers, including three from Belgrave Harriers, entered for this race. One of these was Ray Middleton our 6, 7 and 8 hours record holder. He was going to attempt to break the records from 70 miles to 100 miles. Unfortunately a week or so before the race Ray found that he had problems with his breathing. The failure of the ailment to respond to medical treatment forced him to withdraw from the race. Amongst the 23 competitors who faced the starter at 2pm on Friday the 28th were the 'terrible twins' of the Belgrave long distance walking team, Johnny Morris and John Keown. These two have probably walked more miles together in competition than any other pair of walkers. Each has a great respect for the other's capabilities. Over distances in excess of 20 miles Johnny, when fit, has the edge over John but the reverse is true in shorter races. The race provided a new challenge for the two Belgravians as the maximum time they had previously spent on a track was 65 minutes. Lapping the 400 metres track for hour after hour at approximately 5 mph meant that the temptation to stop was at times overpowering and required great determination to keep going. Right from the 'off' the two Johns settled down to lapping the track together at between 2m 50s and 2m 55s per lap. Every four laps they changed places so that each in turn had the benefit of the inside. Their speed during Friday remained constant so that they reached the 50 mile mark in 9h 52m in 4th and 5th positions. During the night there was a marked drop in temperature but the addition of tracksuits and the supply of hot cups of tea every hour by Carl and Barbara Lawton aided by Steve Sharp enabled the two Belgravians to remain comfortable and in good spirits. A rather bleak dawn saw them still together. By this time they had lost a place to George Eastwood (Woodford Green) who after a very slow start was making up ground rapidly. During Saturday morning a gentle rain persisted for some time. Around the 75 miles mark Morris began to have trouble with a leg which he had injured the previous week whilst trying to start his motorcycle. Treatment at regular intervals from Carl and Steve enabled him for a time to maintain his position. By 80 miles the injury was causing him so much trouble that he lost contact with Keown. The latter now moved steadily away from his fellow Belgravian to reach 90 miles in 18h 20m. Shortly afterwards his luck ran out as his feet, which were badly blistered, began to hurt and he developed a pain in the lower part of his back. These injuries made walking in an upright manner difficult. Despite the expert attention of Carl and John Dunsford Snr, who had joined the club helpers early on Saturday morning, Keown's problems increased until he was walking with a decided 'list to port'! Walking in this fashion caused him to slow considerably. Morris now fully recovered from his leg injury passed his clubmate around the 95 miles mark and went on to complete the 100 miles in 5th position in 20h 46m 36s ( a personal best performance). Reducing speed, Johnny now allowed John to catch him up and together they completed what was supposed to be the one lap required to bring the latter to the 100 miles mark. At this point the announcer gave Keown's position as 6th with a time of 21h 1m 41s. (Later the official result sheet gave the position as 7th, time 21h 4m 41s). Despite the fact that at the 100 miles point the two Belgravians were in the lead in the team race (2 to score), in order to save Keown from possible serious injury both walkers retired at 101 miles. The 'terrible twins' have now successfully completed 100 miles both on the road and the track. Their success at Woodford owes much to the excellent help provided by a small band of Belgravians under the leadership of Carl Lawton our hard working Walking Secretary. Amongst the officials who organised the race was Doug. Fotheringham. He acted as a steward, relief chief recorder and one of the judges. Belgravian Bill True joined the judges on Saturday morning. 100 miles: 1. D.Harrison (Boundary H) 18:04:07; 2. C.Young (Essex Bgls) 18:12:02; 3. P.Worth (Verlea) 19:23:18; 5. items.s: Note on Carl Lawton's sixth place for Great Britain in the 20km walk international against West Germany at Salzgitter on 6 June, with thanks to Barbara Lawton. Carl Lawton gained further international honours when he represented Great Britain over 20 kilometres in the International match against West Germany at Salzgitter on June 6th. The start was at 8 am and the event was won by Olympic Gold Medallist Bernd Kannenberg in 87:11. Carl was 6th in 93:31, his 5km splits being 23:27/46:30/69:40 which demonstrates his pace judgement - one of the hallmarks of a champion. Everyone in Belgrave will congratulate Carl upon his selection and performance. What a worker he is for not only does he put in the training and preparation to reach international grade, but he is also ready to advise newcomers. They all know Carl and by now they must know Barbara - let us finish by thanking her for the support which she gives to our walkers. items.s: R.W.A. 50km Report and result of the R.W.A. 50km Championship at Birmingham on 17 July 1976, where Belgrave were second team and Carl Lawton second individually, with a summary of the club's national walking team positions. R.W.A. 50km JULY 17th 1976 - BIRMINGHAM - R.W.A. 50km CHAMPIONSHIP. Belgrave's undermanned team travelled to Birmingham for what turned out to be a tough national (107 started and 62 finished). The Bels chances of anything were hopeless but it happened, we didn't win but 2nd was good enough. Carl Lawton led the boys home in 2nd position with Ray Middleton 18th. Bob Picton finally showed that perseverance pays off, in this case with a National medal to take home. Dave King completed the team. As a result of this Belgrave still managed third in the year's National Rankings out of 30 clubs. National positions have been: Junior 3rd, 10m 11th 20km 7th, 20m 7th and 50km 2nd. 1. items.label: August 1976
items.sum: Ben Knifton, retired in Portugal, describes walking an 1800 metres race for ages 8 to 80 in Faro, marking his last race after fifty years as a Belgrave member.
items.s: Ben Knifton in action Ben Knifton, retired in Portugal, describes walking an 1800 metres race for ages 8 to 80 in Faro, marking his last race after fifty years as a Belgrave member. Ben Knifton in action Ben Knifton writes from retirement in Portugal and says that he often thinks of all his old friends in Belgrave and sends his warmest greetings to them all. He also tells of his latest race:- When I saw there was a walking race in Faro over 1800 metres for those aged from 8 to 80 I thought "I'll have a go". I had a week in which to prepare and trained on the road after dark each evening because it was too hot during the day. These activities brought curious enquiries from friends locally who had seen me by the head-lights of their cars. I included in my diet salt tablets, wholemeal bread, honey and milk. I lost a pound in weight each day. My leg muscles ached a bit at first so I treated them with hot baths and gave them a good massage using my wife's talcum powder. I never smelled so good and felt so fit! At the venue I joined an enthusiastic crowd. The youngsters were all excited and the handsome athletic youths gave me friendly smiles. It was a good atmosphere in which to be. I was interviewed and my opinion sought on the promotion of the event and the activities of the club. I was photographed wearing their club armband and again with a group of the younger competitors. It was a crowded start in the narrow street and I was nearly tripped headlong. I recovered to see the stalwart youths disappear ahead of me and I was out on my own. I pounded the cobbles in pursuit, encouraged by the crowd. Round the second lap I gained places although my limbs rebelled. Approaching the finish the cheers grew to a crescendo. Who could ask for more? I had always wanted to represent Great Britain and it had come at last! I could even ignore the painful wrench in the muscle of my right thigh! (not enough salt tablets?) I was then photographed with the first and second place winners. Friendly chats followed and a cordial farewell. Back in Albufeira I was asked how I had got on. I produced the standard medal I won in the A.A.A. Championships in 1929, (I always was a braggart!) but they were not fooled. In fact, the Real Amizade Farense presented me with their club badge which I am very proud to wear as a memento of my last race in fifty splendid years as a member of the Belgrave Harriers from 1925 - 1975. Ben Knifton Ben Knifton member 1925-1975; retired in Portugal; walked 1800m race in Faro; won a standard medal at the 1929 A.A.A. Championships A.A.A. Championships Portugal Faro Albufeira Real Amizade Farense Belgrave Harriers

items.s: £180+ Past President Chas Manning thanks the members and others who gave over £180 to a personal fund for John Bicourt's bid for the Montreal Olympics, listing the contributors and quoting their comments. £180+ What can you say? Having been asked to organise the "personal contribution" to John Bicourt, who's obviously not everyone's chalice of hemlock, I thought I'd lent my venerable name to a right deadbeat. But had I? Not a bit - the response was really gratifying - it meant anything but a deadbeat. It meant that Belgravians with their warmth and generosity AND OTHERS believed in him. It meant they had faith in his ability, they had respect for his judgement and it would be a little bit of them out there in Montreal. John carried some of their hopes and their desires. He did them proud. Me? I'd just like to say, as I always seem to be saying, "Thankyou", to all those listed below. Finally, what made me think it really worth while were those comments on the return slips. Anonymous Mrs E.M.Aplin W.Ashford M.Ali John Baker R.L.Barnes Gordon Biscoe L.C.Bishop John Boardman Reg. F.
